units.la: Inclytæ ac Florentissimæ Civitatis GRONINGANÆ Proceribus Dn. CONSULIBUS ac SENAT- ORIBUS Nobilissimis, Consultissi- mis, Amplissimis, Patribus Patriæ,
units.tr: To the Proceres of the Illustrious and Most Flourishing City of Groningen, the Lords Consuls and Senators, Most Noble, Most Learned, Most Distinguished, Fathers of the Fatherland,
To my most gracious lords.

units.la: Magnis verisimisque elogiis consentientis vox Eruditorum celebrat Historiam, quod Origines, Leges, Instituta, Mores, Res gestas gentium diversarum pandens, civilis prudentiæ velut Promptuarium aliquod locupletissimum præstet atque aperiat. Quam laudem cum quævis jure sibi suo arrogare Historia possit, tum eam eximiam meritissimo suo vindicat illa, quæ Reip. domesticæ Antiquitates, Iura, Privilegia, Facta, Formamque complexa, ceu Sacrum Depositum custodit, posterisque propagat. Siquidem Nosse
units.tr: The voice of learned men, agreeing in great and very true praise, celebrates History, because by laying open the origins, laws, institutions, customs and deeds of diverse peoples, it offers and unfolds a most rich storehouse, as it were, of civil prudence. Though History may rightly claim this praise for itself in any case, it claims it most deservedly in a special way for that history which, embracing the antiquities, rights, privileges, deeds and form of the home commonwealth, guards them as a sacred deposit and passes them on to posterity. For to know the state of the commonwealth is the foundation of every counsel, and the fount and most abundant spring of all prudence in governing the commonwealth rightly.

units.la: R E M P. [?] omnis de Rep. consilij fundamentum, omnis in Repub. rectè administrandâ, prudentiæ fons est & scaturigo uberrima. Quare immortales gratias, ut Frisia omnis, sic nominatim Groninga vestra & Omlandia debent æternumque debebunt ingenio clarissimo Historici sui inclyti Ubbonis Emmii, cujus Spiritu Resp. vestra etiam post fata ejus subinde renascitur, nunquam intermoritura. Cui Patriæ suæ [?] cum bonum civem quemvis favere & opitulari, quantum in se est, conveniat, ego meo loco impensâ operâque obstetricari studio curæque habui singulari. Quare non tantum Syntagma illud præclarum, quod Cl. Emmius de statu rerum deque jure Provinciæ hujus felici stylo condiderat, cum distractis exemplaribus passim illud expeti ab amantibus patriæ cognovissem, recudendum suscepi, sed simul operam dedi, ut cultius nitidiusque prodiret, tum aliis, quæ cuilibet perlustranti facile erit agnoscere, tum imprimis Geographicâ tabulâ geminâ, quarum altera Urbis, altera totius Provinciæ situm artifice dextrâ delineatum exhibet. Quod meum studium, operam, curam, Nob. v. Ampl. gratam acceptamque fore, ut nullus dubito, sic me meaque omnia, earundem Ampl. Vest. patrocinio & favori, unicè cupio esse commendata. Groningæ Erif.[?] Nonis Martiis. CIↃ IↃC XLVI.
units.tr: Therefore, as all Friesland, so especially your Groningen and the Ommelanden owe, and will for ever owe, immortal thanks to the brilliant genius of their illustrious historian Ubbo Emmius, by whose spirit your commonwealth is continually reborn even after his death, never to perish. Since it is fitting that every good citizen should favour and assist his fatherland as far as he can, I, in my own place, have set myself with particular zeal and care to help bring this work to birth, with expense and labour. For this reason I undertook to reprint not only that excellent Syntagma which the distinguished Emmius had composed in his felicitous style concerning the condition of affairs and the law of this Province, having learned that, the copies being sold out, lovers of their country were seeking it everywhere; but at the same time I took pains that it should appear more elegantly and brightly, both in other respects, which will be easy for anyone perusing it to recognise, and above all by the twin geographical maps, one of which shows the city and the other the situation of the whole Province, skilfully drawn. That my zeal, labour and care will be pleasing and welcome to your Most Noble and Most Distinguished Lordships, I do not doubt; and so I wish myself and all that is mine to be most earnestly commended to the patronage and favour of your same Most Distinguished Lordships. Groningen, Erif.[?], on the Nones of March. 1646.
Most Noble and Most Distinguished Lordships,
Most devoted,
JOHANNES NICOLAI, Printer.
Chapters of this Syntagma.

units.tr: JUDGEMENTS ON UBBO EMMIUS AND HIS WRITINGS, A FEW FROM MANY.

units.la: JOSEPHUS SCALIGER in epistolâ scriptâ XIII. Kal. Sept. an. MDCVIII.
units.tr: JOSEPH SCALIGER, in a letter written on the 13th day before the Kalends of September, 1608.

units.la: Quam jucundæ, inquit, mihi fuerint priores literæ tuæ, testari possunt ii, qui unà aderant, quum eæ mihi redderentur. Nam quanti & probitatem tuam & doctrinam semper fecerim, non solum ego mihi conscius sum, sed & illi, qui me de te ea narrantem sæpissimè audiverunt, quæ virtus tua & meritum à me expressit. Certè, si nihil aliud, saltem divina historia tua Frisica hoc à me exigebat, quam ego judico non solumjis[?], qui similem scribere volent, conatum, sed & iis, qui jam scripserunt, laudem præripuisse. &c.
units.tr: How delightful your earlier letter was to me, those who were with me when it was delivered can testify. For how highly I have always valued both your uprightness and your learning, not only am I myself aware, but so too are those who have very often heard me speak of you, and whom your virtue and merit drew this from me. Certainly, if nothing else, your splendid Frisian history demanded this of me, which I judge has not only taken away the effort of those who wish to write a similar work, but has also robbed of praise those who have already written. etc.

units.la: JAC. AUG. THUANUS in epist. scriptâ Kal. Sept. an. MDCIV.
units.tr: JACQUES AUGUSTE DE THOU, in a letter written on the Kalends of September, 1604.

units.la: Ad eum annum, hoc est, MD XCIIII. nostra perduximus, optavimusque sæpius, ut quod moliris jam editum esset, antequam quæ de Belgicis scripsimus, te longè secuti & vestigia semper adorantes scripsissemus. Nam citra assentationem dicam, quare enim apud te? nihil simile tuis scriptis post BVCHANANVM in eo genere me legere memini, seu fides, prudentia, ac ingenua libertas, sive orationis elegans simplicitas, ac perspicua brevitas spectetur; ut me temeritatis mee pudeat, poeniteatque, qui ab his omnibus imparatus tantum opus supra vires aggressus sim, & infestiores longe nec scriptis disceptandas animorum contentiones non sine vita discrimine contra me excitaverim. quam ita claudit: Vale doctissime VBBO, & me virtutis ingenijque tui praecipuum admiratorem ac cultorem redamate perge, & cum otium erit diligenter rescribe.
units.tr: We have brought our work down to that year, that is 1594, and have often wished that what you were preparing had already been published, before we wrote about the Low Countries, following you closely and always honouring your footsteps. For, without flattery, why should I say otherwise to you? I do not recall reading anything like your writings in that genre since Buchanan, whether one looks at their faithfulness, prudence and frank liberty, or at the elegant simplicity and clear brevity of your style; so that I am ashamed of my rashness and regret that I, unprepared in all these respects, undertook a work beyond my strength, and stirred up against myself, not without danger to my life, contentions of minds, far more hostile, which were not to be settled in writing. He closes his letter thus: Farewell, most learned Ubbo, and go on loving me, your particular admirer and devotee of your virtue and talent; and when you have leisure, write back to me diligently.

units.la: Idem in epist. alia scripta iv. Kal. Quintil. an. M DC XII.
units.tr: The same, in another letter written on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, 1612.

units.la: Itaque postremis illis tuis, quanquam omnia tua mihi summè grata sunt, non tam laetatus sum quam jactura priorum dolui, gratissimamque longe rem mihi feceris, si earum exemplum, si quod habes, ad me quam primum mittas.
units.tr: Therefore, although everything of yours is most welcome to me, I was not so much glad of your latest letters as I grieved at the loss of the earlier ones; and you would do me a very great favour if you sent me, as soon as you can, a copy of them, if you have one.

units.la: Nam non is sum, qui mea ita amore coecus mei probem, ut non plura amicis, quam mihi in iis corrigendis permittenda censeam; praesertim tibi, cujus & singularem in me humanitatem expertus sum, & facilem in scribendo elegantiam cum acerrimo judicio & Veri amore conjunctam non desino tua cottidie legendo admirari. Itaque te iterum rogo, hanc amico à te suppliciter flagitanti gratiam ne negaveris, tibique sic persuadeas, nullas occupationes, quanquam gravissimis undiq; indies premor, impedimento fore, quo minus sedulo ad tuas rescribam.
units.tr: For I am not the sort of man who approves of his own things, blind with self-love, so that I do not think friends should be allowed more say than myself in correcting them; especially you, whose singular kindness towards me I have experienced, and whose easy elegance in writing, joined with the keenest judgement and love of truth, I never cease to admire as I read your works each day. So I ask you again, do not refuse this favour to a friend who begs it of you humbly, and be assured that no occupations, although I am daily weighed down on every side by very heavy ones, will stand in the way of my writing back to you diligently.

units.la: Idem libr. hist. cxix. pag. 771. sub finem, de Suffrido Petrejo locutus hæc subjicit.
units.tr: The same, in the historical book, page 771, near the end, speaking of Suffridus Petri, adds the following.

units.la: Et posteà à Frisiæ Ordinibus invitatus, origines, colonias, nobilitatem, libertatem, jura gentis suæ illustranda suscepit; in quibus altius repetendis dum admissis fabularum figmentis nimium stylo indulget, multorum reprehensiones incurrit; ut VBBONI EMMIO, qui eam provinciam summâ fide ac admirandâ simplicitate posteà executus est, potius lampâda tradidisse, quam ei in scribendâ patriâ historiâ præluxisse videatur.
units.tr: And afterwards, invited by the Orders of Friesland, he undertook to illuminate the origins, colonies, nobility, liberty and rights of his people; but in tracing these back too far, admitting fabulous fictions, he indulges too much in style and incurs the criticism of many; so that he seems rather to have handed the torch to Ubbo Emmius, who afterwards carried out that task with the utmost faithfulness and admirable simplicity, than to have shed light before him in writing his country's history.

units.la: JANUS DOUSA pater lib. 1. Annal. Holl. pag. 75.
units.tr: JANUS DOUSA the elder, Annals of Holland, book 1, page 75.

units.la: Ideoque nec in Frisiorum gestis recensendis lectoris otio abutemur; supervacaneum existimantes ea iterare, quæ ab UBBONE EMMIO legitimo Frisiæ suæ historico fidelissimè perscripta sunt. Cujus ea in patriæ suæ antiquitatibus investigandis curiositas, ea religio fuit, ut (meo quidem animo) parum seu potius nihil aliorum industriæ reliquum fecisse videatur.
units.tr: Therefore neither shall we abuse the reader's leisure by recounting the deeds of the Frisians, thinking it superfluous to repeat what has been most faithfully set down by Ubbo Emmius, the lawful historian of his Friesland. His curiosity in investigating the antiquities of his homeland was of such a kind, and his scrupulousness such, that (in my own view) little or rather nothing seems to have been left to the industry of others.
From the same author, an impromptu letter.

units.la: Sermo frequens de te, & DOUSAEO multum in ore EMMIUS: Historiae hoc visa merere Fides; Incorrupta Fides. quæ quo per tempora nostra Rarior, hoc pluris est faciunda mihi, Cattigenisq; meis: res quorum ex ordine ge-stas Te sparsim Frisiis inseruisse tuis, Et video, & lætor. quo nullum, hoc scilicet ævo, In genere hoc Belgis clarius extat opus. Vera, nec intestata loquor. scit Grotius istud, Doctrinâ verè Magnus & ingenio: Et norunt alij plures, quid maxima gentis Gloria Gallorum sentiat EMMERIUS; EMMERIUS, de te solitus qui plurima amicè Quærere, & in laudes luxuriare tuas: Ante alia Annales merito admirarier unos, Expensos Frisiis quos tulit UBBO suis. Ter quater ô felix antiqui temporis ætas, Cui facundo adeò contigit ore cani! Vos quoque fœlices tanto scriptore Libelli; Ingenij rari, nec minus artis opus: Vos ego sæpè meo vos Elogio ornaturus, Testabor veterum laudibus esse pares.
units.tr: Emmius often speaks of you, and often has Dousa on his lips: "History seems to deserve this faith: uncorrupted faith." Since such faith is rare in our times, I and my fellow Cattigenes must value it all the more. I see, and rejoice, that you have set out in order the deeds of those people and scattered them among your Frisians. In this age no work of this kind stands out more clearly among the Belgians. I speak true things, and not unattested ones. Grotius knows this, truly great in learning and in talent. Many others also know what Emmerius, the greatest glory of the Gauls, thinks: Emmerius, who often asks kindly about you and delights to heap praise upon you, saying that above all others the Annals that Ubbo has weighed out for his Frisians deserve to be admired alone. Three and four times happy the age of old, to which an eloquent voice fell to so fine a singer! You too, happy little books, written by so great an author, a work of rare talent and no less skill: I, who shall often adorn you with my own eulogy, will bear witness that you are equal to the praises of the ancients.
HIRCI-
On Ubbo Emmius

units.la: HIRCINOS alij folles, plaususque morentur; Præter Monstra, nihil qui didicêre loqui.
units.tr: Let others be content with goatish bellows and applause; beyond monsters, they have learned nothing of how to speak.

units.la: Sit, qui CAVLINIS cingat sua pulpita thyrsis; Nil præter SCAVRVM spectet OTACILIVS;
units.tr: Let one who would crown his stage with Caulinian thyrsi be; let Otacilius look at nothing but Scaurus.

units.la: Eunus APRO tantum studeat sua scripta probari, Ipse uno hoc visus judice VARRO sibi. Contenti AVGVSTO vos miratore THVANO● Vivite; majus enim quid dare Fata queant?
units.tr: Let Eunus strive only for his writings to be approved by Aper, and let Varro seem to himself to need only this one judge. You, content with Augustus Thuanus as your admiring reader, go on living; for what greater gift could the Fates bestow?
Franciscus Gomarus

units.la: Iustus ARISTIDES, doctus PLATO, fidus ACHATES, Eloquio NESTOR, consilioque potens: REX Ponti memoris sit mentis laude superbus, Sic DECIVS patriæ clarus amore suæ. NATHANAEL fraudis expers, pietas SIMEONIS Inclyta, mansuetum SOCRATIS ingenium. Adjice sollicitè varia ornamenta virorum, EMMIUS, in reliquis sparsa, ea cuncta habuit.
units.tr: Just Aristides, learned Plato, faithful Achates, Nestor in eloquence and powerful in counsel; let the king of Pontus be proud in the praise of a retentive mind, and Decius be famous for his love of his country. Nathanael free from deceit, the renowned piety of Simeon, the gentle nature of Socrates: add with care the various ornaments of men, scattered among the rest, Emmius, and he possessed them all.
Daniel Heinsius

units.la: Ἠχέεις Ἡροδότοιο μελισταγὲς ἱπερόπευμα Ἰαδ[?]ᾳ ἀρχαίης ἐςὶ ἡ ἐυεπίης. Ἐννέα γὰρ Μούσας ὀπηδοφαμένη ζηλὶς αὐτῇ, Αὐτὴ δὴ Μυζίων ἐςὶ μοι ἡ δεκάτη. Αὐτὰρ Θεκυδίδαο βαρὺ ςόμα, τῷ μὲν ἀγῶνες Βίβλος ἅπε μόνον τοῖς τότε γινομένοις.
units.tr: You echo the honey-sweet song of Herodotus, the ancient Ionic of eloquent speech [Ἠχέεις Ἡροδότοιο μελισταγὲς ἱπερόπευμα Ἰαδ[?]ᾳ ἀρχαίης ἐςὶ ἡ ἐυεπίης. Ἐννέα γὰρ Μούσας ὀπηδοφαμένη ζηλὶς αὐτῇ, Αὐτὴ δὴ Μυζίων ἐςὶ μοι ἡ δεκάτη. Αὐτὰρ Θεκυδίδαο βαρὺ ςόμα, τῷ μὲν ἀγῶνες Βίβλος ἅπε μόνον τοῖς τότε γινομένοις.]. For this rival, attending the nine Muses, is herself the tenth of my Muses; but the heavy voice of Thucydides, whose book contends only with the events of his own time.
JUDICIA

units.la: Αὐλὸς δ᾽ ἐσομένοισι ποτ᾽ ἀνθρώποις ἐκτολυπεῦσαι στεῦξαι κλῆμα ζοφὸν, πάντοτε δ᾽ ἐσόμενον. Ἱμμιάδα ἢ λόγοισιν ἐπέπλεξεν ἢ χάεις ἀμφοῖν, καὶ πλέον ἢ κενοῖς ἢ χάεις ἀμφιλέροις. Κτῆμα γὰρ ἄμμιν ἐδωκε, ᾧ ἐσομένοισιν ἀγῶνα, τοῦτο μὲν ἐυεπίης, τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐπιλυμίης.
units.tr: A flute, to unroll for men yet to come a dark lament, one that will last for all time. He wove it from words, or from joy in both, and more from empty or ambiguous joys. For he gave us a possession, a contest for those who will come after, this one of good speech and that one of ill speech. [Αὐλὸς δ᾽ ἐσομένοισι ποτ᾽ ἀνθρώποις ἐκτολυπεῦσαι στεῦξαι κλῆμα ζοφὸν, πάντοτε δ᾽ ἐσόμενον. Ἱμμιάδα ἢ λόγοισιν ἐπέπλεξεν ἢ χάεις ἀμφοῖν, καὶ πλέον ἢ κενοῖς ἢ χάεις ἀμφιλέροις. Κτῆμα γὰρ ἄμμιν ἐδωκε, ᾧ ἐσομένοισιν ἀγῶνα, τοῦτο μὲν ἐυεπίης, τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐπιλυμίης.]

units.la: In epist. data Lugd. Bat. prid. Cal. Novembris Anno M DC. XVI.
units.tr: Written in a letter given at Leiden, the day before the Kalends of November, in the year 1616.

units.la: Cum in tam eximio volumine & æterno opere, quo patriam & universum Frisiorum nomen, candore admirabili, summâ industriâ, singulari facundiâ, quamdiu ullum in terris eruditioni erit pretium, tibi obligasti.
units.tr: When, in so excellent and enduring a volume, in which you have bound yourself to our country and to the whole name of the Frisians, with admirable candour, the greatest diligence and singular eloquence, for as long as learning has any worth on earth.

units.la: JANVS GRVTERVS in epist. scriptâ 18. Sept. an 1606.
units.tr: JANUS GRUTERUS, in a letter written 18 September 1606.

units.la: Mi domine habes secundam partem historiæ optimæ, quam transmisit author Præses THVANVS, qui priores suas ad se non recepit. Fac quæso nunc saltem intelligat ipse gratam fuisse & voluntatem ejus & æstimium de te, cui es inter historicos Princeps. Ego jure merito diligo & æstimo virtutes tuas & doctrinas supra seculum suum rectas & erectas. Pergere te in historico illo campo feliciter, votum meum est, & petitio unica.
units.tr: My lord, you have the second part of an excellent history, which the author, President Thuanus, sent, though he did not take back his earlier volumes. Please let him now at least understand that his goodwill and his high regard for you, to whom you are the prince among historians, have been welcomed. I justly love and esteem your virtues and learning, which are upright and raised above their age. That you proceed happily in that field of history is my wish and my one request.
The same.
On Ubbo Emmius
The same.

units.la: QUisque hodie Historiæ numeros implesse putatur; Qui de re quavis dicere plura potest.
units.tr: Anyone today is thought to have filled the ranks of History, if he can say many things about any subject.

units.la: Quive adeo fumos aut somnia vendere doctus, Stemmata cujusvis continuare queat;
units.tr: And whoever is learned enough to sell smoke or dreams can continue the pedigree of anyone at all.

units.la: Fabellasque gravi jacere ac miracula pompà, Quà pueri expaveant, fœmineumque genus.
units.tr: They throw out fables and miracles with solemn pomp, the sort at which boys and the female sex are terrified.

units.la: Paucis culta Fides, paucis reverentia Veri est, Nemo at Mnemosynem demeruisse sitit;
units.tr: Faith is cultivated by few, and reverence for Truth belongs to few; nobody thirsts to deserve well of Mnemosyne.

units.la: Mnemosynem, monumenta suis quæ sola receptat Illa tholis, Vanum inde exulat, inde Nohtum.
units.tr: Mnemosyne, who alone keeps the monuments in her own temples, from there Vanity is banished, and Ignorance from there.

units.la: Non tulit id Phœbus, prolesque novena Monetæ, Corque tibi thyrso terque quaterque ferit, UBBO EMMI. hinc Frisicæ surgunt gesta omnia gentis, Ticta Minerva suo quæ velit esse peplo.
units.tr: Phoebus did not bear this, nor the nine-fold offspring of Memory, and she strikes your heart thrice and four times with the thyrsus, Ubbo Emmius. Hence all the deeds of the Frisian nation rise up, which Minerva wishes to have woven into her own robe.

units.la: Quæque Cupidineæ aurato mucrone sagittæ In tabulis scribat Gratia terna cedri:
units.tr: And what the Graces write on cedar tablets with the golden arrow of Cupid, the three Graces.

units.la: Moxque Honor ac Virtus templo deponat avito, Heic aras ubi habet Anna Perenna suas.
units.tr: Soon Honour and Virtue shall place it in the ancestral temple, here where Anna Perenna has her altars.

units.la: Quottidiè quibus Hora rosas, quibus Hebe amaranthos Sufficit; at nectar ambrosiamque Venus.
units.tr: Day by day Hora supplies roses to those for whom, and Hebe amaranths; but Venus supplies nectar and ambrosia.

units.la: Macte EMMI, hac cura, macte hoc opere; UBBO! perennis. Historiæ tu Dux, tu coryphæum eris.
units.tr: Well done, Emmius, with this care, well done with this work; Ubbo, everlasting one! You will be the leader of History, you its coryphaeus.

units.la: Quamque tibi magis Invidia atque Inscitia dentes Ostendunt, annos hoc magis ipse feres: Perque omnem Europam vectus famæ allice pennâ, Excipiêre hominum dulce Deûmque decus.
units.tr: The more Envy and Ignorance show you their teeth, the more you yourself will endure the years; and carried through all Europe, draw men on with the wing of fame; they will receive the sweet glory of men and gods.
Petrus Scriverius, Dutchman.

units.la: Esse quid hoc dicam? tibi debita fama negatur, V B B O? tibi, patriæ quem voco jure patrem? Nam sine te (verum testor) vir magne fuisset, De Frisiis vanum jam legeretur opus.
units.tr: What shall I say of this? Is the fame due to you denied, Ubbo? To you, whom I rightly call the father of our country? For without you (I speak the truth), great man, the empty work on the Frisians would now be read.

units.la: Jam Suffridæis premerentur nostra Chimæris Tulpita: jam monstris omnia plena forent.
units.tr: Now Suffridus's works would be crushed by our Chimaeras; Tulpita, now everything would be full of monsters.

units.la: Ita verò, explosis fabulatoribus, carmen claudit;
units.tr: And so, having driven out the fabulists, he closes the poem:

units.la: Sed queis judicium, queis est mens sana, pudorque, Lectores libris det DEus VBBO tuis.
units.tr: But may God give judgement, and a sound mind and modesty, to the readers of your books, Ubbo.

units.la: Qui pretium faciant, cedroque & murice donent: Abstineat scabras cætera turba manus.
units.tr: Let them set a value on them and bestow cedar and purple; let the rough crowd keep its hands off the rest.

units.la: Ante focum pueris veterum deliria nutrix Narret, & Occonem garruia[?] laudet anus.
units.tr: Before the hearth let the nurse tell the boys the old delusions, and let the chattering old woman praise Occo.

units.la: Te gravis æternâ commendet voce THUANUS, Noster & ingenti GROTIUS ore legat.
units.tr: Let grave Thuanus commend you with his eternal voice, and let our Grotius read you with his mighty voice.

units.la: Me quoque mirantem generosi fulmina Veri Devinctum sancto pignore pectus habe[?]
units.tr: Me too, wondering at the thunderbolts of genuine Truth, may you hold my breast bound by a sacred pledge.

units.la: HECTOR BOVRICIVS in suprema Frisio-rum curia Senator ad GRONINGAM.
units.tr: HECTOR BOVRICIVS, senator of the supreme court of the Frisians, to GRONINGEN.

units.la: INvicta sedes foederati Belgij, Alumna belli, Martis & Musæ domus, Victrix Marani Baeticique fulminis, Asserta postquam jura, libertas, fides, Te vindicarunt; scilicet parum fuit Quod Marte præstas, quodque limes Belgij Cluis GRONINGA, sede quæ Musas nova Nuper beasti, quæque tot claros viros Jubes vacivos Martias inter minas Labore docto demereri posteros; Beata sedes, quam hospitator EMMIUS, Fax literarum, temporis prisci pater, Vindexque veri, sæculi nostri decus, Ocellus orbis, patriam sumpsit sibi. Quo cive solo gloriari plus potes, Quam cive gaudet Patavinus LIVIO. At hæc prius fuere; nunc jacet jacet Ætate, curis, fractus & laboribus, Fato peremptus, omnium instar EMMIUS. Et tu GRONINGA cive quæ magno cares, Orbata tanto literarum vindice, Scriptore tanto, destituta patriæ, Quæ condis ossa maximi hoc ævo senis, Unum memento, posthac esse neminem, Qui gesta condat, unum præter EMMIUM.
units.tr: Unconquered seat of the allied Netherlands, nursling of war, home of Mars and of the Muses, victor over the Maranian and Baetic thunderbolts: since your rights, your liberty and your faith were asserted and you were vindicated, was it not enough that you excel in arms, and that you, Groningen, on the Cluis, the boundary of Belgium, have lately blessed the Muses with a new home, and that amid the threats of war you bid so many famous men earn the gratitude of posterity by learned labour? Blessed seat, which Emmius, the torch of letters, father of the earlier age, champion of truth, the glory of our century, the eye of the world, took for his own fatherland, as a guest-citizen. In what citizen of that soil can you take more pride than Padua takes in her citizen Livy? But these things were so before. Now Emmius lies low, worn down by age, cares and labours, cut off by fate, equal to all others in death. And you, Groningen, who lack so great a citizen, bereft of so great a champion of letters, so great a writer, deprived of your father, who now hold the bones of the greatest old man of this age, remember this one thing: that hereafter there will be no one, apart from Emmius alone, who will set down the deeds.

units.la: PIERIUS WINSHEMIUS Frisiorum historiogr. in epist. ad GELLIVM HIL- LAMA curiæ Frif. Senatorem.
units.tr: PIERIUS WINSHEMIUS, historian of the Frisians, in a letter to GELLIUS HILLAMA, senator of the court of Friesland.

units.la: Quod ad EMMIVM attinet, is etsi divina sua scripta ad quorundam in gente nostra palatum non temperavit, accedendum tamen in hoc est omnium literatorum judiciis, ne privatis affectibus inetiamur gloriam tam sublimium monumentorum. Vt turpe sit, illi viro, cui quasi totus orbis in scenam prodeunti adsurgit, nos solos iniquiores esse, ac illud nomen temerare, quod & sanctum cunctis[?] gentibus est, & consecravit se æternitati. Pauci enim dies, quibus à cl. Heinsio accepi magni illius AVG. THVANI de Emmio testimonium, quod tale erat, ut vel hujus videndi causa Belgium salutaret, ac coram, quemadmodum adpellat, intueretur hoc naturæ miraculum. Mitto quid uterque DOVSA fecerit. Tantum abest posse virum tam illustrem trahere in despectum, & illius odium tuto nobis concitare, qui in animis hominum ære perennius monumentum reliquit. Ejus enim ut magna admiratio, ita censura difficilis. &c:
units.tr: As for EMMIUS, although he did not season his divine writings to the taste of some in our nation, all men of letters must still agree in their judgement that we ought not to detract, out of private feelings, from the glory of such sublime monuments. It would be shameful for us alone to be more unfair than others to that man, before whom, as he steps onto the stage, the whole world rises, and to tarnish a name that is held sacred by all nations and has dedicated itself to eternity. For only a few days ago I received from the distinguished Heinsius the testimony of the great AUGUSTUS THUANUS concerning Emmius. It was such that he would greet Belgium for the sake of seeing this man alone and would, as he puts it, behold with his own eyes this marvel of nature. I say nothing of what both Dousas did. It is far from the case that we could draw so illustrious a man into contempt and safely stir up hatred against him, a man who has left a monument to himself in men's minds more lasting than bronze. For his great admiration is matched by the difficulty of judging him, &c.:

units.la: DE AGRO FRISIÆ INTER AMASUM ET LAVICAM FLU- MINA.
units.tr: ON THE FIELD OF FRIESLAND BETWEEN THE RIVERS AMASUS AND LAVICA.

units.la: VRbs GRONINGA proximis aliquot sæculis amplissima, splendidissima, & validissima in Frisiis fuit: eademque situ pene medio regionis ab occidente in orientem porrectæ, ideoq; omnibus fere rebus ejus magnis bello ac pace implicita; denique Reip. formâ præ cæteris insignis, atque optime habens. Quapropter operæ pretium visum, seorsim quædam de eâ disserere, & explicare accuratius, eaque explicatione lucem affundere multis partibus Historiæ nostratis. Et primùm quidem de agro dicam breviter, in quo urbs sita est, deque fluminibus agrum percurrentibus: tum de ipsa urbe, de jure Ultrajectino, de pactis & fœderibus ejus, de conatu & armis
units.tr: The city of Groningen was, for some centuries past, the largest, most splendid and most powerful in Friesland; and, lying almost in the middle of the region stretched out from west to east, its great affairs, in war and in peace, were almost all bound up with it. Finally, it was outstanding above the rest in the form of its commonwealth and was in an excellent condition. For this reason I thought it worth the effort to discuss certain matters about it separately and to explain them more carefully, and by this explanation to shed light on many parts of our national history. First, then, I shall speak briefly about the countryside in which the city lies and about the rivers that flow through the land; then about the city itself, the Utrecht law, its agreements and treaties, and its attempts and arms.

units.la: PIERIUS WINSHEMIUS Frisiorum historiogr.in epist.ad GELLIVM HIL- LAMA curiæ Frif. Senatorem.
units.tr: Pierius Winshemius, historiographer of the Frisians, in a letter to Gellius Hillama, senator of the court of Friesland.

units.la: Quod ad EMMIVM attinet, is etsi divina sua scripta ad quorundam in gente nostrâ palatum non temperavit, accedendum tamen in hoc est omnium literatorum judiciis, ne privatis affectibus metiamur gloriam tam sublimium monumentorum. Vt turpe sit, illi viro, cui quasi totus orbis in scenam prodeunti adsurgit, nos solos iniquiores esse, ac illud nomen temerare, quod & sanctum cunctis gentibus est, & consecravit se æternitati. Pauci enim dies, quibus à cl. Heinsio accepi magni illius AVG. THVANI de Emmio testimonium, quod tale erat, ut vel hujus videndi causâ Belgium salutaret, ac coràm, quemadmodum adpellat, intueretur hoc natura miraculum. Mitto quid uterque DOVSA fecerit. Tantum abest posse virum tam illustrem trahere in despectum, & illius odium tutò nobis concitare, qui in animis hominum ære perennius monumentum reliquit. Ejus enim ut magna admiratio, ita censura difficilis. &c:
units.tr: As for Emmius: although he did not always temper his learned writings to the taste of some in our nation, it must nonetheless be granted by the judgment of all scholars that we should not measure the glory of such sublime monuments by private feelings. It would be shameful for us alone to be more unfair to that man, before whom, as he comes forward on the stage, the whole world, as it were, rises, and to besmirch that name which is holy to all nations and has consecrated itself to eternity. For a few days ago I received from the learned Heinsius the great testimony of Augustus Thuanus concerning Emmius, which was such that he would greet Belgium for the sake of seeing this man alone, and would, as he puts it, look upon this marvel of nature with his own eyes. I pass over what Dousa himself did. So far is it from possible that we should drag so illustrious a man into contempt, or safely stir up hatred against him, who has left in the minds of men a monument more lasting than bronze. For, just as his greatness is greatly admired, so is his judgment difficult to match. &c.

units.la: DE AGRO FRISIÆ INTER AMASUM ET LAVICAM FLU- MINA.
units.tr: On the Field of Friesland between the Rivers Amasus and Lavica

units.la: URbs Groninga proximis aliquot sæculis amplissima, splendidissima, & validissima in Frisiis fuit: eademque situ penè medio regionis ab occidente in orientem porrectæ, ideoq; omnibus ferè rebus ejus magnis bello ac pace implicita; denique Reip. formâ præ cæteris insignis, atque optimè habens. Quapropter operæ pretium visum, seorsim quædam de eâ differere, & explicare accuratius, eaque explicatione lucem affundere multis partibus Historiæ nostratis. Et primùm quidem de agro dicam breviter, in quo urbs sita est, deque fluminibus agrum percurrentibus: tum de ipsa urbe, de jure Ultrajectino, de pactis & foederibus ejus, de conatu armis Saxonum, de Edsardi, Geldri, Burgundorum imperio,summatim agam; pòst de αὐτονομίᾳ & præclaro jure civitatis addam nonnulla : postremò ordinem Magistratuum & cæterarum curationum in urbe & extra urbem, totamque formam regiminis civilis exponam. Ager sic habet, quemadmodum & in Historiæ libro primo exposui.
units.tr: The city of Groningen was for several centuries the largest, most splendid and most powerful city in Friesland. Lying almost in the middle of the region stretched from west to east, it was therefore involved in nearly all of its great affairs, in war and in peace, and it was outstanding above the others in the form of its government, which was very well ordered. For this reason it seemed worthwhile to discuss some matters about it separately and to explain them more fully, and by that explanation to throw light on many parts of our national history. First I shall speak briefly of the field in which the city lies, and of the rivers that run through the field. Then I shall deal in summary with the city itself, the law of Utrecht, its pacts and treaties, the attempt of the Saxons by arms, and the rule of Edsard, Gelderland and the Burgundians. After that I shall add some things on its autonomy and its distinguished civic right. Last, I shall set out the order of the magistrates and of the other offices in the city and outside it, and the whole form of civil government. The field is as I set out in the first book of my History.

units.la: Post Lavicæ æstuarium, & alveum ejus penè emortuum, Ostergoæ ac totius Frisiæ Occidentalis terminum, ad quem Visuleta vicus celebris & cœnobium Gerriconium sunt, ager hic noster, de quo agimus, venientibus ab occasu sequitur, longoque litoris tractu non minùs quinis milliaribus secundum latus boreum, ac vadosa æstuaria in ortum porrigitur. Inde in meridiem se referens Amasi fluminis ostio, ac sinu Dullarto, quem à fluctuum rabie sic nominant, ortivo latere claditur, sed sinuosis admodum ac varie flexis litoribus. Nam primùm à septentrionibus, ubi sensim per aliquot passuum millia descendit ad portum fere Delfilanum[?], inde rursum in ortum tum convertitur, Amafo oram radente: mox ad Dullarti initium, in terras fe insinuantis, veluti linguam aut cuneum efformans, cujus in extremitate Reida vicus quondam percelebris, nunc castellum modò militare est, inter meridiem & occasum aliquoufque, deinde quasi incitantibus fe in terram fluctibus, ulteriùs etiam in Occidentem longo spatio litus retrahit, iterum brevi flexu in ortum redit, atque eodem pene, quo in occidentem ierat, spatio, in quo Midwoldicum fanum quatuor turribus conspicuum sese offert, rursus procurrit: postremò aliis etiam minoribus finibus receptis ad terminum austrinum contendit, ubi cœnobium est Hilligerlæum, Hispanicâ clade nuper nobilitatum, & Bellingwoldii. Ab eo termino per palustria & arenosa ad Oftergoæ limitem longo tractu recurrit, Westerwoldios primùm, dein Drentiam ad meridiem habens: idque latus meridionale omnium ejus laterum est maximum, xxvi millibus passuum non brevius. Ager totus dimidio fere, quàm Translavicanus, minor : argilloso ut plurimum, & ubere ad pascua pariter ac frumenta solo : palustris tamen & nemorosus, quâ Dullarto adjacet, quaque Ostergois ad meridiem cohæret, sabulofus hic illic quâ Drentiæ conjungitur. Hanc ego regionem à Lavicâ in Amafum ac Dullartum, minoris Frifiæ nomine affectam interdum avorum & proavorum nostrorum memoriâ reperio. Simul usus dudum invaluit, ab urbe Groningâ, sive quòd in solo ejus hæc fit ad austrinum limitem, (quod tamen in dubium trahunt nonnulli,) sive quòd fœderibus antiquitus cum eâ connexa, seu utramque ob causam simul, Groninganam vocitare. Nunc ex decreto in actis publicis non nisi Vmlandia, id est regio [illegible, ~8 letters] dicitur. Divisa quondam in plures provinciolas, ceu populos quosdam minores, legibus & imperio inter se distinctos, quos tamen commune fœdus & respublica quædam major plerumque in unum rursus colligebat. Et sunt ejus divisionis etiam nunc in usu notissima vestigia, paulò post exponenda.
units.tr: Beyond the estuary of the Lavica and its almost dead channel, which is the boundary of Ostergo and of all West Friesland, where the famous village of Visuleta and the monastery of Gerriconium are, this field of ours, which is our subject, lies, for those coming from the west. It stretches along a shore of no less than five miles on the northern side, and along shallow estuaries toward the east. From there it turns south, and at the mouth of the Amasus river and the bay called Dullart (named so from the fury of the waves) it is closed off on the eastern side, though with a very winding and variously bent shoreline. For first it descends gradually from the north over some miles to almost the harbour of Delfilanum[?]; then it turns again eastward, skirting the coast of the Amasus. Soon, at the beginning of the Dullart, it pushes into the land, shaping itself like a tongue or wedge, at the tip of which lies the village of Reida, once very famous, now only a military fort, extending for some distance between south and west. Then, as if the waves were driving it into the land, the shore recedes a long way further toward the west; again, after a short bend, it returns eastward, and over about the same distance it went westward, it juts out again to where the church of Midwoldicum, visible for its four towers, presents itself. Finally, taking in some smaller districts as well, it heads to the southern boundary, where the monastery of Hilligerlaeum, recently made famous by the Spanish slaughter, and Bellingwoldii are. From that boundary it runs back in a long stretch, through marshy and sandy land, to the border of Ostergo, having Westerwold first and then Drenthe on its south. This southern side is the longest of all its sides, being no shorter than twenty-six miles. The whole field is almost half the size of the land across the Lavica, and it is fairly small. For the most part its soil is clayey and fertile for pasture as well as for grain, though it is marshy and wooded where it borders on the Dullart, and where it joins Ostergo on the south, and sandy here and there where it joins Drenthe. I find that this region, from the Lavica to the Amasus and Dullart, was at times called by the name of Minor Friesland in the memory of our grandfathers and great-grandfathers. At the same time, for a long time the custom prevailed of calling it Groningan, either from the city of Groningen, because it lies in its soil on the southern boundary (though some dispute this), or because it was joined to that city by treaties from ancient times, or for both reasons together. Now by decree in the public records it is called only Vmlandia, that is, the region [illegible, about 8 letters]. It was once divided into several small provinces, like certain lesser peoples, distinct from one another in laws and rule, which a common treaty and some greater commonwealth usually gathered back into one. Even now the most notable traces of that division are in use, to be set out a little later.

units.la: Eandem hanc regionem vel agrum duo amnes præcipui olim percurrerunt, & percurrunt quoque hodie, quanquam nominibus jam aliis noti, nec eodem ubique retento meatu.
units.tr: Two chief rivers once ran through this same region or field, and they run through it still today, although they are now known by other names, and their courses are not everywhere the same as before.

units.la: Alter Hunefiu quondam dictus in Drentia exoriens, collectis primùm aquis palustribus tenuis, deinde lacum Laræum magnum profundumque ingressus ac permensus, ejusque copiâ auctus, justi jam fluminis instar latus atque altus, Gronenbergiam arcem olim haud incelebrem allapsus, imò penè circumlapsus, relictâ ad rv [?] circiter stadia Groningâ, quæ ei ad occidentem & meridiem erat, in circium deferebatur: mox milliari uno magno infra Groningam flexo cursu rectâ occasum versus se incitabat per Hunesgonios, qui ex eo nomen habuerunt, donec in æstuarium Lavicæ, ut nunc quoque facit, exiret, & communi cum eo ostio se exoneraret inter insulas in Oceanum. Nunc oppidanorum studio oppositis aggeribus, obstructo, quâ urbem prætervehebatur, vetere alveo, relicto ad dextram Gronenbergio solo, ad urbem multos ante annos derivatus magno urbis commodo, auctúsque illic amnis Ahæ aquis è Drentiâ similiter venientibus, perque longum spatium infra urbem ejusdem Ahæ alveo vectus Vnderwerumium usque, atque ibi veteri alveo redditus, aggeribus ab urbe ad exitum utrimque compressus, toto hoc infrà urbem spatio ab arundinum copiâ voce Germanicâ Heitdiep vulgò jam nuncupatur, veteri nomine illo Hunesi prorsus obliterato, & accolis etiam omnibus ignoto ac penè inaudito. Quæ verò pars ejus est supra urbem, per Drentiam & Præfecturam suburbanam meâns[?], hodiè à navium certâ specie, quarum in eâ usus est frequens comportandis ad urbem cespitibus, id est, glebis palustribus in usum ignis, vocatur Schutendiep / habetque utrinque agros humiles & uliginosos, per quos decurrit, & præterquam, quâ aggeribus constricta est, eosdem sæpe inundat. At alter amnis è duobus, quos dixi hunc agrum olim secuisse, nomen Fivelâ habuit, jam prorsus etiam ignotum, & è Duerswoldijs finitimis Præfecturæ veteri, aut ex ipsâ Præfectura vetere se proferens primum locumque, ubi nunc cœnobium Werumanum est, antiquitus, deinde mutato cursu modico à cœnobio intervallo humilia camporum perluens, longo ac tortuoso meatu illam agri partem permensus fuit, quæ Amaso propinquat, cuique nomen ex se tribuit Fivelingia, vel Fivelgonia: (utraque enim forma hodie quoque vulgo dicitur) ac demum apud Sondios (id vico tum nomen) se effudit. Verùm is exitus ejus ante annos plus minus cccc objecto aggere transverso oppilatus, & alveus ipse magnam partem unà cum nomine paulatim extinctus est. Collegit ille ex omni fere Fivelgonia aquas eas, & exoneravit, quas jam rivus Dammonensis, hoc nomine hodie notus, eodem ex agro collectas (nam per eundem hunc agrum defluit, & multis locis eundem quoque alveum servat) per canales Delssilanos[?] in Amasum egerit. Et hunc quoque oppidani quàm plurimos ante annos depressa per passuum millia perampla fossa ab eo loco, qui ab aggeris flexu nomen fert, ad mœnia ufque sua derivarunt, meabilem actuariis navibus majusculis, quantæ scilicet per canales Delfsilanos traduci possunt. Quin etiam studio Casparis Roblesii gubernatoris regii non ita multos ante annos claustra ad urbem hujusmodi constituta sunt, ut quoties oppidani velint, amnes hos duos Fivelam & Hunesum ad urbem dudum deductos confundere, rursum per eadem claustra disjungere queant.
units.tr: The first, once called Hunefiu, rises in Drenthe. First it gathers the waters of the marshes into a thin stream; then, entering and passing through the great and deep Lake Laerum, and being swollen by its volume, it becomes a river of proper size and depth. It flows past Gronenbergia, a citadel once not unknown, indeed almost encircling it, and, leaving Groningen about four stadia to its west and south, it was carried toward the northwest. Soon, after a great bend of one mile below Groningen, it hurried in a straight course toward the west through the Hunesgonians, who took their name from it, until it flowed out into the estuary of the Lavica, as it still does now, and discharged itself with the same mouth into the Ocean among the islands. Now, by the zeal of the townspeople, the old channel was blocked off where it ran past the city, by placing dikes across it, and the land by Gronenbergia on the right was left dry. Many years ago it was diverted to the city, to the great advantage of the city. There, the stream was increased by the waters of the Aha, which similarly come from Drenthe, and it was carried for a long distance below the city along the channel of the same Aha, as far as Vnderwerum. There it was returned to its old channel and, pressed in on both sides from the city to its outlet by dikes, the whole of this stretch below the city is now commonly called by the German word Heitdiep, from the abundance of reeds, and that old name Hunesus is completely forgotten, and is unknown and almost unheard of by all the inhabitants. The part of it that lies above the city, through Drenthe and the suburban prefecture, is now called Schutendiep, from a certain kind of boat, of which many were used there for carrying peat to the city, that is, marsh clods for fuel. It has low and marshy fields on either side through which it runs, and apart from where it is confined by dikes, it often floods these same fields. But the other of the two rivers which I said once cut through this field had the name Fivela, now entirely unknown. It rose from Duerswold, near the old prefecture, or from the old prefecture itself, first at the place where the monastery of Werum now stands, in ancient times. Then, after its course was changed a short distance from the monastery, it flowed through the low fields and, through a long and winding course, crossed that part of the field which is near the Amasus. It gave its name to that district, Fivelingia or Fivelgonia (both forms are still commonly used today), and at last it poured itself out at Sondios, which was then the name of the village. But this outlet of the river was blocked by a transverse dike about four hundred years ago, and the channel itself, together with its name, has gradually disappeared for the most part. From nearly all of Fivelgonia it gathered those waters which the stream now known by the name of the Dammonensian stream, collected from the same field (for it flows through this same field and in many places keeps the same channel), discharges through the Delssilan canals into the Amasus. Many years ago the townspeople also dug a deep ditch across many miles from the place that takes its name from the bend of the dike, and diverted it to their walls. It was made navigable for barges and fairly large ships, of such a size as could be brought through the Delfsilan canals. Moreover, through the zeal of Caspar Robles, the royal governor, not many years ago, barriers of this kind were set up at the city, so that whenever the townspeople wish, they can join these two rivers, the Fivela and the Hunesus, which were long since brought to the city, and again separate them through the same barriers.

units.la: Ac Fivela quidem, qui nunc Dammonensis rivus est, (Dammonam quippè duobus milliaribus Germanicis magnis ad ortum solstitialem ab urbe Groningâ perluit) non jam liber, ut Hunesus, in Amasum effunditur, sed exitum ejus quatuor ingentes canales coërcent, tres ad castellum Delffilanum continuis lateribus, quartus propè Farmsumum vicum loco proximo, paucis modò passibus Delffilâ disjuncto. His porrò amnibus, qui hanc Frisiæ partem perluerunt olim, addiderit quis tertium haud minorem prioribus, cui Ea nomen. Is in Monafterienfium finibus ortus, & à meridie in septentrionem se incitans, omnemque agrum Wesferwoldicum primùm, deinde planiciem illâ camporum per quam Dullartus sinus ingens jam se fundit, & lato & profundo alveo permensus, haud procul exitu in occasum, & rursus in boream flexo cursu inter duas Reidas, vicos olim haud incelebres, per septem canales in aggere defossos in Amasum se exoneravit, & agrum hunc quem jam describimus, ab eo qui Frisiæ Orientalis nomine nunc censetur, & Comitatus titulum fert, secrevit. Nunc post Bellenwoldios, qui in ora austrinâ sinus sunt, Dullartinis fluctibus tectus, quanquam alveum sub fluctibus servet, nusquam tamen apparet, ut & cætera omnia, villæ, vici, fana, quæ in eo spatio fuerunt. In hos autem, qui superiunt, amnes, ut & in æstuaria vicina, rivi complures scaphis & lintribus meabiles se effundunt: quorum alii orti ex se, aquis viam sibimet facientibus, alii humanâ industriâ excavati, hic illic regionem secant, & vicos plerosque celebriores alluunt, duplici regionis bono. Nam & humiles atque udos agros aquis levant, commeandi vectandique facultatem incolis commodissimam praestant. Sed qui Hunesum augent, aut in aestuaria aut Dullartum effunduntur, claustris in exitu coercentur: caeteri libero lapsu Fivelae se miscent. Duo etiam ad urbem ipsam Groningam longis brachiis se porrigunt, Honaeus in occidente, Botteranus a borea.
units.tr: The Fivel, which is now the Dammon stream (for it flows past Dammona, two large German miles northeast of the city of Groningen), no longer runs freely into the Ems as the Hunse does. Its outlet is confined by four great canals: three run with continuous banks to the castle of Delfzijl, and the fourth lies near the village of Farmsum, close by, only a few paces from Delfzijl. To these rivers, which once watered this part of Friesland, one might add a third, no less than the others, called Ea. It rises in the territory of the Monasterians and, running from south to north, first traverses the whole Westerwolde district, then the plain through which the great Dollard bay now spreads. With a broad and deep bed, not far from its mouth it turns west and then again north, between the two Reids, villages once not unknown. Through seven canals cut into the dyke it discharges into the Ems, and it separates the region we are now describing from what is now called East Friesland and bears the title of county. Now, beyond the Bellingwolde, which lie on the southern shore of the bay, covered by the Dollard waters, it keeps its bed beneath the waves and nowhere appears, and the same is true of all the other things that were in that area: farmsteads, villages and shrines. Into the streams that remain, as well as into the neighbouring estuaries, several smaller channels pour themselves, navigable by boats and barges. Some of these arose on their own, the waters making their own way, while others were dug out by human industry. They cut through the region here and there and wash most of the more famous villages, to the double benefit of the countryside: they drain its low and wet fields, and they give the inhabitants the most convenient means of travel and transport. But those streams that feed the Hunse either empty into the estuaries or into the Dollard, and are held back at their outlets by sluices; the rest flow freely and mingle with the Fivel. Two channels also stretch out in long arms to the city of Groningen itself, the Honae on the west and the Botter from the north.

units.la: Populorum minorum hanc regionem habitantium nomina, situs, ratio ita habent. Ad occidentem & meridiem Hunesi fluminis Langowoldij Oftergois finitimi, complexi vicos fanis insignes xiii: Fredowoldij in eadem plaga Sylvestribus ac Drentiae propinqui, vicis x comprehensi,tenui in solo utrique: Hummertzij in latere aestuarij Lavicani ad effluxum fluminis jam dicti, eluvionibus ad tres tantum vicos redacti, sed agri felicis, ubi rivus ex Drentia descendens, & Transhunesanam omnem regionem pererrans canali novo ad castellum militare compressus in idem aestuarium exit, & alluvio nunc reddit, quod diluvia quondam & tempestatum vis abstulerunt: Medachij ad ejusdem fluminis ripam introrsum magis pertinentes in vicos ix, in solo perubere ac læto sparsi, ex quibus quinque abbati Adoardio vicino suo parent. Hos vero & Octopagicos olim vocatos, & Hunesgoniis sequentibus accensos deprehendo. Ad orientem & septentrionem amnis Hunesi deinde reliqui Hunesgonij secundùm litus regionis boreum longo tractu extensi, atque hinc interiora versùs, Hummertziis & Medachiis pariter adversâ in ripâ secundùm amnis lapsum oppositi, donec in proxima urbis Groninganæ, & in rivum Dammonensem meridiano latere incurrant, latis simul pro modo priorum, & omni ex parte tum naturâ, tum hominum opere bene cultis finibus; quippè quibus non minùs iv[?] vici cùm singulis fanis contineantur: Distincti in præfecturas minores quinque; quarum ea, quæ ad ostium fluminis vadumque Lavicæ sita est, Marnensis dicitur; altera Vbingana, secundùm superiorem fluminis partem Groningæ in corum vicina, tertia, quam mediam vocant, prioribus confinis, nis, in fluminis ripâ, quâ in occasum se vertere incipit, ad litus boreum pertinens; quarta ab aggere interiore cognominata, in aquilonem ab urbe vergens, rivoque Dammonensi in cæciam ventum ab urbe defluenti contigua; postrema cunctis prioribus major per quina passuum millia juxta litus idem exterius porrecta, pariqué fere spatio intus patescens: Fivelgonij Hunesgonios ad ortum sequentes in Amasi orâ, similiter in duas divisi partes, quarum prior xxxi vicos complexa insignes, nulli superiorum felicitate cedit, tum ob terræ bonitatem, tum ob commoda fluminis vicini: altera vicis rarior, quos ix tantum habet, palustri fere, & passim humili ac uliginoso solo, in austrum priorem sequens, ad interiora vergens, per quam ab ortu venientibus iter Groningam est: eam Duerswoldiam proprio nomine appellitant. Atque hi sunt populi, quos nunc Vmlandes nuncupamus. Cujus quidem vocabuli ἔτυμον[?] si spectas, & si exempla intueharis in literarum nostratium monumentis, non verè proprium id nomen esse, huic tantum regioni competens, sed commune & appellativum, ut loquuntur Grammatici, nec vocem absolutam, sed in genere πρὸς τί referendam ad urbem aut locum aliquem celebrem, circum quem ager populive siti sunt, dubitare non potes. Sic enim est in antiquioribus literis, atque etiam in nuperis ante exortam litem, Die Dimblanden by Groningen / bim Groningen / ban Groningen: quemadmodum alibi, die Dimblanden / bim offte by Franeker / Bolswerdt / Lewerden / & similia: Item Groningen mit ehre dmlanden / ut Oekto thom Bzoeckt / Sibet tho Euftringen mit ehre dmblanden. Sed mitto hoc: ad rem revertor. Omnes hi populi, quos jam recensui, in tres partes, seu membra regionis, hodie divisi sunt, & dudum divisi fuere: quarum prima, quæ trans Hunesum ad occidentem & meridiem est, usque in Lavicam & Ostergoos, ac Occidentalis vulgo nuncupatur: altera Hunesgonios cis Hunesum, tertia Fivelgonios complectitur. Hæ in conventibus generalibus coëunt plerunque, & conjunctim de rebus deliberant, & suffragia ferunt, sæpè etiam, si dissensio sit, singulæ seorsim, disjunctæ cellis, & quò duæ inclinant, eò tertiam quoque accedere ex more aut lege cogunt. Ad juridicos verò confessus superiores, ad quos à tribunalibus inferioribus in singulis territoriis provocatio est, separatim Transhunesani & Cishunesani [?] certis anni temporibus in urbem Groningam convenient, ut nunc mos habet, & diu habuit: quamquam aliquando aliter quoque habuerit. De quâ re rursum dicetur nobis amplius, in sequentibus. A Fivelingiis Præfectura vetus, sequitur, ab Amasio flumine initium sumens, & ad Dullartum sinum toto ejus occiduo ac sinuoso latere, ut hodie res habet, stratæ, vimque ab eo quondam & jacturam passa maximam, agris & vicis fluctu obrutis, ut è magno horum numero vix xvii hodiè, ac plerique semilaceri mutilíque superstint: cujus pars borea Amasio vicina soli pinguis ac argillosi, reliqua ferè exilioris, minusque læti, partim palustris ingenii, partim arenosi, nemoribus frequens; quâ meridionalis maximè, Reideriæ quondam accensa, Tiammâ rivulo è paludibus defluente à proximis dirempta, nomine hoc ne nunc quidem istic obliterato, capite ejus Winscota. Tota verò hæc ab Amaso ad austrinum limitem civitati Groningæ ab annis propè cc bonis conditionibus paret. Ejus austrino limiti ad Dullarti finem Westerwoldij connectuntur, & ipsi Reideriorum quondam pars, hinc porrò in latere ortivo Dullarti ejusdem secundùm Amasum longo tractu duobus magnis milliaribus, & dimidio haud breviore pertinentium: hi vicis censentur quinque, agrumque colunt, nisi quantum Dullarto sinui proximum est, haud felicem, ac paludosæ ferè naturæ: in quos imperium, aut imperii umbram habuit multis sæculis Addingia familia nobilis, Weddæ arcis vetustæ eodem in agro domina, Westerwoldico cognomine posteris quàm gentili notior: nunc ad Arembergios omnia translata.
units.tr: The names, locations and arrangement of the lesser peoples inhabiting this region are as follows. To the west and south of the river Hunse lie the Langowoldij, neighbours of the Oostergoers, comprising thirteen villages notable for their churches. The Fredowoldij, in the same quarter, close to the Sylvestrians and to Drenthe, comprise ten villages, both on thin soil. The Hummertzij, on the side of the Lauwers estuary at the outflow of the aforementioned river, have been reduced by floods to only three villages, but of fertile land, where a stream descending from Drenthe and wandering through the whole region beyond the Hunse is confined by a new canal at the military fortress and flows out into the same estuary. Silt now restores what floods and the force of storms once carried away. The Medachij, lying further inland on the bank of the same river, are spread over nine villages on very rich and pleasant soil, of which five obey the abbot Adoardus, their neighbour. I find that these were also once called the Octopagi, and that they are reckoned among the Hunesgonians who follow. To the east and north of the river Hunse lie the remaining Hunesgonij, extended in a long stretch along the northern coast of the region, and from there, facing inland, opposite the Hummertzij and Medachij on the opposite bank along the course of the river, until they meet the nearby city of Groningen and the Dammon stream on the southern side. They have fields that are broad in proportion to the former, and well cultivated on every side, both by nature and by human labour. Indeed, they contain no fewer than four villages, each with its own church. They are divided into five smaller districts. Of these, the one situated at the mouth of the river and the ford of the Lauwers is called Marne; the second is Ubbegum, on the upper part of the river near Groningen, bordering the former; the third, which they call the middle one, adjoining the first, lies on the bank of the river where it begins to turn westward, reaching to the northern shore; the fourth takes its name from the inner dyke, lies northward from the city, and is contiguous with the Dammon stream flowing from the city toward the blind wind; the last, larger than all the others, extends for five thousand paces along the same outer shore and spreads inland over almost the same distance. The Fivelgonij, following the Hunesgonians to the east on the shore of the Ems, are likewise divided into two parts. The first, which includes thirty-one notable villages, yields to none of the above in prosperity, both for the goodness of its soil and for the advantages of the neighbouring river. The other, sparser in villages, which has only nine, lies mostly on marshy and everywhere low and waterlogged ground, extending southward beside the former and reaching inland, and it is the route for those coming from the east to Groningen. The people call it by its own name, Duerswoldia. These are the peoples whom we now call the Vmlandes. If you look at the etymology [ἔτυμον] of this name, and examine the examples in our vernacular records, you cannot doubt that it is not truly a proper name belonging only to this region, but a common and appellative one, as the grammarians say, and not an absolute term but one to be referred to a city or some famous place [πρὸς τί], around which the land or peoples lie. For so it stands in the older writings, and also in the recent ones before the dispute arose: "Die Dimblanden by Groningen / bim Groningen / ban Groningen," just as elsewhere "die Dimblanden / bim offte by Franeker / Bolswerdt / Lewerden" and similar. Likewise "Groningen mit ehre Dimblanden," as Oekto thom Bzoeckt, and "Sibet tho Euftringen mit ehre Dimblanden." But I pass over this and return to the matter. All these peoples I have just listed are today divided, and have long been divided, into three parts or members of the region. The first, which lies beyond the Hunse to the west and south, extending as far as the Lauwers and the Oostergoers, is commonly called the Western. The second embraces the Hunesgonians on this side of the Hunse, and the third the Fivelgonians. These usually meet together in general assemblies, deliberate jointly on affairs, and cast their votes. Often too, if there is disagreement, each acts separately, apart in their own chambers, and by custom or law compels the third to join whichever side the other two incline toward. For the higher courts of justice, to which appeal is made from the lower tribunals in each territory, the Transhunesians and Cishunesians assemble separately in the city of Groningen at fixed times of the year, as the custom now is and has long been, though at times it has been otherwise. We shall speak of this matter again more fully in what follows. After the Fivelingians comes the old district, beginning at the river Ems and extending to the Dollard bay along its whole western and winding side, as things stand today. It has suffered from the Dollard at its greatest force and loss, the fields and villages being overwhelmed by the flood, so that of the great number of them scarcely seventeen survive today, and most of those half-ruined and maimed. Its northern part, near the Ems, is of rich and clayey soil; the rest is mostly poorer and less fertile, partly marshy in character, partly sandy, and full of woods. Its southern part, once belonging to the Reiders and separated from the nearest by the rivulet Tiamme flowing out of the marshes, still keeps the name Winschoten, which has not been erased even now, its chief town. This whole district, from the Ems to the southern boundary, has obeyed the city of Groningen on good terms for nearly two hundred years. To its southern boundary at the end of the Dollard are joined the Westerwolde, and also a part of the former Reiders, extending from there along the eastern side of the Dollard, following the Ems in a long stretch of two great miles and not less than half a mile. These are counted as five villages and cultivate the land, which, except where it lies next to the Dollard bay, is not fruitful and is of a mostly marshy nature. Over these the noble family of the Addingas had rule, or the shadow of rule, for many centuries. They were lords of the ancient castle of Wedde in the same district, and they are better known to posterity by the surname Westerwold than by their family name. Now all of it has been transferred to the Arenbergs.

units.la: Postremò territorium suburbanum est totius regionis fines ad austrum longo tractu contrà Drentiam tuens, vicos ambitu suo continens xii cum sanis rusticis vi, & cœnobia duo, ambiguo inter Drentiam & eam, quam jam exponimus, Frisiam jure, quibus se debere hinc atque inde decerptis quibusdam partibus coagmentatisque videtur: lingua tamen, legibus, institutis per multa nunc sæcula illam magis quàm hanc referens, & Vltrajectinum Præsulem olim summum Dominum agnoscens. Antiquissimi ejus rectores Gronenbergij feruntur: ab his ad Selverdios, à Selverdiis vicissim ad Vltrajectinos, Geldros, Burgundos ordine pervenit; Burgundi postremò senatui populoque Groningano, nihil imminuto veteri vicanorum jure ac libertate, attribuerunt. Atque hujus in solo, ubi arenis gleba pinguior jungitur, editiore in dorso inter camporum humilia lingua instar se porrigente, sedem habet G R oN I N G A nostra, de quà nunc scribimus potissimum, universæ regionis nunc descriptæ, ut & totius Drentiæ, commune velut horreum.
units.tr: Finally, the suburban territory forms the southern boundary of the whole region. It stretches a long way opposite Drenthe and contains within its bounds twelve villages, with six rural hamlets of sound farmers, and two monasteries. It lies ambiguously between Drenthe and that Friesland whose law we are now setting out, and it seems to owe its shape to certain parts torn off from each and joined together. Yet for many centuries now it has matched Drenthe more than Friesland in language, laws and institutions, and it has long acknowledged the Bishop of Utrecht as its supreme lord. Its earliest rulers are said to have been the Gronenbergs. From them it passed in turn to the Selverds, from the Selverds to the men of Utrecht, then to the Guelders and the Burgundians. Finally the Burgundians handed it over to the senate and people of Groningen, without any loss to the ancient rights and liberties of its villagers. On this soil, where richer clay meets sand, on a raised ridge that stretches out like a tongue among the low fields, stands our Groningen, of which we now write chiefly, the common granary, as it were, of the whole region now described and of all Drenthe.

units.la: Regio universa ab exitu Lavicæ per ambages varias, quà æstuarium se curvat, quà Hunesus egreditur, quà vadum à septentrionibus alluit, quâ Amasus, quâ Dullartus se sinuant, in orâ aggeribus perpetuis, opere difficillimo, sepitur & defenditur contra aquarum influxum: idemque, ut dixi jam ante, secundùm Hunesi lapsum fit non ab urbe solùm, sed & supra urbem, usque ad ejusdem ostium. In eâ post Groningam nobilissima & maxima DAMMONA est, non vilis oppidi instar, si ambitum, & frequentiam habitatorum, si ædificiorum numerum, magnitudinem, formam, si viarum habitum spectes, sed honore moenium, & jure imperii civilis magistratuumque carens, amœna, in circulum feré se colligens, fosaque utplurimùm cingens, templo illustri cum turre latè spectabili insignis; fanum quoque monasticum peramplum, sed extra ambitum, lateri tamen occiduo penè contiguum habens familiæ Augustinianæ, nunc ab omni cultu desertum, ac vix se sustinens: sita ad Fivelam amnem duobus infra Groningam milliaribus cæciam versùs, eodemque amne navigabili media divisa, pontibus intus connexa quinque; unde ad exitum vi, & cœnobia duo, ambiguo inter Drentiam & eam, quam jam exponimus, Frisiam jure, quibus se debere hinc atque inde decerptis quibusdam partibus coagmentatisque videtur: lingua tamen, legibus, institutis per multa nunc sæcula illam magis quàm hanc referens, & Vltrajectinum Præsulem olim summum Dominum agnoscens. Antiquissimi ejus rectores Gronenbergij feruntur: ab his ad Selverdios, à Selverdiis vicissim ad Vltrajectinos, Geldros, Burgundos ordine pervenit; Burgundi postremò senatui populoque Groningano, nihil imminuto veteri vicanorum jure ac libertate, attribuerunt. Atque hujus in solo, ubi arenis gleba pinguior jungitur, editiore in dorso inter camporum humilia linguæ instar se porrigente, sedem habet G R ON I N G A nostra, de quâ nunc scribimus potissimùm, universæ regionis nunc descriptæ, ut & totius Drentiæ, commune velut horreum.
units.tr: The whole region, from the mouth of the Lauwers onward, is enclosed and defended against the inflow of the waters by continuous dikes along the shore, a work of great difficulty, winding in many turns: where the estuary bends, where the Hunse flows out, where the shallows wash it from the north, and where the Ems and the Dollard curve inward. As I said before, along the course of the Hunse this runs not only from the city but also above the city, all the way to the mouth of that river. In this region, after Groningen, the most noble and largest town is Dammona. It is not a mean town in appearance, if you consider its circuit, the number of its inhabitants, the number, size and form of its buildings, and the layout of its streets. But it lacks the honour of walls and the right of civil government and magistrates. It is pleasant, gathered almost in a circle and for the most part surrounded by a moat, and it is distinguished by a famous church with a tower visible from afar. It also has a very large monastery of the Augustinian order, outside the circuit but almost touching its western side, now deserted by all worship and barely standing. The town lies on the river Fivel, two miles below Groningen towards the south, and is divided in the middle by that navigable river, with five bridges joining its two parts. From there to the outlet of the river, where the port and fort of Delfzijl lie, is half a mile. It was once fortified with a rampart, a ditch and gates, by Edzard a hundred years ago. Three years later it was granted the rights of a city and an order of magistrates by George of Saxony. But twelve years after that Edzard stripped it of these, and in the following year the Guelder took them away again and left it bare. At last, in 1535, Tautenburg, leader of the Burgundian soldiers, condemned it to destruction, and it was preserved unharmed only by the prayers of its own people. It was once the capital of Fivelgo. As I have set out in my History, its rights, whatever they were, and its ancient statutes, which the Dammonians call their privileges, were received from the hands of its Orders, handed down and kept in custom. They were reviewed and approved at a solemn assembly in the year 1327 after the birth of Christ, and a few days later they were confirmed by all the Frisians at the general assembly of the whole people at Upstalsboom. The region is thus entirely enclosed and defended against the waters, from the mouth of the Lauwers around to the Ems and the Dollard. In the lesser places, six and two monasteries... (the text here breaks off into the same description of Frisia and of Groningen as its common granary).

units.la: Regio universa ab exitu Lavicæ per ambages varias, quâ æstuarium se curvat, quâ Hunesus egreditur, quâ vadum à septentrionibus alluit, quâ Amasus, quâ Dullartus se sinuant, in orâ aggeribus perpetuis, opere difficillimo, sepitur & defenditur contra aquarum influxum: idemque, ut dixi jam ante, secundùm Hunesi lapsum fit non ab urbe solùm, sed & supra urbem, usque ad ejusdem ostium. In eâ post Groningam nobilissima & maxima DAMMONA est, non vilis oppidi instar, si ambitum, & frequentiam habitatorum, si ædificiorum numerum, magnitudinem, formam, si viarum habitum spectes, sed honore mœnium, & jure imperii civilis magistratuumque carens, amœna, in circulum ferè se colligens, fosaque ut plurimùm cingens, templo illustri cum turre latè spectabili insignis; fanum quoque monasticum peramplum, sed extra ambitum, lateri tamen occiduo penè contiguum habens familiæ Augustinianæ, nunc ab omni cultu defertum, ac vix se sustinens: sita ad Fivelam amnem duobus infra Groningam milliaribus cæciam versùs, eodemque amne navigabili media divisa, pontibus intus connexa quinque; unde ad exitum amnis, ubi Delfsilæus portus & castellum, milliare dimidium: vallo, fossa, portis quondam munita ab Edsardo ante annos centum, & triennio post à Georgio Saxone civitatis quoque jure atque ordine magistratuum donata; sed his ab eodem post annos xii, illis à Geldro anno sequente rursus exuta nudataque: à Tautenburgio demum Burgundiæ militiæ duce anno M. D. xxxv i excidio damnata, & vix precibus suorum incolumis conservata. Ipsa caput quondam Fivelgoniæ: à cujus Ordinibus jura ejus qualiacunque ac statuta vetera, per manus accepta, & in more posita, quæ privilegia sua Dammonenses vocant, solenni in conventu, anno post Natalem Christi M. CCC.XXVII recensa probataque, & mox paucos post dies ab omnibus quoque Frisiis in comitiis universægentis ad Vpstallesbomum confirmata esse, in Historia exposui. In statutis his hæc reperio, Dammonam, ut nunc habet, ita tunc habuisse judices suos ex indigenis lectos: his finito muneris sui tempore (triennè id esse solet) cum primario loci sacerdote jus fuisse, die xxii Februarij fuc-cessores cešores sibi dešignare: hos‽ cognoscendi ju‐dicandi‽; potestatem habuisse de negotiis & querelis omnibus omnium hospitum ac pere‐ grinorum Dammonami venientium, sine contradictione: similiter de contractibus quibusvis coram ipsis judicibus initis, de promissionibus itidem apud eos factis, decisâ æstimationis parte quartâ; prætereâ de dam‐ nis pecudum vi Dammonensi a Dammonensi illatis: at de membrorum mutilatione & de vulneribus judicium eorum non fuisse, nisi facinus patratum esset ipsis præsentibus, aut incendii tempore: Et tamen in eo quoq; casu Consulis, id est, judicis superioris, quem Redgerum dicere mos est, multam ex lege fuisse, non secus ac si ipse judicasset: eosdem judices illos ter quotannis judicia exercuisse per dies quinos: ter item pondera & mensuras examinasse; panis quoq; venalis, cerevi‐ siæ, vini, viarum, puteorum, & similium rationem & curam habuisse, (quod ædili‐ um annonæ præfectorum solet munus esse:) litem introductam ad horum tribu‐ nal, si lis hujusce tribunalis esset, non licuisse litigantibus, judicibus his despectis, alio traducere: si quis contra fecisset, seu actor aėtor sive reus, eum sex solidos judicibus, totidem aditiuis soluere multam oportuisse: cura judicibus ijsdem fuisse, ne facinorosi sedem Dammonæ haberent: si quis Dammonensium (consulatus, id est, imperii ac jurisdictionis superioris jus haberet, idque in alium non Dammonensem conferret, xxx marcas multam populo Dammonensi solvisse: eandem poenam ei fuisse, qui aream suam in oppido venderet extero; quamsi is solvere ob inopiam non posset, aream publico cessisse: & haec si pretium multæ non æquaret, propinquos proximos defectui supplendo x marcas adjecisse: uni eidemq; judici simul & aditiuo esse non licuisse: Dammonensem cultello [?] vulnerantem vicinum suum sex solidos dependisse judicibus his, & totidem aditiuis. His addita de advenis sedem Dammonæ componere, domos emere aut conducere volentibus, deq; nuptiis ac rebus nuptialibus, non inepta certe. Quæ omnia si quis volet considerare attentius, facile intelligit, ampliús tum Dammonensibus jus, & potestatem judicibus eorum ampliorem in jure dicundo fuisse, quam nunc est, & à multis annis fuit. Nam praetorium imperium, & jurisdictionem penè omnem soli Ripperdæi & Houverdæi, aut qui his successere, dudum nunc tenent, & quem volunt, Consulem, id est Redgerum, oppidanis dant. Iudices illorum vix umbram rei, cuius nomen ferunt, retinent, nec vocare quenquam, nec prehendere, nec coërcere, aut in vincula dare, non causas, non crimina cognoscere, nec de his, nec de illis sententias ferre possunt. De Dammona plus satis.
units.tr: The whole region, from the mouth of the Lauwers onward, is enclosed and defended against the inflow of the waters by continuous dikes along the shore, a work of great difficulty, winding in many turns: where the estuary bends, where the Hunse flows out, where the shallows wash it from the north, and where the Ems and the Dollard curve inward. As I said before, along the course of the Hunse this runs not only from the city but also above the city, all the way to the mouth of that river. In this region, after Groningen, the most noble and largest town is Dammona. It is not a mean town in appearance, if you consider its circuit, the number of its inhabitants, the number, size and form of its buildings, and the layout of its streets. But it lacks the honour of walls and the right of civil government and magistrates. It is pleasant, gathered almost in a circle and for the most part surrounded by a moat, and it is distinguished by a famous church with a tower visible from afar. It also has a very large monastery of the Augustinian order, outside the circuit but almost touching its western side, now deserted by all worship and barely standing. The town lies on the river Fivel, two miles below Groningen towards the south, and is divided in the middle by that navigable river, with five bridges joining its two parts. From there to the outlet of the river, where the port and fort of Delfzijl lie, is half a mile. It was once fortified with a rampart, a ditch and gates, by Edzard a hundred years ago. Three years later it was granted the rights of a city and an order of magistrates by George of Saxony. But twelve years after that Edzard stripped it of these, and in the following year the Guelder took them away again and left it bare. At last, in 1536, Tautenburg, leader of the Burgundian soldiers, condemned it to destruction, and it was preserved unharmed only by the prayers of its own people. It was once the capital of Fivelgo. As I have set out in my History, its rights, whatever they were, and its ancient statutes, which the Dammonians call their privileges, were received from the hands of its Orders, handed down and kept in custom. They were reviewed and approved at a solemn assembly in the year 1327 after the birth of Christ, and a few days later they were confirmed by all the Frisians at the general assembly of the whole people at Upstalsboom. In these statutes I find the following. Dammona, as it is now, so then had its own judges chosen from the natives. When their term of office was finished (usually three years), they had the right, together with the chief priest of the place, to designate their successors on the twenty-second of February. These [were to have the power of] hearing and judging cases, and they had authority over all disputes and complaints of all guests and strangers who came to Dammona, without objection. Likewise, concerning any contracts made before the judges themselves, and promises made before them, a fourth part of the estimated value was to be deducted. Besides this, they judged concerning damage done to livestock by or against Dammonians. But judgement over the mutilation of limbs and over wounds was not theirs, unless the deed was done in their presence or at the time of a fire. Even in that case, the fine by law belonged to the Consul, that is the superior judge, whom they customarily call the Redger, just as if he had judged himself. These same judges held court three times a year, for five days each time. Likewise they examined weights and measures three times, and they had charge and oversight of bread for sale, beer, wine, roads, wells and the like, which is usually the duty of the aediles and prefects of the market. A lawsuit brought before their tribunal, if it belonged to this tribunal, could not be transferred elsewhere by the litigants, since these judges would be scorned. If anyone did so, whether plaintiff or defendant, he had to pay a fine of six shillings to the judges and as much to the assessors. The judges were also to take care that criminals did not have a home in Dammona. If any Dammonian, holding the consulship, that is the right of superior rule and jurisdiction, transferred it to someone who was not a Dammonian, he was to pay a fine of thirty marks to the people of Dammona. The same penalty applied to anyone who sold his plot of land in the town to an outsider. If he could not pay the fine because of poverty, the plot was to be ceded to the public. And if the price did not equal the fine, his nearest relatives were to add ten marks to make up the shortfall. No one could be both a judge and an assessor at the same time. A Dammonian who wounded his neighbour with a little knife was to pay six shillings to these judges and as much to the assessors. To these were added rules for newcomers who wished to settle in Dammona, buy or rent houses, and rules concerning weddings and wedding property, which are certainly not foolish. If anyone considers all these things more carefully, he will easily understand that at that time the Dammonians had a wider right, and their judges a greater power in administering justice, than now, and than for many years past. For the praetorian power and almost all jurisdiction have long been held by the Ripperdas and the Houverdas, or those who succeeded them, and they give the townsmen as Consul whomever they wish, that is, a Redger. Their judges retain barely a shadow of the office whose name they bear. They cannot summon anyone, arrest anyone, restrain anyone, or put anyone in chains.
