They cannot examine cases or crimes, nor pass sentence on these or those. Enough about Dammona.

units.la: Reliqua per omnem agrum vici tenent, & in his fanis insignes plus minus CLX[?]; quorum non pauci eâ magnitudine & cultu, ut oppidula videri queant. Cujusmodi sunt Visvleta ad Lavicam, & Northorma in Longowoldiis: Winsumum ad Hunesi flexum uno infra Groningam milliari: Bedumum, Vthusa, Middelsthemum, Warfumum in Hunesgoniis: Loppershemum[?], Berumum, Farmsumum, & quæ nominata jam est Farmsumo proxima, unâque cum eo in orâ Amasi posita ad Fivelæ exitum, Delfsyla, amplis nunc munitionibus & firmis, velut urbs, cin&ta, portu quoque celebris, in Fivelingiis : Winscota, & quondam florens, nunc Huctibus [?] Dullarti attrita, peneque hausta, Midwolda, cum fano quatuor turribus late conspicuo, in praefectura veteri: ut de Reiderwolda iisdem in partibus funditus deleta, qua medius fere Dullartus fluctus nunc agitat, sileam, omnibus prioribus quondam ampliore ac ditiore.
units.tr: The remaining villages throughout the whole district hold their own, and in them there are some 160 notable churches (the numeral is uncertain in the text); not a few of these are so large and so handsomely kept that they might pass for small towns. Examples are Visvleta on the Lauwers, and Northorma in Longo-Woldia; Winsumum at the bend of the Hunze, one mile below Groningen; Bedumum, Vthusa, Middelsthemum and Warfumum in Hunsingo; Loppershemum, Berumum, Farmsumum, and the place already mentioned next to Farmsum, which lies with it on the bank of the Ems at the mouth of the Fivel, Delfsyla. The last is now a town, walled and strongly fortified, enclosed like a city, and famous for its harbour, in the Fivelingo. Then there is Winscota, once flourishing but now worn down and nearly swallowed by the storms of the Dollard; Midwolda, with its church, widely visible for its four towers, in the old district; and Reiderwolda, in the same parts, which was utterly destroyed, where the Dollard's waves now churn in the middle of what was almost the whole region. I say nothing of the others, which once were larger and richer than all of these.

units.la: Egregia ad haec aedificiis ac opulentiâ monachorum & sacrarum virginum Cœnobia in agro fuêre numero xxv: ante cætera vero Adoardia in Medachiis, quinque vicis imperans, famosisque opibus inclyta, superbo imprimis fano, ad modum & dimensionem aedis Claravallensis magnificentissimè structo, visenda, aedificiis variis ac multis frequens, munitionibus & portis, ut oppidum, clausa, familiae Bernardinae: tum Vetus Dammonae vicinum Benedictinarum virginum, & alterum eodem nomine ac ejusdem ordinis in Marnensibus: Rottumum, Warsumum, Thesingaeum, Selwerdia, Grisomonachum, Wittowerumum, Oflerwerumum, Wytwerdia, Hilligerlaea, Schiltwolda; Essena etiam in præfectura suburbanâ. Præterea Præpositurae, sacerdotii genus opimum & honoratum, à Monasteriensi Præsule ἰυ&ξίας[?] ac quietis causâ introductum in hæc loca, quatuor, Farmsumana, Loppershemia, Vsquerdia, Leensia: quinta in Hommertziis jamdudum extrita. Collegium quoque canonicorum, aut ut tum vulgò loquendi mos habebat, ecclesia collegiata apud Bedumanos cum fano ibidem illustri, supra fanorum rusticorum modum; cui primus sacerdos non temerè alius, quàm aut genere aut doctrinae titulo conspicuus solet dari, magno honore atque autoritate in populo. Denique pastura Baffloa in Hunesgoniis, itemque Middelsthemia, vicario munere pro Monasteriensi olim decorate. Nec ad hæc, quod mireris, Regum aut Principum liberalitas quicquam contulit, sed rusticæ plebis studia, paucorumque nobilium ista sanè, quàm pro re ac agri modo majora congesêre.
units.tr: In addition, there were formerly twenty-five monasteries and nunneries in the district, remarkable for their buildings and the wealth of their monks and holy virgins. Above all the rest was Adoardia in Medaa, which ruled five villages and was famous for its great riches, notable especially for its proud church, built on the scale and model of the church at Clairvaux, a sight to behold; crowded with many buildings, and fortified with walls and gates like a town, it belonged to the Bernardine order. Then there was Vetus Dammonae, near Dam, a house of Benedictine nuns, and another of the same name and order in the Marne district. Also Rottumum, Warsumum, Thesingaeum, Selwerdia, Grisomonachum, Wittowerumum, Oflerwerumum, Wytwerdia, Hilligerlaea, Schiltwolda; and Essen in the suburban district. There were also provostships, a rich and honourable kind of benefice, introduced into these places by the bishop of Münster for the sake of ease and quiet: four of them, at Farmsumana, Loppershemia, Vsquerdia and Leensia, and a fifth in Hommerts, long since worn away. There was also a college of canons, or, as the custom of speaking then had it, a collegiate church, among the people of Bedum, with a famous church there, beyond the measure of the country churches. Its first priest was not commonly chosen at random, but usually someone distinguished either by birth or by a title of learning, and he held great honour and authority among the people. Finally there is the pastorate of Baffloa in Hunsingo, and likewise Middelsthemia, once adorned with the office of vicar for the bishop of Münster. Yet, surprisingly, no generosity of kings or princes contributed anything to these; rather the zeal of the rustic folk and of a few nobles, indeed a larger effort than the matter and size of the district would suggest, built them up.

units.la: Quibus omnibus si quis addat] Nobilitatis domicilia toto agro sparsa, cultu & mole magnifica, inveniet nihil ad ejus pulchritudinem ac fortunam pene posse adijci. Castella vero militaria in agri ora, Soltcampæum ad Hunesi ostium, Delfsilæum sæpe jam dictum, præ cæteris ingens, Reidanum in Amasi & Dullarti angulo communi, Bellingwoldium ad Dullarti recessum intimum, Buertangæum in palustribus inter Wefterwoldios & Mo[?]nasterienses mediis, integra adhuc omnia, & præsidiis insessa ad servandos regionis aditus contra hostes: cætera complura jam exarmata.
units.tr: If anyone adds to all these the residences of the nobility scattered throughout the whole district, magnificent in their furnishings and bulk, he will find that almost nothing more can be added to its beauty and wealth. As for the military castles on the edge of the district, there are Soltcampæum at the mouth of the Hunze, Delfsilæum, already often mentioned, enormous beyond the rest, Reidanum at the common corner of the Ems and the Dollard, Bellingwoldium at the innermost recess of the Dollard, and Buertangæum, set among the marshes between the Westerwolde people and the men of Münster. All of these are still intact and garrisoned to guard the approaches of the region against enemies; many others are now disarmed.

units.la: Jurisdictio per omnem agrum (excepto pâ Præfecturâ vetere, quæ ad civitatem, & Westerwoldiis, quæ ad Addingios, & ab his ad Arembergios certis legibus devoluta fuit, & territorio suburbano, cujus etiam peculiaris ratio) cum prædiis antiquitus liberis ac immunibus connexa est, ut qui prædia illa ut sua tenet, jurisdictionem cum imperio quoque teneat. Juris dicundi autem causa agri totius partes illæ jam expositæ in territoria quædam minora sunt subdivisæ. Et horum alia vicos singulos, alia binos, alia ternos quaternoívę complectuntur; quædam etiam singulos vicos disjungunt. Estque in unoquoque territorio certus tribunalis locus. Ac quoniam in territoriis singulis prædia hujusmodi complura sunt, accidit ferè, ut per vices & successiones annuas prædiorum domini jurisdictionem cum imperio habeant, idque secundum modum aut numerum prædiorum, quæ possident. Nam qui prædium hujusmodi unum tantum tenet, unius tantum anni jurisdictionem in eodem territorio habet; qui duo, duobus; qui plura, pluribus: & si quis omnia, perpetuam quoque juris dicundi potestatem eo in tribunali obtinet: idemque valet in iis, qui jus illud prædiis cohærens à præsdiorum dominis prædia ipsa retinentibus, quamquam id veteri instituto plane contrarium sit, pecuniâ, pactione, dono, cessione, denique quoquo modo sibi acquisiverunt. Quâ ratione Dammonense tribunal, quod olim multorum fuit, nunc ad solos Ripperdæos & Houverdæos, aut eos, qui his successêre, Farmsumanum verò vicorumq; aliquot vicinorum ad unos etiam ac solos Ripperdæos devolutum videmus. VI, & cœnobia duo, ambiguo inter Drentiam & eam, quam jam exponimus, Frisiam jure, quibus se debere hinc atque inde decerptis quibusdam partibus coagmentatisque videtur: lingua tamen, legibus, institutis per multa nunc sæcula illam magis quam hanc referens, & Ultrajectinum Præsulem olim summum Dominum agnoscens. Antiquissimi ejus rectores Gronenbergij feruntur: ab hisad Selverdios, à Selverdiis vicissim ad Ultrajectinos, Geldros, Burgundos ordine pervenit; Burgundi postremò senatui populoque Groningano, nihil imminuto veteri vicanorum jure ac libertate, attribuerunt. Atque hujus in solo, ubi arenis gleba pinguior jungitur, editiore in dorso inter camporum humilia linguæ instar se porrigente, sedem habet G R oN I N G A nostra, de quâ nunc scribimus potissimùm, universæ regionis nunc descriptæ, ut & totius Drentiæ, commune velut horreum.
units.tr: Jurisdiction throughout the whole district (except the old outer district, which was handed over under fixed conditions to the city, and Westerwolde, which went to the Addingi and from them to the Arembergs, and the suburban territory, which has its own special arrangement) is bound up with estates that from ancient times have been free and exempt, so that whoever holds those estates as his own also holds jurisdiction together with rule. For the purpose of administering justice, the parts of the whole district just described have been divided into certain smaller territories. Some of these take in single villages, some two, some three or four; some even separate single villages. In each territory there is a fixed place for the court. And since there are many such estates in each territory, it generally happens that by turns, and by annual succession, the owners of the estates hold jurisdiction with rule, and this according to the number of estates they possess. For whoever holds only one such estate has jurisdiction in that territory for one year only; whoever holds two, for two years; whoever holds more, for that many; and if anyone holds all of them, he has the perpetual power of administering justice in that court. The same holds for those who, though the right is attached to the estates, have acquired it for themselves from the owners who keep the estates, by money, agreement, gift, cession, or in whatever way; although this is plainly contrary to the old custom. By this means we see that the Dammonese court, which once belonged to many, now belongs to the Ripperdas and Houverdas alone, or to those who have succeeded them; and the Farmsum court and that of several neighbouring villages has come down to the Ripperdas alone. There are also six and two monasteries, of doubtful status between Drenthe and the Frisia we are now describing; to which they seem to owe allegiance, being pieced together from parts plucked from either side. Yet in language, laws and institutions, for many centuries now, it has resembled the former more than the latter, and it has acknowledged the bishop of Utrecht as its chief lord in the past. Its earliest rulers are said to have been the Gronenbergs; from them it came in order to the Selverds, from the Selverds in turn to the Utrechters, the Gelderlanders and the Burgundians; and at last the Burgundians handed it over to the senate and people of Groningen, with the old rights and liberty of the villagers undiminished. And on the soil of this region, where richer clay is joined to the sand, on a higher ridge stretching out like a tongue among the low fields, lies our Groningen, of which we now write chiefly, the common granary, as it were, of the whole region now described, and of all Drenthe.

units.la: Regio universa ab exitu Lavicæ per ambages varias, quâ æstuarium se curvat, quâ Hunesus egreditur, quâ vadum à septenseptentrionibus alluit, quâ Amasus, quâ Dullartus se sinuant, in orâ aggeribus perpetuis, opere difficillimo, sepitur & defenditur contra aquarum influxum: idemque, ut dixi jam ante, secundùm Hunesi lapsum fit non ab urbe solùm, sed & supra urbem, usque ad ejusdem ostium. In eâ post Groningam nobilissima & maxima DAMMONA est, non vilis oppidi instar, si ambitum, & frequentiam habitatorum, si aedificiorum numerum, magnitudinem, formam, si viarum habitum spectes, sed honore moenium, & jure imperii civilis magistratuumque carens, amœna, in circulum ferè se colligens, fosaque utplurimùm cingens, templo illustri cum turre latè spectabili insignis; fanum quoque monasticum peramplum, sed extra ambitum, lateri tamen occiduo penè contiguum habens familiae Augustinianae, nunc ab omni cultu desertum, ac vix se sustinens: sita ad Fivelam amnem duobus infra Groningam milliaribus cæciam versùs, eodemque amne navigabili media divisa, pontibus intus connexa quinque; unde ad exitum amnis, ubi Delfsilæus portus & castellum, milliare dimidium ; vallo, fossâ, portis quondam munita ab Edsardo ante annos centum, & triennio post à Georgio Saxone civitatis quoque jure atque ordine magistratuum donata ; sed his ab eodem post annos xii, illis à Geldro anno sequente rursus exuta nudataque ; à Tautenburgio demùm Burgundicæ militiæ duce anno m. d. xxxv i excidio damnata, & vix precibus suorum incolumis conservata. Ipsa caput quondam Fivelgoniæ : à cujus Ordinibus jura ejus qualiacunque ac statuta vetera, per manus accepta, & in more posita, quæ privilegia sua Dammonenses vocant, solenni in conventu, anno post Natalem Christi m. ccc.xxvii recensa probataque, & mox paucos post dies ab omnibus quoque Frisiis in comitiis universægentis ad Vpstallefbomum confirmata esse,in Historia exposui. In statutis his hæc reperio, Dammonam, ut nunc habet, ita tunc habuisse judices suos ex indigenis lectos: his finito muneris sui tempore (triennie id esse solet) cum primario loci sacerdote jus suisse, die xxii Februarij suc-cessores cessores sibi designare: hosq; cognoscendi judicandiq; potestatem habuisse de negotiis & querelis omnibus omnium hospitum ac peregrinorum Dammonam venientium, sine contradictione: similiter de contractibus quibusvis coram ipsis judicibus initis, de promissionibus itidem apud eos factis, decisa æstimationis parte quarta; præterea de damnis pecudum vi Dammonensi à Dammonensi illatis: at de membrorum mutilatione & de vulneribus judicium eorum non fuisse, nisi facinus patratum esset ipsis præsentibus, aut incendii tempore: Et tamen in eo quoq; casu Consulis, id est, judicis superioris, quem Redgerum dicere mos est, multam ex legafuisse, non secus ac si ipse judicasset: eosdem judices illos ter quotannis judicia exercuisse per dies quinos: ter item pondera & mensuras examinasse: panis quoq; venalis, cerevisia, vini, viarum, puteorum, & similium rationem & curam habuisse, (quod ædilium annonæ præfectorum solet munus esse:) litem introductam ad horum tribunal, si lis hujusce tribunalis esset, non licuisse litigantibus, judicibus his despectis, alio traducere: si quis contra fecisset, seu actor actor sive reus, eum sex solidos judicibus, totidem adituis solvere multam oportuisse: curae judicibus ijdem[?] fuisse, ne facinorosi sedem Dammonae haberent: si quis Dammonensium (consulatus, id est, imperii ac jurisdictionis superioris jus haberet, idque in alium non Dammonensem conferret, xxx marcas multam populo Dammonensi solvisse: eandem poenam ei fuisse, qui aream suam in oppido venderet extero; quam si is solvere ob inopiam non posset, aream publico cessisse; & hoc si pretium multa non aequaret, propinquos proximos defectui supplendo x marcas adjecisse: uni eidemq; judici simul & adituo esse non licuisse: Dammonensem culte llo vulnerantem vicinum suum sex solidos dependisse judicibus his, & totidem adituis. His addita de advenis sedem Dammonae componere, domos emere aut conducere volentibus, deque nuptiis ac rebus nuptialibus, non inepta certe. Quæ omnia si quis volet considerare attentius, facile intelligit, amplius tum Dammonensibus jus, & potestatem judicibus eorum ampliorem in jure dicundo fuisse, quam nunc est, & à multis annis fuit. Nam praetorium imperium, & jurisdictionem penè omnem soli Ripperdæi & Houverdæi, aut qui his successêre, dudum nunc tenent, & quem volunt, Consulem, id est Redgerum, oppidanis dant. Judices illorum vix umbram rei, cuius nomen ferunt, retinent, nec vocare quenquam, nec prehendere, nec coërcere, aut in vincula dare, non causas, non crimina cognoscere, nec de his, nec de illis sententias ferre possunt. De Dammona plus satis.
units.tr: The whole region is enclosed and defended against the inflow of waters by continual dykes, built with the greatest difficulty, along the shore: from the mouth of the Lauwers, through its various windings, where the estuary curves, where the Hunze flows out, where the shallows wash it from the north, where the Ems and the Dollard wind about. As I said before, this extends along the course of the Hunze, not only past the city but also above it, as far as the river's mouth. After Groningen, the most noble and largest place in it is Dam. It is not a mean town in its circuit, the number of its inhabitants, the number, size and shape of its buildings, or the layout of its streets; but it lacks the dignity of walls and the right of civil rule and magistrates. It is pleasant, gathering itself roughly into a circle, and mostly surrounded by ditches; it is distinguished by a famous church with a tower visible from afar, and also has a very large monastery, outside the circuit, but nearly adjoining the western side, belonging to the Augustinian order, now deserted by all upkeep and barely standing. It lies on the river Fivel, two miles south-east of Groningen, and is divided by that navigable river, with five bridges connecting the two halves within the town. From there, a half mile to the mouth of the river, where the harbour and castle of Delfzijl are, it was once fortified with rampart, ditch and gates by Edzard, a hundred years ago; three years later it was also granted the rights of a city and the order of magistrates by George of Saxony. But after twelve years these were taken away and it was stripped bare by the same George, and the next year again by Gelderland. Finally in 1535, Tautenburg, leader of the Burgundian soldiery, condemned it to destruction, and it was barely kept safe by the prayers of its own people. Dam was once the head of the Fivelgo; the old rights and statutes of that district, however they were, which the Dammonese call their privileges, were handed down from hand to hand by its orders, and were held in custom. These were reviewed and approved in a solemn assembly in the year 1327 after the birth of Christ, and a few days later they were confirmed by all the Frisians in a general assembly of the whole people at Upstallsboom, as I have set out in my history. In these statutes I find the following: that Dam, as it now has, so then had its own judges chosen from the natives; that when their term of office had ended (which is usually three years), they had the right, together with the chief priest of the place, to designate their successors on the 22nd of February; that these judges had the power, without objection, to hear and decide all disputes and complaints of all guests and strangers coming to Dam; likewise to decide, before the judges themselves, any contracts made, and promises made before them, the part of the value being a quarter; and besides, to decide on damage done to cattle by Dammonese, or by Dammonese to others. But their judgement did not extend to mutilation of limbs or wounds, unless the deed was done in their presence, or at the time of a fire. Even in that case, a fine was due from the Consul, that is the superior judge whom custom calls the Redger, just as if he had judged it himself. These same judges held courts three times a year for five days each; likewise they examined weights and measures three times; they also had charge and care of bread for sale, beer, wine, roads, wells, and similar things, which is usually the duty of the aediles and prefects of the grain supply. If a lawsuit was brought before this court, and if it belonged to this court, litigants were not allowed to take it elsewhere, despising these judges; if anyone did so, whether plaintiff or defendant, he had to pay six shillings in fine to the judges and as many to the aedile. The same judges were also to take care that criminals did not have a home in Dam. If any Dammonese, who held the right of the consulate (that is, of superior rule and jurisdiction), transferred that right to someone not of Dam, he had to pay a fine of thirty marks to the people of Dam; the same penalty applied to anyone who sold his plot in the town to a foreigner. If he could not pay it because of poverty, the plot passed to the public; and if the price did not equal the fine, his nearest relatives had to make up the deficit, adding ten marks. The same single judge could not also be the aedile. A Dammonese who wounded his neighbour with a knife had to pay six shillings to these judges, and as many to the aedile. To these were added provisions about strangers wishing to settle in Dam, to buy or rent houses, and about weddings and wedding goods, which are certainly not foolish. If anyone will consider all these things more carefully, he will easily understand that the Dammonese then had more right, and their judges had greater power in administering justice, than now and for many years past. For the praetorian rule and nearly all jurisdiction is now held by the Ripperdas and Houverdas alone, or by those who have succeeded them, and they give the townsmen whatever Consul, that is Redger, they please. Their judges retain only the shadow of the thing whose name they bear; they cannot summon anyone, arrest anyone, restrain anyone, or put anyone in chains; they cannot take cognizance of causes or crimes, nor pass sentence on either these or those. Enough about Dam.

units.la: Reliqua per omnem agrum vici tenent, & in his sanis insignes plus minùs CLX; quorum non pauci eâ magnitudine & cultu, ut oppidula videri queant. Cujusmodi sunt Visvleta ad Lavicam, & Northorma in Longowoldiis: Winsumum ad Hunesi flexum uno infra Groningam milliari: Bedumum, Uthusa, Middelsthemum, Warsumum in Hunesgoniis: Loppershemum, Berumum, Farmsumum, & quæ nominata jam est Farmsumo proxima, unâque cum eo in orâ Amasi posita ad Fivelæ exitum, Delfsyla, amplis nunc munitionibus & firmis, velut urbs, cin&ta[?], portu quoque celebris, in Fivelingiis: Winscota, & quondam florens, nunc Hudtibus Dullarti attrita, peneque hausta, Midwolda, cum fano quatuor turribus late conspicuo, in praefectura veteri: ut de Reiderwolda iisdem in partibus funditus deleta, quâ medius fere Dullartus fluctus nunc agitat, sileam, omnibus prioribus quondam ampliore ac ditiore.
units.tr: The remaining villages occupy the whole district, and about 160 of them are notable. Many are so large and well kept that they could pass for small towns. Such are Visvleta on the Lauwers, and Northorma in the Longo-woldi; Winsumum at the bend of the Hunze, one mile below Groningen; Bedumum, Uthusa, Middelsthemum and Warsumum in the Hunsingo; Loppershemum, Berumum, Farmsumum, and the village named just before, next to Farmsum, which lies with it on the bank of the Ems at the mouth of the Fivel, Delfsyla. Delfzijl is now walled like a city with ample and strong fortifications and is also well known for its harbour; it lies in the Fivelingo. Then Winscota; Midwolda, once flourishing but now worn down and nearly swallowed up by the Dollard, with its church that can be seen from afar with its four towers, in the old prefecture. I pass over Reiderwolda in the same district, utterly destroyed, where the Dollard's waves now surge through the middle, though it was once larger and richer than all the earlier ones.

units.la: Egregia ad haec aedificiis ac opulentiâ monachorum & sacrarum virginum Coenobia in agro fuere numero xxv: ante caetera vero Adoardia in Medachiis, quinque vicis imperans, famosisque opibus inclyta, superbo imprimis fano, ad modum & dimensionem aedis Claravallensis magnificentissimè structo, visenda[?], aedificiis variis ac multis frequens, munitionibus & portis, ut oppidum, clausa, familiae Bernardinae: tum Vetus Dammonae vicinum Benedictinarum virginum, & alterum eodem nomine ac ejusdem ordinis in Marnensibus: Rottum, Warfumum, Thesingaeum, Selwerdia, Grisomonachum, Wittowerumum, Osterwerumum, Wytwerdia, Hilligerlaa, Schiltwolda; Essena etiam in præfectura suburbanâ. Præterea Præpositurae, sacerdotii genus opimum & honoratum, à Monasterienfi Præsule [illegible, ~5 letters] ac quietis causâ introductum in hæc loca, quatuor, Farmsumana, Loppershemia, Vsquerdia, Leensia: quinta in Hommerziis jamdudum extrita. Collegium quoque canonicorum, aut ut tum vulgò loquendi mos habebat, ecclesia collegiata apud Bedumanos cum fano ibidem illustri, supra fanorum rusticorum modum; cui primus sacerdos non temerè alius, quàm aut genere aut doctrinæ titulo conspicuus solet dari, magno honore atque autoritate in populo. Denique pastura Baffloa in Hunefgoniis, itemque Middelsthemia, vicario munere pro Monasteriensi olim decoratæ. Nec ad hæc, quod miretis, Regum aut Principum liberalitas quicquam contulit, sed rusticæ plebis studia, paucorumque nobilium ista sanè, quàm pro re ac agri modo majora congessêre[?].
units.tr: Besides these, there were once in the district twenty-five remarkable convents of monks and holy virgins, rich in buildings and endowments. Foremost among them was Adoardia in the Medacho, which ruled over five villages, famous for its great wealth, above all for its proud church, built with great magnificence in the style and proportions of the church at Clairvaux, and worth seeing; crowded with many buildings, and fortified with walls and gates like a town, it was enclosed and belonged to the Bernardine order. Then Vetus, near Dammona, of Benedictine nuns, and another of the same name and order in the Marne district; Rottum, Warfumum, Thesingaeum, Selwerdia, Grisomonachum, Wittowerumum, Osterwerumum, Wytwerdia, Hilligerlaa, Schiltwolda; also Essen in the suburban prefecture. Besides these there were provostships, a rich and honoured kind of ecclesiastical office, introduced into these places by the bishop of Münster, at one time for the sake of quiet: four, Farmsumana, Loppershemia, Usquerdia, Leensia, and a fifth in the Hommerzijl, long since worn away. There was also a college of canons, or, as the custom of speaking then had it, a collegiate church, among the people of Bedum, with a famous church there, beyond the size of country churches; to it the first priest was usually given not carelessly, but one distinguished either by birth or by the title of learning, with great honour and authority among the people. Finally there is the pastorate of Baffloa in the Hunsingo, and likewise Middelsthemia, once adorned with a vicarship in place of the Münster office. Yet, which you may wonder at, the generosity of kings or princes contributed nothing to these; rather the zeal of the rustic people and of a few nobles, which indeed, considering the matter and the size of the land, gathered together rather great things.

units.la: Quibus omnibus si quis addat] Nobilitatis domicilia toto agro sparsa, cultu & mole magnifica, inveniet nihil ad ejus pulchritudinem ac fortunam pene posse adijci. Castella vero militaria in agri ora, Soltcampæum ad Hunefi ostium, Delfsilaeum sæpe jam dictum, præ cæteris ingens, Reidanum in Amasi & Dullarti angulo communi, Bellingwoldium ad Dullarti recessum intimum, Buertangæum in palustribus inter Westerwoldios & Mo†nasterienses mediis, integra adhuc omnia, & præsidiis insessa ad servandos regionis aditus contra hostes : cætera complura jam exarmata.
units.tr: If one adds to all these the homes of the nobility scattered throughout the whole district, magnificent in their upkeep and bulk, one will find that almost nothing more can be added to its beauty and wealth. The military castles on the coast of the district are Soltcampaeum at the mouth of the Hunze, Delfsilaeum, already often mentioned, by far the largest of them, Reidanum at the common corner of the Ems and Dollard, Bellingwoldium at the innermost recess of the Dollard, and Buertangaeum in the marshes, midway between the Westerwolds and the Münster people; all these are still intact and garrisoned to guard the approaches of the region against enemies. Many others are already disarmed.

units.la: Jurisdictio per omnem agrum (excepâ[?] Præfecturâ vetere, quæ ad civitatem, & Westerwoldiis[?], quæ ad Addingios, & ab his ad Arembergios certis legibus devoluta fuit, & territorio suburbano, cujus etiam peculiaris ratio) cum prædiis antiquitus liberis ac immunibus connexa est, ut qui prædia illa ut sua tenet, jurisdictionem cum imperio quoque teneat. Juris dicundi autem causa agri totius partes illæ jam expositæ in territoria quædam minora sunt subdivisæ. Et horum alia vicos singulos, alia binos, alia ternos quaternóïve[?] complectuntur ; quædam etiam singulos vicos disjungunt. Estque in unoquoque territorio certus tribunalis locus. Ac quoniam in territotiis singulis prædia hujusmodi complura sunt, accidit ferè, ut per vices & successiones annuas prædiorum domini jurisdictionem cum imperio habeant, idque secundùm modum aut numerum prædiorum, quæ possident. Nam qui prædium hujusmodi unum tantùm tenet, unius tantùm anni jurisdictionem in eodem territorio habet; qui duo, duobus; qui plura, pluribus: & si quis omnia, perpetuam quoque juris dicundi potestatem eo in tribunali obtinet: idemque valet in iis, qui jus illud prædiis cohærens à prædiorum dominis prædia ipsa retinentibus, quamquam id veteri instituto plane contrarium sit, pecuniâ; pactione, dono, cessione, denique quoquo modo sibi acquisiverunt. Quâ ratione Dammonense tribunal, quod olim multorum fuit, nunc ad solos Ripperdæos & Houverdæos, aut eos, qui his successêre, Farmsumanum verò vicorumq; aliquot vicinorum ad unos etiam ac solos Ripperdæos devolutum videmus. Nec desunt hujus generis exempla quoque alia, sed & pauca, & fere recentiora. Porrò prædiorum domini aut ipsi jus dicunt, aut aliis hominibus idoneis id delegant, prout cuique commodum aut gratum est. Est enim hoc arbitrii ipsorum. Jus dicens sive jure suo, sive delegato patria lingua Redgerus, nonnusquam etiam in locis ad occidentem Grietmannus more Translavicano vocatur: quæ voces judicem significant. Is unum aliquem, ut nunc lege cautum est (nam plures fuere ante, si territorium vico uno majus esset) è territorio virum honestum dari sibi ab iis, qui territorio comprehenduntur, curat, cui Wedmanno nomen est, qui non solùm assidet jus dicenti, sed judicii quoque minister est, & quædam momenti minoris sine judice per se expedit. Qui in juris dicundi munere est, merum & mixtum imperium habet, mandandi, prehendendi, multandi, coërcendi, capite puniendi potestate præditus est: multas & cætera judicii commoda percipit ipse, aut cum Wedmanno pro rato communicat. Ab his tribunalibus omnibus appellatio est ad conventus juridicos, aut Cameram Hovetmannorum Groningensium, de quibus post nobis erit dicendi locus. Olim autem non Hovetmanni solùm, sed etiam Consules senatusq; Groninganus plerisq; in causis appellati sunt, interponendiq; edicta ac mandata tum suo tum Ordinum agrariorum nomine potestatem habuerunt, causasq; ipsas unà cum cæteris in conventibus juridicis recognovêre & definivêre, ut ex iis, quæ infrà de jure civitatis dicentur, fiet manifestum. Sed & aliud quondam tribunal in agro fuit, & adhuc est, ad crimina graviora, quæ capitalia putantur, controversiasq; de jurisdictionibus cognoscendas & judicandas pertinens, quod vocant communiter Dat Ouerrecht: quod vicos complures ejusdem vicinæ collegit, è quibus ii, qui eo jure præditi sunt, (id similiter ut prius prædiis certis cohærent) vertente anno coëunt certo loco, ubi antiquitus tribunal hoc locatum fuit, & in leges ac incorruptam justitiæ administrationem juramento obstringunt sese, ad quos vi-
units.tr: Jurisdiction throughout the whole district (except the old prefecture, which was transferred to the city, and the Westerwolds, which was transferred to the Addingi, and from them to the Arembergs, on fixed terms, and the suburban territory, which has its own separate arrangement) is joined to the estates which from ancient times were free and exempt, so that whoever holds those estates as his own also holds jurisdiction together with authority. For the purpose of administering justice, those parts of the whole district just described have been divided into certain smaller territories. Some of these embrace single villages, some two, some three or four; some even separate single villages. In each territory there is a fixed place of tribunal. Since there are many such estates in each territory, it generally happens that the owners of the estates hold jurisdiction with authority in turns and by annual succession, and this according to the measure or number of the estates they possess. For whoever holds only one such estate has jurisdiction in that territory for one year only; whoever holds two, for two years; whoever holds more, for more years; and if someone holds all of them, he obtains the perpetual power of administering justice at that tribunal. The same holds for those who have acquired that right, attached to the estate, from the owners who keep the estates themselves, whether by money, agreement, gift, cession, or in any other way; although this is entirely contrary to the old custom. For this reason we see that the Dammona tribunal, which once belonged to many, now belongs to the Ripperdas and Houverdas alone, or to those who succeeded them, and that the Farmsum tribunal and that of several neighbouring villages has been transferred to the Ripperdas alone. Other examples of this kind are not lacking, but they are few and mostly recent. Furthermore, the owners of the estates either administer justice themselves or delegate it to other suitable men, as suits each one's convenience or liking; for this is at their discretion. The person who administers justice, whether by his own right or by delegated right, is called in the native tongue Redgerus, and in some places in the west Grietmannus, in the manner of the Translavian people; these words mean judge. He takes care, as the law now provides (for there were more before, if the territory was larger than one village), that a respectable man from the territory is given to him by those who are included in the territory, and he is called Wedmannus. He not only sits beside the one administering justice, but is also an officer of the court, and settles some matters of lesser weight by himself without the judge. The one who holds the office of administering justice has merum and mixed imperium, and is endowed with the power of commanding, arresting, fining, restraining, and punishing by death; he himself takes the fines and other profits of the court, or shares them with the Wedmannus in agreed proportion. Appeal from all these tribunals lies to the juridical assemblies, or to the Chamber of the Hovetmanni of Groningen, about which we shall have occasion to speak later. Formerly, however, not only the Hovetmanni but also the consuls and the Senate of Groningen were appealed to in many cases, and they had the power of issuing and giving edicts and mandates both in their own name and in that of the agrarian orders; and together with the others in the juridical assemblies they examined and decided the cases themselves, as will become clear from what will be said below about the right of the city. But there was also formerly, and still is, another tribunal in the district, pertaining to the more serious crimes, which are regarded as capital, and to disputes concerning jurisdictions, to be heard and decided; it is commonly called Dat Ouerrecht: it gathers together several villages of the same neighbourhood, of which those who hold that right (which likewise is attached to certain estates) meet once a year at a set place, where this tribunal was established from ancient times, and bind themselves by oath to the laws and to the incorrupt administration of justice; to whom those annual turns return...

units.la: cos[?] ces illæ annuæ redire: iidemque, quoties res poscit, vocati conveniunt eodem, causaque cognoscunt & sententias ferunt: tum domum in diversa recedunt. Et sunt tribunalia hujusmodi cis Hunesum per Hunesgonios & Fivelingios complura, sed alibi eo, quo dixi, vocabulo, alibi <bl>die Landtrechte</bl> Teutonicè nuncupata, nomine non re diversa.
units.tr: ...and whenever the matter requires, those summoned gather in the same place, hear the case, and pronounce judgments; then they return home separately. There are several tribunals of this kind on this side of the Hunze, through the Hunsingo and the Fivelingo, called by different names in different places: here by the word I have mentioned, there <bl>die Landtrechte</bl> in German, with a name different but not different in substance.

units.la: Atqui jus hoc, quod dixi prædiis connexum, in hac ratione nonnunquam vico quoque integro uni aut alteri, id est, toti plebi vicanæ, non prædiis in vico singulis, alicus & uni familiæ nobili pro toto vico cohæret: eique vico aut familiæ nobili potestas hæc est perpetua. Qui potestatem hanc tenet jure loci ejus, ubi sedes judicii est, is stato die cæteros omnes istuc coëuntes sacramenti religione obligat, eosdem, cum opus est, convocat, id quod iis placet, pro sententia pronunciat. Et accidit non raro, ut qui in hoc judicatu est, reliquam quoque jurisdictionem eodem tempore teneat.
units.tr: Yet this right, which I have said is attached to estates, in this arrangement sometimes belongs not to the separate estates in a village but to one or another whole village, that is, to the whole village community, or to some one noble family on behalf of the whole village; and this power is perpetual for that village or noble family. Whoever holds this power by the right of the place where the seat of the court is, binds all the others who assemble there on the appointed day by the religious obligation of oath, summons them again when there is need, and pronounces as judgment what pleases them. And it not infrequently happens that whoever holds this judgeship also holds the remaining jurisdiction at the same time.

units.la: Præter hæc curationes quoque sunt in hac regione binæ, honestissimæ conditionis, nec minus necessariæ Reip. quàm utiles: Quarum altera ad aquarum claustra, & quæ cum his copulata sunt, altera ad aggeres pertinet: illa deducendis è regione aquis pluviis & palustribus, aut rupto aggere infusis; hæc excludendis marinis aut fluvialibus est instituta: utraque cum potestate, & quadam imperii specie; imprimis prior. In eâ qui sunt, non solùm claustris ipsis, quorum maximus usus, maxima impendia, præsunt, sed aquarum quoque ductus, ac derivationes, & pontes amnibus & rivis impositos curant. Divisi in classes aut collegia plura secundùm regiones & claustra diversa: & classes singulæ in gradus distinctæ.In his inferiores <bl>Sÿlrichters</bl>/ superiores <bl>Schepperes</bl>/summi <bl>vpperste Schepperes</bl> vocantur. Et inferiores quidem singulis in classibus, quas <bl>Sÿlvesten</bl> appellant, complures numero sunt, pro multitudine pagorum, qui qualibet classe comprehenduntur. Quilibet enim vicus ex sui medio edit unum duosve per eos, qui hoc jus habent,viros idoneos ac muneris capaces: qui omnes jurati in leges ad hanc rem pertinentes vicissim ex sese edunt duos aut plures superiores velut ἀρχόντες ὑπάτας[?] praeditos potestate majore, & fere ex nobilitate, aut, ut ante haec tempora res habuit, ex ordine antistitum coenobiis praefectorum. Atque his, in classibus tribus, quae totidem claustra Delfensia curant, additus olim abbas Werumanus, velut praeses aut rector summus, penes quem suprema autoritas: in classe Winsumanâ, quae duplex quoque est, praefectus villae, quam in Hunesgoniis Adoardii habebant: in Adoardianâ cellarius, uti vocant, Adoardius: Reliquae classes hoc praeside carent. Et in universum, ut perplexa admodum atque impedita aquaeductuum ratio in hac regione est, dum sibi quisque viciniaeque suae consulit ac studet, ita varia, inter se discrepantia, intricata plurima sunt in toto hoc instituto, aliudque aliis in classibus ac locis valet. Qui in Delficis classibus sunt, trienne munus habent; qui in Winsumanâ, & Adoardianâ, biennes alibi aliter. Potestas omnibus mandandi, vocandi, cognoscendi, mulctandi secundùm leges. Conveniunt quotannis ter in classibus suis deliberandi & statuendi causâ statò tempore & loco. Et ut plerăque alia communia habent, sic hos quoque conventus classes Delficæ propter claustrorum suorum conjunctionem: habent & Winsumanæ duæ, curantes claustra totidem. In his conventibus, si res requirere videatur, decernitur tributum: id colligitur per inferiores: collectum traditur superioribus: ab his apud præsidem summum: ubi præses hujusmodi est, deponitur: is ex decreto communi impendit, quo poscit usus. In controversiis mos fuit in classibus Delficis, (puto etiam in Winsumanâ utrâque & Adoardianâ) si quis læsum se sententiâ aut mandato inferiorum arbitraretur, appellare superiores, post hos ad cognitionem vocare etiam cæteros ejusdem ordinis in classibus iisdem cum summo præside, ab istis quod decretum esset ratum habere, nec tendere longius: Post ex conventione sic institutum inter Delfenses, Winsumanos, Adoardios, ut ab unis ad proximos, à proximis ad ter[?]tios esset provocatio : in tertiorum sententiâ esset litium finis. Atque hoc nunc quoque apud eos in usu manet. In caeteris classibus omnibus, quae Praefecturae veteris non sunt, Hovetmannorum Groningensium summum judicium est. Agerum praefecti, & ipsi secundùm regiones ac loca inter se distinguuntur, potestatemque amplam habent, parem penè cum prioribus, sed decreta omnium extra eandem Praefecturam veterem, Hovetmannis subjecta sunt. In Praefecturâ veteri, ut illi, sic hi quoque senatum urbis summum judicem agnoscunt. Operam dant, ut aggeres fluctuum violentiae objecti sarti tecti serventur, disjecti reficiantur, interdum augeantur, proferantur, contrahantur ex usu patriae. De quibus dicere plura non libet, ne fiam prolixior.
units.tr: Besides these, there are in this region two offices of the highest standing, no less necessary to the commonwealth than useful. One concerns the sluices and what is joined to them; the other concerns the dikes. The first drains rain and marsh water from the region, or water let in when a dike has burst; the second keeps out sea or river water. Both carry authority and a certain semblance of government, especially the first. Those in it not only preside over the sluices themselves, whose use and expense are greatest, but also look after the water channels, diversions, and bridges placed over rivers and streams. They are divided into classes or several colleges according to region and the different sluices, and each class is divided into grades. Among these, the lower officers are called <bl>Sÿlrichters</bl>, the higher <bl>Schepperes</bl>, and the highest <bl>vpperste Schepperes</bl>. The lower officers in each class, which they call <bl>Sÿlvesten</bl>, are numerous, according to the number of villages included in the class. Each village chooses from its midst one or two suitable men, capable of the office, from among those who hold this right. All of these, sworn to the laws relating to the matter, in turn choose two or more higher officers, endowed with greater power and mostly drawn from the nobility, or, as things stood before these times, from the order of prelates set over monasteries. To these, in the three classes that look after the Delfzijl sluices, was formerly added the abbot of Werum as president or supreme ruler, in whose hands lay the highest authority. In the Winsum class, which is also double, the prefect of the estate that the Adoardians held in Hunsingo; in the Adoardian class, the cellarer, as they call him, Adoardius. The remaining classes lack such a president. In general, just as the arrangement of water channels in this region is very complicated and entangled, since each person looks to himself and his neighbourhood, so there are many varied, mutually discordant and intricate features in this whole system, and one thing holds force in one class or place, another in another. Those in the Delfzijl classes hold office for three years; those in the Winsum and Adoardian classes for two; elsewhere it differs. All have power to command, summon, examine and fine according to the laws. They meet three times a year in their classes, at a fixed time and place, to deliberate and decide. As they share many common concerns, so the Delfzijl classes hold these meetings too, because of the union of their sluices; the two Winsum classes do likewise, looking after as many sluices. In these meetings, if the matter seems to require it, a tax is decreed. It is collected through the lower officers, handed on to the higher, and from these to the president-general. Where there is such a president, the money is deposited with him, and he spends it by common decree as need requires. In disputes it was the custom in the Delfzijl classes (I think also in both the Winsum and Adoardian classes) that if anyone thought himself wronged by the sentence or command of the lower officers, he appealed to the higher ones; after them, the others of the same rank in the same classes were summoned to hear the case with the chief president, to ratify what had been decided and go no further. Afterwards, by an agreement thus established among the Delfzijl, Winsum and Adoardian people, appeal was to pass from the first to the nearest, from the nearest to the third, and the judgment of the third was to be the end of the lawsuit. This custom still remains in use among them. In all the other classes that do not belong to the old prefecture, the supreme judgment rests with the Hovetmen of Groningen. The prefects of the land, who are themselves distinguished from one another by region and place, have ample power, nearly equal to the former, but the decrees of all outside that old prefecture are subject to the Hovetmen. Within the old prefecture, these officers as well as the others acknowledge the city senate as the supreme judge. They take care that the dikes set against the violence of the waves are kept whole and repaired when broken, and at times enlarged, extended or contracted, as the good of the country requires. I do not care to say more on these matters, lest I become too lengthy.

units.la: Denique Præpositi, quos dixi, singuli suis in finibus olim descriptis ecclesiasticae præsidebant ante hæc tempora, & sacris de rebus jus dicebant, assidentibus sacerdotibus sacerdotum causas cognoscebant, delicta omnia contra matrimonii leges castigabant, ædium ac rerum sacratarum curam gerebant, rationes æditimorum[?] examinabant, fœneratores comprimebant, pœnas ab iis poscebant. Præter hos Officialis quoque & Commissarius, uti vocabant, in curatione rerum talium pro Episcopo erant: sed in populo libero tantum non poterant, quantum fere aliis in regionibus solent. Quæ omnia durarunt, quandiu regnum Pontificium cum imperio Hispanico hic stetit: eo vero finito, hæc quoque interiere. Quibus quæ successere classibus congregandis, & habendis synodis, ut verbo divino & primævæ Ecclesiæ propiora, sic usu quoque ipso, si pietas modo in utentibus fit, sine dubio meliora.
units.tr: Finally, the provosts I mentioned, each within his own bounds once marked out, formerly presided over ecclesiastical affairs before these times, and pronounced judgment on sacred matters. With priests sitting beside them, they examined the causes of priests, punished all offences against the laws of marriage, looked after the buildings and sacred property, examined the accounts of the sextons, and restrained usurers, exacting penalties from them. Besides these, the official and the commissary, as they were called, acted for the bishop in the management of such affairs; but among a free people they could not wield as much power as they usually do in other regions. All these arrangements lasted as long as the Papist kingdom stood here together with Spanish rule; when that ended, these too perished. The assemblies that succeeded them, for gathering the classes and holding synods, are, as they are closer to the divine word and the primitive Church, so also in practice itself, undoubtedly better, provided piety is present in those who use them.

units.la: Sacerdotes in agro numerati olim supra cc. xx, quantulo in spatio? præter tot monachos & monachas, quot capi tam multis, & quidem peramplis ac opulentis cœnobiis potuêre: quorum numerus fide multo major fuit.
units.tr: Priests in this territory were once counted at more than 220 (how small a space!), apart from as many monks and nuns as so many, and indeed very large and wealthy, monasteries could hold; their number was far greater than one would believe.

units.la: Populus universus cum reliquis Frisiis à temporibus Caroli Magni ad Saxonum arma per annos fere DCC liber fuit, fuiqne[?] juris, Domini nescius: summi principis Cæsaris solummodò majestatem comiter agnovit, nec tributis pressus, nec angariis obnoxius, omnisque adeò servitutis ignarus. Quæ si quis cuncta consideret, intelliget sanè, haud facilè populum alium rus colentem posse reperiri in his orbis regionibus, qui libertate ac felicitate hunc antecesserit. Sed ipsa luxurians ac penè nimia libertas sæpè magno ei malo fuit, veramq; & genuinam libertatem propè evertit. Nam ambitiosa ingenia. factiones peperêre, pestem liberis populis propriam, sibiqúe potentiam struxerunt: inde ad tumultus & bella civilia ventum, regioq; graviter afflicta. Ad hæc singulæ regionis partes separatim sibi consulere, suisque commodis studere, quid in commune omnibus, & toti regioni expediret, non expendere, necistuc consilia referre: hinc rursus simultates, odia, injuriæ: ex injuriis eadem armata vis, & furor intestinus. Nec judicia sine vitiis ingentibus fuêre, gratiâ, pecuniâ, odio, inimicitiâ corrupta: & licentiâ peccatum frequenter: eâ occasione pax turbata. Quibus malis remedium societate
units.tr: The people, together with the other Frisians, was free from the times of Charlemagne until the wars with the Saxons, for nearly 700 years. It knew no lord and acknowledged only the majesty of the supreme prince, the Emperor, in a courteous way. It was neither oppressed by tributes nor bound by forced services, and was wholly ignorant of servitude. If anyone considers all this, he will clearly understand that hardly any other people tilling the land can be found in the regions of the world that surpassed it in liberty and happiness. But its luxuriant and almost excessive liberty was often a great evil to it, and nearly overthrew true and genuine liberty. For ambitious minds bred factions, and built up a plague peculiar to free peoples and a power of their own. From this came tumults and civil wars, and the region was grievously afflicted. Moreover, the separate parts of the region looked after themselves and sought their own advantage, without weighing what was expedient in common for all and the whole region, nor referring their plans to it. Hence again came enmities, hatreds and injuries; from injuries came the same armed force and internal frenzy. Nor were the judgments free of great faults, being corrupted by favour, money, hatred and enmity; and sin was frequent through licence, and on such occasions peace was disturbed. Against these evils a remedy was sought through union

units.la: Groningensium pluries quæsitum, eaque ancorà [?fluctuans], & vix se sustinens libertas periculis erepta firmataque, eo medio judiciorum integritas reparata, & per aliquot sæcula conservata, ac denique licentia repressa fuit.
units.tr: which the Groningers often sought. By this means, their liberty, fluctuating and barely sustaining itself, was snatched from dangers and made firm, and the integrity of judgments was restored and preserved for several centuries, and at last licence was checked.

units.la: In legibus suis populus ista habet memoratu digna, Pacta dotalia ritè inita, ut mos aut jus regionis poscit, rata sunto. Testamenta nisi de bonis acquisitis, non sunto Res soli ex haereditatibus profectae, ædificia, & quicquid in bonis immobilibus, à defuncto relicta ad proximos sanguine devolvuntur, nisi aliter pactis dotalibus sit cautum.
units.tr: Among their laws the people has these worthy of mention: dowry agreements duly made, as the custom or law of the region requires, shall stand. Wills shall not be valid, except concerning acquired goods. Landed property coming from inheritances, buildings, and whatever immovable goods the deceased has left, pass by blood to the nearest kin, unless otherwise provided in the dowry agreements.

units.la: Mobilia omnia, quæ conjuges matrimonium ineuntes possident, & in usum matrimonij conferunt, quæve stante matrimonio ex hæreditatibus accrescunt, omnia item industria conjugum [?cunjugum] acquisita, etiam sine pactis dotalibus cunjugum sunto pari jure, alteroq; defuncto semissis hæredum ejus esto, reliquum superstiti maneto. Donationes inter vivos robur habento, si bonorum cessio à donatore vivente fiat.
units.tr: All movable goods which spouses possess when entering marriage and bring into the use of the marriage, or which accrue during the marriage from inheritances, and likewise all goods acquired by the industry of the spouses, even without dowry agreements, shall belong to the spouses by equal right; and on the death of one, half shall go to the heirs of the deceased, and the remainder shall remain with the survivor. Gifts between the living shall have force if the donor, while living, makes a surrender of his goods.

units.la: Quæ propter nuptias fiunt in pactis dotalibus, ut ratæ sint, in pacta dotalia hæredes proximi, imprimis parentes, avi, avia, fratres, sorores consentiunt. Minores xxv annis nuptias inire, & pacta dotalia scribere si volent, sub curatoribus aut tutoribus agentes, eos scribendo adhibento. Cædes, quæ prius pecuniâ luebantur, nunc ex lege capitis pœnam habent. Cæteris maleficiis omnibus graves quoque pœnæ sunt in legibus descriptæ. Hactenus de Agro seorsim: sequitur de Vrbe.
units.tr: What is given on account of the marriage in dowry agreements, in order to be valid, requires the consent of the nearest heirs, above all parents, grandparents, grandmother, brothers, sisters. Minors under twenty-five years of age, if they wish to enter marriage and draw up dowry agreements, shall act under curators or guardians, who must be present at the writing. Homicides, which formerly were atoned for with money, now carry the penalty of the capital law. For all other crimes, grave penalties are laid down in the laws. So much on the countryside separately; what follows concerns the city.
CONCERNING THE CITY OF GRONINGEN.

units.la: HUius situs sic habet. Decurrunt ex Drentiâ per Præfecturam suburbanam superiorem duo-amnes, quos dixi, Hunesus, & Aha, pariter ab Euronoto in circium euntes, non longo inter se spatio disjuncti, nonnunquam viii, nonnunquam vi, nonnullubi etiam iv tantùm stadiis, feruntúrque per humiles & uliginosos hinc inde agros. In quorum amnium medio ab ipsis humilibus agris, qui latiusculè ab amnium ripis se extendunt, dorsum paulatim se erigit editius, ac molli-
units.tr: Its situation is as follows. Through the upper suburban district there flow down from Drenthe the two rivers I mentioned, the Hunesus and the Aha. Both run from the south-east towards the north-west, separated from each other by no great distance, sometimes eight, sometimes six, and in some places only four stadia, and they wind through low and marshy fields on either side. Between these rivers, rising from the low fields themselves, which spread out fairly broadly from the banks of the rivers, a ridge gradually lifts itself to a greater height and rises gently-
