units.la: 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 Roeden ter declivè utrimque, à Drentiæ campis sublimibus ac spatiosis venièns, velut lingua exilis, sed longa, & sensim se versus finem coarctans, omnem ferè Præfecturam suburbanam percurrens. In ejus dorsi parte penè ultimâ, quâ amnium alter Aha ipsum dorsum propiùs accedens quasi stringit, posita Groninga est, arctior olim & in ipsissimo solùm dorso ædificata, deinde ampliata paulatim, & devexa ac humiliora utrinque largiùs complexa, loco perquàm felice, curribusque & navigiis ad importandum pariter commodo, segetibus & pascuis in ambitu inprimis fortunato. Dorsum autem illud modicè ad bina circiter stadia ultra urbem boream versùs procurrit, ibiqúe molliter se deponens in humilem & æquam planiciem definit, mediâ ferè inter urbem & cœnobium Selwerdicum viâ. Et amnis quidem Aha, ut nunc dudum res habuit, & habet, in angulo urbis, qui inter meridiem & occidentem prominet, mœnibus se insinuat per amplos fornices sub vallo structos, intraq; mœnia occiduo in latere urbem stringens longo tractu, ponte arcuati operis lateritii iunctus tandem in angulo altero occasum æstivum spectante per similes fornices vallo subiectos ex urbe rursum exit alveo profundo & capace multarum navium, ibique in ipso egressu amni alteri Hunefo ad urbem derivato, duobusque à lateribus ortivo & boreo mœnia foris complexo miscetur. Hunefus vero urbi allapsus in ipso orientis angulo, atque ibi muro transverso rejectus, ne ab austrino quoque latere mœnia circumveniat, & eâ parte etiam Ahæ urbem ingressuro se jungat, ortivo latere vallum radens, suburbium ejus loci insigne, duabus objectum portis ab ipsâ urbe secludit, eodemque modo longius progrediens, ac à septentrione in occidentem sensim se flectens tandem eo, quo dixi, loco sub ipsis mœnibus Ahæ confunditur.
units.tr: 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 rods, sloping down on both sides, coming from the high and spacious fields of Drenthe, like a slender but long tongue, gradually narrowing towards its end and running through almost the whole suburban district. Near the far end of this ridge, where the river Aha draws close to the crest and almost grips it, lies Groningen. It was once more confined and built only on the very top of the ridge, but it was afterwards gradually enlarged and embraced the lower, sloping ground on both sides more widely. It is a site exceedingly happy, convenient alike for carts and ships for bringing in goods, and especially fortunate in its surrounding grain fields and pastures. The ridge runs on moderately about two stadia beyond the city towards the north, and there, gently subsiding, it ends in a low and level plain, roughly midway between the city and the monastery of Selwerd by the road. The river Aha, as things have long been and still are, enters the walls at the corner of the city that projects between south and west, passing through wide arches built under the rampart. Inside the walls it runs along the western side of the city for a long stretch, is joined by a bridge of arched brickwork, and at the other corner, facing the north-west, it leaves the city again through similar arches under the rampart, in a deep channel capable of holding many ships. And just at its exit it mixes with the other river, the Hunesus, which has been diverted to the city and embraces the walls on the outside on two sides, the east and north. The Hunesus, having flowed into the city at the very eastern corner and been turned back there by a transverse wall, so that it does not also surround the walls on the southern side and so that it may join the Aha where that enters the city on that side as well, skirts the rampart on the eastern side. It shuts off from the city the famous suburb of that place, which is protected by two gates. Proceeding in the same way further on, and gradually bending from north to west, it finally mingles with the Aha at the place I mentioned, just below the walls.

units.la: V R B S ampla hodie, & spatiosa, ac publicis privatisque ædificiis magnifica, tum foris duobus. & munitionibus maximis superba. Ambitus mœnium ejus in exteriore fossæ labro passibus bis M. DC. XVIII patebat anno M. DC. V, cùm hæc priprimùm, ut in lucem exirent, scriberem, suburbiis exclusis. Postea formâ moenium in latere meridiano multùm mutata, & amplior, multoq; melior facta, cui similem haud facilè alibi hodiè reperias, sive fossam. rarae latitudinis & profunditatis spectes, sive vallum duplex, inferius scilicet, quod & exterius minusque, surgens ex ipso fossae labro, & interius, quod longè majus, & sublimius, cui alterum illud pro loricâ est, quae modico interstitio pedum xxviii interse distant: cui interstitio valli minoris latitudo parte ima fere respondet: altitudo verò ejusdem pedes ix. complectitur. Et nunc hoc, quo ista recognoscimus, ac novae editioni paramus, anno m. dc. xv, in opposito urbis latere longè magis formâ eâdem moenia ampliata, novaeque urbis area urbi veteri spatio cum eâ penè pari adjecta: eoque opere urbs tota multo quàm ante munitior, & contra hostilem vim tutior facta. Fossa hac parte moenia ambiens & profunda, & quâ aquae est Superficies, non minus quam clxx ped. lata est Fana nunc in eâ sunt in universum xii, ex quibus tria sunt parochialia, uti vocant, quinque monastica, quatuor xenodocheis conjuncta. Parochialium amplissimum cum editissima & firmissimi ac peregregij operis turri, quanquam fastigio jam mutila & trunca, Martinianum: Antiquissimum & cum urbe ipsa, aut ante urbem natum, ac, ut quidam putant, superstitioni Ethnicae quondam dicatum. Walburgicum, in eadem quadrata area, seu coemiterio spatioso, cum Martiniano, formae penè rotundae, ac plane diversae à formis templorum communium; cui etiam cohaeret sublimis fastigii turris: utrumque hoc in parte urbis inter orientem & boream proximè ad ipsa moenia, & Martinianum etiam in angulo fori majoris. Tertium in parte urbis in occidentem vergente, ab Aha amne cognominatum, quondam Nicolao, nunc Mariae virgini sacrum, (Vnser lieben Frouwen tho Alha) foro alteri accubans, cum visenda etiam turre altè faftigiata; in qua nolae complures egregio inter se soni temperamento, concentu harmonico horis singulis bellè præcinunt, easdemque in semisses dividunt, cum voluptate civium, & peregrinorum audientium. Et secundùm hæc tria templa tota civitas in tres fuit distincta parochias. Nunc Walburgica Martinianæ addita est, & ex tribus duæ fa-ctæ. Ex monasticis amplifsimum Franciscanum cum cœnobio spatioso in urbis ferè medio; quod cœnobium jam scholæ literariæ sedes est toti civitati communis: alterum Jacobæum cum cœnobio monachorum Dominicanorum in boreo urbis latere ad ipsa mœnia, breuissimo intervallo dissitum ab area, in qua Walburgicum & Martinianum: Tertium monachorum, quos Fratres nuncupabant, modicum, item cum cœnobio in angulo areæ ejusdem Walburgicæ boreo, ac in latere urbis eodem, mœnibus etiam contiguum; id cœnobium ante triginta circiter annos in sedem & aulam Knifiii primi & postremi Episcopi Groningani versum; deinde Gubernatoris provinciæ domicilium factum: quem usum etiam nunc præstat: quartum monialium sororum S. Claræ cum claustro item peramplo, spatio inter Francifcanos & Jacobæos medio: quintum virginum nobilium non initiatarum multo minus cum cohærente domicilio & ædicula familiæ Selwerdicæ, angusto tantum vico ab ædè Francifcana disjunctum ad boream. Ex xenodochicis fanis maximum, & parochici instar, ad S. Spiritum in latere civitatis austrino, cum xenodocheio peramplo, ac ad cœnobii iusti modum: secundum Gertrudis in oppidi parte ortiva juxta mœnia similiter, cum Xenodocheio benè dotato: tertium Iacobi modicum in extremo urbis angulo, qui est versus occasum æstivum, propè portam, quæ à machina tractoria, quam gruem vocant ex similitudine longi colli, nominatur: quartum Antoniani portæ orientali cohærens, omnium minimum: utrumque horum postremorum itidem cum xenodocheo, sed postremum angustum. Fora, ut dixi, in urbe duo insignia & spatiosa; alterum ex latitudine cognominatum (Dat Bzebe Market[?]) rarę magnitudinis, & vix alibi in civitate pari inveniendæ; incipiens ab area Martiniâna, & c. LXXIX passuum spatio inde in occidentem hybernum procurrens, latitudine paulò minore; intra cujus ambitum curia modica, cum œnopolio curiâ haud paulò majore cum turriculâ in vertice, contiguis parietibus: à quo trames perbrevis in alterum superiore etiam longius, Piscarium, quòd piscium illic mercatus sit, nuncupatum; in cujus fine area ac templum, quod dixi, parochiale tertium ab amne Ahâ nomen ferens. Id in longitudinem patet, si templi aream comprehenderis pass. CC. XLI, si non comprehenderis pass. c. XLIII. Ad hæc fora duo, quod mirêris, capita non minùs XVII platearum, & ferè amplissimarum in tota urbe pertinent: è quibus præcipuæ VI à totidem urbis portis [portæ autem sunt in universum VIII ) recta linea veniunt, Polana, Orientalis, Dominica, Pontana, Botterana, Ebbingana; eædem tota ferè urbe longissimæ, excepta Polana, quæ paulò est brevior: omnes suis portis cognomines, præter Pontanam, quæ à ponte Ahæ impositò ad Amnicam portam, unde procedit, nomen invenit. Caeterae duae portae plateas excipiunt etiam suas, sed per angulum à reliquis derivatas, quarum portarum altera à grue machina (Kraenpoorte[?]) altera ab attollendis lapidibus, ut vulgus arbitratur; ut autem veritas habet, à ponticulo lapideo, qui quondam isto in latere civitatis fuit, quem Germani Stetgentil[?] dicunt, (Stelgentilpoorte[?]) nomen ferunt. Plateae in urbe erant, cùm hæc primùm ederem, majores ad xxv I,[?] minores vii, præter angiportus aliquot. Majoribus accessit proximis his annis vicesima septima prorsus nova, ædificijs elegans, à fori majoris angulo, qui occidentem & boream intuetur, per medium hortum cœnobii Franciscani ducta, mittens in regionem, quæ ad amnem porrigitur, ex ipsâ re nova nominata. Minorum quoque numerus crevit. Antiquitus cùm minor esset civitatis fortuna, ut omnia solent à parvis principiis oriri, pro mœnibus usa est septo ligneo è trabibus contexto. Deinde ante annos plùs minùs cccc. I muro lateritio firmo cum fossâ in morem reliquarum urbium cincta fuit, angustiore etiam tum, quàm jam est, ambitu. Nunc ab eo fere tempore, quo tormentorum æneorum usus percrebuit, maximè verò à Caroli bellatoris Ducis Burgundiæ ævo, cùm is arma Frisiæ minaretur, vallo terreo cum fossâ patentiore ampliatis terminis est circumdata: cujus valli ambitus est, in summâ superficie, passuum IIM. LXXXVI, & in eo molæ, quæ ventis agitantur, XII; duæque præter has extra mœnia in latere septentrionali. Hac amplificatione mœnium postrema versus ortum, meridiem, occasum accessio urbi facta; solum latus boreum, abAhâ amne urbem egrediente, portaque vicina cum parte lateris ortivi ad portam usque Polanam, loco motum non est: atque ita Botterana quoque porta, & Ebbingana, & Polana sedem suam retinuêre; reliquæ, maximè Dominica, Orientalis, Steentullana, sunt promotæ. Ex portis his Polana pyramidibus excelsis ac magnæ molis duabus, Orientalis etiam quatuor sed gracilioribus, Dominica quinque similibus magnifica speciè specie longè lateque conspicuæ, decorem civitati non exiguum addidêre. Nunc duæ posteriores quondam contra Carolum Burgundum extructæ, altera à Casparo Roblesio gubernatore consultò anno M. D. LXXV, altera.tormentorum æneorum vi postremâ obsidione, quâ reducta ad fœderis Belgici societatem civitas est, anno M. D. XCIV, pyramidibus privatæ, totoque opere lateritio superiore dejecto humiliatæ sunt, ut jam supra vallum nihil earum appareat. Ad Dominicam verò Hispani ad initia belli hujus Belgici validam & amplam excitaverant arcem quinquangularem, singulis in angulis ingenti propugnaculo terreo instructam, partem mœnium, ipsamque portam complexam, quæ tamen arx antequam perfici posset, à transactione Gandavensi publicatâ, capto à militibus suis Casparo Roblesio gubernatore, per cives rursum eversa est. Omitto propugnacula è terrâ aggeratâ magnæ molis, quorum tria intra fossam vallum ambientem, vallo ipsi connexa, duo ad boream portas tegentia, tertium in austrinâ parte: quartum item, sed extra fossam, nec vallo contiguum, portæ Orientali objectum: adhæc alia duo ejusdem generis, vallo conjuncta sed minora: & præter ea ex lateribus structa VII, quædam turriculis fastigiata, quædam sine fastigijs: omnia muniendæ urbi contra vim hostilem instituta. Quinetiam durante hoc bello Belgico, suburbium, quod ante dixi, & ingens, & ædificiis non infrequens, à navicularijs habitatum, à quorum navigiis & amne nomen quoq; traxit [Schutendiep enim vulgò nuncupatur) duabus portis prætextum, Polanæ ac Steentillanæ, vallo terreo haud infirmo, & fossa benè profunda est incinctum, ut penè non minùs urbe ipsa tutum sitab hostili incursu & vi, ac quasi urbi adjectum. Cætera suburbia egregia, præsertim ante portas Dominicam, Botteranam, Amnicam belli injuris jam perière:quamquam ante Amnicam, vallum cum fossa, castelli in modum, ductum partem suburbii etiam nunc includat; portamque eandem protegat. Id verò suburbium, quod ante portam Dominicam fuit, longissimè procurrens cum pago proximo Helpenâ, qui vi i i stadiis non minus ab urbe recessit, continuâ domorum serie penè se conjunxit. Et præter suburbia hæc totoMeridionali & Septemtrionali latere in eodem dorso editiore, in quo urbs est sita, amœnis ac sumptuosis hortis, & ædificiis elegantibus totus post pomœria locus longè lateque obsitus ac contectus fuit. Taceo insulas virorum nobilium complures in Meridionali potissimùm plaga. Cuncta nunc per bellum vastata, vix pauca hic illic instaurata: in Borea verò plagâ urbis novæ mœnia illa magnifica ac firma, de quibus paulò antè dixi, excitata, sed nondum perfecta. Denique urbis situs in universum hujusmodi, ut quemadmodum per amnes, ac rivos, quos dixi, ex Amaso fl. ac Lavicæ ostio, ipsoque adeò mari, itemque ex agro circumjecto, majoribus minoribusque navigiis, sic per Drentiæ itinera nullo non anni tempore idonea, ex ipsa Drentia & cæteris circumjectis Germaniæ partibus rhedis ac curribus percommodè res omnes importati in eam, & rursum exportari possint. Tantò quidem ipsa etiam hinc felicior, quòd in omni agro in omnem mundi plagam circumfuso sola sine æmulis negotiationes possideat.
units.tr: The city today is large and spacious, magnificent in its public and private buildings, and proud of its two fora and its very strong fortifications. In the year 1605, when I first wrote these things for publication, the circuit of its walls, measured along the outer edge of the ditch, was 2,618 paces, not counting the suburbs. Since then the line of the walls on the south side has changed a good deal, becoming wider and much better built, so that you would hardly find anything like it elsewhere today. Whether you look at the ditch, which is unusually wide and deep, or at the double rampart, the lower and outer part rising from the very edge of the ditch and smaller, and the inner part, which is much larger and higher, with the other standing in front of it as a breastwork at a small interval of 28 feet, you will see it. The width of the lower rampart at its base roughly matches this interval, and its height is 9 feet. Now, in 1615, as I review these things and prepare them for the new edition, the walls have been extended in the same form on the opposite side of the city, and a new area has been added to the old city, nearly equal to it in size. By this work the whole city is much better fortified than before and safer against hostile force. The ditch that surrounds the walls on this side is deep, and where the water lies on the surface it is no less than 170 feet wide. There are now twelve temples in it altogether. Of these, three are parish churches, as they are called, five belong to monasteries, and four are joined to hospitals. Of the parish churches the largest, with its very high and most finely built tower, though now cut short and truncated at the top, is St Martin's. The oldest, which was either born with the city itself or before it, and which some think was once dedicated to heathen superstition, is that of St Walburga. It stands in the same square, or spacious churchyard, as St Martin's, and is almost round in shape, quite unlike the usual form of churches; a tall tower is attached to it. Both of these stand in the part of the city between east and north, very close to the walls itself, and St Martin's also stands at the corner of the great market. The third is in the part of the city that slopes towards the west; it takes its name from the river Aha, and was formerly sacred to St Nicholas but now to the Virgin Mary (Unser lieben Frouwen tho Alha). It lies beside the other market and has a tower, worth seeing, with a high spire; in it several bells, well tuned to one another in harmony, chime sweetly each hour and divide the hours into halves, to the delight of the citizens and of the strangers who hear them. According to these three churches the whole city was once divided into three parishes. Now St Walburga's has been joined to St Martin's, and the three have become two. Of the monastic churches, the largest is the Franciscan, with its spacious monastery in about the middle of the city; this monastery is now the seat of the literary school, common to the whole city. The second is the St James church with the monastery of the Dominican friars, on the north side of the city, right by the walls, at a very short distance from the square in which St Walburga's and St Martin's stand. The third is a small one of the friars whom they called Brothers, also with its monastery, at the north corner of the same St Walburga square, on the same side of the city, likewise adjoining the walls. About thirty years ago this monastery was turned into the residence and hall of Knyphausen, the first and last bishop of Groningen, and afterwards it became the house of the governor of the province, which use it still serves. The fourth is that of the nuns of St Clare, with a very large cloister, in the space between the Franciscans and the St James church. The fifth is that of the noble virgins who were not professed, much less so the house and little chapel of the Selwerd family, lying to the north, separated from the Franciscan church only by a narrow lane. Of the hospital churches the largest, which is like a parish church, is that of the Holy Spirit on the south side of the city, with a very large hospital built in the manner of a full monastery. The second, that of St Gertrude, in the eastern part of the town, likewise beside the walls, has a well-endowed hospital. The third, a small church of St James, is at the farthest corner of the city, which is towards the summer setting sun, near the gate named after the hoisting machine that they call a crane, from the likeness of its long neck. The fourth, that of St Anthony, is the smallest of all, joined to the east gate; both of these last two also have a hospital, but the last one is narrow. As I said, there are two notable and spacious fora in the city. One is named after its breadth (Dat Bzebe, Market[?]); it is of unusual size and can hardly be matched anywhere else in the city. It begins at St Martin's square and runs from there towards the west-south-west for 179 paces, a little narrower in breadth. Within its circuit stand a modest town hall and a much larger weigh-house with a small turret on top, their walls touching. From it a very short street leads to the other market, which lies further on, and which is called Piscarium because the fish market was held there. At its end are the square and the third parish church, which I mentioned, bearing its name from the river Aha. This square is 241 paces long if you include the churchyard, or 143 paces if you do not. Beyond these two markets, and this is remarkable, the heads of no fewer than seventeen streets, some of them very wide, run into the whole city. Of these, six main streets run in straight lines from as many city gates (there are eight gates altogether): Polana, East, Dominica, Pontana, Botterana, and Ebbinga. These are almost the longest in the whole city, except Polana, which is a little shorter. All take their names from their gates, except the Pontana, which takes its name from the bridge over the Aha, laid at the point where it leads out to the river gate. The other two gates have their own streets too, but these are branches that run off at an angle from the rest. One of these gates takes its name from the crane machine (Kraenpoorte[?]), and the other, as the common people think, from the lifting of stones; but in truth it takes its name from a small stone bridge that once stood on this side of the city, which the Germans call Stetgentil [?] (Stelgentilpoorte[?]). When I first published these things there were about 26 larger streets in the city, and seven smaller ones, apart from several alleys. In recent years a twenty-seventh large street has been added to the larger ones, entirely new and elegantly built. It runs from the corner of the great market, which faces west and north, through the middle of the garden of the Franciscan monastery, and leads into the district that stretches to the river; it is named Nova (New) from this very fact. The number of the smaller streets has also grown. In former times, when the city's fortunes were smaller, as everything usually begins from small beginnings, it used as its walls a wooden fence built of beams. Then, about 400 years ago, it was enclosed with a firm brick wall and a ditch, in the manner of the other cities, though at that time its circuit was narrower than it is now. Since about the time when the use of bronze cannon became common, and especially in the age of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, when he threatened the Frisian lands with arms, it has been surrounded with an earthen rampart and a wider ditch, and its boundaries have been enlarged. The circuit of this rampart, measured along its top surface, is 2,086 paces, and on it there are twelve windmills driven by the winds, and two more outside the walls on the north side. By this enlargement of the walls, a new addition was made to the city on its east, south and west sides; the north side, where the river Aha leaves the city, and the gate near it with the east side as far as Polana gate, were not moved; and so the Botterana and Ebbinga gates and Polana kept their places. The others, especially Dominica, East, and Steentullana, were moved outward. Of these gates, Polana was adorned with two high pyramids of great mass, East with four, but more slender, and Dominica with five of similar appearance; they were splendid and visible far and wide, and added no small beauty to the city. Now the two latter gates, built long ago against Charles of Burgundy, one of them deliberately by the governor Caspar Robles in 1575, the other by the force of bronze cannon in the last siege of 1594, by which the city was brought back into the alliance of the Belgic union, have been stripped of their pyramids and lowered, with all the upper brickwork thrown down, so that none of them now appears above the rampart. Near the Dominica gate, at the start of this Belgic war, the Spaniards had raised a strong and large five-cornered fortress, equipped at each corner with a huge earthen bulwark, which enclosed part of the walls and the gate itself; but before it could be completed, after the Pacification of Ghent was published and the governor Caspar Robles had been seized by his own soldiers, it was torn down again by the citizens. I omit the large earthworks: three of them inside the ditch, joined to the rampart that surrounds the city, two covering the northern gates, and a third on the southern side; a fourth, likewise outside the ditch and not touching the rampart, lies in front of the East gate; besides these, two more of the same kind, joined to the rampart but smaller; and in addition seven built of brick, some crowned with small turrets, some without tops, all set up to fortify the city against hostile force. Moreover, during this Belgic war the suburb, which I mentioned before, large and not thinly built with houses, inhabited by boatmen, from whose boats and the river it also took its name (for it is commonly called Schutendiep), is protected by two gates, Polana and Steentullana, and is enclosed by an earthen rampart of no little strength and a fairly deep ditch, so that it is almost no less safe from hostile attack and force than the city itself, and seems joined to it. The other fine suburbs, especially those in front of the Dominica, Botterana and river gates, have already perished in the injuries of war; although in front of the river gate a rampart with a ditch, built in the manner of a castle, still encloses a part of the suburb even now and protects that gate. The suburb that lay before the Dominica gate ran out very far, and together with the nearby village of Helpen, which lies not less than eight stadia from the city, it nearly joined with it in an unbroken row of houses. Besides these suburbs, the whole place behind the city walls, on the southern and northern sides, on the same higher ridge on which the city stands, was widely and thickly covered and clothed with pleasant and costly gardens and elegant buildings. I say nothing of the several islands belonging to noble men, chiefly on the southern side. All these things have now been laid waste by war, and only a few have been restored here and there. On the northern side of the city, however, that new, magnificent and strong wall, of which I spoke a little before, has been raised but is not yet finished. Finally, the situation of the city is, in general, such that just as goods can be brought in and carried out again by larger and smaller boats through the rivers and streams I mentioned, from the Amasus and the mouth of the Lauwers, and indeed from the sea itself, and likewise from the surrounding countryside, so too by the roads of Drenthe, which are suitable at every season of the year, all goods can very conveniently be brought in from Drenthe itself and the other neighbouring parts of Germany by wagons and carts, and again exported. It is all the more fortunate in this respect, because in the whole countryside that surrounds it, on every side of the world, it alone holds the trade without rivals.

units.la: De antiquitatibus ejus primis, & de origine quæ vulgò feruntur, incerta sunt, pleraque etiam indubiè fabulosa, ac inepta: qualia sunt, quæ nugator Kempius memorat. Nomen à viridibus pratis aut arboretis, quæ sunt circùm circa, videri potest deductum; cum quo convenerit Græcum φυλλέιον[?] (si recta hæc lectio) veteribus circiter hæc loca collocatum. Melius forte à Gruno aut Gryno principe vel conditore loci, non illo quidem Trojano, aut Frisonis nepote originis Indicæ (nugæ enim istæ sunt aniles) sed homine Frisio: Quo cum congruere videtur forma vocabuli, quo Frisii & olim & hodiè tám Occidui quàm Orientales appellare hanc civitatem solent, Groninse[?] aut Groense[?] eam vocantes. Est autem frequens in totâ hac vicinià, derivata nomina hujusmodi à propriis hominum, aut fluminum, aut aliarum rerum similium nominibus in fuit, longissimè procurrens cum pago proximo Helpenâ, qui v i i r stadiis non minùs ab urbe receßit, continuâ domorum serie penè se conjunxit. Et præter suburbia hæc totoMeridionali & Septemtrionali latere in eodem dorso editiore, in quo urbs est sita, amœnis ac sumptuôsis hortis, & ædificiis elegantibus totus post pomœria locus longè lateque obsitus ac contectus fuit. Taceo insulas virorum nobilium complures in Meridionali potissimúm plaga. Cuncta nunc per bellum vastata, vix pauca hic illic instaurata: in Borea verò plagâ urbis novæ mœnia illa magnifica ac firma, de quibus paulò antè dixi, excitata, sed nondum perfecta. Denique urbis situs in universum hujusmodi, ut quemadmodum per amnes, ac rivos, quos dixi, ex Amaso fl. ac Lavicæ ostio, ipsoque adeò mari, itemque ex agro circumjecto, majoribus minoribusque navigijs, sic per Drentiæ itinera nullo non anni tempore idonea, ex ipsâ Drentia & cæteris circumjectis Germaniæ partibus rhedis ac curribus percommodè res omnes importati in eam, & rursum exportari possint. Tantò quidem ipsa etiam hinc felicior, quòd in omni agro in omnem mundi plagam circumfuso sola sine æmulis negotiationes possideat.
units.tr: The early antiquities of the city and the origins commonly reported are uncertain, and most of them are plainly fabulous and silly, such as those which the trifler Kempius relates. The name may seem to be derived from the green meadows or groves that surround it. The Greek word phylleion [φυλλέιον] agrees with this, if that is the correct reading, and it was placed near these places by the ancients. Perhaps it comes better from Gruno or Gryno, a prince or founder of the place. This was not the Trojan of that story, nor a grandson of Frisius of Indian origin (for those are old wives' tales), but a Frisian man. The form of the word agrees with this, since the Frisians, both western and eastern, have long and still commonly called this city Groninse or Groense. Throughout this whole neighbourhood, names of this kind are commonly derived from the proper names of men, rivers, or other similar things, and they end in Inge: Hunsinge, Fivelinge, Ostringe, Rustringe, Harlinge, Husinge, Esinge, Wetzinge, Thezinge, Thedinge, Appinge, Cortinge, Iemminge, Pauvinge, Baltringe, Schuringe, Mackinge, Mitlinge, Tinaldinge, and in the city itself Ebbinge, Botteringe, Harderinge, Folkeringe, Gaddinge, Gelkinge. I pass over the countless other patronymics with the same ending in Friesland and Drenthe.

units.la: PRIMAM sub hoc nomine mentionem ejus in probatis & fidis literarum monumentis (nam de tabulæ Romanæ ætate ac fide cur dubitem, demonstratum à me alibi est) usurpatam invenio in instrumento quodam donationis, quod est in tablino Ecclesiæ Ultrajectinæ, scripto & signato anno Christi M. XL: quo in instrumento Henricus III Imperator, cognomento Niger, filius Conradi II Salici, eidem Ecclesiæ tempore Bernoldi præsulis confert jus prædij, quod ipse in villà GRONINGA videbatur possidere. Quâ de donatione pauca dicam, ut & antiquitatem & veritatem in hac re illustrem. Cùm Normanni vastatores totius tractus maritimi Ultrajectum quoque occupassent, sacraque & profana illic diripuissent, cuncta ferro & flammâ pessum dedissent, successoresque Hungeri, qui manus vastatorum vix sugiens evaserat, Daventriæ domicilium ac sedem collocassent, tandem Baldericus è Comitibus Cliviæ prognatus, quintus post Hungerum episcopus, primùm per se vivente adhuc Henrico Aucupe Rege, sed parvo profectu, dein benevolentia & liberalitate Ottonis Imperatoris, & fratris ejus Brunonis, quos ipse in bonis literis erudierat, adjutus eandem urbem instaurare, ac sedem ibidem figere rursum cœpit. Sed exoleverant ferè Episcopatus jura, quæ ex liberalitate priorum Principum ei fuerant collata, amissis unà cum usu ac possessione donationum haud paucis literis; vicinaque Nobilitas, ceu fieri solet, pleraque vacantia invaserat. Itaque instauratis donationibus ad restituendam Episcopatus fortunam fuit opus. Quod inchoatum à Conrado Franco Imperatore, mox ab Henrico Aucupe promotum; ab Ottone I factum multò uberrimè, novaque beneficia ab eo prioribus addita. In his & venationum jus in Comitatu Everhardi in pago Drentiæ fuit; quod cum ex procerum vicinorum ordine nonnulli invito Episcopo usurparent, & traherent ad se, ab Imperatore soli Episcopo, & cui ille permitteret, est tributum, cum annus flueret à nato Christo D. CCCC. XLIV. Idem repetitum ac firmatum ab Henrico II, cui Claudi cognomen, in gratiam Aufridi, anno M. VI. Et ab eodem Comitatus ipse Drentiæ (sic loquuntur tabulæ) Ecclesiæ eidem in gratiam Adelboldi præsulis donatus in perpetuum: eoq; modo imperium regionis hujus in genere, uti ego existimo, juris Ultrajectini factum. Post mortuo Conrado II. Imperatore, cujus ipsius quoq; animus Ultrajectinæ sedi ob episcopum Bernoldum & studio conjugis Giselæ impensè deditus fuerat, cum filius ejus Henricus III, cognomento Niger, intestina defuncti parentis in æde Martiniana ibidem condidisset, donationibus novis priores cumulavit: in quarum una est ea, quam dixi, Groningæ hujus nostræ memoria celebrata. Sic enim illic scriptum, Henricum Regem ecclesiæ Ultrajectinæ in ho-norem Martini structæ, in remedium animæ patris, & sui memoriam perpetuam, præsule tum Bernoldo, concedere & donare tale prædium, quale in villâ GRONINGA nuncupata videbatur tenere, situm in Comitatu Drentiæ, cum areis, ædificiis, mancipiis agris cultis & incultis, pratis, campis, pascuis, aquis, aquarumve decursibus, piscationibus, viis, inviis, exitibus & reditibus, quæsitis & inquirendis, cum omni ejusdem Comitatus strictione, monetis, teloneis, causis agendis, & discutiendis, cum omnibus appendiciis & pertinentiis, quæ ad præsens retineri videntur, aut quicquid in posterum ibi Deo adjuvante acquiri poterit: eo videlicet tenore, ut supradictum prædium perpetuo respondeat servitio & utilitati fratrum ibi Deo servientium incessabiliter: scilicet ut ex ejusdem prædii utilitate quotannis habeant xxx carradas vini; reliquum vero ex prædio proveniens à Præposito in usum eorundem exponatur fideliter; nec liceat quicquam ejus in usus alios conferre, priusquam id quod jam dictum est vinarium tributum fuerit solutum. Quæ verba apud posteros aliter atque aliter accepta, diversas & dissidentes sententias peperêre. Quidam sic acceperê, quasi villa aut civitas Groninga (id enim sine dubio unum & idem) in Comitatu Drentiae dicatur sita, eademque cum omni jure & annexis donata sit his tabulis ecclesiae Vltrajectinae, velut Drentiae membrum. In quorum numero multi fuêre episcopi hujus sedis, & canonici plerique, & eorum ministri, propterea quòd suis rebus eam interpretationem commodam esse arbitrabantur. Fuêre etiam non pauci nostri temporis, qui litis ergô, quam cum civitate habebant, ut se ab eâ sejungerent, è finibus Frisiae hodiernae eam exterminare voluerunt. Alii contrà in alia omnia euntes, & longè quidem rectius judicio meo. Nec enim dici in tabulis regiis, Groningam in Drentiâ sitam, aut ipsam ecclesiae Vltrajectinae donatam, sed praedium, quod Rex videbatur in villâ Groningâ tenere, & id situm in Comitatu Drentiae esse, & dono ecclesiae ei datum, esseque verba Regis donantis in istam sententiam planissima. Id vero praedium Præfecturam suburbanam esse volunt, Dat Ghyo vnd Woltrecht / ut appellavit posteritas, aut certè maximam hujus partem, quam ego jam ante ostendi partim se Drentiæ, partim Frisiæ contiguæ debere: Eam quippe à primâ usque memoriâ ex oppido Groningâ, tanquam præfecti sede, quem dare Vltrajectini solent, fuisse administratum: atque hoc Regem voluisse, cum scriberet, prædium illud in Drentiæ quidem (comitatu situm, in villâ tamen Groningâ se tenere. Atque hæc interpretatio vel eò mihi videtur verosimilior, imò verior, quòd idem Rex eodem anno, adeoque eodem illo die, quo dedit has, (si me antigrapha, quæ vidi, non fallunt: is est dies XII Calend. Iunii) binas quoque tabulas alias signavit, quarum alteris prædia etiam alia in eodem Drentiæ Comitatu posita, in alteris rursum alia in (comitatu Radulfi, & quicquid de iis inter Amasso & Lavefco, id est, inter Amasum & Lavicam locatum, quæ omnia Vffonis & fratrum ejus, hominum nocentium, justo judicio damnatorum prius fuerint, huic eidem sedi Vltrajectinæ eodem modo cum areis, ædificiis, mancipiis, agris, pratis, campis, pascuis, aquis, piscationibus, viis, inviis, exitibus, rediti-bus, bus, cætcrisque priùs recitatis, dono obtulit. Sic enim sentio, has partes omnes trinis his tabulis ab Henrico donatas coaluisse paulatim in unam Præfecturam, quam Gho[?] & Woltrecht nuncupamus, earumque tribunalis sedem in urbe esse collocatam. De Comitatu verò in eâdem Drentiâ, qui Gozelonis Lotharingiæ Ducis (is est, qui in Frisiâ & Hollandiâ res gessit, & imperium aliquandiu tenuit) & altero Vmbalaha dicto[?], qui Comitis Enobardi fuisse perhibentur, & non tam Ecclesiæ, quàm Episcopo ab eodem Rege aliquot annis post donati sunt,ἐπιχω[?]. At hoc ex his omnibus, & compluribus aliis eorum temporum tabulis disco. tum morem suisse, ut Pagus maius aliquid significaret quàm Comitatus, pluresque Comitatus Pago uno, ac prædia plura uno Comitatu comprehenderentur: ita unam eandemque Drentiam, item Tuentiam, item speciales Frisiæ regiones in plures tunc fuisse Comitatus distinctas. Quod in Frisiâ potissimum hæsit diutiusculè, uti est à me alibi demonstratum. Dicebaturque Comes vulgò in his oris, qui ab Imperatore vel Rege jurisdictionem summam in Comitatu aliquo, id est, in dioecesi habebat cum imperio. Sed de sententiarum discrepantia quod dixi, id lectores dijudicanto: ego, quamquam quid sentiam, exposuerim, me tamen judicem controversiæ non interpono. Episcopi certè plerique, qui proximis sæculis secuti sunt, id quod antè etiam notatum à me est, in rem suam, ecclesiæque suæ verba diplomatis traxêre, jùsque in oppidum, prætoriumque in oppido imperium haud minùs quàm Præfecturam suburbanam, quæ eorum sine controversiâ erat, sibi vendicarunt. Et tenuerunt quidem id diu, sed non sine tumultibus crebris ac difficilibus ex hoc fonte enatis, adeò ut armis arma sæpè concurrerint, sæpè castra in oppido castris opposita, bellumque intra mœnia gestum sit. Populus enim ad libertatem respiciens, aut libidini præfectorum, quos in urbe Episcopi habebant, obviam ibat, aut Episcoporum imperium indies latius tendens recusabat. De quibus omnibus prolixè à me in Historiâ est dictum. Attamen prævaluit Episcoporum vis & potentia, quæ magna tum fuit, succincta etiam autoritate sacrosanctâ, & religionis opinione, tenuibus verò adhuc oppidi rebus. Quæ res si tantæ tunc fuissent, quantæ pòst factæ sunt, non minùs hîc quàm in Oftergoâ & Weftergoâ, in quas diplomata similia ab Henrico IV Cæsare impetrata extitêre, eadem ambitio & avaritia episcopalis operam perdidisset. Sic verò observatum de his porrò invenio, vestigia rerum in monumentis sequens, clerum Vltrajectinum in initio præfectum Territorio suburbano dedisse, quem vellet, & in annos, quot vellet; eumque præfectum in urbe sedem & tribunal habuisse: huic simul & prætorium munus gerendum in urbe, & nomen præfecti urbani imposuisse ipsum Episcopum, eumque Sculthesium summum iudicii ministrum, ceu legatum suum, constituisse: mox Præfecturam utramque in seudum perpetuum esse versam: feudum rursum post aliquot sæcula in emphyteuseos conditionem, aut emphyteusi similem commutatum: in feudi possessione fuisse per aliquot ætates Gronenbergios, Supperachios, rursum Gronenbergios, Gronenbekios, Selwerdios, familias nobiles, interdum conjunctim, interdum divisim. Post, cùm ad Coverdios hæreditas Selwerdiorum transisset cum Idâ hærede unicâ atque ultimâ domus istius, Hermanno Coverdio denuptâ, emphyteusis inducta est; jure an injuria, nescio. Emphyteutæ facti Ioannes & Reinoldus Coverdii cum singulis filiis, & Goverdus Hovius anno Christi M. CCC, LXXI, mortuo paulo ante episcopo Ioanne Vernenburgio: lex his dicta, ut emphy-teusis duraret ad tempus vitæ ipsorum. Verùm ut suburbanus præfectus limitibus arctis finitum imperium in plebem rusticam habebat, nec causas cognoscebat, aut sententias ferebat sine collegio judicum, quos plebs ei assessores dabat, plebsque in cæteris libertate fruebatur suâ; sic prætoria potestas in urbe collata ab episcopo jurifdictionem senatus, & imperium ejusdem, ut falsò quidam credunt, non tollebat. Nam senatus pacta sæpè iniit cum vicinis, quo tempore præfecti in urbe erant, quæ sine imperio & jurisdictione haudquaquam locum habere poterant, & de foro in urbe agendo, cognoscendisque controversiis fœdera habuerunt: denique publicæ tabulæ testes sunt, quondam anno à Christi natali M. CC. LXXXIII, cùm præfecti Gronenbergii essent, & forte è Selwerdicâ domo nobili duo criminis publici facti fuissent rei, quæsitum in conventu fuisse, ab Hunesgoniis, an civitate Groninganâ, an denique ab Egberto Gronenbergio, ut Territorii suburbani præfecto, propterea quòd ubi horum omnium fines concurrebant, arx Selwerdia sedem haberet, viderentur judicandi: & cùm ipsis reis permissum esset, ut ex his tribus, quem vellent judicem sibi esse in perpetuum, eligerent, hos Egbertum cum successoribus ejus elegisse. Quibus omnibus locus esse nullo potuisset modo, si judicandi potestatem cum imperio nullam senatus tenuisset. Ad hæc, quamquam præfecto, munerique ejus locum daret, apud se, tamen Episcopi imperium in sese agnoscere, sive ut principi suo aut domino jusjurandum dare, paremque cum ceteris dioeceseos[?] civitatibus conditionem ac legem subirecivitas hæc nostra multo tempore recusavit. Nec exemplis destituebatur aliarum civitatum liberarum, quæ & præsectos hujuscemodi à vicinis reciperent Principibus, & tamen iisdem jurejurando, ut subditæ, se non obligarent. Et cum ipsa in Frisiæ solo,ac Frisici juris esset, relictâ libertate gentis alienigenis dominis se subijcere tergiversabatur. Et quamvis mussarent sæpèEpiscopi,præsertim si qui ingeniis erant ambitiosis, tamen ad vim descendere ob hanc causam ausi non sunt. Nam creverant jam opes civitatis, & fœderum pactis de tuendâ libertate cum vicinis firmabantur. Accedebat, quòd in societatem fœderis Anseatici, cujus tum & magnum robur, & non vilis autoritas, & prompta auxilia erant, civitas jamdudum esset cooptata, nec abjectam conditionem in sociarum civitatum ordine teneret. Quæ cum sic haberent, quamquam Florentius episcopus, familiâ Wevelichovius, vir sapiens & industrius, à Wenceslao Cæsare diploma obtinuisset signatum anno M. CCC. LXXXII, ipsis Calend. Maij, quo diplomate copia ei fiebat repetendi ac recuperandi omnia,quæ incurià antecessorum ipsius, aut quovis modo ab Episcopatu defluxerant, eoque fretus haud segniter res suas curaret, tamen Groningam lacessere armis, aut iniquis urgere postulatis veritus fuit. Demùm, cùm cætera desperaret, per collegium suum ( nam factum hoc vivente adhuc ipso deprehendo, etsi cùm Historiam primò scriberem, secus opinarer ) alio modo sub beneficii specie obligandam sibi aut Ecclesiæ suæ civitatem putavit. Anno enim M. CCC. XCII, qui penultimus vitæ ejus fuit, Collegium summum, cui proprië donatum fuisse prædium illud ab Henrico Rege ostendi, autore hortatoreque ipso, licet pacta cum Coverdiis haberet, tamen posthabitis his, omne jus suum, quod ex Henrici donatione profluebat, sive id in urbe, sive extra urbem esset, certâ lege civitati tradidit. Lex hæc fuit, ut civitas jus & jurisdictionem ipsam à collegio teneret in annos proximos centum, eoq; nomine eidem collegio solveret quotannis canonem scutatorum Francicorum veterum LXXXIII cum dimidios[?] dio, loco & tempore certo; & præter canonem hunc vigesimo quoque anno honorarium munus septem marcarum argenti puri offerret Ultrajecti: exciperentur census, reditus, decimæ & res hereditariæ, qui quæve canonicorum erant in territorio hoc eodem, ex quibus pactione hac nihil iis decederet: Exactis vero centum annis, ut eadem hæc omnia valerent in annos centum alios; si vellet civitas in pactorum fide manens, & ejus rei gratia marcas argenti puri i. ante Calendas Septembris collegio eidem Ultrajecti offerret, novasq; pactionis literas iisdem his verbis scriptas posceret, daretq;: & rursum, his quoque annis finitis, repeterentur eodem modo ac lege omnia; idemq; extenderetur in perpetuum. Cautum tamen duobus Hoviis cum matre ad tempus vitæ ipsorum, quorum triens totius hujus juris ex pacto priore fuerat. Ita civitas Groninga sine controversia, ut ipsa rebatur, undequaque jam libera, ac sui juris facta, & imperio quoque Territorij suburbani aucta, canonis tantulli onus ne sentiens quidem, Episcopi modo honorem ac dignitatem, ut patroni, comiter agnoscens. Sed Frideficus Blanchenhemius in locum Florentij suffectus episcopus, vir ambitiosissimi & inquietissimi ingenii, quamquam per literas solennes fidem civitati dedisset initio regiminis sui, omnia se ei jura ac privilegia conservaturum, pacta cum suis inita rata habiturum, patronum & protectorem ejus ubique ex æquo & bono futurum, aliaque facturum hujusmodi, rursumque à quadriennio peramicè cum eâ convenisset, cùm metus & periculum ab armis Hollandicis urgerent, tamen paulò post, periculo eo metuq; amoto, cùm videret recenti bello externo pariter, ac sociali fessam civitatem, commodum id ratus cupidini suæ, callidissimo consilio novis eam armis domi implicuit. Primùm enim pro exulibus, capitalibus civitatis inimicis, intercessorem se ingessit: mox non impetrata re, quasi supplicibus deesse non posset, simul aliis quoque causis, quas cupido suggerebat, prætextis, bellum movit. Eo moto, quod futurum prævidebat, canonis annui ex pacto Canonicis debiti solutio est impedita. Ita rescindendæ pactionis color aliquis repertus. Inter causas alias hanc jactabat praecipue, quòd civitas imperium omne, quod quoquo modo ex Henrici Imp. dono profluxisse videri poterat, redemisse se pactione nuper censebat, Episcopus autem ad urbanam Praesecturam pactionem non pertinere contendebat, praefecturamque ajebat ab antecessoribus suis dari solitum, à se quoque dari oportere. Nec ante destitit armis civitatem premere, omnia circum circà infesta ei facere, majora minitari, quàm ad dictatas conditiones descendere eam compulisset. Conditiones hæ fuêre. Exules ad sua, ut tum erant, redirent, nec actiones de damno haberent: Canon quinquennio non solutus collegio ob bellum, statim solveretur: Civitas Episcopo jus Praefecturae suburbanae cederet; is praefectum pro arbitrio daret, qui sedem & tribunal haberet in urbe; id est, ut verbo dicam, pactio prior cum collegio esset irrita. Id pridie Michaelis anni M. cccc. v. confectum. Triduo post, de urbano jure sic porrò transfactum: Civitas Groninga e numero civium suorum Sculthetium[?], id est, praefectum ederet quem vellet, munus ei abrogaret, successorem daret, continuaret, quando, quoties, quandiu placeret: editus verò, successorvé datus apud præfectum subvrbanum Episcopi ministrum juraret: juramenti summa hæc esset, JUS ET JUSTITIAM SE ADMINISTRATURUM OMNIBUS INTEGRE ATQUE INCORRUPTE, SECUNDUM MOREM FORI ISTIUS: præfectofubvrbano ultra triduum tergiversante, consuli potestas esset hoc juramentum ab eo recipere eâdem verborum formâ. Pro hoc jure civitas quotannis aureos scutatos Francicos XXVIII penderet Episcopo ipsi Vltrajecti, & vigesimo quoquo anno marcas duas argenti puri cum marcâ triente præfecto Coverdio Coverdia: utrumque ante exitum Octobris: Et hæc pactio vim haberet in annos C. quibus finitis, si civitas ante exitum ejusdem Octobris offerret Episcopo marcas argenti similis XVI, & trientem marcarum duarum, peteretq; ejusdem juris & pacti continuationem, eadem omnia valerent in annos totidem: & ab eorum sine rursum repetitis ijsdem, & pactis purè servatis in annos totidem alios atque alios: idq; extenderetur in perpetuum, nec liceret episcopis abnuere. Sic Episcopi cupidini iniquæ utcunque tum, satis factum belloque finis impositus. Sed ne hic quidem stetit hominis istius immensa ambitio: quinimò cum successu rerum progrediens longius, eò demum rem redegit, ut civitas eadem omnibus vexata incommodis fessaque, quietis ac pacis causa coacta demum fit, ipsi velut domino fidelitatis juramentum dicere, & eandem conditionem parendi cum cæteris civitatibus maioribus dioecesèos Vltrajecto, Daventriâ, Campis, Suollis subire, ac subditam se, membrumq; dioecesèos profiteri, reliquo tamen jure omni incolumi, & salvis, quæ cum vicinis habebat, fœderibus. Factum hoc anno post Christum ex Virgine natum M. CCCC. XIX. Ab hoc autem tempore pax & concordia inconcussa civitati cum Episcopis & dioecesanis stetit, resque in eodem hoc statu mansit, quem iam exposui, ad Davidem usque Burgundum. Hic Vltrajectinis rebus potitus, anno Christi M. CCCC. LX, cùm pecuniæ egeret, acceptis à civitate nostrâ mutuò aureis Rhenanis M. DC, restituit illi suburbanæ Præfecturæ jus ac imperium ad tempus vitæ
units.tr: The first mention of it under this name that I find in trustworthy and reliable written records (for why I should doubt the age and authenticity of the Roman tablet I have shown elsewhere) is in a certain deed of gift, which is in the archive of the Church of Utrecht, written and sealed in the year of Christ 1040. In this deed Henry III, the emperor, surnamed the Black, son of Conrad II the Salian, grants to the same Church, in the time of Bishop Bernold, the right to an estate which he himself seemed to possess in the village of GRONINGEN. I shall say a few words about this gift, so that both its antiquity and its truth may be made clear in this matter. When the Normans, plunderers of the whole maritime region, had also seized Utrecht, plundered both sacred and profane things there, and destroyed everything with fire and sword, and when the successors of Hungerus, who had barely escaped the hands of the plunderers, had established their residence and seat at Deventer, at last Baldric, born of the counts of Cleves, the fifth bishop after Hungerus, first by himself, while King Henry the Fowler was still living, but with little success, and then aided by the goodwill and generosity of the emperor Otto and of his brother Bruno, whom he himself had taught in good letters, began again to restore the same city and to fix his seat there once more. But the rights of the bishopric, which had been granted to it by the generosity of earlier princes, had almost fallen into disuse, since many documents had been lost along with the use and possession of the gifts; and the neighbouring nobility, as usually happens, had seized most of the vacant property. Therefore, the gifts having been renewed, there was need to restore the fortunes of the bishopric. This was begun by Conrad the Frank, the emperor, then advanced by Henry the Fowler, and very richly completed by Otto I, who added new benefits to the earlier ones. Among these was the right of hunting in the county of Everhard in the district of Drenthe; and since some of the neighbouring nobles, against the bishop's will, were seizing this right and drawing it to themselves, it was granted by the emperor to the bishop alone, and to whomever he might permit, in the year 944 from the birth of Christ. The same was repeated and confirmed by Henry II, surnamed the Lame, in 1006, in favour of Aufrid. And by the same man the county itself of Drenthe (so the records speak) was given in perpetuity to the same Church, in favour of Bishop Adelbold; and in this way, as I think, the rule of this region in general became a right of the Church of Utrecht. After the death of the emperor Conrad II, whose own mind also had been greatly devoted to the see of Utrecht on account of Bishop Bernold and through the zeal of his wife Gisela, his son Henry III, surnamed the Black, having buried his deceased father's remains in the church of St Martin there, increased the earlier gifts with new ones. Among these is the one I mentioned, celebrated in the memory of this Groningen of ours. For it is written there: King Henry grants and gives to the Church of Utrecht, built in honour of Martin, for the remedy of his father's soul and for the perpetual memory of himself, Bernold then being bishop, such an estate as he seemed to hold in the village called Groningen, situated in the county of Drenthe, with areas, buildings, slaves, cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, plains, pastures, waters and watercourses, fisheries, roads, wastelands, exits and returns, things acquired and to be acquired, with the full jurisdiction of the same county, coinage, tolls, the conduct and hearing of cases, with all appurtenances and pertinences which are seen to be retained at present, or whatever in future may by God's help be acquired there: on this condition, namely, that the aforesaid estate shall answer perpetually and unceasingly to the service and advantage of the brothers serving God there; so that from the profit of the same estate they may have thirty carts of wine each year; and that the remainder arising from the estate be faithfully expended by the provost for their use; and that it be not lawful to apply any part of it to other uses before the wine tribute just mentioned has been paid. These words, understood differently by later generations, produced different and conflicting opinions. Some have understood them as if the village or city of Groningen (for these are without doubt one and the same) is said to lie in the county of Drenthe, and that the same, with all rights and appurtenances, was granted by these records to the Church of Utrecht, as a member of Drenthe. Among these were many bishops of this see, and most of the canons, and their ministers, because they judged this interpretation convenient for their own affairs. There were also not a few in our own time who, for the sake of the lawsuit they had with the city, wished to cast it out of the borders of present-day Friesland so that they might separate themselves from it. Others, going in the opposite direction, took all the rest, and far more rightly in my judgement. For it is not said in the royal records that Groningen lies in Drenthe, or that it was itself given to the Church of Utrecht, but that the estate which the King seemed to hold in the village of Groningen, and that this lies in the county of Drenthe, and was given to the Church by his gift; and the words of the donating king are most clear to this effect. Those who take this view hold that the estate was the suburban prefecture, Dat Ghyo vnd Woltrecht as posterity called it, or at least the greatest part of it, which I have already shown to belong partly to Drenthe and partly to the adjoining Friesland. For from the earliest memory it had been administered from the town of Groningen, as from the seat of a prefect, whom the men of Utrecht were accustomed to appoint; and that the King meant this when he wrote that estate, situated indeed in the county of Drenthe, but holding itself in the village of Groningen. And this interpretation seems to me all the more probable, indeed truer, because the same King, in the same year, and indeed on the same day on which he gave these (if the copies that I have seen do not deceive me; that day is the 12th before the Kalends of June), also sealed two other documents, of which one offered other estates likewise situated in the same county of Drenthe, and the other again other estates in the county of Radulf, and whatever of them lay between Amasus and Lavicus, that is, between the Amasus and the Lavica, all of which had previously belonged to Uffo and his brothers, men guilty of crime and condemned by just judgement, and he offered them in the same way to this same see of Utrecht, with areas, buildings, slaves, fields, meadows, plains, pastures, waters, fisheries, roads, wastelands, exits, returns, and the other things recited earlier, as a gift. For I think that all these parts, given by Henry in these three documents, gradually coalesced into one prefecture, which we call Gho[?] and Woltrecht, and that the seat of its tribunal was established in the city. As for the county indeed in the same Drenthe, which is said to have belonged to Gozelo, Duke of Lorraine (he is the one who carried on affairs in Friesland and Holland, and held power for some time), and to the other called Umbalaha[?], which is said to have been that of Count Enobard, these were given by the same King some years later, not so much to the Church as to the bishop. But from all these and from many other records of those times I learn this, that the custom then was for pagus to signify something larger than comitatus, and for several counties to be included in one pagus and several estates in one county; so that the one and the same Drenthe, likewise Twenthe, and the particular regions of Friesland were then divided into several counties. This point stuck in Friesland especially for rather a long time, as I have shown elsewhere. And in these parts the word count was commonly used of one who, by the emperor or king, held the highest jurisdiction with authority in some county, that is, in a diocese. But as to the disagreement of opinions which I have mentioned, let the readers judge it; I have set out what I think, but I do not put myself forward as judge of the controversy. Certainly most of the bishops who followed in the following centuries, as I have already noted before, drew the words of the charter to their own advantage and to that of their Church, and claimed for themselves jurisdiction in the town and authority over the praetorium in the town no less than the suburban prefecture, which was undisputedly theirs. And they held this for a long time, but not without frequent and troublesome disturbances arising from this source, so that arms often clashed with arms, camp was often set against camp within the town, and war was waged within the walls. For the people, looking to their liberty, either opposed the lust of the prefects whom the bishops kept in the city, or refused the bishops' rule, which was spreading wider every day. Of all these things I have spoken at length in my History. Nevertheless the power and might of the bishops prevailed, which was then great, and also girded with sacred authority and the reputation of religion, though the affairs of the town were then still slight. If these things had been as great then as they later became, the same ambition and greed of the bishop would not have laboured in vain here, no less than in Oostergo and Westergo, where similar charters obtained from the emperor Henry IV came to light. Thus, following the traces of events in the records, I find further that the clergy of Utrecht at the beginning gave the suburban territory to a prefect whom they wished, for as many years as they wished; and that this prefect had his seat and tribunal in the city; that the bishop himself imposed on this same man the duty of acting as praetor in the city and the name of city prefect, and appointed him as sculthetus, the chief minister of justice, as his deputy; and soon both prefectures were turned into a perpetual fief; and the fief again after some centuries was changed into the condition of an emphyteusis, or something like an emphyteusis. Through several ages the Gronenbergs, the Supperachs, again the Gronenbergs, the Gronenbeeks, and the Selwerds, noble families, held possession of the fief, sometimes jointly, sometimes separately. Afterwards, when the inheritance of the Selwerds passed to the Coverds, with Ida, the sole and last heir of that house, married to Hermann Coverd, an emphyteusis was introduced; whether rightly or wrongly I do not know. John and Reinold Coverd, with their individual sons, and Goverd Hovius, became emphyteutae in the year of Christ 1371, shortly after the death of Bishop John of Vernenburg; the condition was set that the emphyteusis should last for the lifetime of these men. But just as the suburban prefect held a narrowly bounded authority over the rustic commons, and did not hear causes or pronounce sentences without a college of judges, whom the commons gave him as assessors, and the commons enjoyed their own liberty in other matters, so the praetorian power conferred in the city by the bishop did not, as some falsely believe, remove the jurisdiction of the senate or its authority. For the senate often made agreements with its neighbours at the time when the prefects were in the city, which could have no place without authority and jurisdiction, and it had treaties concerning the conduct of the forum in the city and the hearing of disputes. Lastly, the public records bear witness that once, in the year 1283 from the birth of Christ, when the prefects were Gronenbergs, and two men accused of public crime, who happened to be of the noble Selwerd house, had been brought to trial, it was asked in the assembly whether the Hunesgonians, or the city of Groningen, or finally Egbert Gronenberg as prefect of the suburban territory, ought to be judges, because the arx of Selwerd, where the boundaries of all these met, had its seat there; and when the accused themselves were permitted to choose one of these three as judge for themselves in perpetuity, they chose Egbert with his successors. None of these things could have had any place in any way if the senate had not held the power of judging with authority. Moreover, although the bishop gave the prefect and his office a place among them, this city of ours for a long time refused to acknowledge the authority of the bishop among itself, or to swear an oath to him as to its prince or lord, or to undergo the same condition and law as the other cities of the diocese. Nor was it lacking examples of other free cities, which received such prefects from neighbouring princes, and yet did not bind themselves by oath to them as subjects. And since it lay on Frisian soil and under Frisian law, it hesitated to subject itself to foreign lords, having abandoned the liberty of its people. And although the bishops often muttered, especially those of ambitious temper, yet they did not dare to resort to force for this cause. For the resources of the city had already grown, and its liberty was confirmed by treaties of alliance with its neighbours. Added to this, the city had long since been admitted into the society of the Hanseatic League, whose strength was then great, whose authority was not slight, and whose help was ready, and it was not counted among the cities of the league in a humble position. While these things stood thus, although Bishop Florence, of the Wevelichhoven family, a wise and industrious man, had obtained from the emperor Wenceslas a diploma signed on 1 May 1382, by which he was granted the power to seek back and recover everything that had flowed away from the bishopric through the carelessness of his predecessors or in any other way, and relying on this he attended to his affairs not sluggishly, yet he feared to attack Groningen with arms or to press it with unjust demands. At last, despairing of other means, he thought the city, or his Church, could be bound to himself in another way, under the appearance of a benefit, through his college (for I find that this was done while he was still alive, although when I first wrote the History I thought otherwise). For in the year 1392, which was the penultimate of his life, the chapter, to which that estate had properly been given by King Henry, as I have shown, at the instigation and urging of the bishop himself, although it had agreements with the Coverds, nevertheless setting these aside, transferred all its right, which flowed from the gift of Henry, whether within the city or outside it, to the city under a certain condition. This condition was: that the city should hold the right and jurisdiction itself from the chapter for the next hundred years, and on that account should pay to the same chapter each year a rent of eighty-three and a half old Frankish gold shields, at a fixed place and time; and besides this rent, in the twentieth year, it should offer an honorary gift of seven marks of pure silver at Utrecht; the census, revenues, tithes and hereditary property which belonged to the canons in this same territory should be excepted, so that nothing should be lost to them from this agreement: and when the hundred years were over, all these same things should hold for another hundred years, if the city, remaining faithful to the agreements, were willing, and for this purpose offered to the same chapter at Utrecht marks of pure silver before the first of September, and asked for and received new letters of agreement written in these same words; and again, when these years also were finished, everything should be sought back and governed in the same way and by the same law; and the same should be extended in perpetuity. Nevertheless it was provided that, for the lifetime of the two Hoviuses with their mother, a third of the whole of this right, by the earlier agreement, should belong to them. Thus the city of Groningen, without dispute, as it itself thought, now free and under its own right on every side, and increased also by the authority of the suburban territory, scarcely feeling the burden of so small a rent, gracefully acknowledged the bishop only as its patron and the honour and dignity of its patron. But Frederick Blankenheim, appointed bishop in place of Florence, a man of most ambitious and restless temper, although at the beginning of his rule he had pledged his faith to the city by solemn letters, that he would preserve all its rights and privileges for it, hold the agreements made with its people as valid, be its patron and protector everywhere in fairness and goodness, and do other such things; and although, having again agreed with it most amicably about four years later, when fear and danger from Holland's arms pressed, nevertheless a little after, when that danger and fear had been removed, and seeing the city worn out equally by the recent foreign war and by its alliances, he thought this suitable to his desire and entangled it at home with new arms by a most cunning plan. For first he thrust himself in as intercessor for the exiles, the mortal enemies of the city; then, when the matter was not obtained, as if he could not refuse to supplicants, and at the same time under other pretexts which his desire suggested, he began a war. This war having begun, which he had foreseen would follow, payment of the annual rent owed to the canons under the agreement was held back. Thus some pretext for rescinding the agreement was found. Among other causes he particularly boasted that the city had lately thought it had redeemed by agreement all the authority which could in any way be seen to have flowed from the gift of the emperor Henry, but the bishop maintained that the agreement did not pertain to the urban prefecture, and said that the prefecture had been customarily given by his predecessors and ought to be given by him also. Nor did he cease to press the city with arms, to make everything hostile to it on every side, and to threaten greater things, until he had forced it to descend to the dictated conditions. These conditions were: that the exiles should return to their homes, as they then were, and should have no actions for damages; that the canon not paid for five years on account of the war should at once be paid; that the city should cede to the bishop the right of the suburban prefecture; he should appoint a prefect at his pleasure, who should have his seat and tribunal in the city; that is, to put it in a word, the earlier agreement with the chapter would be void. This was concluded on the day before Michaelmas in the year 1405. Three days later, the urban right was transferred on these terms: the city of Groningen should put forward from among its own citizens a sculthetus, that is, a prefect, whom it wished, remove him from office, give him a successor, and continue him, whenever, as often as, and as long as it pleased; and the one put forward, or the successor given, should swear an oath before the bishop's minister, who was prefect of the suburban territory; the sum of the oath should be this: THAT HE WOULD ADMINISTER JUSTICE AND RIGHT TO ALL WITH INTEGRITY AND WITHOUT CORRUPTION, ACCORDING TO THE CUSTOM OF THIS FORUM; and if the prefect of the suburban territory delayed for more than three days, the consuls should have power to receive this oath from him in the same form of words. For this right the city should pay each year twenty-eight old Frankish gold shields to the bishop himself at Utrecht, and every twentieth year two marks of pure silver with a third of a mark to the prefect Coverd, the Coverds; both before the end of October; and this agreement should have force for one hundred years, at the end of which, if the city before the end of the same October should offer the bishop sixteen marks of similar silver and a third of two marks, and ask for the continuation of this right and agreement, all the same things should hold for as many years; and in the same way, when those years were over, the same things should be sought back again, and the agreements kept purely, for as many more years, and so on; and this should be extended in perpetuity, nor should the bishops be allowed to refuse. Thus the bishop's unjust desire was in some measure satisfied, and an end was put to the war. But not even here did the immense ambition of that man stop; rather, progressing further as affairs went well, he at last brought the matter to such a point that the city, worn out and weary from all these troubles, was finally compelled, for the sake of quiet and peace, to swear an oath of fidelity to him as to its lord, and to undergo the same condition of obedience as the other larger cities of the diocese of Utrecht, Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle, and to profess itself a subject and member of the diocese, nevertheless with all its other rights intact, and with the alliances it had with its neighbours preserved. This was done in the year after Christ, born of the Virgin, 1419. From this time onward, however, unshaken peace and concord remained between the city and the bishops and the diocesans, and affairs stayed in the state which I have now set out, until David of Burgundy. He, having taken possession of the affairs of Utrecht, in the year of Christ 1460, being in need of money, having received from our city by way of loan 1600 Rhenish gold guilders, restored to it the right and authority of the suburban prefecture for the term of his life.

units.la: Cupido Friderici Blanckenhemij. suæ,& in sexennium à finitâ vitâ proximum, conditionemq; addidit, ut à civitate penderetur hoc nomine canon annuus aureorum similium centum; nec verò fas esset prius à civitate repetere successores suos Præfecturam dictam, quàm mutuum omne restituissent. Davidi defuncto anno M. CCCC XCVI, successit apud Vltrajectinos Fridericus Badensis: qui cùm nondum quinquennium rebus præfuisset, armis Saxonicis petita civitas est, belloque diuturno æque ac gravi vexata: in quâ cùm auxilium Episcopi, patroni ac principis sui, sæpè rogasset, nec solùm non juvaretur ab eo ita uti par erat ex contractus conditione, sed haud obscurè premeretur etiam, tandem necessitate ultimâ circumventa, & coacta, sequens id, quod erat in pacti {*}formulâ disertis verbis nuncupatum, in fidem principis alius, Edsardi scilicet Frisiæ, quæ ad Orientem Amasi est, Comitis, concessit. Atque hic Ultrajectini juris in civitatem finis fuit. Ab Edsardo deinde ad Carolum Geldrum, à Geldro ad Burgundos imperium hoc devolutum est. Quod quomodò faecclesiæ actum[?], infra monstrabitur. Vltrajectinæ adhæreret, ut solet: alterius principis imperium in [?]fraudem episcopi & Ecclesiæ non subiret, quamdiu vi majore aliud facere non cogeretur: episcopus vicissim in periculis eam summis viribus tueretur.
units.tr: Friedrich of Blankenheim, at his own wish, added the condition that the pledge would hold for his lifetime and for six years after his death, and that the city would pay an annual rent of a hundred gold coins of the same kind for it. His successors were not to reclaim the said Prefecture from the city until they had repaid the whole loan. David died in 1496 and was succeeded at Utrecht by Frederick of Baden. Before he had ruled for even five years, the city was attacked by Saxon arms and harassed by a long and grievous war. Although it often asked its bishop, its patron and its prince, for help, it not only received none, as the terms of the contract required, but was even openly pressed by him. At last, overtaken by extreme necessity and compelled, it submitted to the authority of another prince, Edzard, Count of East Frisia, which lies east of the Ems, as the agreement had expressly named. This was the end of Utrecht's right over the city. From Edzard the power passed to Charles of Guelders, and from Guelders to the Burgundians. How this was done will be shown below. The city adhered to Utrecht, as it usually did: it would not submit to another prince's rule to the detriment of the bishop and the Church, unless it was forced by greater violence to do otherwise. The bishop, in turn, would defend it with all his strength in times of great danger.

units.la: DE CONIUNCTIONE ET FOEDERIBUS CIVI- TATIS CUM ORDINI- bus Agri vicini.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE UNION AND TREATIES OF THE CITY WITH THE ORDERS OF THE NEIGHBOURING COUNTRY.

units.la: PROXIMUM nunc, ut, quæ acta cum vicinis sunt inter Amasum & Lavicam, quæque cum iis jura sociata, videamus. Nec verò hîc ea repetemus, quæ sunt Historiæ Decade prima nobis exposita: sunt enim minus congrua instituto nostro: sed quæ secundâ & sequentibus exposuimus, fusè ac sparsim, eadem breviter contrahemus, & rem totam velut in synopsi Lectori statuemus ob oculos. Finito tandem diuturno & exitiali bello, de quo Decadis primæ libro ultimo in Historia scripsi, quo in Gronenbergios & Gelekingios divisa civitas, & intestinis armis miserrimum in modum afflicta, & cum civitate tota regio vicina in partes distracta, sese attriverant, velut calamitate cautiores factae ab anno M. CC. LII diu deinceps quietae fuere. Post cum minuti tumultus in Agro inter ipsos agrarios ex ambitione hic illic rursus exisserent, deinde majores quoque, imprimis vero in Fivelingiis renascerentur, civitas tamen in quiete perstitit, & quasi spectatrix fabulae fuit. Et quoniam vacillabat saepè jurisdictio in Agro ob partium studia, contumaciamque potentium, quibus pro jure vis ac libido erant, simul etiam commercia actionibus violentis turbabantur, tum firmandorum judiciorum, tum commerciorum tuendorum causa cum his aut illis agri partibus, ut occasio ferebat, pactis fœderibusque eadem se civitas junxit, eoque modo publicae pacis anchora fuit. Atque haec pax cum ad annum usque M. CCC. XXXII stetisset, intereaque opibus & negotiationum multitudine oppidani crevissent, eo, quem dixi, anno in dissensionem cum sociis suis, ex dissensione in tumultus, ex tumultibus in apertum &
units.tr: NEXT, let us see what was done with the neighbours between the Ems and the Lauwers, and what rights were shared with them. Here, however, we will not repeat what was set out for the reader in the first Decade of the History, since it is less suited to our present purpose. What we have described fully and scattered through the second and following Decades, we will summarise briefly, setting the whole matter before the reader as in a synopsis. When the long and destructive war, which I described in the last book of the first Decade, was finally over, the city had been divided into the Gronenbergers and the Gelekingers. Afflicted most wretchedly by civil arms, and with the whole neighbouring region split into factions along with the city, the people had worn themselves out. Made wiser by the calamity, they remained quiet for a long time from the year 1252 onwards. Afterwards, though minor disturbances arose again here and there in the countryside among the countrymen themselves, out of ambition, and then greater ones too, especially in the Fivelingo, the city nonetheless stayed in peace and was, as it were, a spectator of the play. Since jurisdiction in the countryside often wavered because of party zeal and the obstinacy of the powerful, for whom force and desire took the place of law, and since commerce was also disturbed by violent acts, the city therefore joined itself, by pacts and treaties, to one or another part of the countryside as occasion required, both to confirm judgments and to protect trade. In this way it became the anchor of public peace. This peace held until the year 1332. Meanwhile the townspeople had grown in wealth and in the number of their trades. In that year, as I have said, they fell into dissension with their allies, from dissension into tumults, and from tumults into open and great war.

units.la: magnum bellum inciderunt. Eo bello omnes, qui inter Lavicam flumen & Dullartum sinum sunt, exceptis, qui Præfecturam veterem tenent, & cum his bona Drentinorum pars, in civitatem conjurarunt, nec ante destitere, quàm acceptis illatisque gravibus detrimentis anno demum sexto post arma sumpta summis viribus in civitatem euntes in eas eam angustias & necessitatem adegere, ut ipsa intercessorum arbitrio submittere sese, & deditionem facere coacta sit. Conditiones dictæ duæ asperæ ac duræ parentando hostium odio: prior, ut pars muri oppidani longo tractu à porta Ebbingana versus portam Esteranam[?] deiceretur, locus ligneo septo rursum clauderetur: altera, ut sex in urbe domus ex lateritio opere firmæ & sublimes, turrium aut arcium instar, ad medium usque fornicem, ne novis turbis occasioni essent, humiliores fierent. Reliquæ æquiores; quales hæ, ut vetusta pacta & fœdera inter partes servarentur, omnibus jura sua cum jurisdictionibus integra utrimque manerent, oppidani agrarijs in defendendâ [?]libertate[?] auxilio essent, in collybi & commerciorum ratione fraudem ijs non facerent: quaterni ex tribus agri partibus praetores cum quatuor Drentinis, quatuor consulibus Groninganis, duobus item antistitibus Adoardiano & Werumano, quotannis Groningae in curia convenirent, & monetam examinarent, remq; numariam ex commodo totius regionis constituerent. Pronunciatum prid. Petri & Pauli Apostolorum anno M. CCC. XXXVIII[?], sed sigillis tribus tantum signatum, Fivelingio, Hunesgonio, Drentino; reliquis, quibus signari debuerat, Groningano, Fredowoldio, Langowoldio, Hummerzio, Octopagico, non adjectis. Unde suspicio mihi est, conditiones illas duriores recusasse civitatem. Nec tamen eâ minus pax coiit. Ab annis deinde non multis arx[?] Selwerdia bono Reip. à Groninganis, Hunesgoniis, Fivelgoniis, Langowoldiis pecuniâ publicâ empta est, & solo aequata: pecuniaque in hunc usum à sociis omnibus collata. Periculosa quippe arcis ejus firmitas non solum urbi, sed caeteris quoque de libertate suâ sollicitis videbatur. Et cum pecuniae ejus gratiâ controversia inter urbanos magnum bellum inciderunt. Et cùm pecuniæ ejus gratiâ controversia inter urbanos & Langowoldios enata esset, eam anno M. CCC. LXI, die decollationis Ioannis Baptistae, compositam invenio.
units.tr: In that war all who live between the river Lauwers and the Dollard inlet, except those who hold the Old Prefecture, and with them a good part of the Drenthe people, banded together against the city. They did not stop until, after suffering and inflicting serious losses, in the sixth year after taking up arms, they advanced on the city with their full strength and reduced it to such straits and necessity that it was forced to submit to the judgment of the mediators and make a surrender. The two conditions were harsh and severe, dictated by hatred of the enemy. The first was that a part of the town wall should be torn down along a long stretch from the Ebbing Gate towards the Esterana Gate, and the site closed again with a wooden fence. The second was that six houses in the town, built of brick, strong and tall like towers or citadels, should be lowered to the level of the middle vault, so that they would give no occasion for new disturbances. The remaining conditions were milder. These were: that the old pacts and treaties between the parties should be kept; that each side should keep its rights and jurisdictions intact; that the townspeople should help the countrymen in defending their liberty; and that they should not cheat them in matters of the collybus and commerce. Four praetors from each of the three parts of the countryside, together with four Drenthe men, four Groningen consuls, and likewise two chiefs, from Adwerth and Werum, were to meet every year at Groningen in the council chamber, examine the coinage, and set the money matters of the whole region for the common good. This was proclaimed on the day before the feast of Saints Peter and Paul in the year 1338, but it was sealed with only three seals, those of Fivelingo, Hunsingo and Drenthe. The seals of the others, who ought to have sealed it, Groningen, Fredewold, Langewold, Hummerzo and the Eight Parishes, were not added.
