From this I suspect that the city refused those harsher conditions. Nevertheless peace was made all the same. A few years later the fortress of Selwerd was bought with public money by the Groningers, the Hunsingers, the Fivelingers and the Langewolders, for the good of the state, and levelled to the ground; the money for this purpose was collected from all the allies. Its strength was thought dangerous not only to the city but also to the others who were anxious about their liberty. And when a dispute arose between the townspeople and the Langewolders over the money for it, which led to a great war, I find that it was settled in the year 1361, on the day of the beheading of John the Baptist.

units.la: Eodem verò anno M. CCC. LXI. delecti ex Hunesgoniis, Fivelgoniis, Hummerziis, Præfecturâ vetere, & præter hos etiam Ostergoi, Westergoi, Reiderii, Amasani, Broecmerii Groningae congressi cum consulibus ac senatu hujus civitatis, pacis & libertatis Frisicae tuendae ergo fancivere, ut rata essent omnia, quae olim in solennibus comitiis gentis ad Vpstallisbomum fuerant decreta, eademq; sanctè colerentur: Et his addidere alia: ut praetores omnes cum singulis assessoribus suis ac antistitibus aut sacerdotibus quotannis Groningae convenirent ipsis Calendis Iulij, ac de Reip. negotiis deliberarent & constituerent, nec nisi confectis aut definitis negotiis inde discederent sub gravissima poena: ut Selandiis, id est, partibus Frisiae singulis ratæ essent consuetudines suæ in electione iudicum; nesocij à sociis proscriptos receptarent, neve idem novis ac insolitis vectigalibus se mutuò onerarent, ut omnes in defendendà libertate, & repellendà notoriâ injuriâ, si necessitas necessitas premeret, & promptè & tempestive pro modo virium suppetias sibi mutuo ferrent, nec abstinerent ante, quàm periculum esset depulsum: denique si quæ existeret controversia in aliquâ Frisiæ regione, ea ex specialibus illius regionis constitutionibus, consuetudinibus, privilegiis bonis honestisq; finiretur. Hoc modo Groninga id esse cœpit, quod ante Vpstallisbomum fuerat, locus scilicet concilii aut comitiorum universæ nostræ gentis velut proprius, ac Reip. liberæ Metropolis. Certè ab hoc tempore ad Vpstallisbomum in Auricano agro conventus hujusmodi, cujusmodi solent, fuisse non reperio, Groningæ verò sæpe fuisse reperio: ut mirere merito homines, qui ista cum scirent, tamen urbem è Frisiæ regione eliminare litigiis suis conati sunt. Atqui præter hæc totius gentis concilia etiam tum invaluerat mos, ut ii qui Amaso & Lavicâ clauduntur, conventus juridicos seorsim agerent Groningæ, idque vel quotannis, vel quoties commodum videbatur. Nam & loci commoditas alliciebat, & civitas opibus ac magistratuum ordine & sapientiâ valida in societatem judiciorum adscita contumaciæ potentum terrori, & fluctuanti jurisdictioni firmamento ac subsidio erat. Nec enim tum quoque æquabilis in jure dicundo ratio in subselliis prætorum perAgrum ubique servabatur, & qui opibus valebant in nobiliate, non facile se legum scitis & judicum sententiis suæ cupidini adversis subiiciebant: Unde mala metuebantur, quæ affligendæ patriæ, & evertendæ libertati poterant esse. Quæ cùm priori more vix jam reprimi posse videbantur, remedio majore opus esse sapientes in provinciâ, ac patriæ & pacis amantes judicarunt. Itaque omnes omninò inter Amasum & Lavicam, qui potestatis publicæ partem tenebant, quos seorsim per minores populos in oppido coire, & cum oppidanis sententias judicum recognoscere mos ferè ferebat, simul Groningæ adesse jussi sunt, cùm annus ageretur à Christo in terris nato M. CCC. LXVIII, Ibi consensu omnium decretum solenniter, ut bis quotannis judices, qui inter Amasum & Lavicam flumina flumina sedes habebant, in quorum numero expressè Reiderij & Westerwoldij, cum iis qui sunt in Præfecturà vetere, recensentur, semel, die octava post Pentecostes, iterum die xv Septembris, aut sæpius etiam si res poscoret, Groningæ conventum agerent, in eodē[?] causas cum magistratu oppidano recognoscerent. Atque ita legis esse coepit, quod moris liberi esse solet. Suntque multa alia præclara & egregia illic sancita, ad rem judiciariam, totumque jurisdictionis ordinem ac modum, imprimis verò ad judiciorum sanctimoniam atque integritatem pertinentia, quæ nos in Historiâ Decadis II libro IV expressimus: quæ talia sunt, ut ne eruditissimas quidem & sapientissimas civitates eorum merito possit pudere. Ad hæc fœdera vetera instaurata pacis causâ, vis omnis vetita, mulcta violatoribus gravis ære Groningano indicta. Signatum decretum sigillis Reideriorum, Præfecturæ veteris, Westerwoldiorum, Hunesgoniæ, Hummerziæ, Fivelgoniæ, Fredowoldiæ, Langowoldiæ, civitatis Groninganæ, die Magni Martyris. Hujus fœderis & decreti beneficio pax rursum inconcussa stetit in hac regione toto penè decennio. Tum verò, cùm se factiones denuò commovisent, & vis jure potior esse cœpisset, maximè cis ultraque Hunesum amnem, coacti sunt ii, qui partem Reip. in Hunesgonia gerebant, ni remp. & autoritatem suam pariter perditam vellent, arctius se cum civitate rursum conjungere. Conjunctionis præcipuum caput fuit, factionum compressio: quarum causa si civitati ad arma eundum, & in contumaces aut turbulentos ducendum esset, de sumptu omni, & detrimento illi cautum per obsides ex sociis pro arbitrio ejusdem legendos: decretumq;, ut, in quos sumpta sint arma, eorum bona in ærarium referrentur: horum dimidium civitati, reliquum sociis agrariis cederet: agrarii suis sumptibus ac periculo rem gererent: eorum præfectura si dissiderent inter se, cognitio ac judicium civitatis esset: hujus sententiam reliqui exequerentur. Adjecta his omnibus conditio, ut tamdiu valerent, quandiu non esset iis solenniter renunciatum, annoque integro post renunciationem factam. Huic foederi statim se ascripsêre, qui Adoardianis parent, ipsumque collegium Adoardianum :& post semestre Humerzii quoque accesêre Hunesgoniis confines, conditionibus modò de impendiis expeditionum non nihil variatis, & accuratiùs descriptis. Anno deinde M. CCC. LXXXI, cùm princeps nobilitatis in Frisiâ Orientali Occo Broecmerius, studio augendæ potentiæ suæ, in clientelam se Alberti Bavari Hollandiæ & Selandiæ Hannoniæque Comitis, qui jamdudum Frisiis imminebat, contulisset, Frisii omnes inter Flevum & Lavicam flumina Ostergoi, Westergoi, Sevenwoldii, qui erant periculis ab Hollandis proximi, metuentes libertati suæ fœdus cum civitate Groninganâ in hoc summo discrimine percussèrunt. Nam non Broecmerius solùm formidini erat novus Bavari cliens præpotens opibus, qui scindere in partes gentem, propriisque viribus atterere posse videbatur, sed factiones quoque in Fivelgoniâ ac Hunesgoniâ se subrigentes, in quibus Nobilitatis pars eundem Bavarum ac Hollandos spectare ferebatur. His verò periculis nil validius opponi posse omnes existimabant, quàm cum civitate hac nostrâ fœdus. Eo fœdere promisit civitas, fidam se sociam fœderatis, omnibusq; Frisiis liberis futuram, societati huic fortunas & corpora, si posseret res, impensuram; libertatem suam & fœderatorum contra vim peregrinorum Principum quorumvis, & factiosæ Nobilitatis pro viribus defensuram: si qua clades sociis accideret in prælio, iis periculo perculsis & receptum quærentibus, portas se suas aperturam: factiosos in Hunesgouiâ & Fivelgoniâ huic fœderi cbnitentes, & concordiam distinentes, ne Reip. malo sint, compressuram. Idem fœdus anno proximo M. CCC. LXXXII. repetitum solenniter, & amplius quoque factum, asscriptis omnibus, qui inter Lavicam & Amasum colunt, cum conditione temporis in septennium, atque ita è curiâ urbis præconis voce in magnâ hominum frequentiâ publicatum. Itemque anno sequente iteratum similiter. Et cùm triennio post rursus se factiones in agro vicino moverent violentius, ac turbas cædesque cierent, autoresque à civitate & sociis compressi, atque in ordinem redaēti[?] essent, & fœdus hoc denuo sancitum publicatumque, & pax factiosis Fivelgoniis & Hunesgoniis, omnibusque omninò huic fœderi subjectis, severè mandata. Id factum anno M.ccc. LXXXVII. Ita motus, & res novæ à Frisiâ ad tempus tum aversæ. Post annos deinde novem Albertus, expeditione in Frisiam suscepta, & pugna ad Scotersilam commissa, vicit quidem Frisios, sed longius tamen cùm propter cruentam victoriam, tûm propter tempestates, & inclinans in autumnum anni tempus progredi non fuit ausus. Sed à biennio reversus majori cum apparatu & exercitu, anno nimirum M. CCC. XCVIII, victoriâ rursum partâ, & Staverâ, civitatum tunc temporis in iis Frisiæ partibus validissimâ, obsessâ, & deditione capta, omnem regionem indè usque in Lavicam redegit in potestatem omniqué à populo jusjurandum accepit. Sed deditioni qui assentiri nolebant, Groningam & in agrum vicinum se contulerunt. Qua fortuna Alberti commoti, qui in factione erant Vetcoperorum cis ultraque Amalum flumen, (hujus enim factionis principem & patronum se Albertus profitebatur) sustulerunt animos: Et cùm istuc quoque ab Alberto legati de deditione venissent, filius Occonis Broecmerij jam extincti Widsfeldus, & cum eo Folcmarus Allena Osterhusanus, ad ipsum profecti, se & totam illam Orientalem Frisiam, quæ Comitatus nomine hodie censetur, ei tradiderunt hac lege, ut eandem in feudum ab ipso mox reciperent, fierentque ejus beneficiarii. Hoc vero fecêre, cum faciendi ejus jus omnino nullum haberent. Cùm his idem fecêre horum exemplo, animati è Nobilitate quidam in agro hoc Groningano, numero sex, Ailco Onstenius Ferhildemæus, Reinerus Eizingius, Tammo Gockingius, Menno Howerdæus, Omco Snelgeri, Haijo Wibenius, quorum animi jamdudum factionum & rerum novarum studio prurierant: à quibus totus inter Lavicam & Dullartum ager velut ex æquo & bono divisus, ac Alberto datus, ab Alberto verò ipsis in feudum redditus. Quæ omnia literis comprehensa, signataque sunt III Idus Septembris. Et hi ipsi novi clientes polliciti Alberto sunt, datis ei literis, ad subigendam Groningam, si in recusandâ deditione & obsequio ea perstaret, (nam istuc etiam legatos Albertus miserat, & optimis propositis conditionibus, ostentatâque benevolentiâ summa, ad deditionem hortatus cives fuerat, ac ni deditio fieret, obsidionem & vim denunciaverat) summis viribus auxilio se futuros. Quæ omnia cùm vulgò innotescerent, ut erant iniqua & invisa, merito magnas turbas in agro circùm Groningam dedêre. Nam diversæ factionis viri nobiles, & quotquot libertatis amantes erant, exagitato exaggeratoque facinore, & multitudine concitata, nonnullos ex factione adversâ, atque in his unum alterumque, qui regionem Alberto dediderant, per tumultum occiderunt. Sed novis clientibus cùm ab Alberto auxilia aliquot cohortium è vicinià subitò venissent, ii qui antè inimicos suos presserant, vicissim pressi ab iisdem in extremâ necessitate ad urbem Groningam confugerunt. Quibus cùm statim portæ non aperirentur ob insidiarum metum, instantibus & terga pene caedentibus inimicis, perterrita plebs conclamare coepit, si intra portas admissa defenderetur in hoc suo periculo, se in potestate civitatis imposterum futuram. Sic demum propius discreta re, portæ apertæ, multitudo trepida in urbem recepta: hostes a mœnibus rejecti: conditio tamen illa, seu quod in discrimine confuse ac nulla ratione jactata, sive quod ad paucos solum pertineret, pene pro nulla habita. Albertus quamquam rogatus a novis clientibus ac tota eorum factione, exercitumque ingentem in vicinia habens, & in Groninganos odio ardescens, tamen ut progrederetur eo tempore, ac civitatem invaderet, persuaderi non potuit. Nam hyems suberat, & exercitus morbo infestabatur, & erat ipse ob senium tardior, & civitatis oppugnationem exi-stimabat fore difficilem. Quapropter præsidio in castris Ostergoo in littore, & aliis locis reli-cto, cum exercitu in Hollandiam est reversus. Nec multos post menses omnis etiamFrisia in Flevum usque durius a Principe & ministris ejus habita, servireque nescia, constantiaq; Groningensium animata, percusso cum iisdem Groningen-sibus & cæteris Sciringiis fœdere, ab eo rursum defecit, omniaque ejus præsidia, exceptâ Stavera, eorundem quoque auxilio expugnavit, cum ex Hollandiâ domesticis tumultibus impedita suppetiæ venire laborantibus in tempore non possent. Eo facto in omnium ore erat civitas Groninga, ejus penè unius constantiæ accepta ferebatur recuperata libertas. Sic quippè omnes habebant, si hanc quoque urbem suæ potestatis hostis fecisset, haud cuiquam eorum, qui jam parebant, sat animi futurum fuisse, ut se contra eum rursus commoverent; cæteros verò, qui liberi adhuc erant, facilè subijci ex hac belli arce potuisse. Tum, qui Alberto se & patriam tradiderant, nec à proposito volebant discedere, tanquam perduelles à Groninganis & sociis vicinis sunt proscripti. Hi ab Alberto domi occupato deserti ad Fridericum Blanchenhemium Vltrajectinum præsulem, civitati proprias ob causas succensentem, ut ostendi antè, se conse contulerunt, eumque in Frisiam attraxêre cum exercitu. Qui cùm frustrà urbem obsedisset aliquandiu, discedensque Blancowerae uno ab urbe milliari praesidium in eam reliquisset, oppidani & sociii agrarii confecto exercitu res proscriptorum invasere, arcesque redegerunt in potestatem. Haec gesta anno M. CCCC, & M. CCCCI. Manlitque res in eodem hoc statu ad annum usque M CCCC V, quo pax inter Groninganos & episcopum Vltrajectinum reparata, exules quoque perduelles in patriam recepti, & rebus suis restituti, civitati honos quàm maximus ubique habitus. Tranquilla deinde civitati & sociis omnia ad annum M. CCCC. xiii, novis turbis insignem. Nam Hifco Emdanus, oppidi ejus Rector & praepositus, Sciringicarum partium in Amafana [?] regione princeps, à Kenone Broecmerio Occonis filio Emdâ anno praecedente ejectus, fortunâque omni exutus Groningam ad civitatem sociam & amicam confugerat. Ejus in civitatem adventu factiones prisca, jam per aliquot annos quietae sopitaeque, sunt resuscitatae. De reducendo enim Hiscone diversis sententiis inter proceres contendebatur, Ea contentio usque eò exarsit, ut Coppeno Iarcæo duce, qui erat Sciringicarum partium princeps, & acerbus odii persecutor; naturaque turbidus & sævus, aliquos adversæ factionis proceres in curia, in foro, in domibus suis per tumultum sint interempti, reliqui eorundem partium magno numero, & in his viri nobiles consulari & senatoria dignitate, ejecti in exilium: exules ad Kenonem trans Amasuim sunt profecti, auxilii in inimicos communes spe. Sciringii civitate potiti, autore eodem Coppeno, domo egressi ex agro etiam æmulos, adversæ factionis homines ejecerunt. At biennio post, cùm flueret annus à Christo natum cccc xv, Keno Broecmerius assiduis exulum precibus exoratus, & ut suis quoque rebus contra Hiscônem & socios ejus Sciringios consuleret, exercitum clam confecit, captaque per insidias nocturnas urbe, & ejectis cum Coppeno factiosissimis quibusque Sciringicarum partium, exulibus & Vetcoperis cæteris Remp. reddit. Tum Consules creati Reinoldus Hugingius, Conradus Voffius, Arnoldus Steenwicensis, Bruno Clingius: qui omnes in magistratu hoc manserunt, quoad vixere:idemque observatum in Henrico Bruggio & Dutmaro Rengero, qui Voffio & Steenwicensi successerunt. Ab hoc vero tempore, restituti exules sunt, summa concordia inter se civitas atque ordines omnes, qui in agro à Lavica usque in Dullartum sinum sunt, egere, pene ut una esse Resp. videretur.Repetitaque tum statim sunt fœdera & pacta vetera: novaq; veteribus subinde addita, honori commodisque civitatis augendis, & amicitiæ conjunctionisq; mutuæ magsi ac magis firmandæ. Quæ cuncta ut intelligantur planius, distinctè singula, sed æq; succinctè, ut brevitas operis poscet per, summa rerum capita explicabo. Depulso, quod ab Hollandiam penderat periculo, deinde & cum Ultrajectinis bello composito, ordines agrarii experimento edocti, quantum momenti temporibus dubiis in civitate esset, ejusque amicitia ac fides quâ firmum esset contra hostes libertatis præsidium[?], quàm magna in ea vis ad conservandam simul sociorum concordiam & judiciorū integritatem, id consilii habuêre ut eam indies sibi devincirent arctiùs. Itaque que sensim concessa civitati aliqua, quæ decori & emolumento ei ipsi, cui tribuebantur, nec tamen detrimento iis, qui tribuebant, esse posse videbantur. Cujus generis illud est vel maximè de Hovetmannis, quod memorabo postea, non magis honorificum & egregium urbi; quàm ipsis agrariis ob juris & justitiæ administrationem, & contumaciæ coërcitionem salutare: item illud de stapulà, uti vocant, rerum ἐπιχωρίων deque negotiationibus & mercatus jure: & illud de cerevisiæ solius Groninganæ in tabernis aut hospitiis publicis usu; quorum alia maturiùs, alia tardiùs initium habuêre. Hovetmannos primos, de quibus mihi cognoscere licuit hactenus, vidi in indice notatos sola nomina habente, ad annum Christi M. cccc. x, si memini rectè, qui index in chartophylacio est curiæ urbanæ. Proximos ab his observavi memoratos in literis publicis Kenonis Broecmerii in membrana exaratis anno M. cccc. xvi, quæ literæ arguunt, eos .tum colligendo tributo per Agrum præfuisse, quemadmodum per Urbem Consules. Et rursum nominatos inveni in literis Occonis Broecmerii Kenonis filii anno M. cccc. xvii scriptis & signatis mense Augusto, atque ita nominatos, ut tractasse pecuniam publicam totius provinciæ cum Consulibus oppidanis sit manifestum. Iterumque anno M.cccc.xx iv.nomen eorum in publico transactionis instrumento impressum animadverti. Post quod tempus cum exissent adhuc anni xii, jam continuum eorum indicem, qui in eo munere fuerunt ad Saxonica usque bella per annos circiter lxiii, quandiu libera & sine principe Resp. hæc mansit, curia ad servat. Sed de his infra rursum. Urbem autem hancemporium fuisse antiquitus vicinis regionibus, præcipue Staverana fortuna ruente, nec solum propinquas sed etiam longinquas negotiationes factitasse, ac in possessione earum floruisse, maritimaque non minus quam mediterranea commercia coluisse, extra controversiam fiam est. Nec illud dubium, jus atque mercatus solennis aut nondinationem in toto agro vicino, fluminibus Amaso & Lavica clauso, solam hanc si non lege aut pacto ; quod tamen verum reor, at saltem more & tacito consensu, qui pro lege est, etiam multò ante Bavari bellum tenuisse. De stapulà rerum venali-um ἐπιχωρίων quando cœperit, quæri potest : potest etiam de cerevisiæ Groninganæ usu jam dicto. Priorem ego aut post Bavari arma, aut post recuperatam à Kenone Groningam statim initia habuisse, alterum posterius cœpisse existimo, & cur existimem, rationes habeo, quas ex iis, quæ sequuntur, Lector etiam non monitus intelliget. Primum post Hollandica & Ultrajectina arma à civitate cum vicinis percussum fœdus, quod mihi in literas relatum hactenus videre licuit, est quod paulò ante Kenonis advétum, cùm ipsa adhuc à Sciringiis teneretur, cum Hunesgoniorum parte, qui Præfecturæ mediæ nomine censentur, in Kenonem iniit anno M. CCCC. XV., mense Martio: in quo caput præcipuum est, libertatis patriæ contra Kenonem & omnes exteros propugnatio, collatis in eam subsidiis mutuis: & præter hanc quod quisque juris teneret, ejus conservatio, denique reddituum & locariorum familiæ Onsleniæ, quoad ea exul erit, in ærarium asscriptio. Alterum cum Humerziis, Langowoldiis, Fredowoldiis, asscriptis etiam Octopagicis Translavicanis, anno sequente ejectis jam Sciringiis, ipsis Nonis Iunii ictum in proximum decennium, & hoc quoque pro tuenda libertate, & jure patrio, conjuncta opera & opibus contra exteros Principes: in quo porrò cautum expresse ut oppidani eam urbis & finium suorum curam habeant, ne quid ex iis detrimenti sociis possit accidere: ut controversiis componendis arbitri a partibus designentur, qui nisi ante Trinitatis eas composuerint, eadem a conventu juridico omnium sociorum Groninga definiantur: ut conventus hujusmodi quotannis Groninga agatur statô die mense Iunio: nec exules Coppenus Iargaus, Iacobus Scelgius cum sociis recipientur: cætera de pace tenendâ de solvendis captivis, de pœnis cadium & injuriarum aliarum rūm loquuntur. Tertium non fœdus, sed pactum cumOmcone Sneigero & Dammonensibus initum à civitate eodem anno, tantùm de cædibus aliquid determinans: in cujus formula Dammonenses nominatos invenio, de gemeine buren van dem Damme. In eodem verò hoc, ut & in tertio evidens indicium extat, paulò antè cum universis Fivelgoniis & Hunesgoniis in nova pacta& fœdus consensisse eandem civitatem: quotū exempla periisse dolemus. Anno sequente M. cccc. xvii, mense Junio, cùm glisceret rumor de consiliis Ultrajectini (cui sederat in animo, Groningam ad jusjurandum sibi dicendum adigere) & vicissim de Occone Broecmerio Kenonis filio aliquid suspicionis esset, cum Fivelingiis & Hunesgoniis convenit civitati, ne pars altera sine altera de cooptando domino consilia iniret: secus facienti, bis mille scutatorum veterum poena esset. Et cùm biennio post civitas importunitate Episcopi superata in fidem se ejus vel invita contulisset, agrarii ordines quoque hi iidem, & cùm his Humerzii, Langowoldii, Fredowoldii, autore civitate Episcopum etiam eundem pactis conventis sibi obligarunt: quorum hæc summa: Episcopus promisit, juri, libertati, ditionibus ordinum agrariorum, cujusmodi tum erant, impedimento se nunquam futurum, modo ipsi vicissim in Vltrajectinos injurij non sint, & cum civitate Groninganâ in eadem amicitiâ, societate, & institutis præsentibus permaneant constantes, imo contra oppressores gratiâ & consilio ipsis adfuturum, item procuraturum, ne quid injuriæ àsuis, aut perditionem suum cuiquam eorum inferatur impunè: nec ullum se castellum ullamvè munitionem excitaturum aut receptūrum in agro hoc, unde agrariis ordinibus periculum creari queat. Hoc factum ipso æstivi solstitii die. Et cùm suspicionis aliquid, ceu fieri in mutationibus solet, Fivelingiis esset injectum, seorsim rursus hi cum civitate, & civitas cum iis pacti fuēre in fine hujus anni, minuendæ libertatis, ditionum, juris sociorum autores se non futuros ullo tempore, imo minuere conantes alios repressuros pro virium modo, salvis tamen fœderibus, & pactis omnibus prioribus. Interea toto hoc tempore ab ejectis Groningâ Sciringiis, gravi inimicitiâ, adeoque hostili odio inter se arse-rant & adhuc ardebant Cislavicani & Translavicani ( hi enim Sciringicum nomen profitebantur, & multos adversæ factionis in exilia pellebant, quibus Groningæ & apud socios eorum receptus erat ) frustraque legati Sigismundi Cæsaris conati fuerant in concordiam eos reducere. Qui legati cùm Ftisia excessifsent, tandem malorum ex intestina dissensione pertæsæ partes ipsæ anno M. cccc. xxii[?]. Groningæ conventu instituto interse transegêre. De qua re prolixè scribo in Historia. Altero anno post inter præpositum Loppershemium & plebem vicinam lis composita est per arbitros, è quibus tres HOVETMANNOS Groninganos in tabulis transactionis nominatos invenio, quorum duo eodem illo tempore Consules oppidani fuêre: quod noscendæ antiquitatis causa est observandum. Anno M. cccc. xxv. Groningani Hummerzii, Langowoldii, Fredewoldii, cum Vpsteranis trans Lavicam, item idem, & omnes socii in agro vicino cum Octapagicis Transflavicanis anno M. cccc. xxv i. de coercendis furibus pacta iniere. Deinde hæc ad Orientem Amasi inter Occonem & Focconem dissensione enatâ, atque armis commotis, cum Occonis fortuna labasceret, Focco Groninganis succensens Occoni fœderi junctis, trajecto cum suis Amaso, & excitata illic factione sua, prælio Groninganos vicit; victorque in patriam reversus Occonem in pugna cepit: iterumque primo vere anni M.cccc.xxv i i i. Amaso transmisso, aspirante undique fortuna, totum penè agrum, qui inter Amasum & Lavicam est, à civitate avertit, & in novas leges ac nova fœdera eum adegit. Sed Medachiorum,Hummerziorum, Langowoldiorum, Fredowoldiorum multi non assensêre, & fœdus etiam cum Groninganis, finito jam fœdere priore, pro libertate & legibus priscis rursum pepigêre, in quo appellatio ad Hovetmannos urbanos à judicibus cæteris in agro litigantibus permissa, & ut conventus juridici quatuor quotannis agantur in urbe, in urbe, utque non nisi voluntaria tributa sint, exiganturve agrariis, statutum. Quo cognito, Foccoistuc cum exercitu accurrens disjectis, qui se opponere ausi erant, rem turbavit, & in eas angustias civitatem conjecit, ut petitis induciis consulere sibi ipsa necesse habuerit. At domum regresso Foccone, & rebus difficilibus[?] implicito, adeoque in ordinem redacto, omnia priori statui restituta: nominatim cum Fivelgoniis universis, & peculiariter cum Dammonensibus, itemque cum maxima Hunefgoniorum parte foedera repetita & conditionibus novis ampliata. Simul Hamburgensibus Ennonis Grethani & filiorum ejus sociis Emda potitis hominibus negotiationum studio deditis, quibus commodum videbatur, cis ultraque Amafum mercari & quaestum facere, per eos mercatus aut stapulæ jus, in cujus possessione Groningani ex voluntate sociorum erant, imprimis in Amasi & Dullarti ora, turbatum Groninganis suit. Et hæc, reliquis per Agrum quietis, simultatis inter duas civitates æmulas materia tum fuit. Hamburgensibus vero ex Nobilitate quidam, præcipuè Haijo Ripperda Farmsumanus, Ailco Howerda Muntensis, Eppo Gockinga Brocæus, magis odio civitatis quàm amore ipsorum, tacitè studebant. Inter hæc Guilhelmus Wicheringius consulari familiâ Groningæ natus, tum temporis mercatorum præfectus, dum jus civitatis tueri vult, in ditione Ripperdæâ concursu seditiosorum est occisus. Quod cùm ultimum ire captis armis se ostenderent Groningani, Haijo Ripperda, cui cædes accepta ferebatur, timore perculsus, satius esse duxit, placare offensos, quàm vim eorum experiri. Itaque oblatâ satisfactione transegit cum iis, & promisit, in possessione juris Stapulæ seu mercatus se civitatem non turbaturum, sed relicturum ei hoc jus liberum; nec solum non impedimento in hac re, sed auxilio etiam, si usus poscat, futurum: deinde cædis Wicheringia, & aliorum damnorum illatorum causâ se cum suis D. Arnoldicos esse soluturum: ad hæc eosdem cum civitate hostes internos aut externos habiturum, opem ei laturum, arcem suam suam Farmsumanam praesidio ejus pariter & confugio aperturum. Acta haec & signata anno M. CCCC. XXXIV, pridie Laurentii. Hinc post menses fere duos induciae inter Hamburgenses & Groninganos in proximum biennium factae, & per eas liber commeatus negotiantibus utrinque datus: decretum etiam, ut interea de pace perpetua, compositis omnibus dissensionibus, inter has civitates ageretur. Anno sequente seorsim cum vicis quatuor Farmsumano, Weiwerdico, Hevenschaeo, Oterdumaeo, mox cum duobus aliis in eadem vicinia Holaverdico & Mersumano in eandem sententiam, rursumque cum Wijnscotanis, denique cum Finseranis & Egestanis in Præfecturā veteri civitas pepigit: Et cum his quidem postremis sic convenit, ut si universa Præfectura vetus cum civitate fœdus iniret, tum ut ipsi quoque eo comprehenderentur, & his pactis præsentibus non tenerentur amplius: sin minus, hæc valerent in annos XII: cum primis vero & secundis sic, si contingeret civitatem cum Dammonensibus priori fœderis tempore finito, aut etiam ante, in novum fœdus consentire, tum, ut hæc pacta irrita essent: alioquin in annos XII vim haberent. Vinsicotani simpliciter in easdem leges consenserunt cum Dammonensibus, & reliquis Fivelgoniis, ac Huntsgoniis, in annos similiter XII. sed expresserè de provocatione ad tribunal oppidanum, ex formula fœderis Huntsgonij & Fivelgonij, ac more prisco. Eodemque die, quo cum Winscotanis facta conventio, (id fuit V Iduum Aprilis) cum Haijone Ripperdà & filio ejus Bolone,pactio quoque prior iterata, denuóqtie rite signata, & vinculo fidei novo firmata validius. Sic enim obligarunt se Ripperdæi, & hæredes suos, si quid delinquerent contra fœdus aut pacta hæc, ut bona sua omnia, & omnes possessiones caderent in commissum, cederentque civitati. Adjecère etiam, placere sibi, & rata habere, quæ cum vicinis vicis quatuorcivitas pepigisset. Nec diu post Midwoldii, Oostwoldii, Finsterwoldii, Veenhusii, Scemedani, Egistani, Medenses, Muntendammenses, Suidbrokii, Nortbrokii, Wagenborgii, in Præfecturâ vetere omnes etiam ipsi cum civitate pacti sunt in annos totidem. In pactis præcipua fuêre: ut libertas, patria, & jus cuique suum, ditiones, juridisdictiones, illæsæ conservarentur: in exilium sine causa justa nemo pelleretur: judiciis & legibus controversiæ disceptarentur & finirentur: vis omnis abesset: exteri principes aliique libertatem præsturi, aut injurij cuiquam futuri mutuâ ope finibus regionis arcerentur; ad hanc rem non ferenti opem gravis multa esset: multa æqualiter inter socios divideretur: si qua pars agri hujus socii, si quis vicus, si vir nobilis ignobilisve, in fraudem civitatis aut agri præsidium haberet, peregrinumve militem intra fines vocaret, ei iisvè conjunctis omnium viribus resisteretur. Deinde de maleficiis & injuriis coërcendis prolixè, de obsidibus expeditionum tempore in urbe habendis. Tum porrò hæc: à sententiis judicum agrariorum provocatio esset ad tribunal urbanum intra tempus legitimum, æque sententiæ à conventu juridico sociorum omnium in urbe recognoscerentur: conventus juridici quatuor pluresve in urbe quotannis haberentur: violans eumtem ad urbem mercatus causa, aut inde redeunte triplæ pœnæ reus esset: tributum à sociis agrariis non exigeretur, nisi exipsorum consensu. Signata hæc die VIII Maii, anno M. CCCC.XXXV. Eo tempore varia quoque cum Ailcone Houwerdæo, & Eppone Gockinga Brocæo acta. De quibus res monet, ut pauca nunc dicam. Uterque enim opibus validus in præfectura vetere fuit. Ex his Ailco Mennonis Houwerdæi Eboni natifilius, Muntensis, temporibus Kenonis Broecmerii, sive irritatus à Sciringiis, seu sponte sua impulsus, auxilio Kenonis proximos aliquot ejus oræ genere & opibus præcipuos, &, uti reor, Sciringicarum partium suspectos, fortunis & patria ejecerat, domos plerorumque everterat, ex materia earum ipse arcem sibi validam apud Muntensis eâ parte, quæ Holma dicitur, extruxerat, denique se Rectorem vicinorum pagorum inde usque ad Dullarti oram constituerat. Post cum Focco Leranus Uconis filius successione à domo Broecmeriâ facta, belloque Groninganis & sociis, Broccmeriorum parti inhærentibus illato, victoriaque reportata, Ailconem quoque in ordinem redegisset rogatus ab exulibus, atque æqua eum pati coegisset, exules quidem restituti in integrum sunt: sed eodem, domi cùm dominatum struueret, àsuis vicissim in ordinem redacto, Ailco cum HamburgensibusFocconianarum partium hostibus Emdam tum tenentibus societate junƈta, auxilio eorum exules rursum exturbarat oppresseratvé; deinde ut gratum novis sociis faceret,& suas res proveheret, societati civitatis Groninganæ,& iis quæ societatem sequebantur, se cœpit obiicere. Mox exemplum vicinum Ripperdæorum metuens, & simul ab exulibus formidinem habens, ac injuriarum in diversos, adeoque in oppidanos sibi conscius, præsidium sociorum in arcem suam recepit. Eo fretus liberiùs jam societatem & pacta conventa cum Groninganis turbare, commercia impedire, negotiantibus infestus esse. inter Hamburgenses quoque & Groninganos simultas & odia asperari. Intereà & Eppo Gockinga Aiuoldi filius in ea Præfecturæ veteris parte, qua ager palustris & nemorosus est, quæ in Austrum vergit, apud Suidbrocæos sedem habens, svorum hæreditate locuples ac potens, ut est natura hominum, à magnis ad majora contendebat, & jus, quod multorum erat, in se solum sensim trahebat, seque summum prætorem per totam illam oram haberi volebat: atque hanc ad rem amicitia Hamburgensium, & Ailconis Houwerdæi, & affinitate Grethanorum, qui tum in Frisia Orientali supra reliquos in Nobilitate eminebant, quorum erat gener & sororius, abutebatur. Hinc factiones vicinorum contra ipsum, & inimicitiæ mutuæ, interdum & injuriæ: & ipse Eppo turbidior Groninganis, & societati eorum infestus, ac vicissim civitatis animi non satis in eum placati: videbanturque ad arma res tendere, cùm inter Hamburgenses & Groninganos inducia biennes sunt factæ. His induciis durantibus pactiones illæ, de quibus dixi, anno cccc.xxxv cum civitate initæ. At induciis vixdum finitis incrudescere priora, Ailco & Eppo in cives aut socios Groninganos injurii esse, & vicissim à Groninganis pati, quæ nollent: Eppo præcipuè, qui parte opum est ejectus Hamburgensibus in Amasana occupatis. Demum per arbitros rursum inter civitatem utramque atque item cum Houwerdæis res compositæ. Hac compositione, Groninga in possessione juris & pactorum per Agrum[?] relicta ; injuriarum oblivio inter civitatem & Houwerdæos sancita, controversiaeque compositae, Exulibus, quos Houwerdæi, quosque Eppo expulerant, & fortunis everterant, reditus & restitutio decreta. Inter Epponem porrò & civitatem sic convenit, ut Epponi res redderentur cum pace ad biennium: intra hoc biennium controversiae inter eos per arbitros componerentur: sed cùm Ailco & Eppo ad ingenium redissent, & Hamburgensium navarchus Groninganos quoque esset depraedatus, civitas injuriam ultra arcem Muntensem Ailconis invasit, & cum praesidio Hamburgensi redegit in potestatem. Eodem impetu cursu Epponem quoque nuper redditis iterum ejecit, & pluribus aliis exuit: turrim munitam in Bellingwoldiis vi captam solo aequavit. Hoc casu consternatus Houwerdæus cùm à sociis nil auxilii expectaret (erant quippè armis · ab exulibus tum forte lacessiti atqueoccupati ) cum Groninganis transegit in hanc sententiam : ut ipse haberet reliqua sua omnia, prædia, jura, jurisdictiones inter Amasum, & Lavicamfl.[?] Groninganis relinqueret possessionem arcis Muntensis cum agri jugeribus cc inpignus servandæ fidei : id valeret ad transactionem plenam & perpetuam, in quam bini utrinque arbitri deligerentur. Factum, anno M. cccc. xxxviii, die Gereonis. Ludovicus Hornkenius præfectus arci à civitate datus. Nec diu post compositionem hanc Ailco supervixit, & civitas anno proximo, arce minoris Muntæ ab iis, quorum erat, empta, cum Hissa uxore Ailconis vidua, atque item liberis ejus denuò pepigit, in hunc modum : (Civitas Hissæ & liberis ejus omnes eorum res, quæ bono jure & sine controversia eorundem sunt, relinquit usque quò liberi omnes, aut quidam ex iis, ad justam ætatem pervenerint : tum ex formula compromissi, in quâ civitati cum vivente Ailcone convenerat, omnis controversia vel per arbitratores, vel per judices definietur in perpetuum : interea civitas retinet arcem Muntenfem cum jugeribus agri centum e numero ducentorum nec optimis, nec deterrimis, & totam jurisdictionem arci cohaerentem: querele de injuriis aut detrimentis mutuis, quae in bello accidere, omnes suspenduntur tantisper. Signatum anno M. cccc. XL.menseNovembri. Sic civitas in possessione hac, atque administratione juris per omnem illam viciniam volentibus petentibusque vicinis discordiarum & inaequabilis jurisdictionis pertaesis mansit usque in annum M. cccc. LX. Tum vero arbitris cum potestate lectis, hinc Theodorico Scaffero, Gosleno Gravio, inde Gerardo Petcumano, Egberto praefecto Emdano, ita rursum pronunciatum: Hiffa cum liberis etiam reliqua illa centum jugera reciperet, & cum ceteris rebus suis ac jurisdictionibus haberet, iisque uteretur-frueretur: Groningani damna in aedificiis & rebus aliis ex aequo & bono ei repararent: arbitri definirent, an iis quae retinerent, quaeque ex usufructu agrorum percepissent, satisfactum Groninganis pro injuriis effet. Nec quicquam amplius hac de re motum invenio ad annum usque M. cccc. lxxxi. Interim Eppone quoque rebus humanis anno M.cccc. xli i i, aut M. cccc. xliiii. exempto[?], qui in parte juris pristini, quod habere fe à majoribus existimabat, in Præfectura vetere remanserat, Groningani consensu populi, & pacto quodam cum Eppone freti, arcem ejus Brocaeam, dejecto præsidio, & vidua Epponis Frouwa Ulrici Grethani sorore, occuparunt, universumque imperium prætorium secundùm Dullarti oram in se verterunt, salvo reliquo jure, libertate αὐτονομία populi. Datusque à senatu præfectus, qui diceret jus, à quo provocatio ad senatum & civitatem esset. In eaque conditione libens tota illa ora ad Dullarum sine mutatione ulla perstitit usque ad tempora Saxonica, seque à Rep. & societate reliquarum agri hujus partium sejunxit, nec exportandi importandive lege, nec cæteris istarum pactis cum civitate obligata ab eo tempore fuit. Hoc exemplo vicini Westerwoldii commoti, cum longius tendere, quàm à majoribus relictum acceperat, usurpare Eggo Addinga agri Rector videretur, ad hæc violentius etiam quædam ageret, injuriosius indigenas pariter & alios tractaret, judicata pro libidine aut exsequeretur, aut non exsequeretur, judiciaque eluderet, & ipsi quoque cum Groningensibus fœdus inierunt anno M. CCCC. XLVII.: cujus fœderis itidem caput præcipuum fuit defensio libertatis: &cætera pene omnia ex formula ea, qua cum civitate hi, qui in Præfectura vetere ad Dullartum sunt, anno M. CCCC. XXXV. pepigerant.
units.tr: In that same year, 1361, delegates from Hunsingo, Fivelgo, Hummerzijl, the Old Prefecture, and also the Ostergoers, Westergoers, Reiderland, Ems-land, and Broekmerland, met at Groningen with the consuls and senate of this city. For the sake of preserving peace and Frisian liberty, they decreed that all the decisions which had formerly been made at the solemn assembly of the nation at Upstalsboom should remain valid and be scrupulously observed. To these they added other provisions: that all the magistrates, each with their assessors and their bishops or priests, should meet at Groningen every year on the Kalends of July, and deliberate and settle the affairs of the commonwealth, and should not leave until the business was completed or settled, under the severest penalty; that the Selandians, that is, the parts of Friesland, should each keep their own customs in the election of judges; that no one should harbour outlaws proscribed by their allies; that they should not burden one another with new and unusual taxes; that all should, in defending their liberty and repelling notorious injury, if necessity pressed, promptly and in good time bring mutual aid according to their strength, and not withdraw until the danger had been driven off; and finally, that if any dispute arose in some district of Friesland, it should be decided by the special constitutions, customs and privileges of that district, in good and honest fashion. In this way Groningen began to be what Upstalsboom had been before: the place, as it were, of the council or assembly of our whole nation, and the metropolis of the free commonwealth. Certainly from this time I do not find that such gatherings as were customary were held at Upstalsboom in the Auricher region, whereas I often find them held at Groningen. So people may rightly wonder that those who knew these things nonetheless tried, by their lawsuits, to drive the city out of the region of Friesland. Yet besides these councils of the whole nation, a custom had by then taken firm hold: that those who are enclosed between the Ems and the Lauwers should hold their judicial assemblies separately at Groningen, either every year or as often as it seemed convenient. For both the convenience of the place drew them, and the city, strong in its resources, its order of magistrates and its wisdom, admitted into the partnership of justice, was a bulwark and support against the stubbornness of the powerful and against wavering jurisdiction. For in those days too, equal treatment in administering justice was not everywhere maintained in the courts of the prefects in the countryside, and those who were strong in wealth among the nobility did not easily submit themselves to the statutes and to judicial sentences that opposed their desires. Hence evils were feared which could be the ruin of the homeland and the overthrow of liberty. When these seemed scarcely able to be restrained by the former custom, the wise men of the province, and those who loved their country and peace, judged that a greater remedy was needed. So all those between the Ems and the Lauwers who held a share of public power, and who by custom usually met separately in the towns, in their smaller communities, to review the judges' sentences with the townsmen, were ordered to be present together at Groningen, in the year 1368 from Christ's birth. There, by the common consent of all, it was solemnly decreed that twice a year the judges who had their seats between the rivers Ems and Lauwers, among whom the men of Reiderland and Westerwolde are expressly listed together with those of the Old Prefecture, should hold a court at Groningen, once on the eighth day after Pentecost and again on the fifteenth of September, or more often still if the matter required it, and there should review cases together with the town magistracy. And so what had been a free custom began to be law. There are also many other excellent and distinguished provisions laid down there, relating to judicial business and the whole order and manner of jurisdiction, and especially to the sanctity and integrity of judgments, which we have set out in our History, Decade II, Book IV. They are of such a kind that even the most learned and wise cities could rightly be ashamed of not having them. In addition, the old covenants were renewed for the sake of peace, all violence was forbidden, and a heavy fine in Groningen money was imposed on violators. The decree was sealed with the seals of the men of Reiderland, the Old Prefecture, Westerwolde, Hunsingo, Hummerzijl, Fivelgo, Fredewold, Langewold, and the city of Groningen, on the day of the Great Martyr. By the benefit of this covenant and decree, peace stood unshaken again in this region for almost ten years. Then, when the factions stirred again and force began to prevail over law, especially on both sides of the river Hunse, those who held a share of the commonwealth in Hunsingo were compelled, if they wished not to lose both the commonwealth and their authority, to join themselves more closely again with the city. The chief article of the union was the suppression of factions: if the city had to take up arms for their cause and lead them against the stubborn or the troublemakers, the costs and losses should be secured to the city by hostages chosen at its discretion from among the allies; and it was decreed that the goods of those against whom arms were taken should be brought into the treasury, half of them to go to the city and the rest to the rural allies; the rural allies should carry on the business at their own expense and risk; if the leaders of the rural allies disagreed among themselves, the inquiry and judgment should belong to the city, and the others should carry out its sentence. A condition was added to all this, that these terms should hold only so long as they had not been solemnly renounced, and then for a full year after such renunciation was made. Immediately those who obey the Adoardians subscribed to this covenant, and so did the Adoardian college itself; and about six months later the Humsterzijlers also joined, neighbours of Hunsingo, with the conditions about the expenses of expeditions somewhat altered and described more precisely. Then in the year 1381, when Occo Broekmer, the chief of the nobility in East Friesland, in order to increase his power, had placed himself under the protection of Albert of Bavaria, Count of Holland, Zeeland and Hainault, who had long been threatening the Frisians, all the Frisians between the rivers Vlie and Lauwers, the Ostergoers, the Westergoers and the Sevenwolders, who were in danger from the Hollanders as their nearest neighbours, fearing for their liberty, concluded a covenant with the city of Groningen in this great crisis. For Broekmer was not the only source of alarm, a new and very powerful client of Bavaria who seemed able to split the nation into parts and wear it down by his own strength; the factions also rising up in Fivelgo and Hunsingo, in which part of the nobility was said to look toward the same Bavarian and the Hollanders, were a concern. Everyone thought that nothing could be set against these dangers more effectively than this covenant with our city. By that covenant the city promised to be a faithful ally to the confederates and to all free Frisians, to spend its fortunes and persons on this society, if it were able to do so; to defend its liberty and that of the confederates for its strength against the force of any foreign princes whatever, and of the factious nobility; that if any disaster should befall the allies in battle, it would open its gates to them when they were struck down by danger and sought refuge; and that it would restrain the factious men in Hunsingo and Fivelgo who opposed this covenant and disturbed concord, so that they might not be to the harm of the commonwealth. The same covenant was solemnly renewed the following year, 1382, and made more extensive, with all who dwell between the Lauwers and the Ems being enrolled, for a term of seven years; and it was published in this way, by the voice of the city herald from the council house, before a large gathering of people. In the following year it was likewise renewed. And when, three years later, the factions in the neighbouring country stirred up more violently, raising tumults and slaughters, and the instigators had been suppressed by the city and the allies and brought back into order, this covenant was again ratified and published, and peace was strictly enjoined on the factious men of Fivelgo and Hunsingo and on all who were in any way subject to this covenant. This was done in the year 1387. So the movements and new undertakings from Friesland were for the time being turned aside. Nine years afterwards Albert, having undertaken an expedition into Friesland and fought the battle at Scoterslag, indeed defeated the Frisians; but he did not dare to advance further, partly because of the bloody victory and partly because of the storms and the time of year, the autumn being near. But, returning two years later with a greater force and army, in the year 1398, having again won a victory and laid siege to Stavoren, at that time the strongest city in those parts of Friesland, and having taken it by surrender, he reduced the whole region from there as far as the Lauwers into his power, and received an oath of allegiance from the people. But those who would not agree to the surrender withdrew to Groningen and the neighbouring countryside. Moved by this turn of events, the men of Albert's faction, the Vetkopers on both sides of the river Ems (for Albert declared himself the leader and patron of this faction), took heart; and when envoys from Albert had come to the same place concerning the surrender, Widsfeld, son of the late Occo Broekmer, and with him Folkmar Allena of Osterhusen, went to him and handed over themselves and the whole of that East Frisia, which is now reckoned by the name of county, to him, on the condition that they would immediately receive it back from him as a fief and become his beneficiaries. They did this although they had no right at all to make such a grant. Following their example, certain nobles of this Groningen region, animated by the same spirit, six in number, did the same: Ailco Onstenius of Ferwerd, Reiner Eizinga, Tammo Gockinga, Menno Howerda, Omco Snelgeri and Haijo Wibenia, whose minds had long itched for factions and revolutions. By them the whole territory between the Lauwers and the Dollard was, as it were, divided on the basis of equity and right, and given to Albert, and by Albert given back to them as a fief. All this was recorded in writing and sealed on the third day before the Ides of September. These same new clients also promised Albert, by giving him letters, that if the city persisted in refusing surrender and obedience (for Albert had sent envoys there also, and had urged the citizens to surrender, with the best proposals and with great show of goodwill, and had threatened a siege and force if they did not surrender), they would come to his aid with their utmost strength. When all this became generally known, since it was unjust and hateful, it naturally caused great disturbances in the country around Groningen. For nobles of the opposing faction, and all who loved liberty, inflamed and magnifying the outrage, and with the multitude stirred up, killed some men of the hostile faction in the tumult, including one or two who had given up their region to Albert. But when some cohorts of auxiliaries came suddenly to the new clients from Albert from the neighbourhood, those who had earlier pressed their enemies, now pressed in turn by the same enemies in extreme necessity, fled to the city of Groningen. When the gates were not at once opened to them, for fear of ambush, and their enemies pressed on almost cutting them down from behind, the frightened common people began to shout that if they were admitted within the gates and defended in their peril, they would thereafter be in the power of the city. At last, the matter having been more clearly separated, the gates were opened, the trembling crowd was received into the city, and the enemies were driven back from the walls. Yet that condition, either because it had been thrown out in confusion and without reasoned consideration in the crisis, or because it concerned only a few people, was almost regarded as nothing. Albert, although he was asked by his new clients and their whole faction, and although he had a huge army in the neighbourhood and burned with hatred against the Groningers, could not be persuaded to advance at that time and attack the city. For winter was at hand, and the army was troubled by disease, and he himself was slower because of his age, and he thought the siege of the city would be difficult. Therefore, leaving a garrison in the camp at Ostergo on the shore and in other places, he returned with his army to Holland. And a few months later the whole of Friesland, even as far as the Vlie, which had been treated more harshly by the prince and his officials, and not knowing how to be a slave, and inspired by the steadfastness of the Groningers, made a covenant with those same Groningers and the other Scirings, and with their help again revolted from him, and captured all his garrisons except Stavoren, since help from Holland could not come in time to those in difficulty, being hindered by domestic tumults. After this deed the city of Groningen was on everyone's lips, and the recovered liberty was ascribed almost to its constancy alone. For everyone thought that if the enemy of their power had also made this city his own, none of those who were already obeying him would have had the courage to rise up against him again; and that the rest, who were still free, could easily have been subjected from this stronghold of war. Then those who had surrendered themselves and their homeland to Albert, and who did not wish to depart from their purpose, were proscribed by the Groningers and their neighbouring allies as public enemies. Abandoned by Albert, who was occupied at home, they went for help to Frederick van Blankenheim, Bishop of Utrecht, who, as I showed before, was angry with the city for private reasons, and drew him into Friesland with an army. When he had besieged the city for some time without success, and was withdrawing, he left a garrison in Blankenwerf, one mile from the city; the townsmen and the rural allies, having assembled an army, attacked the property of the proscribed and reduced their castles into their power. These events took place in the years 1400 and 1401. And the matters remained in this state until the year 1405, when peace between the Groningers and the Bishop of Utrecht was restored, the exiles and public enemies were received back into their homeland and restored to their property, and the greatest honour was everywhere shown to the city. Thereafter all was calm for the city and its allies until the year 1413, which is marked by new disturbances. For Hisko of Emden, ruler and governor of his town, leader of the Scirings in the region of the Ems, having been expelled from Emden the year before by Keno Broekmer, son of Occo, and stripped of all his fortune, had fled to Groningen, a friendly and allied city. On his arrival in the city the old factions, which had been quiet and dormant for some years, were revived. For there was a dispute among the leading men about restoring Hisko, with opposing opinions. The contention blazed up to such a degree that under Koppeno Jarchama, leader of the Scirings and a bitter persecutor of hatred, a man of violent and savage nature, some leaders of the opposing faction were killed in tumult in the council house, in the forum and in their own homes, and the rest of that party, in great numbers, including nobles of consular and senatorial rank, were driven into exile. The exiles went across the Ems to Keno, hoping for help against their common enemies. The Scirings, having seized the city, on the advice of the same Koppeno, expelled from the countryside also their rivals, men of the opposing faction. But two years later, in the year 1415 from Christ's birth, Keno Broekmer, moved by the constant entreaties of the exiles, and wishing also to look after his own interests against Hisko and his Sciring allies, secretly raised an army, and, taking the city by a night ambush, drove out Koppeno along with all the most factious Scirings of that region, and restored the commonwealth to the exiles and the rest of the Vetkopers. Then the consuls chosen were Reinold Hugingius, Conrad Vossius, Arnold of Steenwijk and Bruno Clingius; all of them remained in this office as long as they lived, and the same was observed in Henry Brugge and Dutmar Rengers, who succeeded Vossius and Steenwijk. From this time the exiles were restored, and the city and all the orders which lie in the countryside from the Lauwers to the Dollard bay lived in the greatest harmony among themselves, so that the commonwealth seemed almost to be one. Forthwith the old covenants and pacts were renewed, and new ones were added to them from time to time, to enlarge the honour and advantages of the city and to strengthen more and more the friendship and mutual union. So that all these matters may be understood more clearly, I shall explain the main headings one by one, distinctly but as briefly as the scope of this work demands. The danger which had threatened from Holland was averted, and then, after the war with the Utrechters had been settled, the rural orders, taught by experience how great a weight the city carried in doubtful times, and how great its friendship and fidelity were, a firm bulwark against the enemies of liberty, and how great its power was in preserving both the concord of the allies and the integrity of the courts, resolved to bind it to themselves more closely day by day. Thus, little by little, some concessions were made to the city which seemed to be an honour and advantage to the very one to whom they were granted, and yet not a loss to those who granted them. Of this kind is especially the matter of the Hoofdmen, which I shall mention later, no less honourable and distinguished for the city than wholesome for the rural orders themselves, in respect of the administration of law and justice and the restraint of the stubborn; likewise that of the staple, as they call it, of local goods, and of the rights of trade and markets; and that of the use of Groningen beer alone in taverns or public inns. Of these, some had their beginnings earlier, others later. The first Hoofdmen of whom I have been able to learn anything I have seen noted in an index which has only names, for the year of Christ 1410, if I remember rightly, which index is in the archive of the city council. The next after these I have noted as mentioned in public letters of Keno Broekmer written on parchment in the year 1416, which letters show that at that time they presided over the collection of tax throughout the countryside, just as the consuls did in the city. And again I have found them named in letters of Occo Broekmer, son of Keno, written and sealed in August 1417, and named in such a way that it is clear they handled the public money of the whole province together with the consuls of the town. And again in the year 1424 I noticed their name printed in a public instrument of agreement. After that time, twelve years having passed, the council kept a continuous list of those who held that office, for about sixty-three years, up to the Saxon wars, as long as this commonwealth remained free and without a prince. But more of this below. That this city was in ancient times a market for the neighbouring regions, especially when the fortune of Stavoren was declining, and that it carried on trade not only with nearby but also with distant places, and flourished in the possession of these, and cultivated maritime commerce no less than inland commerce, is beyond dispute. Nor is there doubt that the right of a market or fair, or a solemn trading day, throughout the whole neighbouring countryside enclosed by the rivers Ems and Lauwers, was held by this city alone, if not by law or pact (which I nonetheless believe to be true), at least by custom and tacit consent, which is law, even long before the Bavarian war. When the staple of local saleable goods began, may be asked; so may the question of the use of Groningen beer just mentioned. I think that the former began either after the Bavarian arms, or immediately after Groningen was recovered by Keno, and that the latter began later; and I have reasons for thinking so, which the reader will understand, even without my pointing it out, from what follows. The first covenant struck by the city with its neighbours after the Hollandish and Utrecht wars, which I have been able to see recorded in writing so far, is one that it entered into with Keno, with a part of Hunsingo which is reckoned under the name of the Middle Prefecture, shortly before Keno's arrival, when the city was still held by the Scirings, in March 1415. Its chief article is the defence of the country's liberty against Keno and all outsiders, with mutual aid contributed for this; and besides this, the preservation of whatever right each man held; and finally, the enrolment in the treasury of the rents and tenants of the Onsteins' family, for as long as that exile shall be. The second was with the Humsterzijlers, the Langewolders, the Fredewolders, and the Octopagians beyond the Lauwers also being enrolled, struck on the Nones of June in the following year, 1416, when the Scirings had now been expelled; it was to last for the next ten years, and was also for the defence of liberty and of ancestral right, by joint effort and resources against foreign princes. In it, moreover, it was expressly provided that the townsmen should take care of the security of the city and its territory, so that no harm could come to the allies from them; that arbiters should be designated by the parties to settle disputes, and if they had not settled them before Trinity, these should be decided by a judicial assembly of all the allies at Groningen; that such assemblies should be held at Groningen every year on a fixed day in June; that the exiles Koppeno Jargau and Jakob Scelgius with their companions should not be received; and other matters concerning keeping the peace, the release of captives, and the penalties for homicides and other injuries. The third was not a covenant but a pact concluded by the city in the same year with Omco Sneiger and the men of Dam, determining only something concerning homicides; in its formula I find the men of Dam named as the common farmers of the Dam. In this same pact, as in the third, there is clear evidence that a little before the city had agreed to new pacts and a covenant with all of Fivelgo and Hunsingo; we grieve that examples of these have perished. In the following year, 1417, in June, when a rumour about the plans of the Utrechter (who had settled in his mind to make Groningen swear allegiance to him) was spreading, and there was some suspicion about Occo Broekmer, son of Keno, the city agreed with the Fivelgoers and Hunsingers that neither party should take counsel about choosing a lord without the other; whoever acted otherwise should pay a penalty of two thousand old gold shields. And when two years later the city, overcome by the importunity of the Bishop, had put itself under his faith even against its will, the same rural orders, and with them the Humsterzijlers, Langewolders and Fredewolders, at the instigation of the city, also bound that same Bishop to themselves by agreed pacts; the sum of these was this: the Bishop promised that he would never be an obstacle to the right, liberty, and jurisdictions of the rural orders, of whatever kind they then were, provided that they in turn did no wrong to the Utrechters; and that they should remain steadfast in the same friendship, alliance, and present institutions with the city of Groningen; indeed, that he would assist them against oppressors with favour and counsel, and likewise see to it that no injury or destruction from his men be inflicted on any of them with impunity; and that he would not set up or receive any castle or fortification in this territory from which danger could arise for the rural orders. This was done on the very day of the summer solstice. And when some suspicion, as usually happens in times of change, had been cast on the Fivelgoers, these again separately made pacts with the city, and the city with them, at the end of this year, that they would never be the authors of any diminution of liberty, jurisdictions or rights of the allies, but would even restrain others who tried to diminish them, to the extent of their strength, saving however all the earlier covenants and pacts. Meanwhile during all this time the Cisla­vicans and the Trans-lavicans (for these claimed the Sciring name and drove many men of the opposing faction into exile, who were received at Groningen and among their allies), who had been expelled from Groningen by the Scirings, had burned with bitter enmity and deadly hatred against each other, and still burned; and the envoys of Emperor Sigismund had tried in vain to bring them back into concord. When these envoys had left Friesland, at last the parties, weary of the evils arising from internal dissension, themselves came to terms with each other in the year 1422 by an assembly held at Groningen. I write about this matter at length in the History. Two years later a dispute between the provost of Loppersum and the neighbouring common people was settled by arbiters, of whom I find three named in the records of the settlement as Groningen Hoofdmen, two of whom were at that same time town consuls; this is to be noted for the sake of knowing antiquity. In the year 1425 the Groningers made pacts with the Hummerzijlers, the Langewolders, the Fredewolders, with the Uptermers beyond the Lauwers; likewise the same, and all the allies in the neighbouring country, with the Octopagians beyond the Lauwers, in the year 1426, concerning the restraint of thieves. Then, when a dissension had arisen between Occo and Focko on the east side of the Ems, and arms were taken up, and Occo's fortune was wavering, Focko, angry at the Groningers who had joined Occo's alliance, crossed the Ems with his men, and, having stirred up his faction there, defeated the Groningers in battle; and returning victorious to his homeland, he captured Occo in the fight. Then again in early spring of the year 1428, with the Ems crossed and fortune smiling on all sides, he turned almost the whole region between the Ems and the Lauwers away from the city, and forced it under new laws and new covenants. But many of the Medemblikers, Hummerzijlers, Langewolders and Fredewolders did not agree; and they made a covenant with the Groningers too, the earlier covenant having now expired, for liberty and ancient laws; in which it was agreed that appeal to the Hoofdmen of the city from the other judges in disputes in the countryside should be permitted, that four judicial assemblies should be held every year in the city, and that only voluntary taxes should be levied on the rural districts. When Focko learned of this, he hurried there with his army, scattered those who had dared to oppose him, and threw the matter into confusion, and drove the city into such straits that, having asked for a truce, it was obliged to look to its own safety. But when Focko had returned home, and become entangled in difficult affairs, and was himself brought into order, everything was restored to its earlier state: the covenants were renewed with all the Fivelgoers, and particularly with the Dammers, and likewise with the greater part of Hunsingo, and enlarged by new terms. At the same time, since the Hamburgers, who had seized Emden under the leadership of Enno Gretha and his sons, were men devoted to business, and wanted to trade and make profit on both sides of the Ems, as seemed convenient to them, the Groningers' right of market or staple, which they had possessed by consent of their allies, especially on the shores of the Ems and the Dollard, was disturbed by them. And these matters, while the rest of the countryside was at peace, were then the material for a feud between the two rival cities. Some nobles, especially Haijo Ripperda of Farmsum, Ailco Howerda of Munte, and Eppo Gockinga of Brokum, secretly favoured the Hamburgers, more from hatred of the city than from love of them. Meanwhile Wilhelm Wicheringa, born at Groningen of a consular family, then prefect of the merchants, while he wished to defend the city's right, was killed in a crowd of seditious men in Ripperda's lordship. When the Groningers showed that they would take up arms to avenge this final outrage, Haijo Ripperda, on whom the killing was charged, struck with fear, judged it better to appease the offended than to test their force. So, having offered satisfaction, he came to terms with them, and promised that he would not disturb the city in its possession of the right of staple or market, but would leave this right free to it; that he would not only not be an obstacle in this matter, but would also give help, if use required it; further, that he would pay, with his men, the Arnoldic men, for the killing of Wicheringa and other injuries inflicted; besides this, that he would have the same enemies as the city, internal or external, would bring aid to it, and would open his castle at Farmsum to its garrison and refuge. This was done and signed in the year 1434, on the day before Saint Laurence. About two months afterwards a truce was made between the Hamburgers and the Groningers for the next two years, and during it free passage for trade was granted to merchants on both sides; it was also decreed that in the meantime a lasting peace should be negotiated between these cities, all disputes having been settled. In the following year the city made an agreement separately with four villages, Farmsum, Weiwerd, Heveskes, Oterdum, then with two others in the same neighbourhood, Holwerd and Mersum, to the same effect; again with the Winsotans; and finally with the Finsers and the Eestrumers in the Old Prefecture. And with these last it agreed in such a way that if the whole Old Prefecture entered into a covenant with the city, then they too should be included in it and no longer bound by these present pacts; otherwise these should hold for twelve years. With the first and second [villages] it was agreed that if the city should agree to a new covenant with the Dammers after the earlier covenant had ended, or even before, then these pacts should be void; otherwise they should have force for twelve years. The Winsotans simply agreed to the same laws as the Dammers and the other Fivelgoers and Hunsingers, likewise for twelve years, but expressly about appeal to the town tribunal, according to the formula of the Hunsingo and Fivelgo covenant and the ancient custom. On the same day on which the agreement with the Winsotans was made, which was the fifth day before the Ides of April, the earlier pact with Haijo Ripperda and his son Bolo was also repeated, and duly signed again, and strengthened more firmly by a new bond of faith. For the Ripperdas bound themselves and their heirs in this way: if they should offend against this covenant or these pacts, all their goods and all their possessions would fall to forfeit and pass to the city. They also added that they approved and ratified what the city had agreed with the four neighbouring villages. Soon afterwards the Midwolders, Oostwolders, Finsterwolders, Veenhuizen, Schiermonnikoog, Eastern and Western Ee­stum, Medemblik, Munten-dam, Zuidbroek, Noordbroek, and Wagenborg, all in the Old Prefecture, also made pacts with the city for the same number of years. The chief articles of the pacts were these: that liberty, country, and each one's right, lordships and jurisdictions should be preserved unharmed; that no one should be driven into exile without just cause; that disputes should be argued and settled by judgments and laws; that all violence should be absent; that outside princes and others intending to deprive them of liberty or to do injury to anyone should be kept from the borders of the region by mutual aid; that a heavy fine should be imposed on anyone who did not bring aid to this cause; that fines should be divided equally among the allies; and that if any part of the territory of these allies, any village, or any nobleman or commoner should harbour a fraud against the city or the defence of the countryside, or summon foreign soldiers within the borders, they should be resisted with the united strength of all of them or of those joined with them. Then there was a lengthy provision for restraining crimes and injuries, and for holding hostages in the city during expeditions. Further, the following: that appeal from the sentences of the rural judges should lie to the town tribunal within the legal time; that the sentences of the judicial assembly of all the allies should likewise be reviewed in the city; that four or more judicial assemblies should be held in the city every year; that whoever violated these things by going to the city for trade, or returning from it, should be liable to a threefold penalty; and that no tax should be exacted from the rural allies except with their own consent. These were signed on 8 May in the year 1435. At that time various matters were also transacted with Ailco Howerda and Eppo Gockinga of Brokum. About these the matter itself advises me to say a few words now. For each of them was powerful in the Old Prefecture. Of these, Ailco, son of Menno Howerda, son of Ebo, of Munte, in the time of Keno Broekmer, either provoked by the Scirings or driven by his own impulse, with Keno's help had expelled from their fortunes and homeland several of the neighbours of that coast who were the most prominent in wealth and, as I suppose, suspected of Sciring sympathies; he had demolished the houses of most of them, and from their materials had built for himself a strong castle at Munte in that part which is called Holm; and finally he had made himself ruler of the neighbouring villages as far as the shore of the Dollard. Afterwards Focko Lerarius, son of Uko, succeeding from the house of Broekmer, and having waged war on the Groningers and their allies who adhered to the Broekmer party, and having won a victory, compelled Ailco too to submit to order, at the request of the exiles; and the exiles were indeed restored in full. But Ailco, while he was building up his domination at home, was in turn brought to order by his own people; and Ailco, having joined himself in alliance with the Hamburgers, then holding Emden and enemies of Focko's party, drove the exiles out again with their help, or oppressed them; then, to please the new allies and advance his own affairs, he began to set himself against the alliance of the city of Groningen and those who followed that alliance. Soon, fearing the nearby example of the Ripperdas, and at the same time having fear of the exiles, and being conscious of his injustices toward various people, and therefore toward townsmen, he took the protection of the allies into his castle. Relying on this, he began more freely to disturb the alliance and the covenants agreed with the Groningers, to hinder commerce, and to be hostile to merchants; and the feud and hatred between the Hamburgers and the Groningers also grew sharper. Meanwhile Eppo Gockinga, son of Aiuold, in that part of the Old Prefecture where the country is marshy and wooded, which faces south, having his seat among the Zuidbroekers, rich and powerful by his inheritance, as human nature is, pressed from great things to greater, and gradually drew to himself alone the right that belonged to many, and wished to be regarded as the chief magistrate throughout that whole coast; and for this purpose he abused the friendship of the Hamburgers and of Ailco Howerda, and the kinship with the Grethas, who at that time among the nobility of East Friesland stood out above the rest, whose son-in-law and brother-in-law he was. From this came factions among the neighbours against him, mutual enmities, and sometimes injuries; and Eppo himself was more troublesome to the Groningers and hostile to their alliance, while the minds of the city were not sufficiently appeased toward him; and matters seemed to be heading for arms, when a two-year truce was made between the Hamburgers and the Groningers. While this truce lasted, those pacts of which I have spoken were made with the city in the year 1435. But the truce had scarcely ended when the former quarrels flared up again: Ailco and Eppo acted unjustly toward the citizens or allies of Groningen, and in turn suffered from the Groningers what they did not want; Eppo especially, who had been driven from part of his wealth when the Hamburgers occupied the Ems region. At last, through arbiters, the matters were again settled between the city and both sides, and also with the Howerdas. By this settlement, Groningen was left in possession of its right and of the pacts throughout the countryside; oblivion of injuries was sanctioned between the city and the Howerdas, and the disputes were settled; for the exiles whom the Howerdas and whom Eppo had expelled and stripped of their fortunes, a return and restoration were decreed. Between Eppo and the city it was further agreed that Eppo's property should be restored to him with peace for two years; within these two years the disputes between them should be settled by arbiters. But when Ailco and Eppo had returned to their old ways, and the Hamburger admiral had also plundered the Groningers, the city attacked Ailco's injury beyond the castle of Munte and, with a Hamburg garrison, reduced it into its power. With the same speed and course it also drove Eppo out again, who had recently been restored, and stripped many others; it took by force and levelled to the ground a fortified tower in Bellingwolde. Dismayed by this blow, Howerda, who expected no help from his allies (for they were then themselves attacked and occupied in arms by the exiles, by chance), came to terms with the Groningers in this sense: that he would keep all his remaining goods, estates, rights and jurisdictions between the Ems and the Lauwers, and would relinquish to the Groningers possession of the castle of Munte, along with two hundred acres of land as a pledge for keeping faith; this should be valid as a full and perpetual settlement, for which two arbiters on each side should be chosen. Done in the year 1438, on the feast of Gereon. Lodewijk Hornken was appointed prefect of the castle by the city. Not long after this settlement Ailco died, and the next year the city, having bought the castle of Lesser Munte from those who owned it, made a new agreement with Hisse, Ailco's widow, and her children, in this manner: (The city leaves to Hisse and her children all their property which is rightfully and without controversy theirs, until all the children, or some of them, reach a lawful age; then, according to the formula of compromise, into which the city had entered with Ailco while he was alive, every controversy shall be decided forever either by arbiters or by judges; in the meantime the city keeps the castle of Munte, with one hundred acres of land out of two hundred, neither the best nor the worst, and the whole jurisdiction attached to the castle; complaints of mutual injuries or losses, which had occurred in the war, are all suspended for the time being.) Signed in the year 1440, in the month of November. So the city remained in possession of this and in the administration of law throughout that whole neighbourhood, as the neighbours, weary of discord and of unequal jurisdiction, wished and asked, until the year 1460. Then, with arbiters chosen with full powers, Dietrich Schaffer and Gosling Gravius on one side, Gerard Petkum and Egbert, prefect of Emden, on the other, it was again pronounced: that Hisse, with her children, should recover those remaining hundred acres, and should have and enjoy them with her other goods and jurisdictions; the Groningers were to repair to her, on the basis of equity and right, the damage to buildings and other property; the arbiters should determine whether what she retained, and what she had received from the usufruct of the fields, was enough satisfaction to the Groningers for their injuries. I find nothing further moved in this matter until the year 1481. Meanwhile Eppo too had departed from human affairs in the year 1443 or 1444, and his widow, Frouwa, sister of Ulrich Gretha, remained in the Old Prefecture, claiming to have in part the old right which he believed he had from his ancestors. The Groningers, with the consent of the people, and relying on a certain pact with Eppo, seized his castle of Brokum, after the garrison had been removed, and the widow, and took over the whole prefectoral authority along the Dollard shore, saving the rest of the right and the liberty and self-government of the people. The senate appointed a prefect to declare the law, from whom an appeal lay to the senate and the city. And on this condition the whole coast as far as the Dollard willingly remained unchanged until the Saxon times, and from that time it separated itself from the commonwealth and the alliance of the rest of this region, and was no longer bound by the export and import law, nor by the other pacts made with the city. Following this example, the neighbouring Westerwolders, stirred up, since Eggo Addinga, the ruler of the territory, seemed to extend his claims farther than he had received them from his ancestors, and was acting even more violently in certain matters, treating natives and others more unjustly, carrying out or not carrying out judgments as he pleased, and mocking the courts, themselves also entered into a covenant with the Groningers in the year 1447. The chief article of this covenant was likewise the defence of liberty, and almost all the other matters were taken from the formula by which those in the Old Prefecture, along the Dollard, had concluded their pact with the city in the year 1435.

units.la: Expresse vero cautum, si judices Territorii (hi XII erant a populo & e populo electi) inique judicasse putarentur, liceret læso [?] senatum Groninganum appellare intra dies X; senatui jus esset, citare judices, & causam recognoscere, & sententiâ suâ [?] vel appellantem temere, vel inique judicasse deprehensos in marcas veteres V condemnare: Atque hæc omnia salvo Eggonis & totius populi jure, & libertate accepta à majoribus, quatenus hujus fœderis capitibus non adversantur. Fœdus vero esset perpetuum. Signatum pridie Bartholomæi. Eo fœdere ex hoc tempore usia civitas est, & ejus metu repressus Eggo minùs exorbitâre ausus fuit, donec tandem projecto metu, fœdereque contempto, profecta jam ætate,Monasteriensium patronorum fiducia insolentior factus ab irritata plebe est interemptus.
