Meanwhile the Groningers were to remain in possession of the staple right, of the markets, of what pertains to beer, and of other similar rights, in the manner in which they had been before this suit was brought by the Saxon, from the most recent memory of men. Butter, cheeses, horses, oxen, cows, and other merchandise of this kind were not to be sold or offered for sale elsewhere than at Groningen in the staple place, in the usual way, nor to be exported or driven to other regions, bypassing Groningen. The exception would be only those goods of this kind that grew on the estates of the noblemen themselves, who would have the right to divide them as they pleased and as suited them. The same would hold for the people of Dam. The old Prefecture also would remain exempt from the staple law, and would enjoy its former right and liberty, to buy and sell beer and brew it at its pleasure, as it was accustomed to do, for as long as this arrangement of sequestration lasted. The Groningers also, in collecting money lent and other revenues throughout the countryside, would keep the right and customary practice, provided that the judge in that court in the city was Thoren himself, or his deputy, or some other sequestrator given for this purpose by the Estates of the Empire. These terms were approved and signed by both parties, and were also secured by the seals of two mediators. Finally, peace was established. Not long afterwards Albert, already sick in body, was carried to Emden and died there. Thoren, however, was called to Friesland too early by Henry, son of Albert, while the evils, not yet well settled, still clung to the alliance of the Companions (for the minds of the rural nobility were inflamed against the city, and the city's in turn against them, by mutual injuries), and it was his duty to interpose himself among them and apply a remedy. Since he stayed longer than was right, he gave an opportunity for arms to be taken up again the following year, and the neglected agreement almost came to nothing.

units.la: DE STATU CIVITATIS SUB EDSARDO ORIENTALIS FRI- SIÆ COMITE, ITEMQUE CA- ROLO GELDRO, DOMO Burgundica & imperio Belgico.
units.tr: THE CONDITION OF THE CITY UNDER EDZARD, COUNT OF EAST FRIESLAND, AND ALSO UNDER CHARLES OF GELDERLAND, OF the Burgundian house and the Belgian empire.

units.la: AQuo tempore repetitis sæpè induciis sustentata diu res, & colloquiis iterum tentata, tandem anno M. D. V. in acerbissimum & maximum bellum erupit. Eo civitas ab omni parte obsessa, & in extremas tandem redacta angustias, ob acerbitatem & [?]Saxonicam, urgente necessitate, duro telo, in fidem demùm Edsardi Comitis Frisiae Orientalis, hactenus hostis sui se contulit. Id enim satius putavit, quàm iis se dedere, quorum verba & facta plusquàm barbara & crudelia in obsidione proximis mensibus audierat, videratque. Id factum anno M. D. VI, mense Aprili. Conditiones sanè durae, quibus se dedidit, & non satis è jure pristino. In quibus fuêre hæ: Ut
units.tr: At this time the affair, long sustained by repeated truces and again attempted by negotiations, finally broke out in the year 1506 into a most bitter and great war. The city was then beset on every side and at last driven into the narrowest straits. Pressed by urgent necessity and by the harshness of the [?] Saxon war, it at last surrendered to the protection of Edzard, Count of East Friesland, until then its enemy. It judged this preferable to surrendering to those whose words and deeds, more than barbarous and cruel, it had heard of and seen during the siege in the preceding months. This happened in April of the year 1506. The conditions on which it surrendered were certainly harsh, and not sufficiently in keeping with the old law. They were these: That

units.la: Edsardus in urbem reciperetur cum armatis DCCC: ut magistratu civesque jurejurando adigeret in fidem suam: ut locum in urbe, quem vellet, muniret, & praesidio insideret: omnia in eventum judicii principum ac reliquorum ordinum Germaniae. Deinde & hæ: Ut idem Edsardus ex ordine honestiorum civium deligeret pro arbitratu suo, qui pecuniae credita judicia, aliaque Hovetmannis solita in urbe exercerent in eos qui agrum habitant; idque more & modo pristino, sed nomine ipsius: Ut frumenta in agro nata, non alibi quam Groningae & Dammonae venirent: de caeteris ἐπιχωρίοις Edsardus adhibitis in consilium Groninganis certi quid statueret, quod esset ex commodo Urbis & Agri. De cerevisiâ nihil mutatum. Cautum, ut omne jus hoc ad hæredes Edsardi & fratris ejus Uconis transiret. Signatum utrinque postridie Georgii. Hoc facto omnium animi suspensi, maximè verò Saxonum, qui quo animo esset Edsardus, erant incerti. Et quia de eventu judicii scriptum in conditionibus intellexerant, ad cognitionem causæ rem deducere maturabant. Cognitioque solennis institura est Constantiæ: sed is eventus ibi fuit, ut civitas haud dubiè jure, Georgius Saxo gratiâ esse superior videretur. Definitum tamen illic nihil. Deinde colloquiis multis & variis per aliquot annos tentatum denuò negotium: sed nec his quicquam profectum. Nam Saxo decedere jure in agrum, & fœderibus renunciare civitatem jubebat: civitas ut id faceret, nullâ ratione persuaderi volebat. Igitur anno M. D. XIII resumptis armis, Edsardo cum civitate in Saxonis gratiam proscripto, concitatâ in hos ma-gnâ Germaniæ parte, belloque summis viribus, summâ contentione longo tempore continuato, Frisiâ Orientali
units.tr: Edzard should be received into the city with 800 armed men; that he should bind the magistrate and citizens by oath to his allegiance; that he might fortify whatever place in the city he wished and garrison it; all these matters to await the outcome of the judgment of the princes and the other estates of Germany. Then these also: That the same Edzard should choose from the order of the more respectable citizens, as he thought fit, men who would hold the courts for money lent and the other matters customarily handled by the Hovetmanni in the city, over those who inhabit the countryside; and this in the old manner and form, but in his name. That the grain grown in the fields should be sold nowhere but at Groningen and Dammona. As to the other local matters, Edzard, taking counsel with the Groningers, should decide on something definite which would be to the advantage of the city and the countryside. Nothing was changed concerning beer. It was provided that all this right should pass to the heirs of Edzard and of his brother Ucko. It was signed on both sides the day after St. George's day. With this done, the minds of all were held in suspense, but above all those of the Saxons, who were uncertain what Edzard's intention was. And because they had understood from the conditions that the matter would turn on a judgment, they hastened to bring the case to a hearing. A formal hearing was to be held at Konstanz, but the outcome there was such that the city seemed without doubt to have the better right, while Duke George of Saxony seemed superior in favour. Nothing was decided there, however. Afterwards the business was again attempted through many and varied negotiations over several years, but nothing came of these either. For the Saxon ordered the city to withdraw its right over the countryside and renounce its treaties, while the city, by no means, would be persuaded to do so. Therefore in the year 1513 arms were taken up again: Edzard, together with the city, was proscribed in favour of the Saxon, a large part of Germany was stirred up against them, and the war was carried on for a long time with the greatest forces and the greatest effort. East Friesland

units.la: data,tribusEdsardi arcibus occupatis,Edsardus imparem se solum tantæ moli sentiens ad Carolum Geldriæ Ducem Gallorum regis socium ; Burgundis & Austriacis inimicum, se contulit, ut auxilia ab eo pararet. Is fortunam sequens versuti princeps ingenii, promisit benignè, pecuniamque etiam in eum finem accepit. Sed miles promissus non ante venit, quàm Dammona quoque vi essèt à Saxonibus occupata, & Groninga in arctum redacta. Et tum Geldri legatus, qui auxiliis præerat ; Guilhelmus Oijensis, in extrema civitatis necessitate cùm differri diutiùs deditio non posse uideretur, profesus etiam est, sic sibi mandatum à principe, ne quid opis pressis ferret, neu rebus Edsardi civitatisque ullo se modo misceret, ni priùs hæc illius fide soluta in Geldricum nomen jurasset: nec enim æquum esse, principem tantam rem tam sumptuosam, difficilem, periculosam aggredi, tanti hostis offensionem in se suscipere, omnemque pene Germaniam irritare, & nullum operæ suæ pretium ferre. His addidit de optima principis voluntate in civitatem, imprimis de privilegiorum ac juris pristini restitutione, deque arcis demolitione, alia, quæ ducendis animis esse putabat. Itaque inclinante huc civitate, ex hominum natura melioris conditionis avida, nec libenter manente in ea fortuna, cujus ipsos pœnitet, Edsardus quoque quamquam inopina oratione attonitus primum & indignans, tamen, quod sapientis erat, parendum necessitati putavit. Nec mora, exautorata ab eo civitas apud Oijensem in fidem Geldriæ Ducis juravit, vergente jam anno M. D. XIIII. Conditionum contractus hujus summa fuit hæc: Geldrus causam civitatis contra Vltrajestinos non solùm auxilia non ferentes laboranti, uti debeant, sed vim quoque cum hoste inferentes, impendio suo, sine molestia & sumptu ipsius, ageret & tueretur: civitas in nomen Geldricum juraret in perpetuum, imperiumque in agrum universum Lavica & Amaso clausum, in quo & Præfectura vetus,
units.tr: having been given up, and three of Edzard's fortresses seized, Edzard, feeling himself alone unequal to so great a burden, betook himself to Charles, Duke of Geldern, an ally of the king of the French and an enemy of the Burgundians and Austrians, to obtain help from him. He, following fortune, as a prince of subtle wit, kindly promised and even accepted money to that end. But the promised soldiers did not come until Dammona too had been seized by the Saxons by force, and Groningen had been reduced to narrow straits. Then the Geldern envoy who was in charge of the aid, Guilhelmus of Oye, when in the city's extreme necessity surrender seemed unable to be deferred any longer, declared that his prince had instructed him not to bring any help to the oppressed, nor to meddle in any way in the affairs of Edzard and the city, unless first these, released from Edzard's faith, swore allegiance to the name of Geldern. For it was not fair that the prince should undertake so great, so costly, difficult and dangerous a matter, take upon himself the enmity of so great an enemy, almost stir up all Germany, and gain no reward for his effort. To these he added concerning the excellent disposition of the prince toward the city, especially concerning the restoration of privileges and of the old law, and concerning the demolition of the fortress, and other things which he thought would win over their minds. And so, as the city inclined that way, being by the nature of men eager for a better condition, and not willingly remaining in a fortune of which they themselves repented, Edzard too, though at first astonished and indignant at so unexpected a proposal, nevertheless, as a wise man would, thought he must yield to necessity. Without delay the city, discharged by him, swore allegiance to the Duke of Geldern before Oye, the year 1514 now drawing to its close. The sum of this agreement of conditions was this: That Geldern should, at his own expense and without trouble or cost to himself, undertake and defend the cause of the city against the men of Utrecht, who not only did not bring help to the afflicted city but even made war on it with the enemy; that the city should swear allegiance to the name of Geldern in perpetuity, and that the rule over the whole countryside enclosed by the Lauwers and the Ems, in which also the old prefecture,

units.la: Principi cederet : prætoriam potestatem à Principe delegatam in res agri tenerent, & velut Principem repræsentarent, unus è consiliariis principis à principe datus, & quatuor viri è numero honestiorum civium ad hoc idoneorum à Senatu urbano electi, iidemque eodem jure essent, quo Hovetmanni illi veteres quendam fuerant ante bellum Saxonicum, eadem omnia, quæ olim isti, haberent & facerent, servato more antiquo: jus stapulæ, quod vocant, omnium rerum venalium quæ in agro sunt, proveniuntve, integrum per omnia maneret civitati eo modo, quo ante hos motus & arma Saxonica fuêre: In frumento quoque & cerevisiâ idem servaretur, quod olim solebat: αὐτονομία civitati & agro, atque usus patriarum legum maneret: quisque jus suum integrum & illibatum retineret, quisque possessiones, res prædia intra extraque aggeres haberet: nec Princeps[?] quicquam novi institueret: idem nullo unquam tempore vel ipse separaret à civitate agrum, vel separari per alium sineret, aut occasionem separationi daret: munitiones quoque omnes in agro demoliretur, nec novas alias extrueret, extruive patere-tur: tur: denique tributo annuo æquo ac tolerabili ex agro sibi hæredibusque suis pendendo cum civibus & agri incolis compararet, à quo nullæ possessiones aut res in agro sitæ immunes essent. Hæc concepta tum, & probata utrimque: sed in solennem formam redacta, & signata post annos demùm tres, cùm ager totus ab hoste quoque liberatus, & Principi subjectus essct. Is fuit annus à Christo nato M. D. XVIII, & mensis Februarij dies XVIII.
units.tr: should yield to the Prince; that they should hold the praetorian power delegated by the Prince over the affairs of the countryside and represent the Prince as it were, one of the Prince's councillors being given by the Prince, and four men from the number of the more respectable citizens, fit for this, being chosen by the city Senate; and these should have the same right that those former Hovetmanni had before the Saxon war, and should have and do all the same things that those formerly did, the ancient custom being kept. The right of staple, as they call it, over all saleable goods which are in or come from the countryside, should remain entire in every respect to the city in the same way as before these disturbances and the Saxon arms. The same should be kept in regard to grain and beer as was formerly customary. Self-government [αὐτονομία] should remain to the city and the countryside, and the use of the native laws should remain. Each should keep his own right whole and unimpaired, each should hold his possessions, goods and estates within and outside the dikes. The Prince should introduce nothing new. Likewise he should never at any time either separate the countryside from the city himself, or allow it to be separated by another, or give occasion for separation. He should also demolish all fortifications in the countryside, and should not allow others to be built anew. Finally, he should arrange with the citizens and the inhabitants of the countryside for a fair and bearable annual tribute to be paid from the countryside to himself and his heirs, from which no possessions or goods situated in the countryside should be exempt. These terms were then drawn up and approved on both sides, but they were reduced to solemn form and signed only three years later, when the whole countryside had also been freed from the enemy and made subject to the Prince. That was the year of Christ's birth 1518, on the eighteenth day of February.

units.la: Deinde anno M. D. XXI inter Principem & Ordines agri in curiâ Groningana per legatos Geldricos senatumque urbanum sic convenit, ut ipsi in fide Principis essent, & hæredum ejus in perpetuum: Princeps & hæredes integra servarent ipsis privilegia, jura, instituta, leges, consuetudines, secundùm fœdera & pacta olim inter ipsos & civitatem inita. Sic in nomen Geldricum ab Ordinibus juratum, præmissâ conditione hac, non diutiùs validam vim juramenti hujus, quàm Geldrus tueri regionem posset. Et mox hæc pacta à Principe sunt signata die Iunii xx. Verùm cum progressu temporis cùm longiùs paulatim tendere, & à pactis recedere, & civitatis jura arctare deprehenderetur Geldrus, à Marwico prætore primùm incitatus, cui simultas cum senatu intercedebat, deinde irritatus, quod, bello pro Balthasaro Esensi in FrisiâOrientali contra Ennonem Comitem vicinum suscepto, in ejus impensas tributum sibi à civitate negaretur, & suapte naturâ potentiæ per fas & nefas augendæ avidus, & turbulentus, occasione raptâ, quam fors offerebat, per Meinhardum Hammenfem clarum militiâ virum, Daniæ regis auspicia profitentem, occultis mandatis suis instructum, adductis copiis tumultus in agro, & ad ipsas portas urbis cieret, suburbia vastaret & incenderet, Dammonam summâ festinatione muniret, postremo in colloquio Essenæ componendæ rei causâ instituto per Henricum Grovium Erclenii dominum legatum suum, & Hacfordum militum præfectum palàm jam posceret, arcem munitam in urbe sibi extrui, Dammonæque munitiones perfici, civitas merito ab eo animis alienata, ad partes Burgundicas se vertit: Nec mora, re cum agrariis ordinibus deliberata, ex eorum consensu ad Georgium Scenkium Teutoburgium, qui Translavicanis pro Carolo v. Imp. tum præerat, legatos misit, ac deditionem obtulit. Atque illi edoctus celeriter de voluntate Mariæ sororis Caroli Imp. Belgii Gubernatricis, ad quam scripserat, sine mora cum iis, quas in promptu habebat, copiis Groningam profectus, cùm de conditionibus imperandi parendique convenisset, civitatem ordinesque agrarios simul in fidem Caroli Imp. Brabantiæ Ducis & Hollandiæ Selandiæque Comitis, & Frisiæ ac Transisalanæ Domini, velut unius Reip. populum recepit die Iunii mensis viii anno, quem dixi, m. d. xxxvi. Eo facto, cum exercitu Dammonam profectus, eam obsedit, occupatoque interea die viii Iulii per deditionem castello Delffilano, quod Geldri quoque tenebant, copiisque, quæ auxilio obsessis à Dano veniebant, duorum circiter millium, concisis, tandem extremas in angustias redactam dedere se coëgit, durissimis conditionibus. Nam sic convenit, ut duces militiæ Meinardus & Hacfordus in vincula Tentoburgio traderentur: reliqui cohortium præfecti ac milites captivorum instar, inermes, virgam albam manu gerentes sine sarcinis exirent, suaque omnia in oppido relinquerent, nec intra tres menses contra Cæsarem militarent: Oppidani Dammonenses male sibi conscii cum militibus conditione eadem egrederentur: cæteri manere volentes excusandi sui, & experiundæ gratiæ facultatem haberent. Facta hæc die vi Septembr. Deinde cum Bruxella responsum venisset, quò retulerat de omnibus Teutoburgius, ex regiñæ mandato captivi Bruxellam missi, Dammonæ munitiones dirutæ: pro oppido ipsoac ædificiis, quæ & ipsa excidio à Regina & Teutoburgio destinata. deque eo mandata jam data Ioanni Hesso, ab amicis per preces intercessum, decretumque suspensum: dein gratia facta. In tanto tum discrimine Dammona fuit, propterea quòd oportuna tumultuantibus & queti publicæ infestis, fortunaque urbanæ inimicis sit. Parendi imperandique leges sub Burgundis hæ scriptæ, signataque : Omnes & singuli totius provinciæ ordines, qui Amasso & Lavicâ continentur, retinerent jura & privilegia sua per manus à majoribus accepta, leges patrias, statuta, consuetudines: imperium Præfectura veteris, & Selwerdicæ suburbanæ esset ac maneret civitatis: munitiones per agrum omnes, quæ jam essent, evertorentur; nec aliæ in futurum extruerentur, nisi id defensionis requireret necessitas: domus Principe digna, sed inermis & immunita Cæsari ædificaretur in urbe, sumptibus provinciæ totius: reditus ex agro solverentur Cæsari & hæredibus ejus quotannis duodecies mille aureorum Carolinorum. Dammona capta à Teuteburgio totâ Drentiâ Geldri ejecti, Wedda, Coverdiaque captæ, bellum ex universâ illâ vicinia, eodem adhuc anno profligatum. Denique Decembri mense pax interBurgundiam domum & Geldrum composita. Conditiones dictæ inter alias, ut fæderi Gallico, Holsatico, aliisque contra Cæsarem & subditos ejus initis, Geldrus renunciaret: valediceret juri omni in civitatem & agrum Groninganum, Drentiam, sic conuenit, ut duces militia Meinardus & Hacfordus in vincula Tentoburgio traderentur: reliqui cohortium praefecti ac milites captivorum instar, inermes, virgam albam manu gerentes sine sarcinis exirent, suaque omnia in oppido relinquerent, nec intra tres menses contra Caesarem militarent: Oppidani Dammonenses male sibi conscii cum militibus conditione eadem egrederentur: caeteri manere volentes excusandi sui, & experiundae gratiae facultatem haberent. Facta haec die VI Septembr. Deinde cum Bruxella responsum venisset, quo retulerat de omnibus Teutoburgius, ex reginae mandato captivi Bruxellam missi, Dammonae munitiones dirutae: pro oppido ipso ac aedificiis, quae & ipsa excidio a Regina & Teutoburgio destinata, deque eo mandata jam data Ioanni Hesso, ab amicis per preces intercessum, decretumque suspensum: dein gratia facta. In tanto tum discrimine Dammona fuit, propterea quod opportuna tumultuantibus & quieti publicae infestis, fortunaque urbanae inimicis sit. Parendi imperandique leges sub Burgun-
units.tr: Then in the year 1521, an agreement was reached in the court at Groningen between the Prince and the orders of the district, through the Guelderland envoys and the city senate, to this effect: that they themselves should be in the Prince's faith, and that of his heirs, forever; that the Prince and his heirs should keep intact for them their privileges, rights, institutions, laws and customs, according to the covenants and agreements once made between them and the city. The orders then swore an oath to Geldrus on this condition: that the binding force of this oath should last no longer than Geldrus could defend the region. These agreements were soon signed by the Prince on 20 June. But as time went on, it was found that Geldrus was gradually extending his reach, departing from the agreements and tightening the city's rights. He was first stirred up by Marwicus, the praetor, who had a feud with the senate, and then provoked further because the city refused to pay him a levy towards the expenses of the war he had undertaken in East Frisia on behalf of Balthasar of Esens against his neighbour Count Enno. By nature greedy for power by fair means or foul, and restless, he seized the chance that fortune offered. Through Meinhard of Hamme, a man distinguished in arms who served under the King of Denmark and was equipped with his secret instructions, he brought troops into the countryside and right up to the city gates, to stir up disturbances. He ravaged and burned the suburbs and fortified Damme with the greatest haste. Finally, at a conference arranged at Essen to settle the matter, through his envoy Henry Grovius, lord of Ercleny, and Hacford, the commander of his soldiers, he openly demanded that a citadel be built for him inside the city and that the fortifications of Damme be completed. The city, rightly alienated from him, then turned to the Burgundian side. Without delay, after consulting the rural orders, with their consent it sent envoys to Georg Schenk of Tautenburg, who at that time commanded the lands across the Lauwers for the Emperor Charles V, and offered its surrender. He quickly learned of the wishes of Mary, sister of the Emperor Charles and Governor of the Netherlands, to whom he had written. Without delay he set out for Groningen with the troops he had at hand. When terms of command and obedience had been agreed, he received the city and the rural orders together into the protection of the Emperor Charles, Duke of Brabant, Count of Holland and Zeeland, and Lord of Friesland and Overijssel, as one people of a single commonwealth, on 8 June of the year I mentioned, 1536. After this, he set out with his army for Damme and besieged it. Meanwhile, on 8 July, he took the Delfzijl castle by surrender, which the Guelderlanders also held. He also cut to pieces about two thousand men of the force the Dane was bringing to aid the besieged. At last he forced Damme, reduced to the utmost straits, to surrender on very harsh terms. For it was agreed that the commanders Meinhard and Hacford should be handed over to Tautenburg in chains; that the remaining captains of the cohorts and the soldiers should leave unarmed like captives, carrying white wands in their hands and without baggage, leaving all their goods in the town; and that they should not serve against the Emperor within three months. The townsmen of Damme, conscious of their guilt, were to leave with the soldiers on the same terms; the others who wished to remain were to have the opportunity to clear themselves and seek pardon. This was done on 6 September. Then, when a reply came from Brussels to which Tautenburg had reported everything, the prisoners were sent to Brussels by the queen's order, and the fortifications of Damme were demolished. As for the town itself and its buildings, these too had been destined for destruction by the Queen and Tautenburg, and an order concerning this had already been given to John Hesse. Friends interceded through prayers, and the decree was suspended, and then a pardon was granted. Damme was then in great danger, because it was a convenient base for rioters and enemies of public peace and of the city's fortunes. The laws of obedience and command were written and sealed under the Burgundians as follows: all and each of the orders of the whole province, which are contained within the Amasus and the Lavica, should keep their rights and privileges received from their forefathers by hand, their native laws, statutes and customs; the government of the old Prefecture and of the Selwerd suburb should belong to and remain with the city; all the fortifications throughout the countryside that already existed should be overthrown, and no others should be built in future unless the necessity of defence required it; a house worthy of the Prince, but unarmed and without immunity, should be built for the Emperor in the city at the expense of the whole province; the revenues from the countryside should be paid to the Emperor and his heirs every year, twelve thousand Carolus gold pieces. Damme was taken by Tautenburg, and the Guelderlanders were driven out of all Drenthe; Wedde and Coevorden were captured, and the war across that whole neighbourhood was brought to an end in the same year. Finally, in December, peace was concluded between the House of Burgundy and Geldrus. The terms agreed included, among others, that Geldrus should renounce the French and Holstein alliances and others made against the Emperor and his subjects, and should relinquish all right over the city and territory of Groningen, Drenthe, [the rest of the passage repeats:] so it was agreed that the commanders Meinhard and Hacford should be handed over to Tautenburg in chains; that the remaining captains of the cohorts and the soldiers should leave unarmed like captives, carrying white wands in their hands and without baggage, leaving all their goods in the town, and that they should not serve against the Emperor within three months; the townsmen of Damme, conscious of their guilt, were to leave with the soldiers on the same terms; the others who wished to remain were to have the opportunity to clear themselves and seek pardon. This was done on 6 September. Then, when a reply came from Brussels to which Tautenburg had reported everything, the prisoners were sent to Brussels by the queen's order, and the fortifications of Damme were demolished; as for the town itself and its buildings, these too had been destined for destruction by the Queen and Tautenburg, and an order concerning this had already been given to John Hesse; friends interceded through prayers, and the decree was suspended, and then a pardon was granted. Damme was then in great danger, because it was a convenient base for rioters and enemies of public peace and of the city's fortunes. The laws of obedience and command were written and sealed under the Burgun-

units.la: dis hæ scriptæ, signataque: Omnes & singuli totius provinciæ ordines, qui Amasso & Lavicâ continentur, retinerent jura & privilegia sua per manus à majoribus accepta, leges patrias, statuta, consuetudines: imperium Præfecturæ veteris, & Selwerdiæ suburbanæ esset ac maneret civitatis: munitiones per agrum omnes, quæ jam essent, everterentur; nec aliæ in futurum extruerentur, nisi id defensionis requireret necessitas: domus Principe digna, sed inermis & immunita Cæsari ædificaretur in urbe, sumptibus provinciæ totius: reditus ex agro solverentur Cæsari & hæredibus ejus quotannis duodecies mille aureorum Carolinorum.
units.tr: dians as follows: all and each of the orders of the whole province, which are contained within the Amasus and the Lavica, should keep their rights and privileges received from their forefathers by hand, their native laws, statutes and customs; the government of the old Prefecture and of the Selwerd suburb should belong to and remain with the city; all the fortifications throughout the countryside that already existed should be overthrown, and no others should be built in future unless the necessity of defence required it; a house worthy of the Prince, but unarmed and without immunity, should be built for the Emperor in the city at the expense of the whole province; the revenues from the countryside should be paid to the Emperor and his heirs every year, twelve thousand Carolus gold pieces.

units.la: Dammona capta à Teuteburgio totâ Drentiâ Geldri ejecti, Wedda, Coverdiaque captæ, bellum ex universâ illâ vicinia, eodem adhuc anno profligatum.
units.tr: Damme was taken by Tautenburg, the Guelderlanders were driven out of all Drenthe, Wedde and Coevorden were captured, and the war across that whole neighbourhood was brought to an end in the same year.

units.la: Denique Decembri mense pax inter Burgundiam domum & Geldrum composita. Conditiones dictæ inter alias, ut fœderi Gallico, Holsatico, aliisque contra Cæsarem & subditos ejus initis, Geldrus renunciaret: valediceret juri omni in civitatem & agrum Groninganum, Drentiam Tuentiam, si quod haberet aut habere se putaret. Ea pax publicata Groningæ die xvii Decembr. lætissimisque animis ab omnibus accepta, cum omnes bellorum tæderet.Ab hoc tempore vixit civitas concorscum agri ordinibus, mansitque in usu ac possessione juris prioris de Hovetmannis & Hovetmannorum potestate, de stapulā rerum venalium, de frumento, de cerevisia ex formula Geldrica, ut de sententia Burgundicæ formulæ, & de mente paciscentium dubitari non posse videatur. Et est ex eadem formula Burgundica, durante eodem, quem dixi, usu, post annos xiv à civitate simul & agrariis ordinibus jusjurandum datum Philippo Caroli filio, Hispaniæ regi, idque conjunctim rursus, ac Philippus jurejurando reciproco his obligatus, nulla tum prodente se controversia, aut controversiæ suspicione. Nam Dammonenses quod moverunt, velut exempti legi communi, ac præcipui aliquid habentes,id cujusmodi fuerit, quamve habuerit rationem, dicam suo loco. Demùm post aliquot annos per Dammonenses incitati agrarii, paucosque alios, quibus negotiatio allubescebat[?], de stapulæ jure, imprimis in rebus exoticis aliunde importatis queri coeperunt,querelasque ad aulam Burgundicam detulerunt. Aula eodem anno, qui erat M. D. LIX, Arembergio Comiti Gubernatori mandavit, ut inter partes amicam transactionem tentaret. Eâ frustrà per eum tentatâ (nam longius paulatim tendebant querentes, totumque penè fori jus studebant convellere, & oppidani de possessione aut jure suo decedere nolebant) Arembergius. idem die xvi Martij, anno M. D. LX jussit utrosque documenta ante exitum sex hebdomadum apud se producere, & ex his sententiam expectare provisionalem, uti vocant, usque dum controversia plenius cognita tota definiretur: interea voluit Oldermannum juris stapulæ præfectum more suo contra delinquentes agere, sed pœnarum exsecutionem usque ad sententiæ provisionalis promulgationem suspendere. Et cùm pars neutra jussui satisfecisse videretur, ad documenta quod attinebat, idem denuò die xiv Maij præcepit utrique, ut apud Hovetmannos cognitores causam agerent ordinario modo usque ad momentum ferendæ sententiæ: Hovetmannos jussit acta ea omnia exhibere sibi: interea Oldermanuus id observaret, quod ante erat mandatum. Quod ipsum cum iniquius putarent oppidani de Oldermanno (nam extractum iri in longum actionem rebantur, atque interea sine nervo futurum jus civitatis) rem ad Margaretam Parmensem gubernatricem Belgii retulerunt. Illa cum senatu suo commodè interpretata sententiam Arembergii benignè respondit, mandavitque ut ab Oldermanno damnati cautionem præstarent in eventum litis de solvendo judicato: & simul quæ species terum[?] venalium litigiosarum intelligerentur sententiâ Arembergii comprehensæ. Id factum Bruxellæ die xiv Maij, anno M. p. LXI. Post quæ pendente judicio rursus institutæ actiones amicæ ad componendam controversiam, demumque hujus ergo cum mandatis in urbem missus Philippus Cobelius ex secreto senatu regio: cujus prudentiâ & industriâ effectum, ut in capita certa, de quibus erat controversia, formata ab ipso pars utraque acquiesceret, & consentiret, quæ vim juris habèrent interea, dum judicio integro tota causa finiretur. Consensus is solenniter initus & signatus in curiâ Groninganâ die iv & v Augusti, anno M. D. LXIV. Capitum præcipua fuêre : Infrumento ἐπιχωείῳ [?] & cervisia idservaretur, quod esset fadere anni M. CCCC. LXXXII definitum: pecora equini & bubuli generis venalia Groninga in foro sisterentur, ista biduo, hac uno die horis antemeridianis: quo facto, liceret, soluto vectigali usitato, quolibet abigere: butyrum, caseì, lardum, sevum, adeps, terga bubula Groninga & non alibi venum proponerentur, venderenturve: peregrino nihil horum, nec pecorum, nec cæterorum emere in agro liceret, in foro Groningano liceret cuivis, civi, agricolæ, peregrino, liberaque emptorum exportatio esset vectigali soluto. Mercatus solennes in commodum negotiationum plures in urbe instituerentur. Exempta fori juri essent pecora pastionis causâ aliunde in agrum adducta: venalia navibus advecta si esculenta & corruptioni subitæ [?] subita obnoxia sint, jus esset ubivis in agro distrahi: reliqua durabilia cujuscunque generis, frumenta, legumina, saperda, aleces salitæ, ligna, lapides, calx, ferrum, carbones, similiaque non venundarentur intra horas XXIV, ut copia veniendi ad portus civibus esset: tum conjunctim cum civibus tantum emerent agricolæ, quantum ad usus suos domesticos haberent opus; & post alteras horas XXIV si quid mercium esset reliquum, id emere etiam institoribus agrariis non esset vetitum.
units.tr: Finally, in December, peace was concluded between the House of Burgundy and Guelders. Among other conditions, Guelders was to renounce the alliance made with France, Holstein and others against the Emperor and his subjects, and to give up every right he had, or thought he had, over the city and territory of Groningen, Drenthe and Twente. This peace was proclaimed at Groningen on 17 December and was received by everyone with the greatest joy, since all were weary of war. From this time the city lived in harmony with the rural orders, and the earlier law concerning the Hoofdmannen and their authority, the staple of goods for sale, grain and beer, according to the Guelderish form, remained in use and in possession. There can be no doubt, it seems, about the meaning of the Burgundian formula or the intention of the parties to it. And under that same Burgundian formula, while the custom I have mentioned continued, the city and the rural orders together gave an oath after fourteen years to Philip, son of Charles and King of Spain, and Philip in turn bound himself to them by a reciprocal oath. No controversy came forward then, nor any suspicion of one. As to what the Dammonians stirred up, as if they were exempt from the common law and had some special privilege, what kind of thing it was and what standing it had, I will say in its proper place. Finally, after some years, the rural men, incited by the Dammonians, and a few others who fancied trade, began to complain about the right of staple, especially in foreign goods imported from elsewhere, and brought their complaints to the Burgundian court. In the same year, 1559, the court commissioned Count Arenberg, the governor, to try to bring the parties to a friendly settlement. When this attempt by him failed (for the complainants gradually reached further and were eager to overturn almost the whole right of the market, and the townsmen were unwilling to give up their possession or their right), Arenberg, on 16 March 1560, ordered both sides to produce their documents before him within six weeks, and to expect from these a provisional judgment, as it is called, until the whole controversy should be fully examined and finally decided. Meanwhile he wished the Oldermann, prefect of the staple right, to proceed against offenders in his usual way, but to suspend the execution of penalties until the provisional sentence was announced. Since neither party seemed to have obeyed the command as far as the documents went, Arenberg again ordered each side, on 14 May, to conduct the case before the Hoofdmannen as examiners in the ordinary way up to the moment of giving sentence; he ordered the Hoofdmannen to hand all those records over to him, and meanwhile the Oldermann was to observe what had been ordered before. The townsmen thought this more unfair to them concerning the Oldermann (for they believed the action would be drawn out at length, and in the meantime the right of the city would be without force), and they referred the matter to Margaret of Parma, governess of the Netherlands. She, after interpreting Arenberg's sentence favourably with her council, kindly replied and ordered that those condemned by the Oldermann should give security for payment of the judgment in case of losing the suit; and at the same time it was to be understood which kinds of goods for sale were covered by the litigation under Arenberg's sentence. This was done at Brussels on 14 May 1561. After this, while the judgment was pending, friendly proceedings to settle the dispute were started again, and for this purpose Philip Cobelius, of the king's privy council, was at last sent to the city. Through his prudence and diligence it was brought about that both parties agreed to the chapters, drawn up by him, on the points in dispute, and consented that these should have the force of law in the meantime, until the whole case was finally decided. This agreement was solemnly entered into and signed in the Groningen court on 4 and 5 August 1564. The chief chapters were these: that in the instrument the local custom [ἐπιχωρίῳ] and the beer should be kept, as had been defined by the agreement of the year 1482; that horses and cattle for sale should be brought to the market at Groningen, the horses for two days and the cattle for one day, in the morning hours; and that once this was done, it should be lawful, on payment of the usual toll, to drive them away to any place; that butter, cheese, bacon, tallow, lard and hides should be offered for sale and sold only at Groningen and nowhere else; that a foreigner might buy none of these things, nor livestock or anything else, in the countryside, but in the Groningen market anyone, citizen, countryman or foreigner, might buy, and the buyers might export freely on payment of the toll. Regular markets were to be held in the city for the benefit of trade. Livestock brought into the countryside for grazing were to be exempt from market law; goods brought by ship for sale, if they were food and liable to sudden spoilage, could be sold anywhere in the countryside; all other durable goods of every kind, grain, pulses, salted herring, salted anchovies, wood, stone, lime, iron, charcoal and the like, were not to be sold within twenty-four hours, so that citizens would have the chance of buying them at the harbours; then the countrymen were to buy along with the citizens only as much as they needed for their own household use; and after a further twenty-four hours, if any goods remained, it was not forbidden for rural traders to buy them too.

units.la: Quin imo si quis agri incola etiam post primas horas XXIV in usum domesticum aliquid emptum ex his vellet, quæ jam à civibus sint empta, mercibus nondum loco motis, ei id negari eodem, quo prima emptio facta, pretio exhibito non liceret. Mercatores agrarij vectigal aut portorium solverent in usum agri.
units.tr: Indeed, if any inhabitant of the countryside wished, even after the first twenty-four hours, to buy for household use any of those goods which citizens had already bought, while the goods had not yet been moved from their place, it would not be lawful to refuse him this at the same price at which the first purchase was made, once the price was paid. Rural merchants were to pay the toll or customs duty for the use of the countryside. Goods which any of the countrymen imported from elsewhere were free of the staple burden, as were all the other things not named in these chapters. Finally, no one was to be made to take an oath before the Oldermann, the judges or the prefects of trade, without a preceding document sufficient under the laws.

units.la: Quæ quis ex agri incolis aliunde importaret, onere stapulæ essent libera, quemadmodum & omnia reliqua in his capitibus non nominata. Postremo nemo ad jusjurandum ab Oldermanno adigeretur apud judices mercatura præfectos sine præcedente documento legibus sufficiente: atque in hoc ipse Oldermannus & judices jusjurandum darent Reip. Verùm cùm ne his quidem conditionibus contenti possent esse agrarii, Albano Duce rerum potiente in Belgio, rursus ad eum querelas detulere: Ille causâ cognita anno M. D. LXXI, die VII Augusti decretum iterum interposuit, verbis varians à capitibus his, re penè idem. Ejus summa haec: Groninganis integrum sit jus stapulae & mercatum in butyro, caseo, pecore equino bovinoque, frumento omnis generis: quorum nihil liceat exportare, nisi Groningae venale habitum ab horâ matutinâ ad meridiem. Nulli peregrino liceat quicquam sive ἐπιχώριον[?] sive ἐπείσακτον in agro emere aut vendere: in urbe liceat: attamen liberum eidem sit ea, quae ipse advexerit, in ipsis portibus, aut prope eos è navigiis venundare, cui volet. Vitandae fraudis causâ, quae Groningae promercalia fuere, ea à praefecto ad id dato in indicem referantur, vasaque butyri notâ insignantur. In trutinâ urbanâ pondera sint uniformia: nec civis, nec agri incola negotiationibus deditus mensibus Majo, Junio, Julio, Augusto jumenta aliave quaestus faciendi causa pet agrum emere jus habeat, reliquo tempori[?] reliqua mercimonia fœdere anni M. CCCC. LXXXII[?] non comprehensa jus habeat quovis loco, nec tamen liceat nundinationes instituere præterquam Groninga. In usum domesticum cuivis in agro quidvis quocunque loco & tempore emere liberum sit. Contrà fecisse deprehensus primò aureos florenos XXV, secundò L Oldermanno pendat; tertiò, & deinceps arbitrali multâ puniatur: multæ trientem civitas, alterum fiscus regius, tertium Oldermannus capiat. Hic juramento neminem adigat, nisi semiplenâ probatione constrictum: citra eam si quem in judicium trahat, insumtus ipse damnetur. Putans se iniquâ sententiâ apud mercatorum aut Oldermanni tribunal gravatum; si ex agro sit, Hovetmannos; si civis, Senatum appellet, nisi aliud à rege decretum fuerit: Hovetmanni & senatus compendiosè litem expediant. Civitas non miscea se vestigali vinario & cervisiario, cui accisæ nomen, in agro: sed id agrariis impendendum usibus agri relinquat. Publicanus aut quæstor rationes de eo reddat quotannis coram prætore regio, aut Hovetmanno, & ab agrariis ad id delectis. His additum aliquid de conventibus Si quid in his dubii inciderit, ejus explicatio aut definitio penes regem sit, ejusve in Belgio gubernatorem. Hoc decreto perempta sint acta omnia priora ad hanc controversiam pertinentia. Sed isto quoque repudiato decreto, quadriennio post, cum Groningæ coissent agrarii, ut se vinculis his semel exuerent, fœderi ac societati omni, quam cum oppidanis habebant, renunciarunt ritu solenni. Id fuit anno M. D. LXXVI, mense Iannuario. Quo facto, cum, pergerent nihilo minus oppidani, uti solent, & possessionem usu tuerentur, illi opposuêre se; protestari acriter, judicii ministros repellere, mandata contemnere, conventus seorsim habere, ad regium senatum provocare: regius senatus praecipitantius quam par erat decernere, & in fraudem civitatis id quod ab Albano scitum interpretati. Interea pace Gandavensi promulgata, capto Groningæ à militibus suis Caspar Roblesio praefecto regio, Georgio Rennebergio in locum ejus ab Ordinibus generalibus suffecto, crescente indies dissensione & odio inter partes, agrariis nova collegia, nova tribunalia instituentibus, re ad tumultus atque arma spectante, tandem Rennebergius velut Reip. studio ad avertenda pericula & constituendam provinciam, conventum Ordinum ejus indixit in urbe ipsis Calend. Novemb. anno proximo M. D. LXXVII. Illic cùm statim in initio altercationes essent ortæ, contumaciusque & ferociùs agere ac loqui agrarii viderentur, quàm ferendum oppidani putabant, quotquot illorum aderant (nec enim venerant omnes) ab his in custodiam sunt dati. Hinc major secuta animorum exacerbatio: cui medendæ, ac sarciendæ concordiæ (periculosus enim ignis ille videbatur, qui toti Belgio in isto rerum statu posset malo esse) ab Auraico Principe & generalibus Ordinibus Groningam missus fuit summi ingenii, summæque doctrinæ & autoritatis vir Philippus Marnixius Aldegondius, & cum eo Sillius jureconsultus Ordinibus à secretis. Eorumque studio tentata pactitataque multa, conditiones scriptæ inducianum litis; postremò cùm confici res non posset, agrariorum nonnulli clam mandatum dedêre Bartholdo Entenio, ut militem scriberet, civitatique bellum faceret: atque ille ut erat naturâ acer, & in partibus fervens, absque morâ mense Februario sequente arma per Drentiam movit. Civitas verò cùm id audisset, celeritate usa, armatis civibus & cohortibus aliquot emissis priusquam copiæ ejus omnes coire possent, disjectis primùm quæ occurrerant, & prætoriâ quoque cohorte fusâ, in arcem Coverdiam malè tum munitam ipsum confugere, & die xxii Februarii sese dedere coëgit, captivumque cum sociis in urbem abstraxit. Quo tempore sanè adeò fuit inopinâ re asperata plebs, ut vix à furore ejus captivum servare rectores potuerint. Sic oleum camino rursus affusum. Et tamen denuò iterumque binis comitiis compositio tentata, sed sine fructu. Demùm legati ad Mathiam Austriacum novum Belgii Gubernatorem, Principemque Auraicum & generalium Ordinum Senatum Antuerpiam à partibus missi. Illic intercedente & allaborante ipso Auriaco cum Comite Suartzburgio, duobusque è senatu aliis, quibus erat id à Mathiâ ac Senatu demandatum, tandem in hæc capita à legatis inita consensio est: Ab armis & vi utrimque abstinereretur, captivi à civitate dimitterentur, restituerenturque in integrum, cum cæteris vim passis; sententiæ à tempore συγγνώσεως[?] hujus latæ haberentur pro nullis, injuriæ alternæ obligione essent inducta. Groningani manerent in possessione juris pristini, præsertim ejus, quod ante annum M. D. LXXI tenuerant, idque tandiu, donec de controversia in judicio esset pronunciatum: cognitores in eam rem darentur à Mathiâ Gubernatore è senatu Ordinum Belgicorum: apud hos utrique rem agerent, & producerent ea, quæ pro causa sua facere arbitrarentur: interim & à cognitoribus transactio amica tentaretur inter partes, conficereturque, si posset. Processus finiretur intra biennium: id si fieri non posset, terminus pro necessitatis ratione à Gubernatore proferretur. Si qua pars cum culpa sua in mora esset, c marcas auri multam daret, & quidem toties, quoties hoc committeret, ac nihilominus pro more judicii in causa pergeretur. Cognitione finita, cuncta ad Gubernatorem referrentur: Gubernator adscitis in consilium sibi e senatu secreto, vel collegio majore Mechliniensi, viris prudentibus tot, quot poscere rem putaret, contra quos excipere partes non possent, ex actis ipsius sententiam ferret, cui sine contradictione parendum utraque a parte esset. Interea utrinque a vi & injuriis mutuis verborum factorumque sibi temperarent sub poena amittendi juris sui, & M. insuper marcarum auri: ac si privatim aliquis contra delinqueret, poenam ferret pro delicti modo.
units.tr: Those goods which a man from among the inhabitants of the countryside imported from elsewhere were to be free of the staple duty, as were all the other items not named in these chapters. Finally, no one was to be put on oath before the judges or the mercantile prefects by the Oldermannus without a preceding document sufficient under the laws; and in this matter the Oldermannus himself and the judges were to take an oath to the commonwealth. But since the countrymen could not be content even with these conditions, they again brought their complaints to Duke Alva, who then held power in the Netherlands. He, having heard the case, in the year 1571, on the seventh day of August, issued a second decree, varying in words from these chapters but almost the same in substance. Its sum was this: The Groningers shall have the full right of staple and of market in butter, cheese, horses and cattle, and corn of every kind; none of these may be exported unless it has been offered for sale at Groningen from early morning until noon. No outsider shall be allowed to buy or sell anything in the countryside, whether [local or imported]; in the town he may. Nevertheless, whatever he has brought in shall be free for him to sell, from the very harbours or from near them off the ships, to whomever he wishes. To prevent fraud, those goods which were formerly dealt in at Groningen shall be entered on a list by the prefect appointed for this, and the butter vessels shall be marked with a sign. The weights in the town scales shall be uniform. Neither a citizen nor a countryman engaged in trade shall have the right to buy beasts of burden or other things for the sake of gain in the countryside during the months of May, June, July and August; at other times he may have the right to trade in other goods not included in the agreement of the year 1482, in any place; but he may not hold markets anywhere except at Groningen. Anyone in the countryside may buy anything, in any place and at any time, for domestic use. On the contrary, one caught doing otherwise shall pay, for the first offence, 25 gold florins to the Oldermannus; for the second, 50; for the third and thereafter he shall be punished with a fine assessed by the judge; of the fines, the city shall take one third, the royal treasury another, and the Oldermannus the third. He shall not put anyone on oath unless the person is bound by a half-proof; if without such proof he brings someone into court, he himself shall be condemned to pay the costs. A person who thinks he has been wronged by an unjust sentence before the tribunal of the merchants or of the Oldermannus shall appeal, if he is from the countryside, to the Hovetmanni, and if a citizen, to the Senate, unless the king has decreed otherwise; the Hovetmanni and the Senate shall settle the dispute summarily. The city shall not interfere in the countryside with the wine and beer excise, which is called the accise, but shall leave it to be spent on the needs of the countryside. The tax collector or treasurer shall render his accounts on this each year before the royal praetor, or the Hovetmannus, and before countrymen chosen for this purpose. Something further is added concerning the assemblies. If any doubt arises on these matters, its explanation or determination shall rest with the king, or with his governor in the Netherlands. By this decree all earlier acts pertaining to this controversy are annulled. But this decree too was rejected; four years later, when the countrymen had assembled at Groningen, in order to free themselves once and for all from these bonds, they renounced, in the solemn manner, the whole alliance and fellowship which they had with the townsmen. This was in the year 1576, in the month of January. When this was done, the townsmen nevertheless continued as they usually did and maintained possession by use; the countrymen resisted them: they protested vigorously, repelled the officers of the court, despised the mandates, held assemblies separately, and appealed to the royal senate. The royal senate decided more hastily than was fitting, and interpreted what had been enacted by Alva to the detriment of the city. Meanwhile the Pacification of Ghent was proclaimed; Caspar Robles, the royal prefect, was taken at Groningen by his own soldiers, and in his place George Rennenberg was appointed by the General Estates. As the dissension and hatred between the parties grew daily, the countrymen setting up new assemblies and new tribunals, and matters tending toward tumults and arms, Rennenberg at last, as if out of zeal for the commonwealth, to avert the dangers and settle the province, summoned an assembly of its Estates in the city on the first of November in the following year, 1577. There, when at the very start disputes had arisen, and the countrymen seemed to act and speak more obstinately and fiercely than the townsmen thought tolerable, as many of them as were present (for not all had come) were put into custody by the townsmen. From this a greater exasperation of minds followed; to heal it and to mend the concord (for that fire seemed dangerous, which in the state of affairs could be harmful to all of Belgium), Philip Marnix of Aldegonde, a man of great talent, great learning and authority, was sent to Groningen by the Prince of Orange and the General Estates, and with him Sillius, a jurist, secretary to the Estates. By their zeal many things were attempted and negotiated, and terms for a truce in the dispute were drawn up; but at last, when the matter could not be concluded, some of the countrymen secretly commissioned Barthold Entens to raise soldiers and make war on the city; and he, being by nature fierce and burning in the party's cause, without delay in the following February moved arms through Drenthe. The city, when it heard this, acting with speed, sent out armed citizens and some cohorts before all his forces could assemble, scattered first those who came in their way, routed also the praetorian cohort, and forced him to flee into the fortress of Coverden, then poorly fortified, and to surrender on the twenty-second day of February; and it dragged him, a prisoner, with his companions, into the city. At that time the common people were so inflamed by this unexpected event that the magistrates could scarcely save the prisoner from their fury. Thus oil was poured again on the fire. Yet again and again a settlement was attempted at two assemblies, but without result. Finally envoys were sent from the parties to Matthias of Austria, the new governor of Belgium, to the Prince of Orange, and to the Senate of the General Estates at Antwerp. There, with the intervention and labour of the Prince of Orange himself, together with Count Swartzburg and two others from the Senate, to whom this had been committed by Matthias and the Senate, agreement was at last reached by the envoys on these terms: Both sides should abstain from arms and force; the prisoners should be released by the city and restored to their former state, together with the others who had suffered violence; sentences passed since the time of the pardon should be held as void; mutual injuries should be cancelled. The Groningers should remain in possession of their former right, especially of that which they had held before the year 1571, and this until the controversy should be decided in court; commissioners for this purpose should be given by Matthias the governor from the Senate of the Belgian Estates; before these the parties should each plead their case and produce whatever they thought would serve their cause; meanwhile a friendly settlement between the parties should also be attempted by the commissioners, and concluded if it could be. The process should be finished within two years; if this could not be done, the term should be extended by the governor according to the need. If either party were in delay through its own fault, it should pay a fine of 100 marks of gold, and indeed as often as it committed this, and nonetheless the case should proceed according to the usual course of judgment. When the inquiry was finished, everything was to be referred to the governor; the governor, taking into counsel from the Senate in secret session, or from the larger college of Mechlin, as many wise men as he thought the matter required, against whom the parties could not object, should pronounce sentence from the acts, to which both parties should submit without contradiction. Meanwhile on both sides they should refrain from force and from mutual injuries of word and deed, under penalty of losing their right and, in addition, 500 marks of gold; and if anyone privately offended against this, he should bear a punishment proportioned to the offence.

units.la: Agrariis vero durante hac actione liberum esset, quoties & quocunque loco vellent obres ad hanc causam pertinentes, quae ad opidanos non pertinerent, imprimis ad conficiendam in sumptus litis pecuniam, convenire agere separatim, & tributum decernere, dummodo oppidanos & eorum res in hunc usum non gravarent: conventione hanc partes utrimque in conventu Ordinum suorum probarent & sibi mutuo caverent, sub poenis ja dictis: quinimò iuramentum darent præsidi provinciæ suæ, (is tum erat Rennebergius, qui cis ultraque Lavicam Frisiæ, item Transfifalanis [?], Drentiæ & Lingæ præerat) fideliter se servaturos ac præstituros hæc omnia, & si quid contrà committerent hi aut illi, executorem pœnæ eundem hunc non recusaturos: postremò, quò firmiora, & certiora essent omnia, partes, conventione hac probatâ, procuratores ex sui medio ederent, scriptisque mandatis ad eam rem idoneis instruerent, iisque porrò Mathiæ & Ordinum seuatui potestatem darent judicandi & condemnandi in capitibus hi omnibus, ut omnia hæc effectum sortiantur. Actum Antwerpiæ die xxxMaij, anno M.D.LXXV ııı. Subscripsēre Princeps ipseGuilhelmus, Guntherus Suartzburgius, N.Lysfeldius, Jacobus Imannus, & duo agrariorum legati duo item oppidanorum, quorum alter clarissimus atque optimus, & magnæ doctrinæ vir Regnerus Alberda urbis Consùl. Sed reversi domum legati animos suorum, adeò etiam tunc exulceratos repererunt, ut exigua spes conficiendæ concordiæ esse videretur. Quapropter idem consul cum senatore prioris quoque legationis socio Antuerpiam remissus fuit : submissusque ei, cum res traheretur propter difficultatem, & negotiorum aliorum multitudinem, Jacobus Hillebrandus ante decennium consulatu functus, vir gravis, propterea quod res nova & inopina rursum interveniens, civitatem offenderat. Nam agrarii plerique, quos comprehensos dixi, quibusque hæc jam gratia a civitate facta erat, ut in libera custodiâ intra urbem degerent, communicato inter se clam consilio contra datam fidem eodem die, eâdemque pene horâ variis usi technis è custodiâ se eripuerant. Tum nequid majoris inde mali forsan existeret, cùm causa integra tam subito cognosci componique, & gratia restitui non posset, ex consilio ac voluntate Principis Guilhelmi, senatusque generalium Ordinum Mathias edictum interposuit. In eo jussit, ut qui apud Groninganos in custodia reliqui erant, atque ipse simul Bartholdus Entenius, statim dimitterentur: omnes à vi & factis sibi temperarent: controversias suas, & hanc captivitatis, fugę, motorum armorum, aliarum injuriarum aut criminum causam judicio aquo & legitimo, quale in conventione priore descriptum, permitterent: dein cætera omnia eådem conventione comprehensa haberent rata, & sine vitio servarent. Entenius, & cæteri è custodia dimittendi obligarent se, judicio se staturos, & judicato satisfacturos. Oppidanis restituretur possessio juris prioris sine defectu & sine morâ, in quâ turbati ab agrariis erant, eaque iisdem maneret ad latam usque sententiam: Similiter agrarii ab oppidanis restituerentur in integrum in rebus unde controversiæ hujus causa erant dejecti. Præses Rennebergius, & reliqui ejus vicinæ præfecti inferiores, viderent, curarentque diligenter, ne quid contra decretum hoc à quoquam committeretur, committentesque ne ferrent impune. Signatum Antwerpiæ die xxiii Octobr. anno eodem M. D. LXXVIII. Nec diu post reversis jam secundo ad suos legatis dimissi captivi reliqui. Sed occultis consiliis Rennebergii Hispanicas partes jam tum respectantis impedita omnia, atque ita sensim directa res, ut oppressis melioribus in civitate, & in carcerem detrusis, conspirantibus cum eo, quibus odium religionis, studium rerum suarum, patriae incuria inerat, civitas in partes Hispanicas sit delapsa. In eo rerum suarum statu civitas actionibus partis adversae provocata controversiam, & conditionem suam ad Principem Parmensem; qui tum pro rege Belgio praesidebat, retulit, ejusque opem rogavit. Parmensis ex libellis & adjunctis documentis causâ cognitâ, & cum secreto Senatu regio communicatâ, ex ejus sententiâ in hunc modum decrevit: Ob studium tuendae servandaeque Romanae Catholicae religionis, & fidem ac obsequium constans erga regem Groningani habento ad tempus totum jus Stapulae rerum promercalium tàm peregrinarum quàm in agro vicino nascentium. Oldermanno potestas esto contra hoc jus delinquentes ad tribunal societatis mercatorum huic quaestioni destinatu m trahere, ac reos agere; condemnatique si velint Senatum civitatis tantum, nec quenquam aliam appellanto:is in executione moderatione & æquitate utitor, ob afflictam fortunam agrariorum. Cerevisiæ in tabernis cauponariis ac diversoriis usus non esto, nisi Groningana: delicta contraria modo solito puniuntor, Opificia per agrum non exercentor in fraudem societatum oppidanarum, servatorque in hoc sententia anni M.D. XX.die Veneris post Pentecostes lata ab arbitris. Ius administrator per legatum regium & quatuor Hovetmannos à Senatu oppidano deleftos morefolito: omnesque agri incolæ potestati & judiciis editisque eorum parento: Iudices & officiarij nuper contra morem solitum judiciorum causa instituti abrogatisunto: tributa aut onera alia publica toti regioni aut provinciæ communia non decerniuntor, promulgantor, colliguntor, nisi Ordinibus per legatum regium & Hovetmannos convocatis, & re in eorum & oppidanorum conventa deliberata & probata. In iisdem conventibus utriusque partis negotia omnia totius Reip. provincialis tractantor. Ærarium commune unum esto: Acta omnia, pacta, fœdera, conventiones, decreta his contraria irrita, ac pro nullis sunto. Hoc decretum valeto, donec Rex ipse causâ cognitâ sententiam ferat. In calce addit, de vectigali petito, se cum commendatione civitatis ob summam fidem & studium in regem & regias partes ad regem relaturum : sperare, si civitas in eâdem fide&studio ac obsequio perstet, regem non negaturum, sed insuper novis & amplis privilegiis ad reparandam pristinam fortunam eandem civitatem ornaturum. Signatum Valenchenæ die xv April. anno M. D. LXXXI. Et hoc decretum Philippus rex, cum ad eum hac de causâ legati in Hispaniam missi essent Joachimus Ubbena Consul, & Joannes Goudanus urbis Syndicus, causamque totam Parmensis commendâsset, prolixo diplomate, repetitis omnibus decreti hujusce verbis, sed abrogata Parmensis sanctione, laudatâ prolixè civitatis fide & constantia, & meritis egregiis, confirmavit Olysippone in Lusitania, cum annus ageretur M. D. LXXXII. die ultimo Octobris: jussitque esse perpetuum, ac pro privilegio à se dato haberi. Simul eodem die locoque aliud diploma civitati dedit de tributo cerevisiario, sanxitque, ut id, quod ex Albani decreto agrarii soli tractarent, & in rem verterent suam, civitati esset cum ordinibus agri commune, eique erarium poneretur in urbe feris clausum duabus, penderetur in res communes parti utrique, ex voluntate & consensu conjuncto : Atque hoc jure usa civitas est, quantum licuit, ad annum usque M. D. XCIIII, quo anno ad societatem foederis Ordinum Belgicorum, relictis partibus Hispanicis, restitutis & ad gubernacula locatis exulibus, magistratu priori exauctorato, rediit. Tum repetitis veteribus querelis ab agrariis, judicium de controversia Ordinibus generalibus integre permissum. Ab his mox in initio tres intercessores aut arbitratores dati, viri clarissimi & πολιτικώτατοι, Elbertus Leoninus Geldriae Cancellarius, Sebastianus Lofe summae in Hollandia Curiae senator, Joannes Wittenius Consul Campensis, intima mecum amicitia cunjunctus, omnes in senatu & consiliis Ordinum generalium diu versati, qui si possent, una cum illustri Gubernatore D. GUILHELMO LUDOVICO Comite Nassavio controversiam inter partes componerent amicè: si non possent, statuerent pro tempore, quod quieti & regimini expedire videretur, tantisper donec pleniore judicio cognitâ causâ omnia definirentur. Ii, adhibita summa diligentia & studio cum gubernatore, cum[?] frustrà diu in compositione controversiæ universæ laborassent tandem ea, quæ ad formam & ordinem politiæ provincialis in hac conjunctione cum Ordinibus fœderatis, & ad pecuniæ communis administrationem faciebant, accepta in id plena à partibus potestate, primum constituerunt. In his sciverunt ante omnia, ut civitas & ager una sint provincia in perpetuum sub uno Gubernatore: ut conventus provinciæ communes sint utrique parti, habeanturque non alibi quam Groninga. In primis collegium novum instituerunt ad modum cæteris in provinciis fœderatis usitatum, in quod quatuor viros oppidani, totidem agrarii darent, conjunctionis atque unitatis vinculum & nervum: ejus collegij munus esset curare & admi-
units.tr: While this action was under way, the agrarians were free to meet and deliberate separately, as often and wherever they wished, on matters pertaining to this cause that did not concern the townsmen. Their chief purpose was to raise money for the costs of the lawsuit, and they could levy a tax, provided they did not burden the townsmen or their property for this purpose. Both parties were to approve this agreement in the assembly of their own Estates and give each other security under the penalties mentioned above. Moreover, they were to swear an oath to the governor of their province (at that time Renneberg, who presided over Friesland on this side of the Lauwers, and likewise over the Transisalana, Drenthe and Lingen) that they would faithfully keep and carry out all these things, and that they would not refuse to accept this same man as executor of the penalty if either side committed any breach. Finally, so that everything might be more firm and certain, once the agreement was approved, each party was to choose representatives from among its own members and furnish them with written mandates suited to the purpose. They were then to give Matthias and the Council of the Estates the power to judge and condemn in capital cases, so that all these provisions might take effect. Done at Antwerp, 31 May, in the year 1575. Signed by Prince William himself, Gunther Schwarzburg, N. Lysfeld, Jacob Imann, and two legates of the agrarians, and likewise two legates of the townsmen, one of whom was the most distinguished and excellent man, a man of great learning, Regnerus Alberda, consul of the city. But when the legates returned home, they found the minds of their own people still so inflamed that there seemed to be little hope of reaching agreement. For this reason the same consul was sent back to Antwerp with a senator, the companion of the earlier embassy. And because the business dragged on on account of its difficulty and the great number of other affairs, Jacob Hillebrand was sent to join him. He was a serious man who had served as consul ten years before. Meanwhile, a new and unexpected event had again offended the city. For many of the agrarians whom I have mentioned as arrested, and to whom the city had already granted the favour of living in free custody within the town, had secretly conferred among themselves, and on the same day and at almost the same hour, in breach of their pledged word, had escaped from custody by various devices. Lest some greater evil should arise from this, since the case, still undecided, could not be so quickly investigated and settled, nor could the grace be restored, Matthias, acting on the advice and will of Prince William and the Council of the General Estates, issued an edict. In it he ordered that those who were still held in custody at Groningen, together with Bartholdus Entenius himself, should be released at once. All were to refrain from violence and acts of force; they were to submit their disputes, and the cause of this imprisonment, flight, armed disturbances and other injuries or crimes, to a fair and lawful judgment such as had been laid down in the earlier agreement; and then they were to hold all other matters comprehended in that same agreement as binding and keep them without fault. Entenius and the others who were to be released from custody bound themselves to abide by the judgment and to satisfy whatever was decided. The townsmen were to have restored, without delay and without fail, the possession of their former right of which the agrarians had deprived them, and this was to remain with them until the sentence was pronounced. Likewise the agrarians were to be restored by the townsmen to their former position in the property from which they had been ejected in connection with this dispute. Governor Renneberg and the other lesser officials of the neighbouring districts were to see to it, and to take care, that nothing was done by anyone contrary to this decree, and that those who did so should not go unpunished. Signed at Antwerp, 23 October, in the same year 1578. Not long afterwards the remaining prisoners were released, when the legates had returned to their people for the second time. But through the secret schemes of Renneberg, who already then looked to the Spanish party, everything was obstructed and the affair was so gradually steered that, with the better men in the city overpowered and thrown into prison, and with those who conspired with him, in whom there was hatred of religion, zeal for their own interests and neglect of the fatherland, the city slipped over to the Spanish side. In this state of its affairs, the city, provoked by the actions of the opposing party, referred the dispute and its own situation to Prince Parma, who then governed as the king's lieutenant in the Netherlands, and asked for his help. Parma, after examining the petitions and the accompanying documents, and after communicating the case with the royal Council, decided in the following manner, by its judgment: Because of their zeal in defending and preserving the Roman Catholic religion, and their constant faith and obedience towards the king, let the Groningers have for all time the whole right of staple for goods for trade, both those brought from abroad and those produced in the neighbouring countryside. Let the alderman have the power to bring to the tribunal of the merchants' guild, appointed for this inquiry, those who transgress this right, and to prosecute them as defendants; and if the condemned wish to appeal, let them appeal only to the city Senate and to no one else. In carrying out this, let him use moderation and fairness, because of the afflicted fortunes of the agrarians. Let there be no use of beer in taverns and inns except Groningen beer; offences against this are to be punished in the usual way. Crafts are not to be practised in the countryside to the detriment of the townsmen's guilds, and in this matter the judgment given by the arbiters on the Friday after Pentecost in the year 1520 is to be observed. Justice is to be administered, as usual, through the royal legate and four headmen chosen by the town Senate; and all inhabitants of the countryside are to obey its authority, its courts and their edicts. Judges and officials recently appointed for the courts, contrary to the customary practice, are to be abolished. Taxes or other public burdens common to the whole region or province are not to be decreed, promulgated or collected, except when the Estates have been convened by the royal legate and the headmen, and the matter has been discussed and approved in their assembly and that of the townsmen. In these same assemblies all business of both parties concerning the whole provincial commonwealth is to be transacted. Let there be one common treasury. All acts, pacts, covenants, agreements and decrees contrary to these are void and of no effect. This decree shall stand until the king himself, once the case has been examined, pronounces sentence. At the end he added that, regarding the tax on beer that had been requested, he would refer the matter to the king, commending the city for its great loyalty and zeal towards the king and the royal party; he hoped that, if the city persisted in the same loyalty, zeal and obedience, the king would not refuse, but would moreover adorn the same city with new and ample privileges for restoring its former fortunes. Signed at Valenciennes, 15 April, in the year 1581. And this decree was confirmed by King Philip at Lisbon in Portugal, on the last day of October in the year 1582, when Joachim Ubbena, consul, and John Goudanus, syndic of the city, had been sent to him as legates in this cause, and Parma had commended the whole matter to him. He confirmed it by a lengthy diploma, repeating all the words of this decree, but with Parma's sanction annulled; he praised the city's loyalty and constancy at length and its outstanding services, and ordered that it should be perpetual and held as a privilege granted by himself. On the same day and in the same place he gave the city another diploma concerning the beer tax, and he provided that what the agrarians alone had dealt with and turned to their own profit under the decree of Alva should be common to the city and the country Estates, and that the revenue should be placed in a treasury in the city closed with two locks, and be paid out for common purposes to each party, by mutual will and consent. The city enjoyed this right, as far as it was allowed, until the year 1594. In that year, having abandoned the Spanish party, and with the exiles restored and placed back in power, and the former magistracy removed, it returned to the union of the Belgic Estates. Then, with the old complaints renewed by the agrarians, the judgment on the controversy was entrusted entirely to the General Estates. Soon at the outset they appointed three intermediaries or arbitrators: men most distinguished and most skilled in public affairs, Elbert Leoninus, chancellor of Gelderland; Sebastian Lofe, senator of the high court in Holland; and John Wittenius, consul of Kampen, who was joined to me in close friendship. All of them had long been involved in the Senate and councils of the General Estates. They were to settle the dispute between the parties amicably, if they could, together with the illustrious governor, Lord William Louis, Count of Nassau. If they could not, they were to decide for the time being whatever seemed expedient for peace and government, until the whole matter was settled by a fuller judgment after the case had been examined. After these men had, with the greatest diligence and zeal, and together with the governor, laboured for a long time in vain over the settlement of the whole controversy, they at last first established those matters which pertained to the form and order of the provincial polity in this union with the allied Estates, and to the administration of the common treasury, having received full authority from the parties for this purpose. In these matters they resolved above all that the city and the countryside should be one province for ever under one governor; that the common assemblies of the province should belong to both parties, and be held nowhere else but at Groningen. First of all they set up a new college, after the manner customary in the other provinces of the union, to which the townsmen and the agrarians should each give four men, as the bond and sinew of this union and unity. The duty of this college was to take care of and administer the money of the province arising from the tax and excise, for the uses of peace and war, and likewise the monastic goods that had been transferred to the common treasury. In addition, it was to take care that the true religion should be propagated and preserved, and that no place be given to the exercise of error,...

units.la: Decretum III.viro-rū ab Ordinibus generalibus delegatorum. [?]nistrare pecuniam provinciæ ex tributo & vectigali provenientem in usus pacis & belli, bona item monastica in ærarium commune relata: adhæc dare operam, ut religio vera propagetur & conservetur, exercitio erronea locus non detur, ne qua fraus bonis Ecclesiasticis & similibus ad pios usus à majoribus destinatis fiat: provinciæ ordines ad conventus, cum opus est, absente Gubernatore convocare, in conventibus deliberanda proponere, Ordinum suffragiis decreta exequi, denique partem curæ & potestatis in iis, quæ belli [?]sunt, cum Gubernatore tenere. Collegii caput sit Gubernator, isque in eo compareat quoties velit aut possit: collegæ vicissim præsideant per septimanas, & alternatim ex urbe aut agro. Collegio quæstor etiam additus communibus suffragiis legendus tractandæ pecuniæ, itidem scriba à secretis, ostiarius, ministrique inferiores alii: Præterea sic studio atque autoritate eorundem inter partes convenit, ut duo semper ex hac provincia assessores sint in collegio generalium Ordinum, qui cum cæteris deliberandi & statuendi potestatem de rebus fœderis habeant, alter ex oppidanis, ex agrariis alter: unus item in ordinum senatusenatu, & unus in senatu rerum maritimarum, idque alternatim, ita ut si iste ex urbe fuerit, hic sit ex agro, & contra: Provincia pro modo virium certam partem sustineat onerum, quae tuendo fœderi sunt necessaria: in negotiis provincialibus aut communibus uno utatur sigillo ex urbano & agrario confecto. Civitas in consessibus & actionibus ac rebus omnibus priores partes teneat, agrarij secundas: in suffragiis tamen pares sint: quæ si discrepent, delectis pari numero utraque à parte permittatur res: qui & ipsi si nequeant consentire inter se, Gubernator suffragio suo dissensionem dirimat. Et hæc ex partium consensu. De mercatus jure, & controversis rebus aliis sic, uti judices, pronunciarunt. Civitas in possessione juris Stapulæ pariter in rebus in agro natis & peregrinis maneto: propolæ & propolia in agro non sunto: de cerevisiæ usu res maneto in eo statu, in quo solet ex fœdere esse: Hovetmanni quoque ad judicandas res relinquuntor iidem, & eádem in potestate, qui & quâ in potestate, constituti sunt ab Ordinem senatu statim in initio dedita Groninga. Cuncta hæc valento, quoad ab Ordinibus generalibus in pleno possessorio, aut petitorio aliter fuerit definitum. Quae contra haec ab agrariis quoquo modo acta, coeptaque, irrita sunto; nec fas esto, imposterum quicquam eosdem impediendis his tentare: contra commissa ex legibus puniuntor: quaestio de accisis, uti vocant, evanescito ex partium consensu.
units.tr: Decree of the three deputies of the General Estates. [?]nistrare the money of the province arising from the tax and excise, for the uses of peace and war, likewise the monastic goods transferred to the common treasury. Besides, they are to take care that the true religion is propagated and preserved, that no place is given to erroneous worship, and that no fraud is committed against ecclesiastical goods and the like, which our ancestors destined for pious uses.
