The provincial Estates are to convene the assemblies when needed in the Governor's absence, to propose matters for deliberation there, to carry out decrees by the votes of the Estates, and finally to share with the Governor the care and power over those matters which concern war. The Governor is to be head of the college, and he is to attend it as often as he wishes or is able. The colleagues in turn are to preside by weeks, alternately from the city and from the countryside. A quaestor is also to be added to the college, chosen by common vote to handle the money, likewise a secretary, a doorkeeper, and other lesser officers: Besides, through the zeal and authority of the same men, it was agreed between the parties that there should always be two assessors from this province in the college of the General Estates, who together with the others are to have the power of deliberating and deciding on matters of the covenant. One of them is to come from the townsmen, the other from the rural party. Likewise, one is to sit in the senate of the Estates and one in the senate for maritime affairs, alternately, so that if the one is from the city the other is from the countryside, and vice versa. The province is to bear, according to its strength, a certain share of the burdens necessary for defending the covenant. In provincial or common business it is to use one seal, made from the city and rural parts together. In assemblies, proceedings and all matters the city is to hold the first place and the rural party the second; in votes, however, they are to be equal. If these disagree, the matter is to be left to chosen men, equal in number from each side; if they too cannot agree, the Governor is to settle the disagreement with his vote. And these things were agreed by consent of the parties. Concerning the right of the market and other disputed matters, the judges gave the following ruling: The city is to remain in possession of the staple right, equally in matters produced in the countryside and in foreign goods. Hawking and hawkers are not to be in the countryside. As to the use of beer, the matter is to remain in the state it usually is in under the covenant. The Hovetmen are also left to judge cases, the same men and with the same power by which they were appointed by the Estates' senate at the beginning, given at Groningen. All these shall hold good until the General Estates decide otherwise in a full possessory or petitory action. Whatever the rural party has done or begun against these in any way shall be void, and it shall not be lawful for them to try to hinder these things in future. Offences committed against them are punished by the laws. The inquiry concerning the excise, as they call it, shall lapse by consent of the parties.

units.la: Omnia haec, quae hac sententia definita sunt, ut effectum suum sortiantur sine mora ac sine vitio, & sarta tecta serventur, Gubernator, & Hovetmanni operam danto. Pronunciatum praesente Gubernatore, & parte utraque die xvii Februar. Juliani, anno M. D. xcv Groningae. Sed agrarii autore Verrucio Syndico, jurisconsulto eximio offensi pronunciato non solum abrogationem hujus, sed etiam reformationem aut reductionem totius causae Ordines generales flagitarunt. Ab Ordinibus novi judices numero ix, peritissimi quique dati, hisque cognoscendi definiendique summa potestas tributa. Hi tota re diligenter excussa & considerata tandem anno M. D. xcvii, die xi Januarii Juliani in consessu generalium Ordinum, patentibus conclavis valvis, sententiam tulêre. Quæ ut intelligi possit, quæ partium postulata fuerint, aperiendum. Agrarii ordines secuti vestigia consiliorum priorum de solvendo fœdere, divortium postulaverunt, separationem integram per quam sibi consulerent seorsim, suamque tenerent remp. divisam à civitate, nec quicquam cum hac haberent commune, præter viciniam & commercia libera. Speciatim verò Hovetmannorum à senatu oppidano datorum jurisdictionem recusabant omninò, conventus habere suos, quando & ubi commodum sibi, seclusa civitate, in iis de rep. consultare & statuere, collegium provinciale suum tenere, judices summos exse [?] edere volebant: jus fori rerum venalium in oppido, & id quod de frumento & cerevisia dixi, ex fœderibus promanans, in universum rescissum cupiebant. Minora mittoCivitas contra, conjunctionem solitam summa ratione institutam olim, longissimoque tempore probatam, transactionibus & decretis multis roboratam, poscebat: Hovetmannorum electionem & potestatem ex more prisco, quæ cum eâ cohærent, pactum item vetus de cerevisia, legem de frumento Σιτωνείῳ[?], denique stapulæ jus integrum in omnibus rebus venalibus domi natis aut peregrinis&importatis, relinqui sibi, & firmari petebat. Judices pronunciarunt hoc modo: Sententia trium virorum deputatorum anno M. D. xcv lata abrogata esto. Civitas & ager una provincia, una ditio sunto, & conjunctim ab ordinibus suis reguntur. Omnia jura & reditus, qui quondam Principis fuêre, omnes item ex tributis recentibus omnis generis provenientes pecunia exercentur, & impendantur, quò debent, ex consensu communi partis utriusque: monasteria & bona monastica, & quæ ejus generis in urbe & agro, item in Præfectura vetere & suburbanâ conjunctis sententiis conferuntur in usus pios: ad administrationem pecuniæ publicæ & censuum, ac ad ea, quæ ab ordinibus decernentur exequenda & efficienda deliguntur viri idonei pari numero utraque à parte, iisq; mandata & munerum limites præscribuntor, cujusmodi è re esse provinciæ ordines putabunt: interea collegium ante biennium institutum, eâ formâ, quâ institutû est, maneto tantisper donec nec hæc erunt confecta: munera à Principe conferri aut committi solita ab ordinibus conjunctim conferuntor & demandantor. Camera justitiæ, uti vocant, id est tribunal Hovetmannorum, & ejus præses (legatum dicunt) & officiarii cæteri illuc pertinentes, exceptis ipsis Hovetmannis, quos sola civitas edet, constituuntor, committuntor, juramento obligantor conjunctim ab ordinibus provinciæ, ut nomine reip. aut potestatis superioris jus dicant ex legibus provincialibus, & consuetudine antiquitus receptâ, in causis ab anno M. D. XXI, ad annum M. D. LX in hoc tribunali cognosci solitis: provinciæ totius negotia neutra pars seorsim, nec quisquam omnino partis alterius extra conventus provinciales tractato. Agrariis liberum esto negotiari cum quibuslibet, quocunq; loco, quibuscunq; in mercimoniis iis libitum erit: exceptis rebus quę in agro proveniunt aut sunt, ut butyro, caseo, equis, bubus, frumento, quarum exportatio vetita esto, nisi ante Groningæ promercales fuerint: Et tamen agrarii jus habento mercâdi & vendendi mutuò in usus rei suæ familiaris, etiam ea, quæ Groningæ promercalia non fuere. units.tr: All these things defined by this sentence are to take effect without delay or fault, and to be kept whole and intact; the Governor and the Hovetmen are to see to it. Pronounced in the presence of the Governor and both parties, on 17 February, Julian style, in the year 1595 at Groningen. But the rural party, offended by the pronouncement, at the urging of Verrucius the syndic, an outstanding jurist, demanded from the General Estates not only the repeal of this but also a reform or reopening of the whole case. The Estates appointed new judges, nine in number, all of great experience, and gave them the highest authority to hear and decide the matter. After examining and weighing the whole affair carefully, they at last pronounced their sentence in the year 1597, on 11 January, Julian style, in the assembly of the General Estates, with the doors of the chamber thrown open. So that it may be understood what the demands of the parties were, this must be explained. The rural Estates, following the steps of their earlier plans to dissolve the covenant, demanded a divorce, a complete separation by which they might look after themselves apart and keep their own commonwealth divided from the city, having nothing in common with it except neighbourhood and free trade. In particular they utterly refused the jurisdiction of the Hovetmen appointed by the city senate. They wanted to have their own assemblies, whenever and wherever it suited them, excluding the city, to consult and decide on public affairs there, to keep their own provincial college, and to issue supreme judges of their own. They also wanted the right of the market for goods sold in the town, and what I have said about grain and beer, which arises from the covenants, to be rescinded altogether. I omit the minor points. The city, on the other hand, demanded and asked that the long-established union, founded of old on the highest reasoning, long approved and strengthened by many agreements and decrees, be upheld; that the election and power of the Hovetmen by ancient custom, which are bound up with it, be kept; likewise the old agreement about beer, the law about grain, and finally the full staple right over all goods for sale, whether produced at home or brought in from abroad, be left and confirmed to it. The judges ruled as follows: The sentence of the three deputies pronounced in 1595 is to be repealed. City and countryside are to be one province, one dominion, and jointly governed by their Estates. All rights and revenues that once belonged to the Prince, and all revenues of every kind arising from the recent taxes, are to be spent and applied, where they ought to go, by the common consent of both parties. Monasteries and monastic goods, and such property of that kind in the city and countryside, likewise in the old and suburban Prefecture, are by joint sentence to be devoted to pious uses. For the administration of public money and levies, and for carrying out and effecting what the Estates decide, suitable men are to be chosen, equal in number from each party; their commissions and the limits of their offices are to be prescribed as the provincial Estates think fitting for the province. Meanwhile the college instituted two years earlier is to remain in the form in which it was set up, until these matters are settled. Offices which were customarily conferred or committed by the Prince are to be conferred and entrusted jointly by the Estates. The Court of Justice, as they call it, that is, the tribunal of the Hovetmen, and its president (they call him the legate) and the other officials pertaining to it, except the Hovetmen themselves, whom the city alone shall nominate, are to be appointed, commissioned and bound by oath jointly by the Estates of the province, so that in the name of the commonwealth or the higher power they may administer justice according to the provincial laws and the custom received from of old, in cases which from 1521 to 1560 were usually heard in this tribunal. The affairs of the whole province are not to be handled separately by either party, nor by anyone at all of one party outside the provincial assemblies. The rural party is free to trade with anyone, in any place, in whatever goods they please, except products of the countryside or things that are there, such as butter, cheese, horses, cattle and grain, whose export is forbidden unless they have first been offered for sale at Groningen. Yet the rural people are to have the right to trade and sell among themselves for the needs of their own households, even in goods that were not offered for sale at Groningen. If the parties cannot agree among themselves on the form and manner of holding the market

Hi à biennio, anno scilicet M. D. XCIX, die XXVII Febr. Juliani partim interpretantes sententiam priorem, partim illiquida definientes, hunc in modū pronunciarunt denuò: Omnes merces aut res importatæ in agrum, etiamsi in agro jam sint, non sint obnoxiae stapulae juri, easque emere, vendere, commutare inter se agrariis liceat: exceptis equis, hinnulis, bubus, vaccis, trimestre longiusve tempus in agro pastis, qui in agro natis accenseri & fort[?] oppidani juri subjecti esse debent. In agro nata & stapulae subjecta non alia censeri debent quàm haec: butyrum, caseus, equi, pulli, boves, vaccae, triticum, secale, hordeum, avena, far: atque haec omninò, ni antè promercalia Groningæ[?] fuerint, distrahere in agro licitum non sit. Sub iis, quae in usum rei familiaris vendere & emere licet, etiam eu comprehendantur, quae lanij, pistores, propolae, aut institores in usum rei suae in agro coëmunt, ut minutim rursum vendant. Agrarius peregrino vendens res suas fori juri subjectas immunis à poena sit, nisi constiterit, scisse, peregrinum esse, quo cum contraxit. Hovetmanni ab oppidanis electi, ab Ordinibus totius provinciae potestatem judicandi accipiant, & iis, ac apud eos sacramento se obligent ex formâ solenni, in sententia ascripta. Ante hoc sacramentum praestitum Hovetmanni pro Hovetmannis non habeantur, & acta eorum velut non acta censeantur. Præses, Hovetmanni, scribę à secretis, accensi, in fide sint utriusque partis pari modo, nullo præcipuo civitatis iure præter Hovetmannorum electionem & officii limites ab utraque parte iis præscribantur. Præses & Hovetmanni solam jurisdictionem tractent in causis solitis ab anno M.D.XXI ad annum M.D.LX, potestatem reliquam magistratus, & politicum regimen agri non attingant: agrariis liceat separatim suos conventus habere in causis ad ipsos seorsim sine civitate pertinentibus. Ordines huius provinciæ, Ordines urbis Groningæ, & Omlandiæ, agrarios solos Omlandios inter Amasum & Lavicam appellare, rectum sit. Agrarii vectigalia nulla, mercatus solennes, trutinas publicas instituant sine consensu Ordinum provinciæ omnium: agrariorum postulatum de subdivisione tributorum & onerum inter civitatem & agrum adhuc non audiatur: interim quod in onerum modo, quem pro rato provincia hæc tenetur sustinere, ex tributis & censibus jam usitatis solvi non poterit, id conficiatur ex quinta census aut proventus omnium bonorum immobilium, agrorum pariter & adi[?]ficiorum, rusticorum urbanorumque, ex formâ anni M. D. LXXVII : & hoc fervetur, donec de modo alio partes convenerint, aut aliter ab Ordinibus generalibus fuerit decretum. Cætera actionis hujus nondum satis explicata ac probata explicentur & probentur plenius, ut ferri sententia possit; & tenen-tur oppidani rei respondere peremptoriè.

[...] for use in the household [...] in taverns or inns [...] except Groningen [...] the former place [...] opinion, votes [...] votes in provincial matters [...] likewise [...] received [...] but while [...] to find [...] Let no one attempt anything similar in future: concerning aid sought from the country people for payment of the old debt and the necessary expenses, since the matter is not yet sufficiently clear, the same parties are to lay that debt and the necessary expenses before the General Estates, so that once the matter is known they may settle and pronounce a judgement. All this is to be done saving the right of the treaties and agreements between the allied provinces in Belgium, and without diminishing the authority of the General Estates and of the Governor, which is owed from the Groningen settlement of 1594 or otherwise. Finally, the remaining demands of the parties are rejected, and costs are compensated. Pronounced on 11 January 1597. Signed on behalf of the General Estates, C. Aerssen. But since from the wording of this judgement a new dispute arose between the parties, it was referred back to the General Estates, and they delegated cognizance and the power of judging to the earlier judges. These, after two years, namely on 27 February 1599, partly interpreting the former judgement and partly settling matters not yet clear, pronounced again in this manner: All merchandise or goods imported into the countryside, even if they are already in the countryside, are not subject to the staple right, and the country people may buy, sell and exchange them among themselves: excepting horses, foals, oxen and cows pastured in the countryside for a term of three months or longer, which are to be counted as native to the countryside and must be subject to the townsmen's law. The things born in the countryside and subject to the staple are to be counted as only these: butter, cheese, horses, foals, oxen, cows, wheat, rye, barley, oats, spelt; and these, unless they were first offered for sale at Groningen, it is not lawful to sell in the countryside. Among the things which it is permitted to buy and sell for the household, those also are to be included which butchers, bakers, retailers or hawkers buy in the countryside for their own use, to resell in small quantities. A country man selling his goods, which are subject to the market law, is to be free from penalty, unless it is shown that he knew the person with whom he dealt to be a foreigner. The headmen, chosen by the townsmen, are to receive the power of judging from the Estates of the whole province, and are to bind themselves to them and before them by oath in the solemn form written in the judgement. Before this oath is taken, the headmen are not to be regarded as headmen, and their acts are regarded as not acts. The president, the headmen, the secretary and the officers are to be equally faithful to both parties, with no special right of the city apart from the election of the headmen and the limits of their office, which are to be prescribed to them by each party. The president and the headmen are to deal only with the jurisdiction in customary cases from the year 1521 to 1560, and are not to touch the remaining power of the magistrate or the political government of the countryside; the country people may have their own separate assemblies in cases belonging to themselves apart from the city. It is right that the Estates of this province, the Estates of the city of Groningen and of Omlande, call only the country people between the Ems and the Lauwers "Omlanders." The country people are not to institute any tolls, solemn markets or public scales without the consent of the Estates of the whole province; the country people's demand for a division of taxes and burdens between the city and the countryside is not yet to be heard; meanwhile, what cannot be paid from the taxes and levies already in use, in the measure of the burden which this province is bound to bear in proportion, is to be made up from a fifth of the assessment or income of all immovable goods, of fields as well as buildings, rural and urban, according to the form of the year 1577; and this is to be observed until the parties agree on another method, or the General Estates decree otherwise. The remaining matters of this action, not yet sufficiently explained and proved, are to be explained and proved more fully, so that a judgement can be pronounced; and the townsmen are bound to answer peremptorily.

units.la: Interea quæ servanda sint in usu juris stapulæ, recensent & præcipiunt ex formulâ (cobelia aut Albanâ), de tempore proponendi in publico merces, de loco, de indice earum, ex quibus vectigal forisfolutum, de modo vectigalis certo in singulas mercium species: interdicuntque oppidanis institutione novorum vectigalium & aggravatione veterum: addunt de trutinæ curâ & inspectione contra fraudes.
units.tr: Meanwhile they recount and prescribe what is to be observed in the use of the staple right, following the formula (Cobelia or Albana): concerning the time for setting goods out in public, the place, the list of them by which the toll is paid in advance, and the rate of the toll fixed for each kind of merchandise; and they forbid the townsmen to introduce new tolls or to increase old ones; they add provisions on the care of the scales and their inspection against fraud.

units.la: Denique de Oldermanno, & iis, qui illo in subsellio de Stapulæ jure judicant, subijciunt, statuuntque, ne Oldermannus carens semiplenâ probatione quenquam ad jusjurandum adigat, utque accusatus in hoc casu velut innocens absolvatur. Oldermannus verò insumptus, & pœnam pro excessus modo arbitrariam condemnetur: ut semiplena probatio habeatur: testimonium affirmativum testis jurati, modò is non fit in ministerio ipsius Oldermanni, qui reijci[?] ut suspectus potest. Oldermannus & judices hi nihil potestatis, aut jurisdictionis sibi usurpent in agrarios praeter id, quod ad ipsorum cognitionem proprie pertinet: Idem Oldermannus ad hoc tribunal suum neminem citet ex agro nisi per mandatum Camerae provincialis, id est, Praesidis & Hovetmannorum: agrarii & peregrini à sententia hujus tribunalis Hovetmannos cum praesidè, cives senatum urbanum appellent, & recognitionem petant: Huic sententiae in consessu Ordinum generalium pronunciatæ, & nomine eorundem à summo scribâ à secretis subscriptæ, addidere judices iidem aliam quoque eodem die & loco. In eâ concedunt agrariis ad exsolvendum æs alienum tributum agro toti imponere secundum jugera per octennium eo modo, quem ipsi sufficere arbitrabuntur, atque insuper ex bonis monasticis ex decreto Ordinum generalium aureorum xvi millia caperę[?]. Ut tamen æs hoc alienum priùs liquidum fiat apud ipsos provinciae Ordines, nec excedat summam lxiv millium aureorum, quam summam ipsi agrarii antè erant professi lento, quoad ab Ordinibus generalibus in pleno possessorio, aut petitorio aliter fuerit definitum. Qua contra hæc ab agrariis quoquo modo acta, cœptaque, irrita sunto; nec fas esto, impositerum quicquam eosdem impediendis his tentare: contra commissa ex legibus puniuntor: quæstio de accisis, uti vocant, evanescito ex partium consensu. Omnia hæc, quæ hac sententiâ definita sunt, ut effectum suum sortiantur sine mora ac sine vitio, & sarta tecta serventur, Gubernator, & Hovetmanni operam danto.
units.tr: Finally, concerning the Oldermannus and those who sit on the bench of the Staple court to judge, they lay down and decree that the Oldermannus, lacking a half proof, shall not put anyone to the oath, and that the accused in this case shall be acquitted as innocent. But if the Oldermannus has been contrary to this, he shall be condemned to a penalty to be assessed according to the degree of his excess, so that a half proof is held to exist when a sworn witness gives affirmative testimony, provided he is not in the service of the Oldermannus himself, and may be rejected as suspect. The Oldermannus and these judges shall not usurp any power or jurisdiction over the agrarians beyond what properly belongs to their own cognizance. The same Oldermannus shall summon no one from the country to this his tribunal except by a mandate of the provincial chamber, that is, of the Governor and the Hovetmanni. The agrarians and foreigners may appeal from the sentence of this tribunal to the Hovetmanni with the Governor, the citizens to the city senate, and may ask for a review. To this sentence, pronounced in the assembly of the General Estates and signed in their name by the chief secretary, the same judges added another, on the same day and in the same place. In it they grant the agrarians, for paying their debts, a tax to be laid on the whole land by the yoke for eight years, in whatever manner they themselves judge sufficient, and in addition that sixteen thousand gold pieces be taken from the monastic goods by decree of the General Estates. However, so that this debt be first made clear before the provincial Estates themselves, and not exceed the sum of sixty-four thousand gold pieces, which sum the agrarians had earlier professed, until the General Estates have decided otherwise in a full possessory or petitory action. Whatever the agrarians have done or begun in any way contrary to these things shall be void; nor shall it be lawful for anyone to attempt to hinder them in these matters; offences committed against this shall be punished according to the laws; the inquiry concerning the excise, as they call it, shall lapse by agreement of the parties. The Governor and the Hovetmanni shall see to it that all these things, defined by this sentence, take effect without delay and without fault, and are kept whole and intact.

Si de formâ ac modo habendi fori convenire inter se partes non potuerunt, compendio ea, quæ controversa ipsis sunt, exponunto; sententiam generalium Ordinum de iisdem expectanto. Agrariis: liberum esto cerevisiam in usum familia suæ coquere; venundandi quæstusque faciendi causa, non esto; nec in tabernis aut diversoriis ullius cerevisiæ præterquam Groningane usus per totum agrum concessus habetor. Groningani in possessione loci prioris in scribendo, signando, sedendo, suffragiis ferendis manento, pariaque suffragia in actionibus & deliberationibus provincialibus retinento.Suffragiis inter se pugnantibus omnes modi & rationes æquæ & usitatæ adhibentor ad ea concilianda: si id non successerit per Gubernatorem, & delectos ab utraque parte parinumero dissensio dirimitor, usque dum modus alius melior fuerit ad hanc rem repertus & introductus: conventus Ordinum indicuntor suffragiis Ordinum eorundem congregatorum, aut edicto Gubernatoris, aut denunciatione eorum, qui eâ de re mandata habebunt, idque iis locis, qui idonei maximè videbuntur. Acta, novationes, usurpationes, quæ adversantur his, ac impedimento sunt, abrogata & pro nullis sunto, nec quicquam impsleo[?]imposterùm simile tentator: De subsidio ab agrariis petito ad solutionem aris alieni veteris, & impensas necessarias, quoniam non satis adhuc res liquet, iidem tenentur es illud alienum & impendia necessaria apud Ordines generales exponere, ut re cognita ab iis statui & ferri sententia possit. Omnia hæc salvo jure fœderum & pactorum inter provincias socias in Belgio, & sine diminutione auctoritatis Ordinum generalium & Gubernatoris, quæ ex transactione Groningana anni M. D. XCIV, aut alias his debetur. Postremò postulata reliqua partium reiiciuntur, & sumptus compensantur. Pronunciatum die XI Januar. anno M. D. XCVII. Subscripsit nomine Ordinum generalium C. AERSEN. Verum ex sententiæ hujus verbis cum nova lis esset orta partibus, ea ad Ordines generales iterum relata, ab iis cognitio & judicandi potestas prioribus judicibus delegata fuit. Hi à biennio, anno scilicet M. D. XCIX, die XXVII Febr. Juliani partim interpretantes sententiam priorem, partim illiquida definientes, hunc in modum pronunciarunt denuò: Omnes merces aut res importatæ in agrum, etiamsi in agro jam sint, non sint obnoxiæ stapulæ juri, easque emere, vendere, commutare inter se agrariis liceat: exceptis equis, hinnulis, bubus, vaccis, trimestre longiusve tempus in agro pastis, qui in agro natis accenseri & fori oppidani juri subjecti esse debent. In agro nata & stapulæ subjecta non alia censeri debent quàm hæc: butyrum, caseus, equi, pulli, boves, vaccæ, triticum, secale, hordeum, avena, far: atque hæc omninò, ni antè promercalia Groningæ fuerint, distrahere in agro licitum non sit. Sub iis, quæ in usum rei familiaris vendere & emere licet, etiam ea comprehendantur, quæ lanij, pistores, propolæ, aut institores in usum rei suæ in agro coëmunt, ut minutim rursum vendant. Agrarius peregrino vendens res suas fori juri subjectas immunis à pœna sit, nisi confiteritur, scisse, peregrinum esse, quo cum contraxit. Hovetmanni ab oppidanis electi, ab Ordinibus totius provinciæ potestatem judicandi accipiant, & iis, ac apud eos sacramento se obligent ex formâ solenni, in sententia ascripta, Antè hoc sacramentum præstitum Hovetmanni pro Hovetmannis non habeantur, & acta eorum velut non acta censeantur. Præses, Hovetmanni, scribę à secretis, accensi, in fide sint utriusque partis pari modo, nullo præcipuo civitatis iure præter Hovetmannorum electionem & officii limites ab utraque parte iis præscribantur. Præses & Hovetmanni solam jurisdictionem tractent in causis solitis ab anno M. D. XXI ad annum M. D. LX, potestatem reliquam magistratus, & politicum regimen agri non attingant: agrariis liceat separatim suos conventus habere in causis ad ipsos seorsim sine civitate pertinentibus. Ordines hujus provinciæ, Ordines urbis Groningæ, & Omlandiæ, agrarios solos Omlandios inter Amasum & Lavicam appellare, rectum sit. Agrarii vectigalia nulla, mercatus solennes, trutinas publicas instituant sine consensu Ordinum provinciæ omnium: agrariorum postulatum de subdivisione tributorum & onerum inter civitatem & agrum adhuc non audiatur: interim quod in onerum modo, quem pro rato provincia hæc tenetur sustinere, ex tributis & censibus jam usitatis solvi non potest, id conficiatur ex quintâ censûs aut proventûs omnium bonorum immobilium, agrorum pariter & adi-ficiorum, ficiorum, rusticorum urbanorumque, ex forma anni M. D. LXXVII : & hoc servetur, donec de modo alio partes convenerint, aut aliter ab Ordinibus generalibus fuerit decretum. Cetera actionis huius nondum satis explicata ac probata explicentur & probentur plenius, ut ferri sententia possit, & teneantur oppidani rei respondere peremptorie. Interea quoque servanda sint in usu juris stapula, recensent & praecipiunt ex formula Cobelia aut Albana, de tempore proponendi in publico merces, de loco, de indice earum, ex quibus vectigal forisfolutum, de modo vectigalis certo in singulas mercium species: interdumque oppidanis institutione novorum vectigalium & aggravatione veterum: addunt de trutinae cura & inspectione contra fraudes. Denique de Oldermanno, & iis, qui illo in subsellio de stapulae jure judicant, subjiciunt, statuuntque, ne Oldermannus carens semiplena probatione quenquam ad jusjurandum adigat, utque accusatus in hoc casu velut innocens absolvatur, Oldermannus verò insumptus, & poenam pro excessu modo arbitrariam condemnetur: ut semiplena probatio habeatur: testimonium affirmativum testis jurati, modo is non sit in ministerio ipsius Oldermanni, qui reijci ut suspectus potest. Oldermannus & judices hi nihil potestatis, aut jurisdictionis sibi usurpent in agrarios praeter id, quod ad ipsorum cognitionem proprie pertinet: Idem Oldermanuus ad hoc tribunal suum neminem citet ex agro nisi per mandatum Camerae provincialis, id est, Praefidis & Hovetmannorum: agrarii & peregrini a sententia hujus tribunalis Hovetmannos cum praesidè, cives senatum urbanum appellent, & recognitionem petant: Huic sententiae in consessu Ordinum generalium pronunciatae, & nomine eorundem a summo scribâ a secretis subscriptae, addidêre judices iidem aliam quoque eodem die & loco. In eâ concedunt agrariis ad exsolvendum aes alienum tributum agro toti imponere secundum jugera per octennium eo modo, quem ipsi sufficere arbitrabuntur, atque insuper ex bonis monasticis ex decreto Ordinum generalium aureorum xvi millia capere. Ut tamen aes hoc alienum prius liquidum fiat apud ipsos provincias Ordines, nec excedat summam lxiv millium aureorum, quam summam ipsi agrarii ante erant professi: utque quotannis de hoc tributo apud generosum Gubernatorem, & delectos Ordinum provincialium rationes reddantur, ut agrariis iisdem liceat vectigal cerevisiæ & vino in tabernis aut diversoriis publicis imponere, & singulis semestribus locare tanti, quanti id proximè fecerant oppidani, pecuniamque illam stipendiis impendere, ac salariis ossiciariorum suorum, & negotiis aliis necessariis: quod si tamen vectigal annuum excefserit aureos quatermille, excedens pars ut cedat in erarium commune, ejusque quæstori numeretur. In hoc statu res ista hæsit, donec à Dammonensibus solis omnium agrariorum, haud invitis tamen cæteris, novus est pulvis civitati excitatus: de quo paulò post rursum. Anno verò M. DC. cùm jamcontroversiæ, quæ hactenus partes distinuerant, compositæ viderentur, in comitiis provinciæ, leges latæ sunt ab Ordinibus quibus munus & potestas collegii Deputatorum fuêre definita: Earum hæc summa. Deputati in collegio sint vi. pari numero utrimque lecti, patriæ amantes ac fidi, viri integri, bonique nominis, religioni reformatæ addicti, qui cum Gubernatore collegium conficiant. Hi jurent, provincia fideles in omnibus se futuros, operamque daturos, ut transactio cum civitate inita ab Ordinibus generalibus anno M. D. XCIV, cum civitas societati foederis communis redderetur, item sententia inter diffidentes partes anno M. D. XCVII, & M. D. XCIX lata, sine vitio serventur: jurent quoque sine partium harum aut illarum studiis, affectibusque in suos abdicatis, animis puris, atque integris communes provinciae res se diligenter & fideliter curaturos administraturosque, uti maxime ex usu atque utilitate totius provinciae esse existimabunt: munera & ministeria alia si qua teneant, interea se posituros, decreta comitiorum praeterita & futura quam exactissime executuros: nullius jura in hac provincia in exercenda jurisdictione, in conferendis beneficiis, in vocandis rite ecclesiarum ministris & similibus rebus impediant: simul videant, ne quisquam bona hujusmodi piis aut publicis usibus dicata in usu proprios vertat, neu qui jus vocandi & conferendi habet, eam rem ultra tempus receptum hebdomadum sex differat: per collegas duos & Quaestorem generalem tributa & vectigalia jam usitata tempestive singulis semestribus locent, quanti omnino queant, & a conductoribus publicanis sponsiones idoneas dari curent, per quas Respub. indemnis esse possit, nec permittant, ut Quaestor aut quisquam alius munus a provincia acceptum gerens, aut pecuniam provinciae tractans, vectigalia tributaque huiusmodi conducat, aut in societate cum conductorum quoquam sit, aut etiam sponsorem se praestet: denique ut in eo sint, ne quid in fraudem provinciae tota hac in re a quoquam committatur, non a publicanis, non a provincialibus; ne publicanis fraus ulla fiat, ve ipsi praeter legem provinciales affligant, ut lites inter eos orta, quam citissime expediantur: ut potestatem habeant cum(Comite gubernatore militares praefecturas superiores & inseriores vacantes conferendi, modo ii, quibus conferuntur, non displiceant provinciae Ordinibus, quod cognoscendum proxime futuris comitiis: a reliquis vero curationibus aut muneribus quaestorum, secretariorum, armamentarii magistrorum, similiumque tribuendis abstineant, eamque curam comitiis relinquant: cum militares praefecturas conferent, intraneos, modo idonei sint, extraneis praeferant ferant: tributa ab omnibus provincialibus exigant severè, & nusquam conniventes, eaque in nullum finem alium, quàm in quem destinata sunt, impendant; tributorum onerumve aliorum nihil sine consensu & mandato Ordinum populum poscant, hoc verò agant sedulò, ut qui Reip. tributi aliquid residuì debent, si quàm maturimè ad id solvendum compellantur. Porro cùm quid cuiquam solvendum decernent, consignent hoc manibus suis si non omnes, saltem bini ex oppidanis, & totidem ex agrariis, & subsignet scriba à secretis, isque decretum hoc statim in volumen actorum referat: secùs si quid h ujus generis fiat, id in reddendis rationibus locum non habeat. Idem collegæ [?] deputati in eo sint, ut qui Reip. militant, iis stipendia integrè singulis quadrimestribus aut diebus CXXV I solvantur:curent quoque, ut quod cohortium præfeētis [?] numeratur in stipendia militum, hoc militibus statim pendatur sine fraude, sine quæsito eâ in re ullo quæstu, utque in eos, qui contra delinquere deprehensi fuerint, animadvertatur graviter, sive exautoratione, sive aliâ pœnâ graviore: hocq; observetur etiam hac in re, ut stipendii residuum[?] praefectis cohortium non ante solvantur, quàm manibus suis testati fuerint inferiora militiae munera in cohorte gerentes, militibus esse satisfactum; ac ut rationes acceptorum & expensorum quadrimestres non concludantur, nisi coram utroque collegio & deputatorum, & λογιςῶν[?]: curent similiter, ut equites pariter peditesque tum justo numero in alis & cohortibus suis sint, tum armis pro ordinum ratione probè instructi: ut armamentario ne quid desit, quod ad apparatum pertineat; ut ex eo nec ipsi, nec alii, qui Remp. gerunt, quaestum ullum faciant, aut negotiationi hujusmodi quoquo modo se misceant: conveniant quotidiè exceptis diebus Dominicis & festis celebrioribus, aut iis qui supplicationibus publicis sunt destinati, idque bis, semel ante meridiem, iterum post meridiem, sintque in actione per horas plus minus binas, prout negotia poscent. Praeses post dictas ad Deum preces proponat agenda, singulorum collegarum sententias roget, ex consensu plurium concludat, conclusum per eum, qui à secretis est, in chartam referat, id executioni mandare satagat, secreta collegii revelari non patiatur: operam det, ut in comitiis proponenda & agenda biduo anté comitiorum initium inscriptis exhiberi possit duplici exemplo, altero in oppidanorum, altero in agrariorum usum : ut comitiorum decreta in mundum relata & oppidanis & agrariis tradantur : manu suâ subsignet acta & epistolas collegii; scribæ à secretis instet, ne is officio usquam desit, sed omnia collegii acta, decreta, literas in volumen redigat : sigilli quoque custos sit, eoque recte utatur: extraordinarios sumptus collegium ne faciat, non ædificet, dona tribuat, pensiones assignet, munia nova instituat, sine consensu, aut jussu Ordinum, eorumve, qui ab iis potestatem habent: denique cum generalibus Ordinibus, qui Hagæ sedem habent, & cum Ordinum eorundem senatu, adeoque cum iis, qui rebus maritimis præsident, consiliorum consociationem habeat: Reliqua sunt de curarum & laborum, quos pro Rep. sustinent, præmiis. In jurejurando quod Reip. dant, promittunt, regi Hispaniæ, & omnibus qui cum ipso faciunt, hostes se futuros, eorum consiliis & conatibus obviam ituros, fœderi sociarum provinciarum fideliter ac sine vitio adhæsuros, ad propagandam, promovendam , tuendam religionem reformatam, & ad conservanda defendendaque jura, privilegia, libertatem provinciarum fœderatarum generatim, & provinciæ hujus inter Lavicam & Amasum speciatim: postremò munus sibi commissum cum fide & diligentiâ administraturos, concordiæ & amicitiæ colendæ sincerum studium habituros, Reip. provinciali salutem pro viribus procuraturos. Ab hoc tempore bonorum monasticorum administratio desiit esse penes hoc collegium, translataque est ad collegium aliud huic curæ peculiariter destinatum, de quo dicam postea. Et jam Dammonenses in causâ suâ agendâ erant toti, contendebantque, se eo jure, quod cæteris Ordinibus agrariis per sententiam irrogatum esset, haud teneri, quippè qui aliquid præ iis haberent præcipuî, repetita memoria actorum tempore Mariæ gubernatricis Belgii cœptorum. Tandem verò disceptato, quantum satis erat, negotio, à judicibus delegatis ex voluntate collegii generalium Ordinum Hagæ duæ sententiæ sunt latæ alia post aliam, prior anno superiore, altera hoc ipsom.DC.XV; ambæ verò eo verborū textu ac formâ, ut pars utraque in se victoriam trahat, ac non minùs quàm antè juris sui etiam nunc maneat incerta. Simul verò eodem hoc jam labente anno latum aliquid est ab iisdem judicibus de sententiis, quæ in Camerâ provinciali ab Hovetmannis pronunciantur, recognoscendis, quod revisionem vulgo nuncupant. Sed & hoc tale esse videtur, ut qui eo subsidio uti velint, non multi futuri esse putentur, propter impendia, aleamque dubiam.
units.tr: Pronounced in the presence of the Governor, with both parties present, on 16/17 February (Julian), 1595, at Groningen. But the agrarians, led by the Syndic Verrucius, a distinguished jurist, were displeased with the pronouncement. They demanded from the General Estates not only its repeal but also a reform or reopening of the whole case. The Estates appointed nine new judges, all of them very skilled, and gave them full power to hear and decide the matter. After examining and weighing the whole affair with care, they finally gave judgment on 11 January (Julian) 1597, in a session of the General Estates, with the doors of the chamber thrown open. To make clear what each party had demanded, the following must be explained. Following the path of their earlier plans for dissolving the covenant, the agrarians demanded a divorce, a complete separation by which they could look after themselves apart and keep their own state, divided from the city, with nothing in common with it except neighbourhood and free trade. In particular, they refused altogether to accept the jurisdiction of the Hovetmen appointed by the city council. They wished to hold their own assemblies whenever and wherever suited them, to deliberate and decide on public affairs without the city, to keep their own provincial college, and to appoint their own chief judges. They wanted the right of the market-place in the town, and what I have said about grain and beer, which arose from the covenants, cancelled entirely. I pass over smaller matters. The city, on the other side, demanded and asked that the old union, established with the greatest wisdom long ago, proved by long use, and strengthened by many agreements and decrees, be kept; that the election and powers of the Hovetmen be retained in the ancient manner, along with what belongs to them; that the old agreement on beer and the law on grain be upheld; and finally that the staple right in all goods for sale, whether home-produced or foreign and imported, be left and confirmed to it in full. The judges pronounced as follows: The sentence of the three deputed men, given in the year 1595, is to be repealed. The city and the country shall be one province, one jurisdiction, and be ruled jointly by their Estates. All rights and revenues which once belonged to the Prince, and likewise all the proceeds of the recent taxes of every kind, are to be administered and spent, as they are owed, by the common consent of both parties. Monasteries and monastic goods, and such property of that kind in the city and the country, and likewise in the old and suburban prefecture, are by unanimous decision to be applied to pious uses. For the administration of public money and of the levies, and for carrying out and completing what the Estates decide, suitable men are to be chosen in equal numbers from each side, and their commissions and the limits of their duties are to be prescribed as the Provincial Estates think fit for the good of the province. Meanwhile the college instituted two years earlier is to remain in the form in which it was set up, for as long as these matters are being completed. Offices that were usually conferred or committed by the Prince are to be conferred and entrusted by the Estates jointly. The Chamber of Justice, as they call it, that is the court of the Hovetmen, together with its president (whom they call the legate) and its other officers, excepting the Hovetmen themselves, whom the city alone shall nominate, are to be appointed, commissioned, and bound by oath, jointly by the Estates of the province, so that in the name of the commonwealth or the higher authority they may declare law according to the provincial laws and the custom received from antiquity, in the cases which from 1521 to 1560 were usually heard in this court. Neither party is to deal with the affairs of the whole province separately, nor shall anyone from one side deal with them outside the provincial assemblies. The agrarians shall be free to trade with anyone, in any place, and in whatever goods they please, except for products of the land, such as butter, cheese, horses, oxen and grain, whose export is forbidden unless they have first been offered for sale in Groningen. Yet the agrarians shall have the right to buy and sell among themselves for the needs of their own households, even of those goods that were not offered for sale in Groningen. If the parties have not been able to agree on the form and manner of holding the market, they are to set out briefly the points in dispute, and await the decision of the General Estates on them. The agrarians shall be free to brew beer for their own households, but not for sale or profit; and no beer other than that of Groningen is to be used in taverns or inns throughout the whole country. The Groningers shall keep their former precedence in writing, sealing, sitting and giving votes, and shall keep equal votes in provincial actions and deliberations. When votes conflict, every fair and customary method is to be used to reconcile them. If this does not succeed through the Governor and an equal number of men chosen by each side, the dispute is to be settled until some better method has been found and introduced for this matter. Meetings of the Estates are to be called by the votes of the Estates assembled, or by the edict of the Governor, or by notice from those who have been commissioned for the purpose, in those places which seem most suitable. Acts, innovations, and usurpations that oppose or hinder these arrangements are to be repealed and regarded as void, and no one is to attempt anything similar in future. As for the subsidy the agrarians asked for, to pay off their old debts and meet necessary expenses, since the matter is not yet clear enough, they are bound to set out that debt and those necessary expenses before the General Estates, so that when the matter is known they may decide and pronounce judgment. All this is to be done without prejudice to the right of the covenants and agreements between the allied provinces in the Netherlands, and without diminishing the authority of the General Estates and the Governor, which is owed by the Groningen agreement of 1594 or otherwise. Finally, the remaining demands of the parties are rejected, and the costs are set off against each other. Pronounced on 11 January 1597. Signed on behalf of the General Estates: C. Aersen. But since, from the words of this sentence, a new dispute arose between the parties, the matter was referred again to the General Estates, and they gave the power of hearing and judging it back to the former judges. These, two years later, on 27 February (Julian) 1599, partly interpreting the earlier sentence and partly settling unclear points, pronounced again as follows: All merchandise or goods imported into the country, even if they are already in the country, are not subject to the staple right, and the agrarians may buy, sell and exchange them among themselves: except horses, foals, oxen and cows that have been pastured in the country for a term of three months or longer, which are to be counted as home-bred and made subject to the town market right. Products of the land not subject to the staple are to be counted only as these: butter, cheese, horses, foals, oxen, cows, wheat, rye, barley, oats, and spelt; and these may not be sold in the country unless they have first been offered for sale in Groningen. Among the goods that may be bought and sold for household needs, let there also be included those which butchers, bakers, retailers, or traders buy in the country for their own use, in order to sell them again in small quantities. An agrarian selling his goods to a foreigner, which are subject to the market right, shall be free from penalty, unless he admits that he knew the person he dealt with was a foreigner. The Hovetmen, chosen by the townsmen, shall receive from the Estates of the whole province the power of judging, and shall bind themselves before them by oath in the solemn form written in the sentence. Until this oath has been taken, the Hovetmen shall not be considered Hovetmen, and their acts shall be regarded as if they were not acts. The president, the Hovetmen, the secretary, and the officers shall be equally trusted by both parties, with no special right of the city beyond the election of the Hovetmen, and the limits of their office shall be prescribed to them by both parties. The president and the Hovetmen shall deal only with the jurisdiction in the cases customary from 1521 to 1560, and shall not touch the remaining power of the magistrate or the political government of the country. The agrarians may hold their own separate assemblies in matters that concern them alone, without the city. It shall be proper that the Estates of this province and the Estates of the city of Groningen and of Omlanden call the agrarians alone Omlanders, those between the Ems and the Lauwers. The agrarians shall not set up any tolls, public markets, or public weighing-houses without the consent of the Estates of the whole province. The agrarian demand for dividing taxes and burdens between the city and the country is not yet to be heard; meanwhile, whatever cannot be paid from the taxes and levies already in use, in the proportion this province is bound to bear, is to be raised from a fifth of the assessment or income of all immovable goods, of lands and of buildings, rural and urban alike, according to the scheme of the year 1577. This shall be kept until the parties agree on another method, or the General Estates decide otherwise. The remaining points of this action, not yet sufficiently explained and proved, are to be explained and proved more fully, so that a sentence can be pronounced, and the townsmen are to be bound to answer peremptorily. Meanwhile the staple rights are also to be kept in use, and they lay down and prescribe, following the Cobelia or Alban formula, the time for offering goods in public, the place, the list of them on which the toll is due, and the amount of the toll for each kind of goods; and sometimes they add to the townsmen the setting up of new tolls and the increase of old ones. They add provisions on the care and inspection of the weighing-house against frauds. Finally, concerning the Oldermann and those who sit on that bench to judge the staple right, they lay down and decide that the Oldermann, lacking a semi-full proof, shall not bind anyone to an oath, and that an accused person in such a case shall be acquitted as innocent, while the Oldermann, if he has acted presumptuously, shall be condemned to a penalty fixed at his discretion according to the offence; that a sworn witness's affirmative testimony shall count as a semi-full proof, provided he is not in the service of the Oldermann himself, since he may be rejected as suspect. The Oldermann and these judges shall not claim for themselves any power or jurisdiction over the agrarians beyond what properly belongs to their own cognizance. The same Oldermann shall not summon anyone from the country to his court except by a mandate of the provincial chamber, that is, of the President and the Hovetmen. Agrarians and foreigners may appeal from the sentence of this court to the Hovetmen with the president, and townsmen to the city council, and ask for a review. To this sentence, pronounced in the assembly of the General Estates and signed in their name by the chief secretary, the same judges added another on the same day and in the same place. In it they grant the agrarians leave to impose a tax on the whole country by the morgen for eight years, in whatever way they think sufficient to pay off their debts, and in addition to take 16,000 gold pieces from the monastic goods by decree of the General Estates. However, this debt must first be made clear before the provincial Estates themselves, and must not exceed the sum of 64,000 gold pieces which the agrarians themselves had earlier declared. And every year an account of this tax shall be rendered before the noble Governor and the chosen men of the provincial Estates, so that the same agrarians may be allowed to impose a tax on beer and wine in taverns or public inns, and to let it out every six months for as much as the townsmen had recently let it for, and to spend that money on the wages of their officers and on other necessary business; but if the annual tax should exceed 4,000 gold pieces, the excess shall pass into the common treasury and be paid to its quaestor. In this state the matter stuck, until, through the Dammonenses alone among all the agrarians, though not against the wishes of the rest, a new dust was stirred up against the city, about which I shall speak again shortly. But in the year 1600, when the disputes which had hitherto divided the parties seemed settled, laws were passed by the Estates at the provincial assembly, by which the duty and power of the college of deputies were defined. The sum of these was as follows: The deputies in the college shall be six, chosen in equal numbers from each side, lovers of their country and faithful men, upright and of good name, adhering to the reformed religion, who with the Governor shall form the college. They shall swear that they will be faithful to the province in all things, and will take care that the agreement made with the city by the General Estates in 1594, by which the city was restored to the common confederacy of the covenant, and likewise the sentence given between the disagreeing parties in 1597 and 1599, are kept without fault. They shall also swear, laying aside all partisan zeal and feelings for one side or the other, with pure and upright minds, to manage and administer the common affairs of the province diligently and faithfully, as they judge most useful for the whole province. Whatever other offices and duties they hold, they will set aside meanwhile, and will carry out the decrees of the assemblies, past and future, as exactly as possible. They shall not hinder anyone's rights in this province in exercising jurisdiction, in conferring benefices, in properly calling ministers of the churches, and in similar matters. At the same time they shall see to it that no one turns to private use goods of this kind dedicated to pious or public uses, and that whoever has the right of calling and conferring does not delay that matter beyond the customary six weeks. Through two colleagues and the General Quaestor, they shall let out the taxes and tolls already in use every six months, at the best price they can get, and shall see to it that suitable guarantees are given by the publicans, by which the commonwealth can be kept safe; and they shall not allow the Quaestor or anyone else who holds an office from the province or handles provincial money to lease such taxes and tolls, or to be in partnership with any of the lessees, or even to stand surety. Finally, they shall take care that no one, neither publicans nor provincials, commits any fraud against the province in this matter; that no fraud be done to the publicans, nor the provincials be oppressed by them contrary to law; and that lawsuits arising between them be settled as quickly as possible. They shall have the power, together with the Governor, of conferring the vacant higher and lower military prefectures, provided those to whom they are conferred are not displeasing to the Estates of the province, which is to be examined at the next assembly. But from the other charges or offices of quaestors, secretaries, masters of the arsenal and similar posts they shall abstain, leaving that care to the assembly. When they confer military prefectures, they shall prefer those from within the country to outsiders, provided they are fit. They shall exact the taxes severely from all provincials, never conniving, and spend them for no other end than that for which they are destined; they shall demand nothing from the people beyond the taxes and other burdens without the consent and mandate of the Estates; and they shall take care that those who owe any remaining tax to the commonwealth are compelled to pay it as soon as possible. Further, when they decide that anything is to be paid to anyone, they shall sign it with their own hands, if not all, then at least two townsmen and as many agrarians, and the secretary shall countersign it, and he shall immediately enter this decree in the register of acts; otherwise, if anything of this kind is done otherwise, it shall have no place in the rendering of accounts. The same colleagues and deputies shall see that those who serve the commonwealth are paid their wages in full every four months, or every 125 days; they shall also see that what is allotted to the prefects of the cohorts for the soldiers' pay is paid to the soldiers at once, without fraud, and without any gain made from it, and that those who are caught offending in this are punished severely, whether by dismissal or by some heavier penalty; and this shall also be observed in this matter: the remaining wages shall not be paid to the prefects of the cohorts until they have attested with their own hands that the inferior officers of the cohort have satisfied the soldiers. And the quarterly accounts of receipts and expenditure shall not be closed except in the presence of both colleges of deputies and of the auditors. They shall likewise see that the horsemen and foot soldiers are present in their wings and cohorts in the right number, and are properly equipped with arms according to their rank; that nothing is lacking in the arsenal that pertains to the equipment; and that neither they nor others who serve the commonwealth make any profit from it, or mix themselves in any such trade in any way. They shall meet every day, except on Sundays and the more solemn feast days, or on those days appointed for public supplications; and they shall meet twice, once before noon and again after noon, and the session shall last about two hours, or as the business requires. After the prayers offered to God, the President shall propose the matters to be dealt with, ask the opinion of each colleague, conclude by the agreement of the majority, and have the conclusion written on paper by the one who is secretary; he shall take care to carry it into execution, and shall not allow the secrets of the college to be revealed. He shall take care that the matters to be proposed and dealt with at the assembly can be presented in writing two days before the assembly begins, in two copies, one for the use of the townsmen and the other for the agrarians, so that the decrees of the assembly, once drawn up, may be handed to both townsmen and agrarians. He shall sign the acts and letters of the college with his own hand; he shall press the secretary not to fail in his duty anywhere, but to put all the acts, decrees and letters of the college into the register; he shall also be keeper of the seal and use it properly. The college shall not incur extraordinary expenses, nor build, give gifts, assign pensions, or set up new offices without the consent or order of the Estates, or of those who have authority from them. Finally, it shall hold a consultation with the General Estates, who have their seat at The Hague, and with the council of the same Estates, and so with those who preside over maritime affairs. The rest concerns rewards for the cares and labours they undertake for the commonwealth. In the oath which they give to the commonwealth, they promise that they will be enemies of the King of Spain and of all who act with him; that they will oppose their counsels and attempts; that they will adhere faithfully and without fault to the covenant of the allied provinces; that they will work, as far as they can, for the spread, advancement and protection of the reformed religion, and for the preservation and defence of the rights, privileges and liberty of the united provinces in general, and of this province between the Lauwers and the Ems in particular; and finally, that they will administer the office entrusted to them faithfully and diligently, will have a sincere zeal for cultivating concord and friendship, and will work for the welfare of the provincial commonwealth as far as their strength allows. From this time the administration of the monastic goods ceased to be in the hands of this college, and was transferred to another college specially appointed for this care, about which I shall speak later. And now the Dammonenses were busy pleading their own cause, and they argued that they were not bound by the right which had been imposed on the other agrarian Estates by sentence, since they had certain privileges before them, recalling the memory of the proceedings begun in the time of Mary, Governess of the Netherlands. At last, however, when the matter had been sufficiently debated, two sentences were given at The Hague by the judges delegated by the will of the college of the General Estates, one after the other: the first the year before, and the second in this very year 1615. Both, however, were so worded and framed that each party claims the victory for itself, and no less than before their right remains uncertain. At the same time, in this year now passing, the same judges have also ruled something about reviewing the sentences pronounced by the Hovetmen in the provincial chamber, which they commonly call revision. But this also seems to be such that few are likely to want to use that remedy, on account of the expense and the uncertain outcome.

units.la: ALIA PRÆCLARA CI- VITATIS JURA ET LEGES.
units.tr: Other Distinguished Rights and Laws of the City

units.la: HABET vero præter hæc alia quoque præclara jura civitas hæc nostra. Inter quæ illud censeri po-test, quod in toto ANGLIAE regno commerciorum ac negotiationum libertatem jam CCC. L. ante annos cives habuerint, cum conditionibus haud pœnitendis: ut testatur diploma Henrici III regis anno regni ejus XLI signatum, quod est in Reip. archivis illæsum. Deinde illud etiam, quod ante complures hominum ætates amplissimo FOEDERI ANSEATICO civitas ascripta fit, locumque in eo perhonestum inter civitates socias tenuerit semper, & adhuc teneat. Sed hoc nobilius & illustrius prioribus, quod privilegio ornata sit à majoribus accepto, & Cæsarum diplomate confirmato, & sine vitio ad hoc usque tempus continuato, ne cuiquam omnino vel regi vel principi vel ordini liceat quenquam, qui civis aut incola civitatis sit, aut quoquo modo civitati subjectus, judicii causâ, è civitate evocare, aut ad ullum tribunal exterum citare. Nec eo inferius id, quod nulla sit à Senatus sententia aut decreto provocatio, nulla alterius judicis tanquam superioris appellatio, nec in civilibus nec in criminalibus causis: quo sanè nihil amplius, nihil majus, nihil sublimius dari civitati potest : quod denique tale est, ut in nullâ civitate Germaniæ extra Helvetiam, nullâ Belgii, nullâ Galliæ, Angliæ, Scotiæ, Poloniæ, Ungariæ, Sueciæ, Daniæ simile queat inveniri. Nec solùm Senatus hoc jure pollet, sed & collegium Hovetmannorum, quam Cameram vulgò vocant, à cuius iudicio decretove similiter appellatio non est, non plebejo, non nobili. Nec aliud in conventu juridico Ordinum agrariorum valet, in quo maxima autoritas Hovetmannorum nunc est, & fuit per centum fere annos, olim vero ante Saxonica tempora stante integra Reipub. libertate, universi senatus cum Hovetmannis esse solet, qui conventus non alibi quoque quàm in urbe agitur. Nam ultrà hujus tribunal tendere nemini licet. Nec vero istud in postremis privilegiorum hujus civitatis posuero, quod legum & statutorum suorum ipsa domina est: ipsa ferendi abrogandique potestatem liberrimam habet, nec necessum habet ad voluntatem & consensum cuiusquam [illegible, ~6 letters] respicere alterius : atque ita sciscit & antiquat, quemadmodum temporum ratio ac usus postulat. Eandemque potestatem in suas leges & statuta agrarii tenent, si se cum civitate conjungant, & ex voluntate consilioque ejus potestate utantur : sirie[?] eâ autem hac in parte nihil possunt, quamquam antè Kenoniana ac Focconiana inde illud etiam, quod ante complures hominum ætates amplissimo FOEDERI ANSEATICO civitas affcripta fit, locumque in eo perhonestum inter civitates socias tenuerit semper, & adhuc tenet. Sed hoc nobilius & illustrius prioribus, quod privilegio ornata sit à majoribus accepto, & Cæsarum diplomate confirmato, & sine vitio ad hoc usque tempus continuato, ne cuiquam omninò vel regi vel principi vel ordini liceat quenquam, qui civis aut incola civitatis sit, aut quoquo modo civitati subjectus, judicii causâ, è civitate evocare, aut ad ullum tribunal exterum citare. Nec eo inferius id, quod nulla sit à Senatus sententia aut decreto provocatio, nulla alterius judicis tanquam superioris appellatio, nec in civilibus nec in criminalibus causis: quo sanè nihil amplius, nihil majus, nihil sublimius dari civitati potest: quod denique tale est, ut in nullâ civitate Germaniæ extra Helvetiam, nullâ Belgii, nullâ Galliæ, Angliæ, Scotiæ, Poloniæ, Ungariæ, Sueciæ, Daniæ simile queat inveniri. Nec solùm Senatus hoc jure pollet, sed & collegium
units.tr: Besides these, our city also has other distinguished rights. Among them may be counted this: that the citizens enjoyed freedom of trade and commerce throughout the whole kingdom of England more than 350 years ago, on conditions that are not to be regretted, as is attested by a charter of King Henry III, sealed in the forty-first year of his reign, which is preserved intact in the city archives. Next, many generations ago the city was enrolled in the most illustrious HANSEATIC LEAGUE, and it has always held, and still holds, a most honourable place among the allied cities. But this is nobler and more illustrious than the earlier privileges, in that it is adorned with a privilege received from our ancestors, confirmed by an imperial charter, and maintained without fault to this day: that no king, prince or order may be permitted to summon out of the city, for the purposes of a lawsuit, anyone who is a citizen or resident of the city, or in any way subject to it, or to cite him before any foreign tribunal. Nor is this inferior to it: that there is no appeal from the sentence or decree of the Senate, and no appeal to any other judge as to a superior, either in civil or in criminal causes. Nothing greater, nothing higher, nothing more exalted can be granted to a city than this. Finally, it is such that nothing similar can be found in any city of Germany outside Switzerland, or in any city of Belgium, France, England, Scotland, Poland, Hungary, Sweden or Denmark. Nor does the Senate alone enjoy this right, but also the college of the Hovetmen, which they commonly call the Chamber, from whose judgment or decree there is likewise no appeal, whether for commoner or for noble. Nor does anything else hold in the judicial assembly of the Ommelandic orders, in which the greatest authority now belongs to the Hovetmen, and has belonged for nearly a hundred years. Formerly, before the Saxon times, while the liberty of the commonwealth remained whole, the whole Senate was wont to sit with the Hovetmen, and this assembly is held nowhere else than in the city. For no one is permitted to appeal beyond this tribunal. Nor have I placed among the last of this city's privileges the fact that it is itself the mistress of its own laws and statutes: it has the most free power of enacting and repealing them, and it need not look to the will and consent of anyone else; and so it decrees and abolishes them as the condition of the times and custom require. The rural districts also hold the same power over their laws and statutes, if they join themselves to the city and exercise that power by its will and counsel; but in this matter they can do nothing on their own, although before the Kenonian and Focconian [disturbances] ... [the passage here repeats the preceding privileges:] many generations ago the city was enrolled in the most illustrious HANSEATIC LEAGUE, and it has always held, and still holds, a most honourable place among the allied cities. Nam ultrà huius tribunal tendere nemini licet. Eandemque potestatem in suas leges & statuta agrarii tenent, si se cum civitate conjungant, & ex voluntate consilioque ejus potestate utantur: sine eâ autem hac in parte nihil possunt, quamquam ante Kenoniana ac Focconiana niana, & iis priora tempora haud dubie potuerint. Denique hoc etiam civitati egregium, quòd argentea aereaque pecunia signanda ab annis non minus ccc. aurea ve-, rò ab anno (Christi M. CCCC. LXXXVIII [?] jus habuerit, adeoque nunc quoque habeat. Porrò in legibus Reip. hujus ita scriptum, Ut CONSULES officio decedentes die VIII Calend. Martii novis arcam publicam cum sigillo civitatis & clavibus tradant, rationesque expediant intra dies XIV; & si quid aeris publici residui habeant penes se, id exsolvant: ut consulum quilibet cum assessoribus suis in praetorio rationes reddat accepti, & reliqui coram quaestore Reipub. & Triumviris concilii jurati: ut causae majores non cognoscantur nisi in senatu: ut senatus controversias expediat celeriter, & quidem intra XII septimanas à lite conclusa: idem ut in rebus difficilibus senatum veterem, aut si placeat, alios etiam è civium numero prudentiores vocet in curiam; vocati tamen suffragium non habeant, sed consilio tantum senatum juvent; penes quem solum suffragii jus: Provocans à consulis & assesso-
units.tr: { } Privilege of non-evocation. Nor is this inferior: that there is no appeal from the sentence or decree of the Senate, nor any appeal to another judge as superior, either in civil or in criminal cases. ... Finally, this too is an outstanding feature of the city: it has had, from not less than 300 years ago, the right to coin silver and copper money, and gold money from the year 1488 (?), and so it still has it now. Furthermore, the laws of this commonwealth contain the following: that the CONSULS, when they leave office, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, hand over the public chest to their successors, with the city seal and keys, and render their accounts within fourteen days; and if they have any public money left in their hands, they shall pay it out; so that each of the consuls, with his assessors, shall render his account of receipts in the court-hall, and the remainders before the treasurer of the commonwealth and the Triumvirs of the sworn council. That greater cases shall not be heard except in the Senate; that the Senate shall settle disputes quickly, and indeed within twelve weeks from the closing of the suit; that in difficult matters the Senate shall summon the old senators, or, if it is pleasing, other more prudent men from among the citizens, into the curia; but those summoned shall not have a vote, but shall only assist the Senate with counsel; the right of voting belongs to the Senate alone. Whoever appeals from the sentence pronounced by the consuls and assessors in the court-hall to the whole Senate, and loses the case, shall pay one mark to the commonwealth as a fine.

units.la: rum [?]um sententiâ in prætorio latâ ad senatum totum, & causâ cadens, ut mulctam Reip. solvat marcam unam: ut eundem appellare senatum, qui pronunciavit, si quid per errorem pronunciatum videatur liceat intra diesx:ne quis eorum, qui in senatu sunt, intercedat pro quoquam qui Reip. mulctam debet: si fecerit, x aureos Rhenanos Reip. pendere damnas sit. Cōsul senatorve in munere suo non fideliter versari compertus loco moveatur, nec unquam ad Remp. aditum rursum habeat. Item, iidem mulctam, si quam debent, ante aliòs Reip. solvant, nec fas sit reliquos cogere, priusquam ab his factum, quod oportet. Nec hi, nec Schulthesius, nec tabellarius Reip. verba pro altero in senatu aut judicio faciant, nisi tutores pupilli sint, cujus de re agitur. Cum senatus habetur, nemo emansitet impunè, aut sero veniat: acta dictaque in senatu nemo eliminet: cognati partium in senatu ferendis sententiis non intersint. Si quis causam suam, quam senatus semel definivit, finito eorum munere, qui eam definierunt, ad successores eorundem retulerit iterum, marcas x Reip; pendat.
units.tr: That he may appeal to the same Senate which pronounced the sentence, if it seems that something was pronounced in error, within ten days. That none of those who are in the Senate shall intercede on behalf of anyone who owes a fine to the commonwealth; if he does so, he shall be liable to pay ten Rhenish gold guilders to the commonwealth. A consul or senator found not to have acted faithfully in his office shall be removed from his position and never again have access to the commonwealth. Likewise, they shall pay any fines they owe to the commonwealth before others, and it is not lawful to press the rest until what is due has been done by them. Neither these men, nor the Schulthesius, nor the public messenger shall speak on behalf of another in the Senate or in court, unless they are guardians of the minor whose case is being treated. When the Senate is convened, no one may stay away with impunity, or come late; no one may remove the acts and statements made in the Senate; relatives of the parties shall not take part in giving sentences in the Senate. If anyone brings back to the successors of those who decided it his case, which the Senate has once settled, after the term of office of those who decided it has ended, he shall pay ten marks to the commonwealth.

units.la: Olim si qui solvendo non erant, mos fuit, ut nomina eorum certo tempore, exeunte nimirum anni quadrante, quo quis consulum in senatu praesederat, si poscerent creditores, ex sublimi curiae fenestra concurrente ad hanc rem frequenti civium turba recitarentur: eoque facto illi non solum infames fierent, sed & legum patrocinio exuerentur, non contra contumeliam, non contra vim ac ferrum essent tuti. Nunc cætera manent, postremum tantum est sublatum. Proclamatus hoc modo honore suo, & bono nomine cadit, officii publici nullius capax est; in judicio stare, respondere, testimonium dicere non potest. Hoc ad fidem fori & contractuum colendam servandamque sanctius est institutum. Quondam uti in agro, sic in civitate testamenti factio nulla omnino fuit. At pactorum dotalium jus viguit, eaque pacta servare necessum fuit, si rite legitimeque essent confecta. Legitimum vero in his erat, ut etiam nunc est, præsentibus & consentientibus agnatis & cognatis proximis, quorūnive maximè interesset, ea iniri-& scribi, ac ad senatum signandi causâ referri. Nec in his hodiè quicquam mutatum.
units.tr: In former times, if people were unable to pay their debts, the custom was that their names, at a fixed time, namely at the end of the quarter-year in which one of the consuls had presided in the Senate, were read out, if the creditors demanded it, from the high window of the council house, with a large crowd of citizens gathered for this purpose; and when this was done, those persons not only became infamous, but were also stripped of the protection of the laws, and were not safe against insult, violence or the sword. Now the other things remain, only the last has been abolished. One proclaimed in this way is deprived of his honour and good name, and is incapable of any public office; he cannot stand in court, answer, or give testimony. This was instituted more strictly to preserve and maintain trust in the market and in contracts. Formerly, just as in the countryside, there was no testamentary capacity at all in the city. But the law of marriage settlements prevailed, and such agreements had to be kept, if they had been drawn up properly and lawfully. Now, what was lawful in these matters, as it still is, was that they were entered into and recorded in the presence and with the consent of the agnates and nearest cognates, or of those most concerned, and were referred to the Senate for sealing. Nothing has been changed in these matters even today.

units.la: De testamento nunc aliud jus ante annos aliquot inductum. Nam quibus ætatis anni sunt, si liberis legitimis carent, his de bonis suis omnibus non haereditariis, sed acquisitis, ni obstent pacta dotalia, testari liberè pro libitu licet: De haereditariis non nisi ex semisse licet. At quibus liberi legitimi sunt, totius substantiae suae semissem relinquere iisdem coguntur, nisi justam causam, senatuiq; probatam contra eos, aut eorum aliquem habeant. De altero semisse pro arbitrio suo disponere similiter servatis iisdem possunt. Sed in his omnibus opus, ut à sanis lectóve non affixis, ac mente integris id fiat, referaturque ad senatum, aut testantis manu scriptum senatui osseratur, & sigillo publico civitatis muniatur.
units.tr: Concerning wills, a different law was introduced some years ago. Those who have reached adulthood and have no legitimate children may freely make a will as they please regarding all their goods that are acquired rather than inherited, unless dowry agreements stand in the way. Of inherited goods, they may dispose of only half. Those who have legitimate children are compelled to leave half of their whole estate to them, unless they have a just cause against them or one of them, approved by the senate. They may similarly dispose of the other half at their own discretion, observing the same conditions. But in all these cases the act must be done by those who are sound of body, not confined to bed, and sound of mind, and it must be reported to the senate, or the testator's handwritten will must be presented to the senate and secured with the city's public seal.

units.la: Quod si liberorum aliqui exhæredes scribuntur, his tamen ex fructibus partis suae alimenta debentur; pars ipsa liberis iporum, si quos habent, aut haeredibus proximis accrescit. In successionibus olim hæc valuêre. In bona parentum liberi succedebant, & potissimum mares: ii vero ex consilio & judicio propinquorum æquam dotem sororibus, si quæ erant dabant, nec licebat ipsis quicquam rerum patrimonialium alienare, priusquam cum sororibus de dote convenissent. Si per propinquos confici res inter fratres & sorores non posset, autoritas senatus interveniebat. Quinimò nepotes ex filiis potiores filiabus erant in successione hac, si filiæ dotem jam accepissent: sin[?] minùs, filiæ cum fratris defuncti liberis æqualiter in capita hæreditatem parentum dividebant; cum plurium vero fratrum defunctorum liberis utriusque sexus succedebant in stirpes. Liberorum unus si decessisset parentibus adhuc vivis, non parentes, sed fratres & sorores utroque parente cum defuncto conjuncti aut conjunctæ hæreditate capiebant, maribus tamen hic quoque sexu altero potioribus: uterinis autem & consanguineis parentes præferebātur: fratres vero uterini aut consanguinei, itē sorores hujusce modi, si propiores hæredes alii non essent, fratris aut sororis defuncti defunctæve bona æquis portionibus inter se partiebantur. Conjuges genitis & defunctis communibus liberis, ac liberorum liberis, sibi mutuò succedebant:succeduntque etiam nunc;ex asse[?]: si liberos communes non genuissent, moriente eorum altero superstes ex semisse hæres ejus erat, ut etiam hodiè est: sin genuissent, iisque moriente altero in vivis essent, superstes nihilominus semissem capiebat, reliquum liberis communibus relinquebat: idemque valebat,si vitâ decedens liberos legitimos ex alio matrimonio procreatos haberet superstites. Nec aliter quoque hoc tempore res habet.
units.tr: If any of the children are written down as disinherited, they are nevertheless owed maintenance from the income of their share, and the share itself passes to their own children, if they have any, or to the nearest heirs. In the past these rules held in matters of succession. Children succeeded to their parents' goods, and especially the sons; these, by the counsel and judgment of relatives, gave a fair dowry to their sisters, if any there were, and no one could alienate any of the patrimonial property before agreeing about the dowry with the sisters. If the matter between brothers and sisters could not be settled by relatives, the authority of the senate intervened. Indeed, the sons' children took precedence over the daughters in this succession, if the daughters had already received their dowry; but if not, the daughters and the children of a deceased brother divided the parents' inheritance equally by heads. Where there were several deceased brothers, the children of both sexes succeeded by stocks. If one of the children died while the parents were still living, the parents did not take the inheritance; rather the brothers and sisters who were joined to the deceased by both parents did, with males again preferred to the other sex. Among uterine and consanguineous siblings, however, the parents were preferred. Uterine or consanguineous brothers, and likewise sisters of this kind, if there were no nearer heirs, divided the goods of the deceased brother or sister between themselves in equal shares. Spouses succeeded one another when there were common children, and their children's children; and they still succeed in the whole estate today. If they had no common children, when one died the survivor was the heir to half, as is still the case today.
