If they had children, and one of them died while the children were alive, the survivor nevertheless took half and left the remaining half to the common children. The same held if a dying spouse left surviving legitimate children born of another marriage. Nor is the position different at the present time.

units.la: Defuncti defunctæque nepotes & neptes ex filiis excludebant ejusdem fratres & sorores; item ex filiabus nepotes & neptes, si ex filiis non essent: filiæ verò præferebantur filiarum liberis. Impuberis defuncti hæreditas, non existentibus parentibus, devolvebatur ad patruum & avunculum, & non ad amitam & materteram, nec ad avum & aviam, excepto casu, si amita unica cum unico avunculo, aut matertera una cum uno patruo superesset : tum enim hæreditas tota in duas partes pares dividebatur. Nec aliud in puberis defuncti bonis valebat. Sed avunculum & patruum, item materteram&amitam altero tantùm parente conjunctos cum parentibus defuncti avus & avia à successione ejusmodi excludebant. Uterini & consanguinei fratres, item sorores, si patrui, avunculi, amitæ, materteræ non essent, succedebant sibi mutuò, exclusis patruis, avunculis, amitis, materteris magnis. Privignus ex vitrico aut novercâ genitus sorores habens uterinas vel consanguineas à morte matris aut patris sui tenebatur cum vitrico aut novercâ eas alere, elocare,dotare. Quod si in matrimonio secundo filii quoque geniti essent, hos quoque oportebat cum fratre ex priore matrimonio orto, & cum patre, idem sororibus suis germanis præstare. Sed pleraque horum correcta nunc jure novo. Id sic habet. Liberi parentum suorum hæredes sunto sine discrimine sexus in mobilibus pariter & immobilibus: verùm filius duplum semper capito, soror simplû. Fratres & sorores præferuntor parentibus in bonis defuncti fratris aut sororis, & servator quoque hic eadem proportio. Si moriens liberos relinquat superstites, & simul liberorum præmortuorum liberos, hi locum parentum in adeundâ hæreditate tenento, & succedunto cum illis in stirpes, non in capita. At si moriens relinquat in vivis avum, aviam, fratres, sorores ex altero tantummodo parente, germanorum fratrum,& germanarum sororum liberos, patruum quoque avunculum, amitam,materteram,omnes pariter ad successionem vocantor.Marito potestas non esto vendendi, permutandi, ære alieno gravandi quicquam rerum conjugis suæ, quæ immobiles sunt, sine expresso&liberrimo ejus consensu. Uxori similiter non permittitor non solùm mariti res sed suas quoque vivente marito quoquo modo alienare, aut gravare sine ejusdem consensu libero puroque: alioqui mariti & uxoris bona omnia statim à nuptiis aut cum nuptiis communia fiunt utrique jure pari. Lex quoq; olim fuit, & est eadem non ita nuper renovata, ut sacro lavacro non ini- tiati ritè ex more Ecclesiæ, capaces hæerditatum non sint. Clandestinæ ruptiæ etiam graviter vetitæ, quibus qui se implicant, quinque marcas multam dant: at si propinqui querelas de his ad senatum deferant, exulare coguntur, quoad uterque vivunt; altero vero mortuo alteri conceditur jus civitatis exilio amis- sum pecuniâ reparare. Homicidium capite, adulterium pecuniâ ex legibus plectitur. Omnibus Reip. partem gerentibus interdictum stipendio extraneo; cogunturque munus inituri jurare, non se, non liberos suos, non conjugem, nec quenquam alium nomine suo stipendio hujusmodi autoratos esse: idemque ante annos LXVI ad omnes omninò cives, & inquilinos, ipsosque adeò sacerdotes extensum, pœnäque contrâ facienti irrogata bonorum omnium confiscatio. Servis possessiones tenere, aut habitare in urbe, extraque urbem sub imperio senatûs non licet: eorumque, si illic moriantur, hæreditas ærario adscribitur. Hæreditatem ad exteros, qui ultra Lavicam & Amasum, ultraque Coverdiam Drentiæ habitant, devolutarum pars quarta ærario similiter accrescit. Reliqua prætereo, ne modum operis excedant; & quæ restant de Reip. formâ, in civitate expediam.
units.tr: The grandsons and granddaughters of the deceased through sons excluded the deceased's brothers and sisters; likewise the grandsons and granddaughters through daughters, if there were no sons; but daughters were preferred to the children of daughters. The inheritance of a deceased minor, when there were no parents, passed to the paternal and maternal uncles, and not to the paternal and maternal aunts, nor to the grandfather and grandmother; except in the case where a single aunt survived with a single uncle, or a single maternal aunt with a single paternal uncle; for then the whole inheritance was divided into two equal parts. Nor did anything else apply to the goods of a deceased adult. But grandfather and grandmother excluded from such succession the maternal and paternal uncles and aunts who were related to the deceased through only one parent, together with the parents. Uterine and consanguineous brothers, and likewise sisters, if there were no paternal or maternal uncles or aunts, succeeded one another, excluding the great-uncles and great-aunts. A stepson born of a stepfather or stepmother, having uterine or consanguineous sisters, was bound, after the death of his mother or father, to maintain them with his stepfather or stepmother, and to portion them off and provide their dowries. If children had also been born in a second marriage, it was also required that they provide the same for their full sisters, together with the brother from the first marriage and the father. But most of these rules have now been corrected by the new law. It stands thus: the children are heirs of their parents, without distinction of sex, in movables and immovables alike; but a son always takes a double share, a daughter a single share. Brothers and sisters are preferred to parents in the goods of a deceased brother or sister, and the same proportion is observed here too. If a dying person leaves surviving children, and at the same time the children of children who died earlier, these shall hold the place of the parents in taking up the inheritance, and shall succeed alongside them by stocks, not by heads. But if a dying person leaves alive a grandfather, a grandmother, brothers and sisters through only one parent, the children of full brothers and full sisters, and also paternal uncles, maternal uncles, paternal aunts and maternal aunts, all of these are called equally to the succession. A husband shall have no power to sell, exchange, or burden with debt any of his wife's property that is immovable, without her express and wholly free consent. Likewise a wife is not permitted, while her husband is living, to alienate or burden in any way not only her husband's property but also her own, without his free and unqualified consent; otherwise all the goods of husband and wife become common to both, on equal terms, from the wedding or with the wedding.

units.la: FORMA REIP. IN UR- BE, ET MAGISTRATU- UM ORDO.
units.tr: THE FORM OF THE COMMONWEALTH IN THE CITY, AND THE ORDER OF THE MAGISTRACIES.

units.la: FORMA Reip. in urbe ARISTOCRATICA est, modicè in DEMOCRATIAM declinans quam exponere nunc animus est, Antiquitus, cùm minor adhuc civitatis fortuna esset, RATIONALES quatuor, OLDERMANNI VIII eam administrarunt. Nunc verò ab annis amplius trecentis CONSULES quatuor summum locum in eâ tenent dignitatis. His additi olim XVI, nunc & proximis sæculis XII SENATORES: qui omnes senatum conficiunt, totius Reip. caput. Penes hunc senatum est jurisdictio urbana, potestasque in rebus urbanis edicendi, decernendi, vocandi, prehendendi, in custodiam dandi, coëtcendi, supplicia extrema irrogandi, gratiæ faciendæ, pecuniam publicam tractandi, plerosque magistratus alios creandi, imprimis Hovetmannos illos, de quibus dixi sæpè, Præfectos item territoriorum extra urbem designandi, Delectos edendi; qui in collegiis sedeant domi ac foris, Quæstorem, Ædilem Reip. æditUOS publicanos eligendi, legationes mittendi: denique hujus officii est, toti Reip. consulere, &c in eam curas suas intendere. Senatorium munus bienne est, ita comparatum ut quotannis media senatûs pars, [Senatûs voce Consules quoque comprehendo) cui duo anni in munere expleti sunt collegio decedat; decedentium loco totidem alii numero octono succedant, collegiumque compleant. Quorum designatio quomodo fiat, post exponam. In senatu consules dignitate, honore, authoritate antecedunt: suffragii vi ac jure senator consuli par, idemque par referendi potestate. Sed consulum nec inanis est nec inefficax auctoritas in dicendis sententiis: quorum jus est, per vices ternis mensibus eo ordine, quem sors dat, senatui præfidere : quique eorum praesidet, is & sigilli publici custos est, apparitoribus aut accensis stipatur, vocationem prehenfionemque habet, plura penè solus ad senatum refert, quam cæteri in senatu omnes, senatum suffragia rogat,id quod majori parti placet, pro sententiâ totius senatûs pronunciat: denique si ingenio & industriâ pollet, si valet facundiâ, si animo non abjecto est,magnum momentum afferre rebus in omnem partem potest. Idem verò etiam cum tribus senatoribus, quos vel fors vel comparatio cum collegis ei junxit, certo tempore in prætorio jus civibus dicit litigantibus inter se, aut iis, quibus contra cives actio est, idque fere minores ob res, aut ad fidem solutionis pertinentes, nec nisi à meridie dimisso jam senatu. In quo tribunali jurisdictio ejusmodi est, ut quàm celerrimè litigantes expediat, maximè antequam prætoris vices exeant, atque ita fori debitorumque fidem tueatur. Ab eo qui vult, ad senatum provocandi jus habet: à senatu provocatio ulterior non est. Post senatum, ut Hovetmannos hîc prætereiam, de quibus est dictum jam sæpiùs, & dicendum post rursum, collegium aliud in civitate est virorum xxiv ex honestissimo civium ordine, quod CONCILIUM JURATUM vocant, propterea quod quotannis, non minùs quàm senatus, se solenni jurejurando obstringit Reip:&in collegio Trium-viri velut collegii præsides ac rectores, qui ex eo quòd nomine reliquorum verba faciunt in senatu, aut ubi res poscit, Talemanni sunt dicti. Et horum quoque, qui in concilio hoc sunt, munus biennè est, xii quotannis decedentibus, & totidem in decedentium locum surrogatis. Munus quod sit, ex ipsâ juramenti formulâ, quâ se Reip. obligant, est manifestum. Jurant autem apud consulem in senatu quotannis, vocatos in curiam se venturos, Reip. cum senatu consulturos, senatuique auxilio futuros, coitiones seorsim non facturos, nec factiones instituturos. Itaque longiùs si tendant, & non jussi à Senatu si coeant, ossicii limites excedere, & turbulentius agere putantur. Usus autem recepit, ac in morem abiit, ut rerum graviorum, quæ ad totam Remp. pertinent, nihil agat senatus, aut de iis constituat, nisi ex assensu concilii hujus: Cujusmodi sunt, bella suscipere & finire, fœdera inire, leges ferre & abrogare, munitiones novas, aut alia opera publica magni momenti instituere, in re monetariâ aliquid mutare, alieno ære civitatem gravare. De quibus cùm agitur, solet senatus eos, unâ cum iis, qui senatu proximè decesserunt, quos senatum veterem vocant, in curiam accersere, & rebus diligenter deliberatis & excussis, ex eorum assensu aut dissensu de iis statuere.Hoc ad robur decretorum, & retinendam civitatis concordiam non parum profore, majoribus est visum.
units.tr: The form of government in the city is aristocratic, tending moderately towards democracy. I now intend to set it out. In antiquity, when the city's fortunes were still smaller, four Rationales and eight Oldermanni administered it. But for more than three hundred years now, four Consuls have held the highest rank in it. To these were formerly added sixteen, and in more recent centuries twelve Senators. Together they make up the Senate, the head of the whole commonwealth. The urban jurisdiction rests with this Senate, and with it the power to issue and decree edicts in urban affairs, to summon, to arrest, to commit to custody, to coerce, to impose capital punishment, to grant pardons, to handle public money, and to appoint most of the other magistrates. Especially they appoint those Hovetmanni of whom I have often spoken, and likewise the Prefects of the territories outside the city, and they issue the Delegates, who sit in the colleges at home and abroad. They also elect the Treasurer, the Aedile of the commonwealth, and the public keepers of buildings, and they send embassies. Finally, it is the duty of this office to look after the whole commonwealth, and to direct its cares towards it. The office of senator lasts two years, and is so arranged that each year the middle part of the Senate (under the name Senate I include the Consuls as well) who have completed two years in office leaves the college. In place of those who leave, the same number, eight, succeed them and fill up the college. How these are designated I shall explain later. In the Senate the Consuls surpass the others in dignity, honour and authority. In the power and right of voting a senator is equal to a Consul, and likewise equal in the power of proposing motions. But the authority of the Consuls in delivering opinions is neither empty nor ineffective. It is their right, in turns of three months each, in the order that the lot gives, to preside over the Senate. The one who presides is also the keeper of the public seal, is attended by the official attendants or the accensi, has the power of summoning and arresting, and almost alone reports more business to the Senate than all the others in the Senate together. He asks the Senate for its votes, and what pleases the greater part he pronounces as the opinion of the whole Senate. Finally, if he is strong in talent and diligence, if he has eloquence, and if his spirit is not downcast, he can bring great weight to affairs in every direction. The same Consul, together with three senators whom either the lot or his agreement with his colleagues has joined to him, at a fixed time in the praetorium gives judgment to citizens who are litigating with one another, or to those who have an action against citizens. This is mostly for minor matters, or for matters concerning the security of payment, and only after the Senate has been dismissed at midday. In this tribunal the jurisdiction is of such a kind that it dispatches the litigants as quickly as possible, especially before the term of the praetor ends, and so it protects the good faith of the market and of debtors. Anyone who wishes has the right of appeal to the Senate, and from the Senate there is no further appeal. After the Senate, I shall pass over here the Hovetmanni, of whom I have already spoken often and shall speak again. There is another college in the city, of twenty-four men from the most honourable rank of citizens, which they call the SWORN COUNCIL, because, every year, no less than the Senate, it binds itself to the commonwealth by a solemn oath. In this college three men, like presidents and governors of the college, who speak in the Senate in the name of the rest, or where the matter requires, are called Talemanni. The office of those who are in this council also lasts two years, with twelve leaving each year and the same number being substituted in their place. What the office is can be seen plainly from the very formula of the oath by which they bind themselves to the commonwealth. They swear before the Consul in the Senate each year that, when summoned to the council chamber, they will come, that they will advise the commonwealth together with the Senate, that they will be of help to the Senate, that they will not hold separate meetings, and that they will not form factions. So if they strive further, and meet without being summoned by the Senate, they are thought to exceed the limits of their office and to act too turbulently. Custom, however, has taken hold, and has passed into a habit, that the Senate does nothing about matters of greater importance that concern the whole commonwealth, nor decides on them, unless with the assent of this council. Such matters are: to undertake and end wars, to enter into treaties, to pass and repeal laws, to begin new fortifications or other public works of great importance, to change something in the coinage, or to burden the state with foreign debt. When such matters are under discussion, the Senate usually summons into the chamber those who have just left the Senate, whom they call the old Senate, together with the council, and after the matters have been carefully deliberated and thrashed out, it decides on them with their assent or dissent. Our ancestors judged that this would contribute not a little to the strength of decrees and to keeping the concord of the state.

units.la: Cujus rei gratiâ interdum etiam alios ex honestiorum civium ordine senatus convocat, ut hujusmodi deliberationibus intersint, & maximè ædiles duos tribunitiæ potestatis, qui societatum, in quas opificum plebs est divisa, magistri & patroni sunt, easque in omnem movere partem possunt. Sed Concilium hoc juratum ut consilii potestatem habet,ita imperii aut jurisdictionis partem nullam, ideoque nec accensum aut apparitorem habet. Verum aliud est ad munus Concilii hujus pertinens non postremum, designare quotannis viros VIII, qui biennium in senatu sint, & Reip. consilio & potestate praesint: quod jus sane amplum. Designatio autem fit hoc modo. Concilium ad VI Idus Febr. ex voluntate senatus coactum in curia coram senatu per sortem designabat olim ex suo numero viros IX, proximo autem saeculo tantummodo v,quos nunc Gubernator adhuc ex pacto designat. Hi [?] praesente senatu, consule verbis praeeunte, jusjurandum dant, nil gratiae, odio, invidiae, cupidini se daturos, soliusque Reip. rationem habituros: mox, digresso senatu, reliquisque e concilio, in conclavi inclusi non ante inde discedunt, quam in viros VIII liberis suffragiis lectos consenserint. Legunt autem non tam quod certa jubeat lex, quam quod more sic fit receptum, plerumque duos, qui ex collegio Hovetmannorum, eodem forte tempore decedunt, deinde eos, qui in senatu prius fuerunt, nisi quid obstet, denique optimum quemque ex honestissimo civium ordine, maximeq; ex concilio aut collegio suo, velut ex seminario Senatus. Eo facto, electos sine mora senatui in curia congregato edunt, domumq; discedunt: senatus editos per viatorem confestim in curiam vocat. Qui si electioni assentiantur, quod fere accidit, eodem momento ad praetorium deducti, ibi aperto sub coelo circumfusi corona populi, qui excitus signo nolae majoris, & moris hujus gnarus huc frequens concurrit, solenni juramento, praeeunte verbis praeside consule e fenestrâ praetorii prospectante, stantes Reip. se obligant unâ cum caeteris in senatu mansuris, in annum proximum: postridie; cum iisdem collegis congregati, cumque iis in suffragia occulta missi, consules e suo collegarumque numero designant aut duos, si totidem loca vacant, id quod accidit ut plurimum, duobus fere quotannis e Consulatu decedentibus, aut tres, aut etiam nonnunquam quatuor, nonnunquam quoq; unum tantum. Designant autem ante alios plerumque eos, si eorum copia sit, qui consulatu ante sunt functi, judicesque inter agrarios fuerunt. Sic demùm die ab eo xiiii, qui Apostolo Petro sacer est, decedentibus veteribus totidem, munus suum capessunt. Quod si contingat, ut ex electis his unus pluresve delatum honorem recusent, eos Reip. mulctam dare aureos scutatos vicenos olim oportuit, nunc autem latiâ non multos ante annos lege aut capessere munus, aut civitate discedere oportet. Idque cùm accidit (accidit autem raro) itemque si quae alioqui senatorum consulumve loca seu morte, sive quacunque ratione alia vacent, non jam Quinquevirorum, aut jurati Concilii est (quamquam olim id etiam, sed ante aliquot sæcula fuisse videatur) verum ipsius senatus, alios sufficere, & collegas cooptare. Octiduo deinde post quàm haec senatus electio facta, coacto rursum Concilio jurato, simili ratione quinque ex ipsis alii, ut nunc mos habet (olim verò hac quoque in re ix,) eodem in loco sorte ducuntur. Per hos xii designantur ex eo civium ordine, qui lautioris fortunæ sunt, aut dote aliquâ animi commendati, qui decedentibus è collegio totidem, biennium jam munere functis succedant, & cum iis, qui annum tantum in collegio fuerunt, Reip. consulant. Tum totum collegium tres è sui medio capit, autoritate & usu rerum cæteris præstantiores, qui collegium regant sententiamque ejus, ubi opus est, velut oratores exponant: quos Talemannos ex ea re appellatos dixi. Et olim quidem ante tumultus hos civiles, ita in rebus his observatum, non lege quidem, sed more inveterato, ut in senatum nisi ex familiis nobilibus aut patriciis nemo ferè legeretur, nec temerè ex iisdem, nisi qui esset aut suisset è Concilio jurato tanquam senatus seminario, operamque & fidem suam Reip. minoribus in muneribus, in procuratione ædium, ac aliarum rerum sacratarum, & similibus probassent: In Concilium autem juratum similiter ex iisdem familiis frequentes cooptarentur, quoad ejus fieri posset, aut ex reliquo civium ordine honestissimo, ut quisque erat vel eruditione, vel alia aliqua præ cæteris dote conspicuus & commendatus; ex opificum autem aut institorum collegiis aut nunquam, aut omninò rarissimè quisquam caperetur. Indignum enim id concilio honoratissimo, & Reip. periculosum propter abjectos hujusmodi hominum sensus praeter lucrum penè nihil spectantes, aut magni facientes putabatur. Hoc verò praetereundum hic silentio non est, non semul accidisse olim rebus sic poscentibus, aut factionum vi, ut exposita ratio in designandis quotannis Consulibus duobus dimidiaque senatûs parte observata non fit; sed consules iidem omnes vel biennium, vel ad annos complures, vel denique ad vitae exitum in munere ac honore permanserint: idemque sit factum in reliquo senatu. Est praeterea aliud in civitate collegium, partem Reip. curans, negotiantium scilicet disciplinae, ac juri nautico tuendo, & dirimendis indè natis controversiis olim praesectum, cujus tribunal Gilderecht [?] lingua Teutonica ex re nominatum. Octo viris constat hodiè; quorum etiam, ut senatorum, & eorum qui sunt in concilio jurato, munus est bienne, quaternis similiter quotannis collegio decedenti-[?]
units.tr: For this reason the Senate sometimes also summons others from the more honourable rank of citizens, to take part in such deliberations, and especially the two aediles of the tribunician power, who are masters and patrons of the guilds into which the common people of the craftsmen are divided, and who can move them in every direction. But this sworn council, while it has the power of counsel, has no part of command or jurisdiction, and therefore has neither an accensus nor an attendant. But there is another function of this council, not the least, which pertains to it: to designate each year eight men who are to be in the Senate for two years, and to preside over the counsel and power of the commonwealth, which is indeed a broad right. The designation is made in this way. The council, summoned by the will of the Senate on the sixth of the Ides of February, in the chamber before the Senate, used formerly to designate by lot nine men from its own number, and in the last century only five, whom now the Governor still designates by agreement. These [?], with the Senate present and the Consul leading the words, swear that they will give nothing to favour, hatred, envy or greed, and that they will have regard to the good of the commonwealth alone. Then, when the Senate has withdrawn and the rest of the council has departed, they are shut up in a room and do not leave from there until they have agreed on eight men chosen by free vote. They choose, however, not so much because a fixed law commands it, as because it has been received by custom: usually two who, by chance, are leaving the college of the Hovetmanni at the same time; then those who were previously in the Senate, unless something stands in the way; and finally the best man from the most honourable rank of citizens, especially from the council or from their own college, as from a seedbed of the Senate. This done, they bring out the chosen men without delay to the Senate gathered in the chamber, and go home. The Senate, when the men have been brought out, at once summons them by a messenger into the chamber. If they assent to the election, which usually happens, they are at once led to the praetorium and there, in the open air, surrounded by a crowd of people, who, roused by the sign of the larger bell and aware of this custom, come together in numbers, they bind themselves to the commonwealth with a solemn oath. The Consul presiding leads the words, while the Consul looks out from a window of the praetorium. They swear standing, together with the others who are to remain in the Senate, for the following year. The next day, gathered with the same colleagues and sent to secret voting along with them, the Consuls designate from their own number and that of their colleagues either two, if as many places are vacant (which usually happens, since about two Consuls leave office each year), or three, or sometimes even four, and sometimes only one. They usually designate first, if there is a supply of them, those who have already completed the consulship and have been judges among the agrarian judges. Thus, on the day after the fourteenth, which is sacred to the Apostle Peter, when the same number of old members have left, they take up their office. But if it happens that one or more of those chosen refuse the office offered, they used formerly to owe the commonwealth a fine of twenty gold scudi, but now, by a law passed not many years ago, they must either take up the office or leave the city. When this happens (though it happens rarely), and likewise if any places of senators or consuls are otherwise vacant, whether by death or by some other cause, it is not the business of the Quinqueviri or of the sworn council (although formerly this seems to have been so, some centuries ago), but of the Senate itself to appoint others and co-opt colleagues. Eight days after this election by the Senate, the sworn council is summoned again, and in a similar way five others from among themselves, as the custom now is (formerly nine in this matter), are drawn by lot in the same place. Through these twelve are designated from that rank of citizens who are of more affluent fortune, or who are commended by some gift of mind, and who are to succeed the same number leaving the college, which has completed two years in office, and together with those who have been in the college only one year, they advise the commonwealth. Then the whole college takes three from its midst, who are superior to the rest in authority and experience, who govern the college and, where necessary, set out its opinion as speakers. I have said that they are called Talemanni for this reason. And formerly, before these civil tumults, it was observed in these matters, not by law indeed but by long-standing custom, that scarcely anyone was elected to the Senate except from noble or patrician families, and not rashly even from these, unless he had been, or had been, from the sworn council, as from the seedbed of the Senate, and had proved his effort and loyalty to the commonwealth in lesser offices, in the management of buildings and of other sacred matters, and in similar things. Likewise, into the sworn council were frequently co-opted from these same families, as far as that could be done, or from the rest of the most honourable rank of citizens, each as he was conspicuous and commended for learning or for some other gift above the others. But from the guilds of craftsmen or shopkeepers, either no one or very rarely anyone was taken. For this was thought unworthy of the most honourable council, and dangerous to the commonwealth, because of the base feelings of such men, who look to almost nothing but gain, or who value it above all. Yet this must not be passed over here in silence: it has not happened at the same time, that the explained method of designating two Consuls and half the Senate each year has not been observed, when affairs so demanded, or by the force of factions. But the same Consuls have remained in office and honour for two years, or for many years, or finally until the end of their lives, and the same has been done in the rest of the Senate. There is also another college in the city, which takes care of a part of the commonwealth, namely the discipline of merchants and the protection of maritime law, and which was formerly set over the settling of the controversies arising from it. Its tribunal is named from this matter in the Teutonic tongue Gilderecht [?]. Today it consists of eight men. The office of these, as of the senators and of those in the sworn council, lasts two years, with four similarly leaving the college each year [?]

units.la: { } Catchword "tibus" read from the foot of the page at the right; taken as the next word. tibus ac totidem succedentibus. Id hoc modo fit. Senatus ea pars, quæ magistratu abit, quatuor viros eligit singulos è singulis civitatis regionibus, ( hæ quatuor omnino sunt ) honestissimos & gravissimos quosque ex omni populo, nulla alia tum potestate publica præditos. Hi quatuor electi totidem aliis, quibus expletum biennium est, suffecti, cæteris, qui annum in munere fuere, adduntur. Cuncti hi statim ad VIII Calend. Martij ex sui medio Seniorem designant, quem OLDERMANNUM vocant, & duos Fisci magistros, <bl>Die Bußherren</bl> dictos, fiscelli scilicet numarii curam habentes, omnes in his officiis annuos: præter quos reliqui quinque societatis judices, <bl>Die</bl> <bl>Gildtrichters/</bl> nuncupantur. Senior, in collegio actor præcipuus, velut advocatus Reip. in tuendo stapulæ jure, de quo dixi supra, ejusque custos ac vindex, si quem contra id delinquere deprehendit, eum multam poscit, tergiversantem apud duum-viros fiscales postulat, aut ad totum collegium rem defert: sententiam pronunciatam ipse exequitur, nisi reus ad superius tribunal aut Senatûs aut Hoyetmannorum provocet. Duùm-viri fiscales fisci curam habent cum Oldermanno,atque albi mercatorum: oportetque eos, qui mercatui operam dare volunt, apud hos priùs nomina sua profiteri; fine quo nemini id facere licet. Et sunt iidem ὑπεύθυνοι[?] id est, reddendis apud Consulem rationibus obnoxii quotannis cum eodem Oldermanno: quibus expeditis, successoribus fiscellum tradunt, pecuniæ reliquum ærario Reip. inferunt. Sed est collegii hujus curæ antiquitus commissa præcipuè custodia tota juris nautici, in codice Reip. diligenter descripti, jurisdictioque universa ad res navales & maritimas pertinens. Verùm collegium hoc ipsum collegarum quoque numero olim duplo fuit majus, (xiii enim præter Oldermannum & duùmviros fisci curatores fuere) & electionis ratio ab eâ, quæ hîc exposita, diversa. Nunc cum numero potestas quoque non nihil arctata. Electio olim sic habuit. Senatûs pars munere decedens è fui medio sortitò edebat quàtuor: hi cum Oldermanno & duobus fiscelli magistris eodem die viros xvi eligebant optimos quosque secundum urbis regiones, quorum nullus eo anno in senatu esset, aut senatu decessisset. Electi xvi-viri ex suo numero Oldermannum statim designabant hac lege, ut per vices ex urbis regionibus aliis post alias designaretur in singulos annos; habebaturque ea ratio propinquitatis, quae in senatu eligendo solet haberi. Caeteta similia his, quae jam dixi. Deinde praeter hos alii quoque sunt O-ctoviri, urbis magistri, bini ex singulis regionibus delecti, honore & autoritate non postremi; bis quotannis censum agunt omnium civium, & quid quisque eorum gerat, quae negotia tractet, quibus se suosque tueatur, inquirunt, desides aut noxios Reip. cedere cogunt: ne quis aedificans publice privatimve noceat, aut bono officiat, ne quid vitii canalibus ad deducendas aquas ac sordes per urbem accidat, quaeque alia ad mundiciem urbis pertinent, providentur: denique si diligentes sunt, perutilem operam Reip. praestant
units.tr: tibus ac totidem succedentibus. This is done in the following way. The part of the Senate that is leaving office chooses four men, one from each of the city's districts (there are exactly four), the most honourable and respected men from the whole people, who hold no other public office at that time. These four elected men are added to the others whose two-year term has been completed, and they replace an equal number of others, while those who have served the year in office are also added. All of these, at once, on the eighth day before the Calends of March, designate from among themselves a senior, whom they call the Oldermann, and two treasury masters, called the Die Bußherren, who hold the care of the fiscal purse and the money. All hold these offices for one year. Besides these, the remaining five are called the judges of the guild, Die Gildtrichters. The Senior, the chief actor in the college, acts like the advocate of the commonwealth in defending the staple right, of which I spoke above. He is also its guardian and avenger: if he finds anyone offending against this, he demands a fine, and if the offender shifts his ground, he brings him before the two fiscal magistrates, or refers the matter to the whole college. He himself carries out the sentence once pronounced, unless the accused appeals to a higher court, either of the Senate or of the Hoyetmannen. The two fiscal magistrates have charge of the treasury together with the Oldermann, and of the merchants' register. Those who wish to engage in trade must first enter their names with these men, and no one may do so without this. They are also [ὑπεύθυνοι], that is, bound to render accounts yearly to the Consul together with the same Oldermann. When these are finished, they hand the purse to their successors and pay the remaining money into the public treasury. But the chief charge entrusted to this college from of old is the whole guardianship of maritime law, which is carefully written down in the code of the commonwealth, and the entire jurisdiction pertaining to naval and maritime affairs. Yet this college itself was formerly twice as large in number of members (for there were thirteen, besides the Oldermann and the two fiscal treasurers), and the method of election was different from the one set out here. Now, with the number reduced, its power has also been somewhat narrowed. Formerly the election went like this. The part of the Senate that was leaving office drew lots from among its own members for four men, and these four, together with the Oldermann and the two treasury masters, on the same day chose sixteen of the best men, according to the city's districts, none of whom was then in the Senate or had left the Senate. The sixteen elected men designated the Oldermann from their own number, under this rule: that he should be designated in turn from the city's districts, one after another, year by year; and the consideration of kinship, which is usually observed in electing senators, was also observed. The rest was similar to what I have already described. Besides these there are also the Octoviri, the city magistrates, two chosen from each district, not the least in honour and authority. Twice a year they take a census of all the citizens, and inquire what each one does, what business he conducts, and how he protects himself and his family; they compel the idle and the harmful to withdraw from the commonwealth. They provide that no one building, publicly or privately, does harm or injury to the good; that no defect arises in the channels that carry water and filth through the city; and whatever else pertains to the cleanliness of the city. In short, if they are diligent, they render very useful service to the commonwealth.

units.la: Quinetiam scloppetariorum praefecti quatuor diu in civitate fuere, à senatu quoque designati, perpetui. Hi curam armorum habebant, juventutemque maximè exercebant in tractandis scloppetis, foro venalis annonæ, quæ ad urbem defertur quotidie, præstant: à pistoribus & iis, qui cerevisiam coquunt, ne quid fraudis committeretur, ut justa esset ponderum & mensurarum ratio in officinis, cœnum ut publicis locis amoveretur, procurabant. Quæ omnia nunc ad centuriones oppidanos octo, qui iis successêre, translata sunt. Denique ÆDILES duo in Reip. sunt Trib. potestatis, quam non lege datam, sed paulatim nitendo longiùs tubulentis[?] actionibus quæsitam proximis sæculis usurparunt non magno sanè Reip. bono. Horum magnum esse nomen solet. Et quoniam cum plebe opificum & institorum connexi sunt, ac ab eâ dependent, de plebis hujus ordine & distinctione paucâ hic dicam. Dividitur ipsa secundùm artificiorum aut rerum, quas tractant, genera diversa in societates XVIII: exceptis, qui cerevisiæ coquendæ officinas exercent, ac negotia majora in emendo & vendendo gerunt. Dignioris quippè ordinis miscere se vilioribus nolunt habenturque post nobilitatem inter honestissimos totius civitatis. Hæ societates singulæ ternos sibi præfectos suffragiis designatos creant quotannis mox à Paschatos: & in his primum quemque Seniorem vel Oldermannum, velut totius societatis præsidem, reliquos binos capita societatis dicunt: omnes universum numero LIV. Et hi vicissim circiter idem tempus mox ab electione sui in cœnobio Jacobæo congregati, Ædiles, quos dixi, edunt, non aliunde quàm ex his ipsis societatibus. Quamquam fuit quondam tempus, quo duobus istis tertius quoque è Senatu adjungebatur, qui dudum nunc collegio defluxit. At Ædiles patronos se plebis professi, quam & suopte ingenio, & per præfectos in omnem facilè impellere partem poterant, haud dissimiles veteribus in Reip. Rom. Tribunis, ab humili initio eò tandem progressi sunt, dum curam patrociniumque egenæ & circumventæ præterexunt plebeculæ, multitudine freti, ut in morem abierit, nulla recipere de majore re decreta, quibus assensum hi ipsi Ædiles non adhibuissent. Itaque quoties hujusmodi aliquid actum, cum concilio jurato & cæteris isti quoque in curiam sunt vocati. Qui si, cæteris accedentibus sententiæ senatus, vel soli dissensissent, levantes se ultimis subselliis intercedebant: vetabantque senatum & reliquos progredi, ac decernere aliquid, priusquam ad societatum plebejarum præfectos, vel ad ipsas integras societates, si ita præfectis videretur, res esset relata. Sic convocatis primùm præfectis, qui erant, ut dixi, numero omnes LIV[?], in conclavi apud Jacobæos res in medium proponebatur. Eá[?] si difficilior videretur, societates totæ certis adesse locis jubebantur, & seorsim consulebantur à suis quæque præfectis. Earum sententiâ, quam plerumque præfecti dictabant, ad ædiles, ab ædilibus ad senatum & consilium juratum relata, de negotio ac Rep. statuebatur. Itâ fiebat, ut optima quæque consilia, ac Reip. profutura plerumque corrumperentur, impedirenturve. Nam Ædiles cum præfectis hisce ex opificum officinis; infimaque plebe prorepentes, ac vilibus rebus innutriti Reip. benè gerendæ ferè ignari sunt, improvidi, & supra ea, quæ ante pedes sunt, nihil sapientes, gratiæque inscitæ multitudinis dediti. Quo nomine, id quod plerumque tum fiebat, si se plebi probassent, complures etiam annos suo in munere continuabantur. Asenatu tamen, ut cæteri omnes, qui aliquid publici muneris aut potestatis habent, sic hi quoque Ædiles suum jus & olim accepêre, & hodie etiam accipiunt, cùm sacramentum apud eum dicunt quotannis: Suntque ea, quæ exorbitarunt in hac re, salubriter jam correcta, & ad metam revocata. Porrò de societatibus his plebeis ita in legibus civitatis perscriptum est, non licere ipsis inconsulto, aut non probante senatu statuta sibi condere, aut fœdera facere: præfectos verò earum teneri, vocante senatu, in curiâ se sistere; instrumenta statutorum & privilegiorum suorum senatui exhibere, profiterique iuratos[?], præter ea nihil se statutorum in societatibus suis habere: præterea, si quæ societas civitati inutilis aut noxia videatur, in potestate senatus esse, eam abrogare: item, si quis in societate quid committat, quo se indignum societate secisse videatur, deque eo controversia existat, ejus cognitionem senatui deberi cum tribus societatis præfectis: ad hæc, societates cum præfectis suis teneri, summa ope, summis viribus ut tueantur dignitatem & jus senatus, eique auxilio & firmamento sint, ac pœnas contumacium, cum res requirit, promoveant. Habent tamen societatum præfecti in suâ quisque societate potestatem cognoscendi controversias quasdam ad societatem pertinentes, easque definiendi, ac multas quoque capiendi ab his, qui contra societatis leges deliquisse deprehenduntur. Sed id totum sic habet, ut jurisdictionis species aut pars videri nequeat.
units.tr: Moreover, four prefects of the musketeers were for a long time in the city, likewise designated by the Senate and holding office for life. They had charge of the arms, and chiefly trained the young men in handling muskets. They also supervised the market for provisions, which is brought to the city every day. They saw to it from the bakers and the brewers that no fraud was committed, and that the system of weights and measures in the workshops was just; and they took care that the mud was removed from public places. All these duties have now been transferred to the eight town centurions, who succeeded them. Finally, there are two Aediles in the commonwealth, with the power of tribunes. In recent centuries they have usurped this power, which was not granted by law but gained little by little through pressing their claims further and further, to no great benefit of the commonwealth. Their name is usually held in high esteem. And since they are connected with the common people of craftsmen and shopkeepers and depend on them, I shall say a little here about the order and division of this common people. It is divided, according to the kinds of crafts or of the goods they deal in, into eighteen guilds, with the exception of those who run the brewing houses and conduct larger businesses in buying and selling. For these, being of a more distinguished rank, do not want to mix with the lower sort, and they are counted, after the nobility, among the most honourable of the whole city. Each of these guilds creates for itself three prefects, designated by vote, every year soon after Easter. Of these, the first is called the Senior or Oldermann, as president of the whole guild, and the other two are called heads of the guild. All together they number fifty-four. These in turn, gathering about the same time, soon after their own election, in the Jacobean monastery, elect the Aediles I have mentioned, and they choose them from none other than these same guilds. Yet there was once a time when a third man from the Senate was added to these two, but he has long since dropped out of the college. But the Aediles, professing themselves patrons of the common people, whom by their own nature and through the prefects they could easily drive in any direction, though at the beginning little like the old tribunes of the Roman Republic, have at last advanced so far that, while they took up the care and protection of the needy and oppressed little people, relying on their numbers, they have, as has become the custom, received no decrees on any major matter to which the Aediles themselves had not given their assent. So whenever anything of this kind was discussed, the sworn council and the others were also summoned to the senate-house together with these men. If these men, when the others agreed with the opinion of the Senate, or if they alone dissented, rising from the lowest benches, interposed their objection: they forbade the Senate and the rest to proceed and decide anything before the matter had been referred to the prefects of the plebeian guilds, or to the guilds themselves whole, if the prefects thought fit. Thus, when the prefects were first called together, who, as I said, numbered fifty-four in all, the matter was put before them in a room at the Jacobeans. If it seemed rather difficult, the guilds as wholes were ordered to attend at certain places, and each was consulted separately by its own prefects. The opinion of these, which the prefects for the most part dictated, was reported to the Aediles, and from the Aediles to the Senate and the sworn council, and a decision was made on the business and on the commonwealth. In this way it happened that the best counsels, and those most beneficial to the commonwealth, were for the most part corrupted or hindered. For the Aediles, together with these prefects, who came up from the workshops and the lowest common people, and who were brought up on humble things, are for the most part ignorant of how to manage the commonwealth well: they are shortsighted, wise in nothing beyond what lies at their feet, and devoted to the favour of the ignorant multitude. For this reason, which was then commonly the case, if they pleased the common people they were kept in their office for several years. Yet, as with all others who hold some public office or power, these Aediles too have both received their right from the Senate, and still receive it today, when they take their oath before it each year. And the abuses that crept into this matter have now been wholesomely corrected and brought back within their bounds. Furthermore, concerning these plebeian guilds it is written in the laws of the city that they may not draw up statutes for themselves, or make alliances, without the consent or approval of the Senate; that their prefects are bound, when the Senate summons them, to appear in the senate-house; to show the Senate the documents of their statutes and privileges, and to declare under oath that they have no statutes in their guilds beyond these. Moreover, if any guild seems useless or harmful to the city, it is in the power of the Senate to abolish it. Likewise, if anyone in a guild commits something by which he seems to have shown himself unworthy of the guild, and a dispute arises about it, the hearing of the case belongs to the Senate together with three prefects of the guild. In addition, the guilds with their prefects are bound to defend with all their strength the dignity and right of the Senate, to be its aid and support, and to enforce penalties against the disobedient when the matter requires it. Nevertheless, the prefects of each guild have the power, within their own guild, to hear certain disputes pertaining to the guild, to settle them, and also to exact fines from those who are caught breaking the guild's laws. But all of this is so arranged that it cannot appear to be a kind or part of jurisdiction.

units.la: Et si quis eo lædi se injuste à præfectis existimet, is pro more Ædiles, tanquam societatum summos magistros atque ἐφόρους[?] appellat, ab his porrò, si placet, ad ipsum quoque senatum provocat. Postremo societatum præfecti terni jurati, ut est in iisdem civitatis legibus, rationes accepti & expensi reddunt Ædilibus. Æ- diles pecuniam impendunt ædificiis & structuris publicis, unde nomen iis datum, ac vicissim accepti & impensi calculum ponunt apud eosdem hos præsectos,adeoque apud consules,si vel hi vel illi hoc requirant. Est verò etiam perhonesta in civitate procuratio Ædituorum, quæ sacras ædes, & quæ istuc pertinent, tuentur, bonaque in eum usum à majoribus collata administrant: delecti feré ex patritiâ nobilitate, & bini aut terni in singulis parochiis: eaque procuratio si senatoriis hominibus commendata non est, viam saltem procuratoribus ad honorem atq; ordinem eum sternit.Et cum his pari penè passu incedunt PROVISORES quos vocant, aut curatores ptochodochiorum, quæ quatuor esse in urbe dixi, maximè ejus, quod est ad S. Spiritum, & alterius ad S. Gertrudem, propter magnitudinem & possessiones ac reditus eorum peramplos· Ad quam administrationem senatorii quoque ordinis viri saepè vocantur, aliique qui lautissimæ conditionis inter cives sunt. Nec prætereundi hic, qui ædibus præfecti sunt, quas FRATRUM vulgò vocant, in quibus adolescentes literarum & pietatis studio dediti alii gratis, alii pretio modico, pro cujusque fortunâ ac loco aluntur & habentur honestè, iisque omnibus morum & studiorum inspector atque exactor præest: quorum præfectorum ratio quoque par cum prioribus. Et sunt hæ curationes omnes, quas recensui, non annuæ, nec determinati temporis, sed in arbitrio consulum; deque his rationes apud eosdem redduntur consules, quoties & cùm placet id ipsis. Quid de SCHOLARCHIS dicam ? quibus Scholæ & totius rei Scholasticæ literariæ cura, pecuniæque in hunc usum destinatæ quæstura, denique; omnium huc pertinentium ἐφόρεια[?] senatu demandata est: quorum alter consularis, alter senator, aut ordinis senatorii hactenus fuit.
units.tr: If anyone thinks he has been unjustly wronged by the prefects, he appeals in the customary way to the aediles, who are called the chief masters of the guilds and ephors [ἐφόρους], and from them, if he wishes, further to the senate itself. Finally, the guild prefects, three sworn men as the same city laws require, render their accounts of receipts and expenditure to the aediles. The aediles spend money on public buildings and works, which is where their name comes from, and in turn they submit their account of receipts and expenditure to the same prefects, and so to the consuls, if either party requires it. There is also a most honourable office in the city, that of the church wardens (aedituorum), who look after the sacred buildings and the matters that belong to them, and manage the goods handed down for that use by our ancestors. They are chosen mostly from the patrician nobility, two or three in each parish. Even if this office is not entrusted to senators, it at least opens a path to honour and rank for the wardens. Walking almost step for step with them are the so-called PROVISORS, or overseers of the almshouses. I said there were four of these in the city, the greatest being the one at the Holy Spirit and the other at St Gertrude's, because of their size and their very large possessions and revenues. Men of the senatorial order are often called to this administration, as are others of the most distinguished condition among the citizens. Nor should I pass over those who are set over the houses commonly called the BROTHERS' houses, in which young men devoted to learning and piety are maintained and kept respectably, some free of charge and some for a modest fee according to each one's means and station. Over all of them presides an inspector and overseer of morals and studies. The accounts of these prefects are also rendered in the same way as those of the former. All these offices I have listed are not annual, nor for a fixed term, but at the discretion of the consuls, and accounts are rendered to the same consuls whenever they wish and as often as they please. What shall I say of the SCHOLARCHS, to whom the care of the schools and of all the scholastic and literary business, and the treasury of money destined for this use, and finally the supervision [ephoreia] of all matters pertaining to these, has been committed by the senate? One of them has hitherto been a consul, the other a senator, or of the senatorial order.

units.la: Quid de Reip. QUAESTORE, qui pecuniæ, ac omnium redituum eius conquisitor & custos est, acceptique ac expensi indices servat, atque ex his rationes sena tui debet. Quid de Trium-viris, vectigalium, portoriorum accisarum, uti vocant, magistris, ad forum & curiam loco idoneo negotio huic & muneri suo vacantibus? Quid de iis, qui pecuniam Sacerdotiis olim legatam, solvendo minis-tris Ecclesiae stipendio, & sartis tectis tenendis eorum domiciliis colligunt, & expendunt? Quid de orphanotropheij curatoribus, & eleemosynariis pauperum domi sedentium alimoniae praepositis? qui omnes ex honestissimis civium ordinibus a senatu leguntur, in tempus incertum, ab ejusque arbitrio pendent. Adde ante hos nominandum honoris causa jurisconsultum, quem S Y N D IC U M dicunt, liberali Reip. stipendio ornatum, summaque dignitate: qui & a consilio est senatus, & ejusdem orator, adeoque universae civitatis advocatus: quem locum amplissimus & consultissimus, clarissimusque vir, amicus singularis, P A N C R A T I U S C A S T R ICOMIUS I. U.D. jam ab annis aliquot, & nunc; dum haec recuduntur, tenet. Adde & Scribas duos ut jam res habet(nam unus tantum fuit) qui senatui eidem à secretis, & epistolis, scribendisque & custodiendis actis publicis sunt: quorum munus perhonestum & quaestuosum est. Et ad hos armamentarij publici, id est, tormentorum aeneorum, pulveris nitrosi,& omnis instrumenti ac apparatus huc pertinentis, fabrûm quoque & fabricarum publicarum, itemque vigilum praefectos, manipulorumque magistros: praefectum insuper noctis, nocturnis facinoribus civium reprimendis, accenso ministrisque armatis fultum. Et hi quidem omnes, quos recensui, rem urbanam curant, è quibus alii verè Reip. alii senatûs ministri sunt. Praeter eos verò collegium in urbe est juris dicundi causâ antiquitus institutum, & saepiùs jam ante nobis in hoc libro memoratum, perampla praeditum potestate ac honore, quod HOVETMANNORUM CAMERAM vulgò in-digetant. Id autem quamquam non in civves, sed in eos, qui vicinum agrum foederre quondam civitati junctum inhabitant, jurisdictionem directam habet, tamen non abs're hoc loco potissimum recenseo. Nec enim solùm in urbe semper, nec usquam alibi, sedem tenet, & jus dicit, sed etiam praeter cives opibus & dignitate praecipuos, & in his haud temerè alios quam consulatu functos, collegas non admittit: nec ulli praeter senatum edendorum collegarum potestatem habent, nec aliunde quam ab eodem senatu expectare & accipere stipendia antiquitus ante dimissam integram libertatem collegae solent. Quo de collegio quamquam multa sparsim hoc libro dicta sint, tamen ut res manifestior fiat, paulo altiùs hic quoque quaedam repetenda. Et primùm, quae prima collegii hujus, aut Hovetmannorum origo, quod principium,dicere non possum. Nec enim id literis proditum usquam, quod sciam.Primos verò in monimentis Reipub. mihi lectos Hovetmannos Kenonianis temporibus, post annum M cccc à natali Domini Servatoris nostri,superiùs ostendi, eosq; tum tributis & tractandae pecuniae per agrum praefuisse memoravi. De his porrò, vestigiis[?] monumentorum veterum insistens, & omnia expendens diligenter, sic reperi: Cùm concors cum ordinibus agri vicini civitas ageret, ac foedera in certos annos percussa identidem prorogaret, prope ut una utrorumque Respublica videretur, ex consensu sociorum eos profluxisse, rectius atque aequalius expediundi juris, & tenendae concordiae, conservandaeque quietis publicae causa: electos esse ex spectatissimis & integerrimis quibusque in civitate, interdum etiam ex iis, qui e nobilitate agrariâ in urbem commigrarant, & jus civitatis acquiserant: quinos & quinos in collegio suisse perannos amplius ix[?], eosque incerta ratione, prout operam suam probassent, aut grati Reipubl. essent, aut casus daret, vel permutatos successoribus: vel per annos complures, quod erat frequens, continuatos: praetoriam potestatem tenuisse in omnes per agrum habitantes, eaque usos totius provinciae, id est, agri & civitatis nomine, edictisque nomen senatus cum nomine suo subscripsisse, & civitatis sigillo edicta & literas signasse: jus dixisse iis, qui fraudem sibi fieri apud reliquos per agrum judices, aliòve modo suum se consequi, non posse querebantur, exceptis successionum causis, quarum cognitio pervetusto more conventui jurediciali, de qno ante dixi relinquebantur: Et tamen de his quoque causis appellatos fuisse, decretumqee suum, usque in conventus tempus interposuisse: denique huic etiam conventui aut solos, aut cum senatu civitatis interfuisse, imò praesedisse, aut saltem non ultimas in ea partes tenuisse, à sententiis decretisque eorum, nisi ex partium consensu, provocationem non fuisse: imprimis vero operam dedisse, & auxilio fuisse iis, qui crediti debitive aliquem eorum, qui in agro habebant sedes, cujuscunque is ordinis esset, postulabant: nec declinare cuiquam cognitionem, nec latâ sententi-tiâ tergiversari licuisse: ita celerrimè jus fuisse expeditum, & suum cuique tributum: multosque adeò contractus tum paulatim eam conditionem habere coepisse, ut non alios apud judices, quàm hos, si quid controversiae forte incideret, aut in solvendo morâ exisseret, causa ageretur : id institutum cùm alias ob res, tùm ob fidem contractuum & commerciorum tuendam salutare communi Reip. visum, probatumque in morem ivisse, atque ita vim legis tenuisse.
units.tr: What of the city QUAESTOR, who collects and keeps guard over the money and all its revenues, keeps the lists of receipts and expenditures, and must render accounts to the senate from these? What of the three TRIUMVIRS, masters of the tolls, customs and excises, as they are called, who attend to this business and their office in a suitable place by the market and the town hall? What of those who collect and spend the money once bequeathed to the priesthoods for paying the ministers of the Church and for keeping their dwellings in good repair? What of the curators of the orphanage and of the almoners who oversee the support of the poor living at home? All of these are chosen by the senate from the most honourable ranks of the citizens, for an indefinite time, and depend on its discretion. Add before these, to be named out of respect, the jurist whom they call the SYNDIC, adorned with a generous salary from the commonwealth and of the highest dignity. He is both a member of the senate's council and its spokesman, and so the advocate of the whole city. This office is held, and is held even now while these pages are being reprinted, by the most distinguished and learned man, a famous and singular friend, PANCRATIUS CASTRICOMIUS, doctor of both laws, who has held it for some years. Add also the two clerks (as things now stand, for there was only one before), who serve the same senate as secretaries and letter-writers, and who write and keep the public records. Their office is most honourable and profitable. To these must be added the prefects of the public arsenal, that is, of the bronze guns, saltpetre powder, and all the equipment and apparatus pertaining to them, and also of the public smiths and workshops, and likewise the prefects of the night watch and the officers of the bands, and the prefect of the night, who restrains citizens' nocturnal crimes, supported by the herald and armed attendants. All these I have listed look after civic affairs, and some of them are truly servants of the commonwealth, others of the senate. Besides these there is in the city a college, established long ago for the purpose of administering justice and already mentioned more than once earlier in this book, endowed with very great power and honour, which is commonly called the Chamber of the Hovetmanni. Although its direct jurisdiction extends not over the citizens but over those who inhabit the neighbouring countryside, which was once joined to the city by treaty, I do not think it inappropriate to list it here especially. For it not only always holds its seat and gives judgment in the city and nowhere else, but, apart from citizens outstanding in wealth and dignity, and among these rarely anyone except those who have held the consulship, it admits no colleagues. Nor do they have the power to appoint colleagues except by the senate, and in ancient times, before complete liberty was lost, they were accustomed to expect and receive their salaries from the same senate. Although many things have been said here and there in this book about this college, nevertheless, so that the matter may be clearer, some points must be gone over here again in greater detail. First, I cannot say what the first origin or beginning of this college, or of the Hovetmanni, was, for as far as I know it has never been recorded in writing. But I have shown above that the earliest Hovetmanni I have read of in the records of the commonwealth were in the time of Keno, after the year 1400 from the birth of our Saviour, and I noted that at that time they presided over taxes and the handling of money throughout the countryside. Following the traces of the old records about these men, and weighing everything carefully, I have found the following. When the city, in harmony with the orders of the neighbouring countryside, was carrying on its affairs, and was repeatedly renewing treaties struck for fixed years, so that the commonwealth seemed almost to be one for both, it came about by agreement of the allies that, for the sake of more correct and equal administration of justice, of keeping concord, and of preserving public peace, men were chosen from the most respected and upright of the citizens, sometimes also from those who had moved into the city from the landed nobility and had acquired citizenship. Five and five were in the college for more than nine years, and they were changed for successors, or continued for many years (which was common), according to no fixed rule, depending on whether they had approved their work and pleased the commonwealth, or as chance would have it. They held praetorian power over all who lived in the countryside, and used it in the name of the whole province, that is, of the countryside and the city. In their edicts they signed the name of the senate together with their own, and sealed the edicts and letters with the city seal. They gave judgment to those who complained that they could not obtain their due from the other judges in the countryside, or that they were being cheated in some other way, with the exception of cases of inheritance, which were left to the judicial assembly, the very old institution I mentioned before. Yet even in these cases appeals were made to them, and they interposed their own decree until the time of the assembly. Finally, either alone or with the senate of the city they were present at this assembly, indeed they presided over it, or at least held no lowest place in it; and there was no appeal from their sentences and decrees except by agreement of the parties. Above all they took care to help those who demanded payment of debts owed to them or by them from any of those who lived in the countryside, whatever their rank; no one could decline their jurisdiction, nor evade a sentence once given. Thus justice was dispatched very quickly, and each received his due. And so many contracts gradually began to be on this footing, that cases were pursued before no other judges than these, if any dispute arose or delay in payment occurred. This arrangement, both for other reasons and for the sake of protecting good faith in contracts and dealings, was thought beneficial to the common commonwealth, and having been approved it grew into custom, and thus held the force of law.

units.la: Ad hæc animadverti, eosdem, qui Hovetmanni erant, simul eodemque tempore nonnunquam consules quoq; aliquando, aut senatores Reip. urbanæ fuisse, rationes eidem Reip. ejusve senatui reddidisse, edicendi mandandique jus ac potestatem non solùm apud Cislavicanos, sed etiam trans Lavicam habuisse : quod argumento irrefragabili est, non ab agrariis ordinibus vicinis eos electos fuisse, nec ab iis pependisse, delegatámve ab iisdem potestatem tenuisse, sed à solâ civitate :
units.tr: I have also noticed that the same men who were Hovetmanni sometimes at the same time, and occasionally as consuls or senators of the city government, rendered accounts to that government or its senate. They held the right and power of issuing and enforcing edicts not only among the Cislavicani but also across the Lauwers. This is an irrefutable proof that they were not chosen by the neighbouring rural orders, did not depend on them, and did not hold their power by delegation from them, but by the city alone.

units.la: „nec enim ideò hos à Translavicanis munus accepisse, aut in eorum fide fuisse legimus aut credimus, quod apud eos edicendi judicandique potestatem ex fœdere tenuêre; nec vero congruum est, eorum se potestati & judicio Translavicanos subjicere voluisse, quos Cislavicanis ordinibus agrariis obligatos esse, & ab illis leges accipere nosent, quippè qui non cum his ipsis, sed cum civitate fœdus percuterent. Inveni etiam hoc collegium colligendis in agro tributis, si quando tributis, opus, præfuisse, eamque pecuniam tractasse, aggerum, viarum, aquæductuum curam habuisse, judices agrarios ad faciendum officium compulisse, exorbitantesque eosdem compressise, ad conventus ordines convocasse, denique velut ad clavum Reip. sedentes, quietis & εὐζωΐας[?] custodes in tota provincia fuisse. Et hæc ad SAXONUM usque tempora. Ii partim sua sponte, partim stimulantibus nonnullis, qui ferre imperium non poterant, hac potestate spoliare civitatem conati sunt. E DSARDUS jus hoc in arctum redegit[?] : quippe sui arbitrii electionemHovetmannorum ex civium numero fecit, & jurisdictionem angustioribus terminis clausit. GELDRUS electionem senatui reddidit, & jurisdictionem restituit solitam, sed quatuor Hovetmannis à senatu lectis[?] ex suis addidit quintum, qui præses collegii esset, ac legatus ipsius, atque hi omnes ipsius quoque homine, atque ipsius[?] mandato jus dicerent. Nec quicquam CAROLUS CAESAR, aut filius ejus PHILIPPUS mutarunt, eoque modo res ad hæc postrema tempora pervenit. Tum lis de toto fœdere, totaque hac cum civitate conjunctione mota. Eam resuscitatam nuper ORDINES GENERALES eo, quo exposui, modo definierunt.
units.tr: "For we read or believe that the Translavicani did not receive this office from them, nor were they under their trust, because they held the power of issuing edicts and judging among them by covenant. Nor is it fitting that the Translavicani wished to submit to their authority and judgement, when they knew that they were bound to the Cislavicani rural orders and received laws from them, since they made their covenant not with these men themselves but with the city. I have also found that this college presided over the collection of taxes in the countryside, whenever taxes were needed, handled that money, had charge of the dikes, roads and aqueducts, compelled the rural judges to perform their duties, restrained them when they overstepped, summoned the orders to assemblies, and finally, sitting as it were at the helm of the commonwealth, were the guardians of peace and of the good life [εὐζωΐας] throughout the whole province. And this continued down to the times of the Saxons. Some of them, partly of their own accord and partly urged on by others who could not bear authority, tried to strip the city of this power. Edzard reduced this right to narrow limits: for he made the choosing of the Hovetmanni his own decision, selecting them from the number of the citizens, and he confined their jurisdiction within narrower bounds. Geldern returned the election to the senate and restored the jurisdiction as it had been, but he added from his own people a fifth Hovetman, who was to be president of the college and his deputy, and all of them were to pronounce judgement by his own man and at his own command, although four had been chosen from the senate. Neither Charles Caesar nor his son Philip changed anything, and in this way the matter came down to these latest times. Then a dispute arose over the whole covenant and the whole union with this city. The States General recently revived this dispute and settled it in the manner I have described."

units.la: Sed aliud quoque imperium in agro civitas habet haud spernendum. Id duas amplectitur Præfecturas majores, eamquam VETEREM nominant, & SUBURBANAM : quarum illa vicos egregios XVII, hæc XII tantum, nec prioribus pares habet : & in his cœnobia quoque v. Utrique[?] à senatu præfectus datur, mutaturque pro arbitrio. Præfectus prioris ferè consularis, ac genere nobili natus, alterius etiam haud temere alius, quàm senatorius. Atque ille quidem cum judice, ex indigenis plerumque ei additio, jus dicit, cæteraque imperii peragit senatus nomine, sed non aliter, quàm secundùm leges & morem patrium, à quo recedere non licet. Ex hoc more Præfectura in territoria distinguitur quinque, quorum quodlibet tribunal suum habet, in quo præfectus vicissim certis temporibus jus dicit de criminibus, rebus soli, ædificiis, ac similibus momenti majoris: nec licet præfecto, cùm de his agitur quemquam extra territorium suum evocare: in cæteris, ut crediti debitique, negotiis maximè licet. Nec fas est, nisi in territorio suo, in quo quis vel sedem habet, vel in maleficio prehensus est, maleficum supplicio afficere, aut custodiæ mandare. Et usus recepit, ut præfecto jus dicenti assideant aliquot, qui in plebe territorii eminent, honoris causâ: utque Wedmannus (judicii minister) in unoquoque territorio sit, isque & minora quædam, quæ judicum solent esse, pro judice agat, & custodiæ præsit, prehendendique potestatem habeat. Territoria hæc sunt: Muntense, Midwoldicum, Finserwoldicum, Brocæum, Wijnscotanum, Alter in Præfecturâ suburbanâ jus dicit, hoc modo. Habet Octo-viros præfectura, optimos quosque&maximè idoneos è plebe: quorum quatuor singulis bienniis munere decedunt, & totidem alii ab iis, qui in munere manent, collegæ adsciscuntur, semel adsciti, quadriennium in munere continuant, munusque jurati gerunt: jurant fecundùm morem & leges patrias incorruptè fe judicaturos. Ad hæc forte è numero suo Octo-viri ducunt duos, qui minoribus causis expediundis omnibus diebus Veneris & Saturni Groningæ (hæc tribunalis hujus sedes est) præfecto assideant in trimestre, & cum eo jus dicant, idque vicissim, donec circumactus fit totus annus. Reliqui cum assessoribus his & cum præfecto ter stato tempore singulis annis, aut quoties res poícit, graviores controversias foli ac similes cognoscunt&judicant,simulque fi quâ de re minore ad hunc eorum confessum provocatum fit à præfecti duûm-virûmque sententia, eam quoque definiunt. Ab eo verò, quod ab his præside præfecto definitum est, quemadmodum & à prioris præfecti sententiis ac decretis in præsecturâ vetere, ad Senatum urbanum provocatio est, fi quis eâ uti velit. In senatûs sententiâ litium finis est.
units.tr: But the city also has another jurisdiction in the countryside, not to be despised. It embraces two greater prefectures, the one they call the Old and the other the Suburban. The former has seventeen notable villages, the latter only twelve, and it is not equal to the former; in these there are also five monasteries. A prefect is appointed to each by the senate and changed at its discretion. The prefect of the Old is usually a former consul and born of a noble family; the other, too, is hardly ever anyone but a senator. The former, together with a judge, usually added from among the natives, pronounces judgement and carries out the other duties of his office in the name of the senate, but only according to the laws and the ancestral custom, from which it is not permitted to depart. In accordance with this custom the Prefecture is divided into five territories, each of which has its own tribunal, where the prefect in turn at fixed times pronounces judgement on crimes, property in land, buildings and similar matters of greater importance. When these matters are being heard, the prefect may not summon anyone from outside his own territory; but in other matters, such as debts and credits, he may do so freely. Nor is it lawful, except in his own territory, where a man either has his residence or has been caught in wrongdoing, to punish a wrongdoer with death or commit him to custody. Custom has also established that some men of distinction among the common people of the territory sit beside the prefect when he judges, as a mark of honour; and that a Wedmannus (minister of the court) is present in each territory, who acts as judge in certain minor matters that are usually the business of judges, presides over custody, and has the power of arrest. These are the territories: Muntense, Midwoldicum, Finserwoldicum, Brocaeum, Wijnscotanum. The other one, in the Suburban Prefecture, pronounces judgement in the following way. The prefecture has eight Octoviri, the best and most suitable men from the common people, of whom four retire from office every second year, and as many others are added as colleagues by those who remain in office. Once added, they continue in office for four years and perform their duty under oath: they swear that they will judge uprightly according to the custom and laws of their country. Moreover, the Octoviri choose from their number two men who, every day of Friday and Saturday in Groningen (this is the seat of this tribunal), sit with the prefect for a quarter of a year to dispatch the minor cases, and pronounce judgement together with him, taking turns until the whole year has passed. The rest, with these assessors and with the prefect, at fixed times three times each year, or as often as the business requires, hear and decide the weightier disputes concerning land and similar matters; and if in any matter an appeal is made from the decision of the prefect and the two men to this their assembly, they decide that too. From what this president prefect has decided, just as from the judgements and decrees of the prefect of the Old Prefecture, there is an appeal to the city senate, if anyone wishes to use it. The senate's decision is the end of lawsuits.

units.la: Præter has SENATUS idem ditiones quoque minores per reliquum agrum habet, in quas judices mittit. Sed ab his non ad Senatum, sed ad conventum judicialem totius agri, de quo supra dixi, aut aut Hovetmannos patet ap-pellatio.
units.tr: Besides these, the senate also holds smaller jurisdictions throughout the rest of the countryside, into which it sends judges. But from these the appeal lies not to the senate but to the judicial assembly of the whole countryside, of which I spoke above, or to the Hovetmanni.

units.la: DE MUNERIBUS TOTI PROVINCIÆ COMMUNI- BUS.
units.tr: Of the Offices Common to the Whole Province

units.la: FINIREM hîc de rebus civilibus, nisi sui monerent me munera, quæ cum fœdere Belgico nata fuêre, & civitati agroque sunt communia. De quibus quamquam & priùs dicta quædam mihi sunt, tamen & obiter modò id factum, & brevius quàm res videtur poscere. Sunt ea duplicia: quorum foris alia, alia domi geruntur. Quæ foris, sessiones sunt in collegiis amplissimis, quæ communia sunt omnibus in fœdere comprehensis; eaque sunt tria. Primum est id, quod GENERALIUM ORDINUM nomen habet, honore potestateque summum, totius foederis ac Reip. communis caput, à quo cætera pendent, & leges accipiunt, longè lateque inclytum, haud dissimile concilio Achaico veteri, aut Ætolico in Græciâ, aut Panionio in Asiâ, sed perpetuum. Sedes ei Hagæ in Hollandiâ, in quod mittuntur ex omnibus provinciis sociis [illegible, ~6 letters] viri summis. Alterum dignitate & potestate proximum huic, bellica potissimum curans. SENATUS ORDINUM nuncupatur: quod, quoties res ardua ac magna incidit, quæ consilio decretoque habet opus, in partem curæ & consilii vocatur, & nunc seorsim deliberat de eâ, sententiamque suam ad collegium superius refert, nunc cum eodem in deliberando conjungitur. Eodem quippè loco, eâdem in arce sedem habet, quo expeditior sit conjunctio. Tertium & ipsum illustre & magnarum virium est, MA-RITIMIS REBUS, quæ maximæ in Belgio sunt, PRAEFECTUM, distinctum in collegia minora velut membra totius,quorum unum inSelandia Middelburgi;alterum Roterodami, tertium Amsterodami, quartum Hornæ vel Enchusæ in Hollandia; quintum in FrisiaDoccumi sedem nunc tenet. In collegium Ordinum Generalium civitas èsuis, agerque item.è suis mittunt assessorem spectatissimum ac prudentissimum quemque in toto utroque corpore; eisque vel prorogant honorem,quoties & quamdiu volunt, vel successores dant: plerumq; verò in complures annos in munere relinquunt. Et sunt hi duo munere & honore pares, nec alter altero plus potest. Sic tamen observatur, cùm præsentes pariter sunt in collegio, ubi præsidendi vices ad hanc provinciam venêre, ( per hebdomades enim vicissim provinciæ id jus habent) ut urbanus verè eum locum teneat, verbaque faciat, agrarius nunquam, nisi urbano absente. Uterque non solùm deliberat cum cæteris de tota Rep. sociorum, & decernit, sed à suis accipit, quæ res poscit, eaque ad collegium refert. Quæ si ad totam provinciam pertinent, conjunctim hoc faciunt, eaque à collegio accipiunt[?] provinciali: sin solius civitatis sunt, à senatu certior fit urbanus, & solus collegio generali exponit. Idem sæpè aut solus, aut cum collega vel præsens, vel per literas ex Ordinum Generalium voluntate ad suos, quæ sunt opus, refert. Uterque à collegio provinciali per literas publicas in possessionem muneris mittitur. De eo, qui in senatu Ordinum sessurus est, (uni quippe hic tantummodo è provincia nostra locus) sic nunc inter oppidanos & agrarios est comparatum, ut illi in biennium, quem velint suorum designent, idemq; in alterum biennium faciant agrarii. Sed in collegiü rerum maritimarum, quod Doccumi nunc est, utraque pars è suis unum legat. Et tres hi, nimirum qui in senatu Ordinum futurus est, & qui in collegio Doccumano, literis collegii provinciæ hujus instruuntur, at scedendi, remq; publicam gerendi potestatem à summo Generalium Ordinum collegio accipiunt, ac in munus suum immittuntur: eique jurejurando se obstringunt: omnes spectatæ dignitatis virtutisque inter suos, & è civitate non nisi consulares aut senatorii. Atque omnia hæc non honorata solùm[?],sed lauta quoque munera sunt, & opima. De cæteris, quæ collegio Doccumano cohærent, ut Scribæ & Fisci præfecti,quæ provinciæ huic cum Translavicanis sunt communia, & quæ his similia alia, dicere non libet, ne prolixior fiam. Et hæc quidem foris : reliqua domi. Horum primum&præcipuum Provinciale collegium, ut initio institutum fuit, collegas octo habuit, deinde post sexennium sex habere cœpit, & adhuc habet, pari numero hinc inde lectos : de quorum munere amplissimo ante nobis dictum. Oppidanos senatus edit, & ferè ex his, qui in consulatu aut senatu fuêre, eosque pro arbitrio suo aut mutat anno exacto, aut in munere manere patitur. Nec alius agrariorum mos, qui reliquos designant. Collegæ, ut antè ostendi, per vices, atque in orbem præsident, alternatimque oppidanus & agrarius:vices septimana finiuntur. Quæstor autem collegii, cui amplissima pecunia tractanda committitur, item Scriba à secretis, conjunctim ab oppidanis & agrariis eliguntur in conventu communi, ab iisdemque pendent ; munusque habent perpetuum, si cum fide in eo versentur. Reliqua in serioris notae ministeria ostiariorum, scribarum amanuensium, tabellariorum in potestate collegii sunt. Dein Quatuor-viri sunt, ab iisdem utrisque pari numero electi, quos Rationum magistros appellant, & his scriba adjunctus, chartarum custos. Horum officium est, indices censuum ac reditum omnium provinciae in promptu habere, & hos nervos Reip. ad unguem nosse: largitiones, quae ex publico fiunt ab Sexviris, aliasque item pecuniae assignationes censurae subijcere suae, easque vel calculo suo facere ratas, vel, si iniquas aut decretis Ordinum non congruas putent, suspendere, ac de suspensis Sexviros monere, & si sit opus, ad conventum Ordinum referre: rationes quoque, quoties libet, quaestores poscere: denique curare, ne tardatis solutionibus fraus aerario fiat neve pecuniaria res provinciae quoquo modo detrimentum patiatur. Utilissimum institutum, si acribus hominibus atque integris, & boni publici studiofis, contraque gratiam & offensam infractis fuerit commissum. Accessit proximis annis totidem virorum collegium tertium, cui cura demandata est bonorum monasticorum totius provinciæ, quæ priùs ad collegium primum pertinebat. Causa instituti hujus fuit, quòd credere-tur, collegium primum rebus omnibus, quæ illi çommissæ erant, non sufficere. Sedent in eo duo à senatu oppidano dati è civium numero, duo ab ordinibus agrariis ex eorundem medio. Designantur in comitiis. Curatio eorum annua, nisi fiat prorogatio, quæ fit sæpè. Duo ex his, alter ex oppidanis ex agrariis alter,actorum & rationum indices aut libros tenentur conficere, capiuntque stipendium è publico Carolinos aureos ccc; cæteri verò cc tantùm.
