Omnes, cùm locandum aliquid, aut controversia inter Quæstorem & conductores finienda, quod officii eorum est, ex Sex-viris collegii primi duos sibi adjungunt, oppidanum unum, agrarium alterum, & cum his expediunt omnia, aut si major controversia sit, quàm ut expediri ab ipsis recte possit, remittunt muni, ab iisdemque pendent ; munusque habent perpetuum, si cum fide in eo versentur. Dein Quatuor-viri sunt, ab iisdem utrisque pari numero electi, quos Rationum magistros appellant, & his scriba adjunctis, chartarum custos. Iidem Quatuor-viri soli, si qua vendenda ex rebus monasticis, quae usum jam non habent, vendunt: de pecunia, quae ex locariis, aut rebus venditis provenit, secundum leges sibi disponunt, quibus solvendum, solvi jubent: id curae habent, ne qua fraus à conductoribus quoquo modo Reip. fiat, ne Quaestores solutiones quae controversia vacant, tardent, neu quicquam cuiquam solvant temere aut pro arbitrio suo. Usi sunt prioribus annis ministerio Quaestorum duorum: nunc utuntur unius. Is à conductoribus exigit locaria annua, & si quid censuum aliorum, exacta, & in indices suos relata ex voluntate Quatuor-virum horum manibus ipsorum signata rursum expendit: omnium rationes reddit cum libris Quatuor-virum collatas, auscultantibus etiam iis, quos Ordines provinciae ad eam rem edunt. Quaestura ista perpetua plerumque & fructuosa. Horum collegiorum omnium sedes in urbe est, urbemque hominum frequentia, ac quaestu auget. Postremò publicanorum ordo in Reip. provinciali est, in urbe & agro degens, invisus hominum vulgo, sed in hoc statu & fortunâ Reip. planè necessarius. Hi vectigalia, portoria, tributa, & si quid aliud census hujusmodi est, conducunt in semestre, locante collegio provinciali, certamque Reip. summam promittunt, prædesque dant: ipsi suo periculo colligunt, atque interdum acerbiùs, quàm gratum provincialibus, exigunt, ut indemnes se præstent: quos fraudis compertos habent, ex legibus gravissimè multant: interdumque fit, ut si nimis magno conduxerint, cedere foro & facultatibus, aut cum Rep. transfigere cogantur. Ministris utuntur compluribus, & in omnes res omniaque loca intentos oculos habent, ne quid per fraudem sibi decedat. Denique totum hoc genus à Romano more illo vetere non multum discedere videtur.
units.tr: I would end my discussion of civil affairs here, were it not that the offices themselves call me to speak of them. These were created along with the Belgic covenant, and they are common to the city and to the countryside. I have already said something about them earlier, but only in passing and more briefly than the subject seems to deserve. They are of two kinds: some are carried on abroad and some at home. The foreign ones are the seats in the most distinguished assemblies, which are common to all the members of the covenant. There are three of these. The first is the body called the States General, the highest in honour and power, the head of the whole covenant and commonwealth, on which everything else depends and from which it takes its laws. It is famous far and wide, not unlike the old Achaean council, or the Aetolian in Greece, or the Panionian in Asia, but it is permanent. Its seat is at The Hague in Holland, and to it the allied provinces send their most eminent men. The second, next in dignity and power to this, has chiefly to do with war. It is called the Council of State. Whenever some weighty and important matter arises that needs deliberation and a decision, it is called in to share the care and counsel. At times it deliberates on the matter separately and then refers its opinion to the higher body; at other times it joins with that body in deliberation. It has its seat in the same place and the same citadel as the other, so that the joining together is easier. The third, also distinguished and of great importance, is the office of the Admiralty, which is the greatest in the Netherlands. It is divided into smaller colleges, as it were members of the whole: one at Middelburg in Zeeland, another at Rotterdam, a third at Amsterdam, a fourth at Hoorn or Enkhuizen in Holland, and a fifth, which now has its seat at Dokkum in Friesland. To the college of the States General, the city sends from its own members, and the countryside likewise from its own, the most respected and prudent men in the whole of both bodies. These men the provinces either continue in office for as long as they wish, whenever they wish, or they appoint successors. Most often, however, they leave them in the office for many years. These two are equal in office and dignity, and neither has more power than the other. Yet this is observed: when both are present together in the college, and the turn to preside has come to this province (for each province holds this right in turn by weeks), the town representative alone takes that place and speaks, and the country representative never does, unless the town representative is absent. Each of them not only deliberates with the others about the whole commonwealth of the allies and decides, but also receives from his own people whatever business requires it and brings it before the college. If the matters concern the whole province, they do this jointly and receive instructions from the provincial college. If they concern only the city, the town representative is informed by the Council, and he alone sets them out to the General College. Often the same man, either alone or with his colleague, whether present or by letter, reports to his own people by the will of the States General whatever needs to be reported. Each is sent into possession of his office by the provincial college through public letters. As for the man who is to sit in the Council of the States (for only one place falls to our province), the arrangement now made between the townsmen and the countrymen is this: the townsmen name whomever they wish for two years, and the countrymen do the same for another two years. But in the College of Maritime Affairs, which is now at Dokkum, each side chooses one of its own. These three men, namely the one who is to sit in the Council of the States and the two in the Dokkum college, receive letters of commission from the provincial college of this province, and they receive the power of sitting and managing public affairs from the supreme College of the States General. They are sent into their office, and they bind themselves by oath. All of them are chosen from among their own people for distinction and virtue, and from the city only consular or senatorial men are chosen. All these offices are not only honourable but also lavish and rich. As for the others that belong to the Dokkum college, such as the clerks and the prefects of the treasury, which are common to this province and the lands beyond the Lauwers, and other similar offices, I do not wish to speak of them, lest I become too long. These are the offices abroad; the rest are at home. The first and chief of these is the Provincial College. As it was originally set up, it had eight colleagues. Then, after six years, it began to have six, and it still has six, chosen in equal numbers from each side. I have already spoken before of its very distinguished office. The Council draws its townsmen, and mostly from among those who have served as consuls or senators. After a year has passed, it either changes them at its own discretion or allows them to remain in office. The countrymen have no different custom in choosing their own. The colleagues preside in turn and in rotation, alternately a townsman and a countryman; each turn lasts a week, as I showed above. The treasurer of the college, to whom a very large sum of money is entrusted, and likewise the secretary, are chosen jointly by the townsmen and the countrymen in a common assembly. They depend on those same men, and they hold their office for life, provided they conduct themselves faithfully in it. The remaining lesser offices of doorkeepers, scribes, copyists, and couriers are at the disposal of the college. Then there are four men, chosen in equal numbers by both sides, whom they call the Masters of Accounts, with a scribe attached to them as keeper of the papers. Their duty is to keep at hand the registers of all the census and revenues of the province, and to know these sinews of the commonwealth to a nicety. They are to subject to their own scrutiny the largesses that are made from public funds by the Six Men, and likewise other assignments of money. They are either to approve these by their own calculation, or, if they think them unjust or not in accordance with the decrees of the States, to suspend them, warn the Six Men about those suspended, and, if need be, refer the matter to the assembly of the States. They may also demand accounts from the treasurers whenever they like. Finally, they see to it that by delayed payments no fraud is done to the treasury, and that the financial affairs of the province suffer no loss in any way. It is a most useful institution, provided it is entrusted to keen and upright men who are zealous for the public good and proof against favour and resentment. In recent years a third college of the same number of men has been added, to which the care of the monastic goods of the whole province has been committed; these had previously belonged to the first college. The reason for this institution was the belief that the first college was not sufficient for all the matters committed to it. Two men sit in it, given by the town Council from among the citizens, and two from the countryside orders, chosen from among themselves. They are designated at the assemblies. Their charge lasts a year, unless it is extended, which is often done. Two of them, one a townsman and the other a countryman, are charged with keeping the records of proceedings and accounts, or the books, and they receive a salary from the public treasury of 300 gold Carolus coins, while the others receive only 200. Whenever something is to be let out, or a dispute between the Treasurer and the tenants has to be settled, which is part of their duty, they take to themselves two of the Six Men of the first college, one townsman and one countryman, and with these they settle everything. If the dispute is greater than they can properly settle themselves, they refer it to the ordinary judges. These same Four Men alone, if anything from the monastic properties which is no longer in use is to be sold, sell it. They arrange by law the money that comes from the leases or from the goods sold, and they order to whom it is to be paid and paid out. They take care that no fraud is done to the commonwealth by the tenants in any way, and that the Treasurers do not delay payments that are free from dispute, nor pay anything to anyone carelessly or at their own pleasure. In earlier years they used the services of two Treasurers; now they use one. He collects from the tenants the annual rents, and any other census dues, and when these are collected and entered in his registers, he disburses them again, with the approval of these Four Men, under their hands and seals. He renders the accounts of all, compared with the books of the Four Men, with those whom the orders of the province appoint for this purpose also listening in. This treasurership is usually lifelong and profitable. The seat of all these colleges is in the city, and the city is enlarged by the crowds of men and by the profit they bring. Lastly, there is the order of tax farmers in the provincial commonwealth. They live in the city and the countryside, and are generally hated by the common people, yet in this condition and fortune of the commonwealth they are absolutely necessary. They lease the excise duties, tolls, taxes, and whatever other revenues are of this kind, for six months at a time, the provincial college letting them out. They promise a fixed sum to the commonwealth and give sureties. They collect at their own risk, and sometimes they exact more harshly than is welcome to the provincials, so that they may keep themselves unharmed. Those whom they find guilty of fraud they punish severely under the laws. And sometimes it happens that, if they have leased at too great a price, they are compelled to give up their property and possessions, or to come to terms with the commonwealth. They employ many servants and keep watchful eyes on every matter and every place, lest anything be lost to them by fraud. In short, this whole class does not seem to differ much from that old Roman custom.

units.la: In omnia autem hæc, quæ provinciæ totius sunt, conventus provincialis quem comitia dicunt, potestatem summam obtinet, omnibusque leges dat, mutat in iis & statuit pro arbitrio, si consentiat, modò ne quid contra leges foederis communis, & conditiones, quae in deditione urbis & conjunctione cum reliquis foederatis perscriptae sunt. Conventus hujus sedes antiquissimo more Groninga est: convocaturque, quoties res postulat. Constat duobus membris, uti tota provincia, quam civitas agrique ordines constituunt. Civitatis locum in conventu solus senatus tenet. Agri ordines quondam antiftibus coenobiorum, nobilitate agrariâ, & plebe rusticâ censebantur, antistitelque & praecipua nobilitas nominatum vocabantur: plebs reliqua vicatim plerumque suos cum potestate & mandatis ad conventus mittebat. Nunc antistites dispuncti sunt, resque ad solam nobilitatem, & delectos plebis cum mandatis suorum instructos rediit. Conventui aedificium in urbe peramplum & spatiosum destinatum est, in usum scholae quondam exstructum, distinctum conclavibus diversis. In eorum maximo conveniunt omnes. Et si praesens Gubernator est, in capite conclavis loco summo confidet ad mensam, juxtaque eum, qui in collegio sunt provinciali. Deinde ad dextram Gubernatoris, atque in latere conclavis dextro consules & reliquus senatus sedem tenent: alterum latus cum sedilibus reliquis agri ordines occupant. Proponit in consessu gubernator quæ agenda, aut collegii præses. Eo facto interdum manet collegium loco suo, interdum, si causa requirit, discedit. Re deliberatâ senatus priore loco sententiam dicit per Syndicum suum, si adest, aut per consulem. Sequuntur agrarii. Quibus si inter se convenire nequit, secedentes deliberant, & suffragiis inter se certant; nonnunquam etiam tripartitò dividunt sese, ut supra ostendi, cùm de agro agerem seorsim: atque itâ, si duæ partes in unam sententiam eant, tertiam quoque trahunt. Tum, quod sentiunt, per Syndicum quoque suum, quem habent, senatui exponunt. Post disputationes ubi consensere senatus agrarìque, decretum conficitur, atque in publicum librum refertur. Id totam obligat provinciam, ac pro lege habetur. Si consensum inire haud possint, reijcitur res in comitia proxima, aut omit-titur. titur.Convocatio horum comitiorum penes Gubernatorem & collegium Sex-virûm Deputatorum est, qui scripto eam expediunt, & conveniendi causas praecipuas eodem scripto strictim comprehendunt. Stata verò & ordinaria comitia quotannis habentur mense Februario, in quibus ii, qui in collegiis omnibus sessuri sunt, eliguntur, oppidani à senatu, agrarii à suis, Quaestores provinciales, collegiorum duorum Scribae à secretis cum loca vacant, designantur suffragiis utriusque partis communibus: idque sit non solùm his statis, sed etiam quibusvis aliis Comitiis, pro ut res poposcerit. Post haec peracta, si quid temporis superest, quod accidit rarius, id negotiis aliis, quae agi in comitiis solent, impenditur. Sed comitia in leges & instituta, ac jura civitatis potestatem nullam habent, nec in ea, quae propria sunt agri. Tantùm subjecta sibi habent illa, quae toti provinciae sunt communia.
units.tr: In all these matters that belong to the whole province, the provincial assembly, which they call the comitia, holds supreme power: it gives laws to all, changes and establishes them at its discretion, provided it agrees, but only so long as nothing is contrary to the laws of the common covenant and the conditions drawn up in the surrender of the city and its union with the other confederated states. The seat of this assembly is Groningen, according to the most ancient custom, and it is convened whenever business requires. It consists of two members, as does the whole province, which the city and the orders of the countryside make up. In the assembly the city's place is held by the senate alone. The orders of the countryside were formerly counted among the abbots of the monasteries, the landed nobility and the rural commons, and the abbots and the leading nobility were called by name; the rest of the commons usually sent their own representatives, with authority and instructions, to the assemblies by village. Now the abbots have been removed, and the business has come back to the nobility alone, together with chosen men of the commons furnished with instructions from their own people. For the assembly a very large and spacious building in the city has been set apart, built formerly for use as a school and divided into several chambers. All gather in the largest of them. If the governor is present, he sits at the head of the chamber, at the highest place at the table, and beside him those who belong to the provincial college. Then, to the governor's right, and on the right side of the chamber, the burgomasters and the rest of the senate hold their seats; the other orders of the countryside occupy the other side with their own benches. The governor, or the president of the college, lays before the assembly what is to be done. This done, the college sometimes remains in its place and sometimes, if the matter requires it, withdraws. When the matter has been debated, the senate gives its opinion first, through its syndic if he is present, or through a burgomaster. The countryside men follow. If they cannot agree among themselves, they withdraw and deliberate, and contend with one another by votes; sometimes they also divide themselves into three parts, as I showed above when I treated of the countryside separately; and so, if two parts go over to one opinion, they draw the third along too. Then they set out what they think before the senate, through their own syndic, whom they have. After the discussions, when the senate and the countryside have agreed, a decree is drawn up and entered in the public book. It binds the whole province and is held as law. If they cannot reach agreement, the matter is deferred to the next assembly or is dropped. The calling of these assemblies rests with the governor and the college of the Six Deputies, who prepare the summons in writing and set out briefly in the same writing the chief reasons for meeting. The fixed and ordinary assemblies are held every year in February, in which those who are to sit in all the colleges are chosen: the townsmen by the senate, the countrymen by their own people, the provincial treasurers, and the secretaries of the two colleges when places fall vacant, are appointed by the common votes of both parties. This is done not only at these fixed assemblies but at any other assembly whatever, as business may require. When these matters are finished, if any time is left, which happens rather rarely, it is spent on other business that is usually transacted in the assemblies. But the assemblies have no power over the laws, institutions and rights of the city, nor over those things that are proper to the countryside. They have under their authority only those things that are common to the whole province.

units.la: DE RE ECCLE- SIASTICA IN URBE.
units.tr: ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL AFFAIRS IN THE CITY.

units.la: Sic Civilia: restat ut Ecclesiastica perstringam. Solent in urbe esse, ut in principio ostendi, parochiae tres cum totidem sanis. In his sacerdotes sacris operantes numero XXI: in quibus pastores tres singuli in sanis ac parochiis. Tandem anno M. CCCC. LXXX unus ex his editus velut ἐφορῷ[?] totius rei ecclesiasticae in urbe & urbis vicinia, quem PERSONAM more suo vocabant: isque erat velut minor quidam episcopus, aut episcopi vicem gerens, magna potestate & multis privilegiis ornatus a Romano Pontifice. Hunc caeteri pastores, & duo seniores urbis consules eligebant, & in munus suum immittebant, in magnoque honore habebat tota civitas. Deinde anno M. D. LXVIII, cum mutatio-nibus Belgicis via divinitus strueretur, novique episcopatus passim in his regionibus instituerentur, episcopus quoque huic civitati datus Joannes Cnifius ex ordine cucullatorum Ultrajectinus, Personae nomen munusque peremptum, canonici constituendo collegio electi, his alendis tuendaeque episcopi dignitati census omnes coenobii Werumani a rege ac pontifice versi, Adoardii quoque annua aliquot millia huc conferre coacti: coenobium Fratrum domicilium episcopi factum, Martiniana aedes cathedrali honore donata. Sed raro fato unus idemque primus & ultimus episcopus Groningae Cnifius fuit: quo vitâ functo, cum annus flueret M. D. LXXII, res in priorem statum relapsa est. Nunc abrogatâ Romanensi superstitione & ἱεραρχία[?] is quoque statu cum caeteris corruit. Sacerdotum loco introducti sunt ecclesiae ministri, suffragiis ejusdem ecclesiae electi, volente & probante senatu, qui purum Dei verbum docent, & sacramenta ex forma divinitus tradita administrant duobus in templis, ipsi numero sex: quorum nullus potestate eminet supra caeteros, omnes agunt aequaliter inter se, quamvis alii alios, prout dotibus instructi ornatique sunt, autoritate & gratiâ praeeant. His seniores additi numero feré xvi, qui cum iisdem presbyterium conficiunt, cui commissa custodia disciplinae & eutaxiae ecclesiasticae. Coit hoc singulis septimanis semel, aut quoties res requirit, & de rebus ecclesiasticis deliberat atque agit: civile nihil attingit. Seniores, qui in hoc collegium cooptantur (quod ab ipso fit collegio) non genere aut opibus aut potentiâ spectantur, sed pietate & integritate vitæ, & necessariâ prudentiâ, famâ denique inculpata. Et hi additi doctoribus sunt velut senatus ecclesiasticus. Præter hos & diaconi sunt in ecclesiâ numero plerumque xvi, qui peculiare collegium constituunt, & conventus suos habent: interdum etiam, ubi res poscit, imprimis tertio quoque mense disciplinae causa cum presbyterio conjunguntur, & unum velut collegium cum eo faciunt. Hi similiter ex integerrimis ecclesiae civibus electi pecuniam pauperum tractant, eleemosynas colligunt, & distribuunt, ac de omnibus rationes reddunt publicè, ad quas cuilibet, cui animus licet accedere. Ac sunt hi diversi ab iis, de quibus in exponendis rebus civilibus dixi. Eliguntur à presbyterio, ut isti à senatu. Nec est hoc munus perpetuum, sed triennio aut quadriennio exspirat substitutis novis: fereque ex his, qui bene hoc munere functi sunt, presbyteri cooptantur. Est & invisendis, solandis, erudiendis, exhortandis aegrotis, ac in mortis periculo constitutis praefectus, quem visitatorem nuncupant, ex iis plerunque delectus, qui in munere docendae Ecclesiae in urbe vel in agro versati sunt. Is presbyterii pars est. De schola litteraria hic dicere prolixius nihil attinet, quam liberalibus stipendiis constitutis in usum docentium senatus hic instituit aut instauravit post urbem foederi Belgico rursum conjunctam. Nam ordo ejus typis publicatus extat. Hoc solum hic repeto, docere in ea praeceptores vii, qui stipendia à Rep. capiunt aureos Carolinos non minus bis mille sexcentos octuaginta, & domicilia habent libera ab omni onere, δωρεάν[?] autem à discipulis non capiunt. Sedes scholae in coenobio Franciscano, ut dixi ante, situ in urbe medio. Porrò Ecclesiæ ministri diebus dominicis ter docent in templo utroque, atque insuper, reliqua hebdomade bis in Martiniano, semel in Mariano aut Amnico: baptismum iisdem in templis finitis concionibus præsente ecclesiâ administrant: Cœnam domini summâ cum reverentia quolibet trimestri distribuunt communicantibus, idque vicissim in templis jam dictis, nec quenquam ad mensam hanc sacram admittunt, nisi ante de mysterio benè edoctum, & capitum doctrinæ Christianæ præcipuorum mediocriter gnarum, & in vita probum piumque: cæteros ab ea arcent. Reliqua quoque ministerii sui ritè expediunt. In primis quolibet mense semel cœtum vel conventum agunt in urbe cum ministris ecclesiarum vicinarum quæ in præfectura sunt suburbana, disciplinæ & exhortationis mutuæ causa. Quotannis autem semel delecti eorum, reliquique presbyterii synodo intersunt ministrorum universæ hujus provinciæ inter Amasum & Lavicam, in quam delecti singularum classium coëunt, nunc in urbe, sæpius in agro, locis celebrioribus. Cæteroqui, ad conventus menstruos & ordinarios quod attinet, nihil habent urbani cum ministris agrariis commune.
units.tr: So much for civil affairs; it remains for me to touch briefly on ecclesiastical ones. As I showed at the beginning, the city has three parishes, each with a number of districts attached. In these, twenty-one priests serve the sacred office, and in each district and parish there was one minister. Then, in the year 1480, one of these was appointed as a kind of overseer [ἐφορῷ] of all ecclesiastical affairs in the city and its surrounding area, whom they called the Persona, after their own fashion. He was, as it were, a lesser bishop, or one who acted in the place of a bishop, endowed with great authority and many privileges by the Roman Pontiff. The other ministers and the two senior consuls of the city elected him and installed him in his office, and the whole community held him in great honour. Then, in the year 1568, when the Belgian upheavals were being divinely prepared and new bishoprics were being established throughout these regions, John Cnijf of the Utrecht order of hooded friars was also given as bishop to this city. The name and office of the Persona were abolished, and a canonry was set up by election. To support the canons and to maintain the dignity of the bishop, all the revenues of the Weerum monastery were turned over by the king and the pope, and some annual sums were also compelled to be paid here from Adoardus. The Franciscan house became the bishop's residence, and the Martinian church was given the honour of a cathedral. But by a rare fate, Cnijf was the one and the same first and last bishop of Groningen. When he died, in the year 1572, the matter fell back into its former state. Now, with the Roman superstition and the hierarchy [ἱεραρχία] abolished, that office too has fallen with the rest. In place of the priests, ministers of the church have been introduced, chosen by the votes of that same congregation with the approval and consent of the senate. They teach the pure Word of God and administer the sacraments in the form divinely handed down, in two churches, and there are six of them. None of them stands out above the others in authority; all act equally among themselves, although some lead others in influence and esteem, according to the gifts with which each is endowed and adorned. To these are added about sixteen elders, who together with the ministers form the presbytery, to which the guardianship of church discipline and good order is entrusted. It meets once a week, or as often as the business requires, and deliberates and acts on ecclesiastical matters; it touches nothing civil. The elders who are co-opted into this college (which is done by the college itself) are chosen not for birth, wealth or power, but for piety, integrity of life, necessary prudence, and in short, an unblemished reputation. These, added to the teachers, form, as it were, the ecclesiastical senate. Besides these there are deacons in the church, usually sixteen in number, who form a separate college and hold their own meetings. Sometimes, when the matter requires it, especially every third month, they are joined with the presbytery for the sake of discipline and make one body with it. Likewise chosen from the most upright citizens of the church, they handle the money of the poor, collect and distribute alms, and render accounts of everything publicly, which anyone who wishes may inspect. These men are distinct from those I spoke of in describing civil affairs. They are chosen by the presbytery, as the others are by the senate. This office is not for life, but expires after three or four years, with new men substituted; and usually those who have discharged this office well are co-opted into the presbytery. There is also a prefect for visiting, comforting, instructing and exhorting the sick, and those in danger of death, whom they call the visitor. He is usually chosen from among those who have been engaged in teaching the Church in the city or in the countryside, and he is part of the presbytery. There is no need to speak at greater length here about the literary school, except to note that the senate established or restored it, after the city was joined again to the Belgian union, by setting up liberal stipends for the teachers. For its order has been published in print and survives. I will only repeat here that seven masters teach in it, who receive stipends from the Republic of not less than 2,680 Carolus guilders, and they have free lodging with every burden removed; but they take nothing from the pupils [δωρεάν]. The seat of the school is in the Franciscan house, which, as I said before, lies in the middle of the city. Further, the ministers of the church preach three times on Sundays in the two churches, and in addition twice in the rest of the week in the Martinian church and once in the Marian or Amnican church. They administer baptism in these same churches, at the end of the sermons, in the presence of the congregation. They distribute the Lord's Supper with the greatest reverence every three months to those communicating, again in the churches just mentioned. They admit no one to this sacred table unless he has first been well instructed in the mystery and is moderately acquainted with the chief heads of Christian doctrine, and is upright and pious in life; the rest they keep away from it. They also properly carry out the other parts of their ministry. Above all, once a month they hold a meeting or gathering in the city with the ministers of the neighbouring churches that lie in the suburban prefecture, for the sake of mutual discipline and exhortation. Moreover, once a year their chosen representatives, along with the rest of the presbytery, attend the synod of the ministers of this entire province between the Ems and the Lauwers, to which the chosen men of each class assemble, sometimes in the city, more often in the countryside, in the more frequented places. Otherwise, as far as the monthly and ordinary meetings are concerned, the city people have nothing in common with the country ministers.
On the Workhouse at Groningen

units.la: LIbet hoc loco nunc inserere institutum tum temporis nondum hîc natum, cùm libellum hunc in lucem primùm emitterem, sumptum à sociis vicinis, Reip. haud inutile. Id ἐργαςτήριον[?] est castigandæ exultantinequitiæ & ignaviæ, quale in urbe Leowerdia descripsi. Locus ei est in parte cœnobii Dominicani sumptu provinciæ totius adornatus, variè in cellulas & ossicinas distinctus, institutoque tali accommodatus, nebulonum & inertium hominum carcer. Nam qui coërceri domi à suis, & in obsequio ac officio retineri non possunt, item errones, moribus profligati, prodigi rerum suarum, ignaviæ dediti, cæteris noxii, facinoribus quoque inquinati, quos capite plectere non libet, cujusvis generis, sexus, ætatis, in hunc abducuntur, & laboribus variis exercentur, durioribus aliis, aliis leviori-bus, diuturniore vel breviore tempore, prout cujusque mores & commissa merentur. Nonnunquam etiam aliunde è regionibus vicinis facinorum rei, qui suis domi pudori ac infamiæ sunt, huc mittuntur. Laborandum in eo omnibus aut esuriendum. Si qui aliis laboribus idonei non sunt, & corpore valent, tophos tundendo minuunt, & in usum cœmenti præparant: multa artificia docentur & factitant, quibus impostrum è carcere emissi vitæ præsidia parare sibi possint: secluduntur in diversis ac distinctis cellis: ne alij alios turbent. Datus iis exactor est opera severè urgens, curansque, ne quid nequiter aut protervè, ne quid [?]ἀκοσμως agatur, sed ut omnia fiant ordine & decenter, ut est singulis imperatum. Et huic præfecti sunt viri quatuor, bini ex urbe agroque à suis designati, hi à detores à Quæstore censuum, monasticorum, uti est decreto Ordinum statutum; de qua quotannis mense Februario in Camera rationum præsentibus Ordinum delectis calculum ponere coguntur. Voluntatem horum exactor exequitur: & rationes menstruas de iis, quæ ejus curæ commissa sunt, apud hos eosdem reddit. Et licet etiam curatoribus adsciscerè sibi matronas duas honestas rei œconomicæ peritas, quæ partem curarum & inspectionis in se recipiant, sed gratuitò similiter, ut ipsi curatores. Hoc ἐργαστή-ριον[?] multis malis terrori, multis etiam emendationi est, à disciplina & coërcitione nuncupatum.
units.tr: It is worth inserting here, though the practice did not yet exist in this place when I first published this little book, an institution taken from our neighbouring allies that is of no small use to the commonwealth. This is the workhouse [ἐργαστήριον] for correcting exuberant wickedness and idleness, of which I wrote a description in the city of Leeuwarden. It is housed in part of the Dominican convent, fitted out at the expense of the whole province, divided into various cells and workshops, and adapted to this purpose: it is a prison for scoundrels and idle people. Into it are taken people of every kind, sex and age whom their own families cannot restrain or keep in obedience and duty: vagrants, men of ruined character, spendthrifts who have squandered their own property, those given to idleness, those harmful to others, and those stained with crimes but not deserving the death penalty. They are set to various labours, some harder and some lighter, for a longer or shorter time, according to what each one's conduct and offences deserve. Sometimes also offenders from neighbouring regions, who have become a shame and disgrace to their own homes, are sent here. Everyone in it must either work or go hungry. Those who are not fit for other labours but are physically able break up tufa stone and prepare it for use in mortar. Many crafts are taught and practised, by which those released from the prison can provide for themselves in future. They are shut up in separate and distinct cells so that they do not disturb one another. A supervisor is appointed over them, who presses the work hard and takes care that nothing is done wickedly or insolently, nothing [done] in disorder [ἀκόσμως], but that everything is done in order and decently, as each person has been instructed. Over this institution are four men, two from the city and two from the countryside, designated by their own people; these are appointed by the Quaestor of the monastic revenues, as the decree of the Estates provides, and they are required each year, in the month of February, in the Chamber of Accounts and in the presence of the deputies of the Estates, to render their reckoning. The supervisor carries out their wishes and gives them a monthly account of the matters entrusted to his care. The curators may also associate with themselves two respectable matrons skilled in household management, who take on part of the care and oversight, but they too serve without pay, just like the curators themselves. This workhouse, named after discipline and restraint, is a terror to many evils and a means of amendment to many people.

units.la: DE ACADEMIA GRONINGÆ NU- PER INSTITUTA.
units.tr: On the Academy of Groningen Recently Founded

units.la: CORONIS mihi esto hujus libelli recogniti Academia in hac urbe ab Ordinibus provinciæ studio procerum eruditorum anno superiore M.DC.XIV instituta, & solentores à Quæstore censuum, monasticorum, uti est decreto Ordinum statutum; de qua quotannis mense Februario in Camera rationum præsentibus Ordinum delectis calculum ponere coguntur. Voluntatem horum exactor exequitur: & rationes menstruas de iis, quæ ejus curæ commissa sunt, apud hos eosdem reddit. Et licet etiam curatoribus adscisceré sibi matronas duas honestas rei œconomicæ peritas, quæ partem curarum & inspectionis in se recipiant, sed gratuitò similiter, ut ipsi curatores. Hoc ἐγκρατεῖον[?] multis malis terrori, multis etiam emendationi est, à disciplina & coërcitione nuncupatum.
units.tr: Let this be the crown of this revised little book: the Academy in this city, founded last year, in 1614, by the Orders of the province through the zeal of learned nobles. The payers are obliged to render an account each year, in February, in the Chamber of Accounts, before the chosen members of the Orders, for the Quaestor of the monastic revenues, as the Orders' decree has laid down. The collector carries out their will and renders monthly accounts of what has been entrusted to his care, before these same men. The curators may also take to themselves two respectable matrons skilled in household management, who will undertake part of the care and oversight, likewise without pay, as the curators themselves serve. This house of self-restraint [ἐγκρατεῖον], named for discipline and correction, is a terror to many evildoers and a means of reform to many others.

units.la: DE ACADEMIA GRONINGÆ NU- PER INSTITUTA.
units.tr: On the Academy of Groningen, Recently Founded

units.la: CORONIS mihi esto hujus libelli recogniti Academia in hac urbe ab Ordinibus provinciæ studio procerum eruditorum anno superiore M. DC. XIV instituta, & solenapta. Sublevandis studiosorum sumptibus mensa communis instituta in capita xl: qua qui utuntur, in annum Oeconomo pendunt aureos Carolinos xlv, quorum quilibet æstimatur ftuferis xx: reliquum refp. solvit. Victus in ea sufficiens & mundus ex lege œconomo dicta. Sternitur & instruitur mensa quotidie ter, jentaculo, prandio, cœnæ. Academiæ initia hactenus felicia: & speramus cum tempore majora: speramns inquiam:Nam & nos pars ejus qualiscunque fumus. Hoc vero studii habemus ex voluntate optimorum curatorum procerumque nostrorum, ne pro libertate legitima ac honesta exlex licentia, multorum malorum causa, apud nos inolescat, regnumque sibi paret; utque ii, qui literarum studiofos apud eosdem nos fe profitentur, non solum doctiores, sed etiam virtute ac pietate meliores reddantur. DEUS OPT. MAX. gratia sua conatibus his adsistat,& laboribus docentium & discentium benedicat;
units.tr: Let this be the conclusion of this revised little book: the Academy in this city, founded and celebrated last year, in 1614, by the Orders of the province with the zeal of distinguished scholars. To relieve the expenses of the students, a common table has been set up for forty persons; those who use it pay the steward forty-five Carolus gold pieces a year, each of which is valued at twenty stuivers, and the rest is paid by the city. The food is sufficient and clean, according to the rule laid down by the steward. The table is laid and served three times a day: breakfast, dinner, and supper. The beginnings of the Academy have so far been happy, and we hope for greater things with time; we hope, I say, for we too are a part of it, such as we are. We have this purpose from the will of our excellent curators and nobles, so that, instead of legitimate and honest liberty, lawless license may not take root among us, to the cause of many evils, and seize power for itself; and so that those who profess themselves students of letters under these men may be made not only more learned but also better in virtue and piety. May God, best and greatest, support these endeavours with His grace, and bless the labours of teachers and learners.
AMEN.
THE END.

units.tr: * Privilege granted to the city and confirmed by the bishop of Utrecht, Florentius, in cases of the bishop, that no one be summoned beyond Holwerd.

units.tr: † The Groningers, the Oostergoërs and Westergoërs, and the rest of their neighbourhood made a covenant to defend their liberty.

units.tr: * When the Frisians were again defeated by Albert, and Stavoren and the whole region beyond the Lauwers were occupied, certain Cistavician nobles gave the entire Cistavician district to him without consulting the people, and received it back from him as a fief.

units.la: Compositio inter Occonem Broecmerium & Fœcconem Vconis F. autorib. Groninganis.
units.tr: Settlement between Occo Broecmer and Focco, son of Vcko, made by the Groningen authorities.

units.la: Focco bellum infert Groninganis, & agrum ab ijs separat.
units.tr: Focco makes war on the Groningers and separates the district from them.

units.la: Focco novarum legum per agrum autor est.
units.tr: Focco is the author of new laws for the district.

units.la: ‡ Tumultus in Frisia Orientali, contra Fœcconem & socios, autoribus Grethanis, fœdusque pro libertate percussum.
units.tr: ‡ Uprising in East Friesland against Focco and his allies, instigated by the Gretheans, and a covenant struck for liberty.

units.la: Fœdera a vicinis cum civitate Groning. instaurata.
units.tr: Covenants with the neighbours of the city of Groningen renewed.

units.la: ‡ Emda per insidias ab Hamburgensibus occupata sociis Grethanorum.
units.tr: ‡ Emda taken by treachery by the Hamburgers, with the allies of the Gretheans.

Count Ulricus was proclaimed before the people.
The riverside church at Groningen was built higher.
Count Ulricus died.

units.la: Dammonenses ob coctam contra pacta cerevisiam venalem multati.
units.tr: The Dammonians, fined for selling beer brewed contrary to the agreements.

units.la: Fœdus civitatis cum Collumanis in annos XXX.
units.tr: A treaty of the city with the Kollumers for thirty years.
The Martini tower collapsed.

units.la: ‡ Mœnia urbis Groning. ampliata versus Austrum & Occasum, vallumq; novum excitatum, adjuvantibus agrarijs, opus triennij labore absolutum.
units.tr: ‡ The walls of the city of Groningen were enlarged towards the south and west, and a new rampart raised with the help of the country folk; the work completed after three years' labour.
Charles of Burgundy demanded that the city be surrendered to him.

units.la: Ioan. Tedema videtur aut perperā poni aut mortuum esse in consulatu.
units.tr: John Tedema seems either to have been placed here in error or to have died in office.

units.la: Moritur Wefselus Gansfortius, Groningensis, vulgò LVX MVNDI dictus conditus infamo[?] cœnobij Virginum, Spiritualium, uti vocant, humili sepulcro & vix noto posteris
units.tr: Wessel Gansfort of Groningen, commonly called Lux Mundi, died. He was buried in a humble grave in the monastery of the so-called Spiritual Virgins, and is scarcely known to posterity.
A very famous covenant with the Ostergoers.
A covenant with the people of Leeuwarden[?].

units.la: Fœdus Ostergoum longius promotum per Westgoam. Eneca duris conditionibus dedita.
units.tr: The covenant with the Ostergoers was extended further through Westergo. Eneca surrendered on harsh terms.

units.la: Otto Langius legatus Cæsaris in Frisia, inimicus fœderi Croningano.
units.tr: Otto Langius, the Emperor's legate in Friesland, was hostile to the Groningen covenant.

units.la: Fœdus Ostergoū a Maximiliano Cæsare confirmatum Campoduni.
units.tr: The covenant with the Ostergoers was confirmed by Emperor Maximilian at Campen.
Consular Fasti

units.la: Fœdus nouum ci-vitatis cum Westergois, Ostergoo simile. Albertus Saxo militem sub præfectis diuersis in Frisiam mittit, ut eam at-terat.
units.tr: A new covenant of the city with the Westergoers, similar to that with the Ostergoers. Albert of Saxony sends soldiers under various commanders into Friesland to wear it down.

units.la: * Foxus auspiciis Alberti Frisiam invadit, & in agrum Groning. venit.
units.tr: (*) Foxus, under the auspices of Albert, invades Friesland and enters the territory of Groningen.

units.la: Albertus Saxo a Cæsare Gubernator Frisiæ designatur.
units.tr: Albert of Saxony is designated by the Emperor as governor of Friesland.

units.la: † Albertus Saxo in Frisiam venit & homagium recipit.
units.tr: (†) Albert of Saxony comes into Friesland and receives homage.

units.la: Cum Groninganis colloquia instituit. Groningani Dammonam præsidio Edsardi munitam per Vlricum Dorn. tentant.
units.tr: He opens negotiations with the Groningers. The Groningers attempt to take Dammona, which was held by a garrison of Edzard's men, through Ulrich Dorn.

units.la: ‡ Albertus e Misnia reuersus cum exercitu, filio obsidione Franekerae liberato, Groningam obsidet. Bellum pacatione dirimitur studio Georgij Thorcnij & Fri-
units.tr: (‡) Albert returns from Meissen with an army. After his son is freed from the siege of Franeker, he besieges Groningen. The war is ended by a peace brokered through the zeal of Georg Thorenius and Frederick

units.la: Denuo cognitio controversiæ instituta Novesij, actore Saxone, reis Edsardo & Groningani.
units.tr: A renewed examination of the dispute was instituted at Neuss, with Saxony as plaintiff and Edzard and the Groningers as defendants.

units.la: Idem repetitum Coloniæ præsente ac præside ipso Maximil. Cæsare.
units.tr: The same matter was taken up again at Cologne, in the presence and under the presidency of Emperor Maximilian himself.

units.la: Gerbrandus Moccama, & Gemma Iuwsma capite multati Leoardiæ.
units.tr: Gerbrand Moccama and Gemma Iuwsma were executed at Leeuwarden.

units.la: † Actio de reconciliatione inter partes Monasterij: & alia Adoardiæ.
units.tr: (†) A legal action concerning reconciliation between the parties of the monastery, and another at Aduard.
A proscription was declared against Edzard.

units.la: ‡ Edsardus, item Groningani proscripti. Bellū atrox cis ultraque Amasum illatum. Dammona à Saxonibus vi capta. Groninga Iuris Geldrici facta.
units.tr: (‡) Edzard and likewise the Groningers were proscribed. A fierce war was waged on both sides of the Ems. Dammona was taken by force by the Saxons. Groningen was made subject to Gelderland law.

units.la: § Ius Frisicū a Georgio Saxone in Carolum Burgund. pr. Geldros in Frisia occid. Doccumum a Burgundis & Burgundicis reconciliatio Sneca obsessa. Longus Geldricis recepsum.
units.tr: (§) Frisian law [was invoked] by George of Saxony against Charles of Burgundy; the Gelderlanders [were] in western Friesland. Doccum [was taken] by the Burgundians, and a Burgundian reconciliation followed; Sneek was besieged. Longus was withdrawn by the Gelderlanders.

units.la: Edfardus cum Brunfuigijs & Saxonibus transegit, arcemque Stichusam recepit.
units.tr: Edzard came to terms with the Brunswickers and Saxons, and recovered the fortress of Stickhusen.
(†) A charter was given to the Groningers by the Duke of Guelders.

units.la: ‡ Henricus & Fridericus Gaikinga in cænobio Adoardia[?]no a monachis occisi.
units.tr: (‡) Henry and Frederick of Gaikinga were killed by the monks in the monastery of Aduard.

units.la: Controversia inter societates pleb. & cænobia per agrum de opificijs composita.
units.tr: A dispute between the commoners' societies and the monasteries over the land was settled concerning trades.
(§) The agrarian orders of Guelders rendered homage to the Duke.

units.la: Bellū inter Campenses & Suollenses orum, cui se Geldrus miscuit. Bel-lum quoque in Frisia Occidentali rez[?] cruduit inter Burgund. & Geld.
units.tr: War between the Campenses and the Zwollenses, in which Guelders took part. War also broke out in western Friesland between the Burgundians and the Guelders.

units.tr: (†) With Doccum and the other places lost, the Guelders were at last expelled from western Friesland by Duke Wassenaer. A truce was made between Guelders and Burgundy.

units.la: Annus tumultibus infamis. Groninga quoq; seditione laboratū. Dissensio inter Ducē Geldriæ & civitatem composita.
units.tr: A year infamous for tumults. Groningen also troubled by sedition. The dispute between the Duke of Gelderland and the city settled.
Troops of soldiers in West Friesland.

units.la: Rursum plebs commota Groningæ. Et bellum resuscitatum in diœcesi Vltra-jectina.
units.tr: The common people stirred up again at Groningen, and war renewed in the diocese of Utrecht.
Count Edzard dies.

units.la: Pax composita inter Carolū V. Cæs. & Carolū Geldrū.
units.tr: Peace concluded between Charles V, Emperor, and Charles of Gelderland.

units.la: Simultas inter Groninganos & Emdanos orta portorio Emdano.
units.tr: A quarrel arose between the Groningers and the Emdeners over the Emden toll.

units.la: Esena obsessa ab Ennone Comite Edsfardi F. eiq; dedita cum Balthasare.
units.tr: Esens besieged by Enno, Count, son of Edzard, and surrendered to him along with Balthasar.

units.la: Maria Ieverana authore Boiingo Oldersh. ab Ennone deficit.
units.tr: Maria Ieverana, at the instigation of Boiingo of Oldersum, deserts from Enno.

units.la: Balthasar Esensis neglecto jurejurando in fidem Caroli Geldri se conferri, & bellū Ennoni movet.
units.tr: Balthasar of Esens, disregarding his oath, betakes himself into the protection of Charles of Gelderland and makes war on Enno.

units.la: Ordines agrarii civitatis Groning. controversiam moverunt de quibusdā adjus stapulæ pertinentibus.
units.tr: The agrarian orders of the city of Groningen raised a controversy concerning certain matters pertaining to the staple right.

units.la: Delegati Ordinum Groningæ & Omlandiæ ad Regē Hispaniarum Gans[?]davi Anno 1559. Johan de Mepsche Johan Sickinge. Gert Horenken. Johā Rengers tē post Haye Westerwolt Secret. Eyb. Alting.
units.tr: Delegates of the Orders of Groningen and Ommelanden to the King of Spain at Ghent, in the year 1559: Johan de Mepsche, Johan Sickinge, Gert Horenken, Johan Rengers te Post, Haye Westerwolt, secretary, Eyb. Alting.
Margaret of Parma issued a decree.

units.la: Pacta conventa inter partes intercef-fore Philippo Corelio, de jure stapulæ.
units.tr: Agreements made between the parties, with Philip Corelius intervening, concerning the staple right.

units.la: authore Rennenbergio. Templa duo exercitio religionis reformatae aperiuntur Groningae decreto publico. * Groninga fraude Rennebergij in partes Hisp. delapsa, optimis quibusque in carcerem datis. Eadem obsessa ab exercitu Ord. Pugna Hardenbergia.
units.tr: By the authority of Rennenberg. Two churches opened for the exercise of the reformed religion at Groningen by public decree. Groningen, through the treachery of Rennenberg, fell to the Spanish party, and all the best men were thrown into prison. The same city besieged by the army of the Orders. Battle at Hardenberg.
Various modes of war in the Groningen countryside.
Decree of the Prince of Parma concerning the staple right.
Fierce battle at Noordhorn, won by the Spanish.

units.la: * Diploma a Philippo rege Hisp. Groningānis datum de jure stapulæ.
units.tr: Charter granted to the Groningers by Philip, King of Spain, concerning the staple right.
Most of the captive citizens escaped from their prisons.

units.la: † Vicus Oterdumæus a Wigboldo Eusumano captus, & munitus.
units.tr: The village of Oterdum captured and fortified by Wigbold of Oosum.

units.la: ‡ Illustriss. Princeps Auraicus Guilhelmus Nassovius scelere nequissimi hominis Delfis interimitur.
units.tr: The most illustrious Prince William of Orange, of Nassau, killed at Delft by the crime of a most wicked man.

units.la: Clades Buxumana in Frisia occid. vincentibus Hispanicis.
units.tr: Defeat at Buxum in West Friesland, the Spanish victorious.

units.la: Castella Emotillanum, Reidanū, Solt camp. ab Ordinibus fœderatis duce Guilhelmo Comite Nassovio Hispanicis addempta.
units.tr: The castles of Emmetillan, Reidan and Zoltkamp taken from the Spanish by the confederated Orders under William, Count of Nassau.

units.la: Emotillā Hispanici recuperant. Ager omnis in ora a milite Ordinū affligitur.
units.tr: The Spanish recover Emmetillan. The whole coastal country is harassed by the soldiers of the Orders.

units.la: Groninga ab Ordinibus confœderatis, ducibus Nassavis obsidione nequicquā tentata: Delfsila, Upslachtum, Emotilla, captæ.
units.tr: Groningen attacked in vain by the confederated Orders under the Nassau leaders in a siege; Delfzijl, Uithuizen and Emmetillan captured.
Steenwijk and Coevorden captured by the Nassaus.

units.la: Castellum apud Bellingwoldios excitatum. Groninga ab Hispanicis res mendacis [?] sustentata.
units.tr: A fort built at Bellingwolde. Groningen's affairs sustained against the Spaniards.

units.la: Groninga obsessa dedita, & Ordinum general. societati reddita. Ei & agro gubernator datus illustris Comes GUIL. LUD. NASS.
units.tr: Groningen besieged and surrendered, and restored to the general society of the Orders. The illustrious Count Willem Lodewijk of Nassau was given as governor both to the city and to the land.

units.la: Sententia a tribus Ordinum legatis inter civitatem & agrarios lata.
units.tr: Sentence pronounced between the city and the landholders by three legates of the Orders.
Beginning of the Emden movement.

units.la: Sententia prima definitiva Hagæ inter partes eajdem [?] lata.
units.tr: First definitive sentence pronounced at The Hague between the same parties.
Second and third sentences pronounced there.

units.la: In sententia II, de quinta censuum quod erat scriptum, id eodem vergente anno & sequente ab Ordinibus [?] general. explanatum.
units.tr: In the second sentence, what had been written about the fifth of the levies was explained by the Orders in general in the same year and the following year.
City and land struck by an unexpected storm.

units.la: Emda armis infelicibus a Comite Ennone petita, magno totius regionis malo,
units.tr: Emden, by unlucky arms, sought from Count Enno, to the great harm of the whole region,

units.la: Hi omnes accepti & expensi rationes reddiderunt soli civi-tati Groningane: & civitas sola fructus Camerae percepit, & in suum usum vertit, ut ex vetustis Rationum indicibus, qui in publicis libris servantur, licet intelligere.
units.tr: All of these rendered accounts of receipts and expenditures to the city of Groningen alone; and the city alone received the revenues of the Chamber and turned them to its own use, as may be understood from the old indexes of accounts, which are kept among the public books.

Jasper Marwick, GOVERNOR.

units.la: Cum pagella hæc esset vacatura, non inconsultum visum hic exhibere apographum literarum venerandæ antiquitatis, in chartâ pergamena scriptarum, sigilloque ceræ viridi impresso appendente munitarum, quibus prima fundatio templi Amnici continetur.
units.tr: Since this little page would otherwise be left blank, it seemed not unwise to include here a copy of the letters of venerable antiquity, written on parchment and secured by a green wax seal hanging from them, which record the original foundation of the riverside temple.
Thus those letters read.

units.la: IN nomine sanctæ & individuæ trinitatis Amen. Otto Dei gratiâ Trajectensis Episcopus universis in Christo fidelibus ad quos hoc scriptum pervenerit, salutem in salutis auctore. Notum esse volumus ætati præsentium & posteritati futurorum quomodo novam plantationem Capellæ in Groninge ad honorem Dei & ejus sanctæ Genetricis Mariæ, nec non & sancti Nicolai, omniumque Sanctorum à civibus de Groninge olim laudabiliter inchoatam ad petitionem ipsorum Civium bonæ memoriæ, prædecessor noster Loci Diæcesanus Otto Trajectensis Episcopus approbans, eisdem indulserit ut ipsa Capella Ecclesia sit Parochialis, & in eadem Cimiterium, sepultura mortuorum fidelium, & pueros baptizandi sacramentum, cum cæteris officiis & sacramentis ad Christianitatis fidem pertinentibus in perpetuum habeatur, quod per memoratum prædecessorem nostrum dictis civibus est indultum firmitatis robur habere decrevimus, salvo jure eligendi & præsentandi personam idoneam loci Diœcesano qui pro tempore fuerit eisdem Parochianus. Volumus etiam ut personæ, dignitate & ratione personatus a præmissæ Ecclesiæ, Sacerdote Legitimo quatuor libræ Groningensium ut olim in festo sancti Michaelis exhibeantur, & per hoc Ecclesia ante dicta ab omni jure & potestate personæ sit exempta, & quod præmissa Ecclesia a civibus in Vtingaeluch & Westercluch ut prius frequentetur. Vt autem hæc rata maneant & inconvulsa munimine scripti nostri & sigilli impressione ea corroboravimus. Siquis autem quod huic scripto nostro sit obvium præsumpserit attemptare, indignationem Dei omnipotentis & nostram excommunicationem se noverit incursurum. Acta sunt hæc apud Groninge, anno Domini millesimo ducentesimo quadragesimo sexto feria quarta post Palmas, Testibus his. Fratre præposito Tilensi, Hermanno & Gerhardo scriptoribus nostris a Druine, Alberto & Swethero de Worsts, Hijseberto de Bucharst, Waltero Radingo & Bartoldo Radingo & aliis quam pluribus.
units.tr: IN the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Amen. Otto, by the grace of God Bishop of Utrecht, to all the faithful in Christ to whom this writing shall come, greeting in the Author of salvation. We wish it to be known to the present age and to future generations how the new planting of a chapel in Groningen, to the honour of God, of his holy Mother Mary, and also of St Nicholas and of all Saints, which the citizens of Groningen had praiseworthily begun long ago, at the petition of the same citizens of good memory, our predecessor Otto, Bishop of Utrecht and diocesan of the place, approving, granted to them that this same chapel should be a parish church, and that in it there should be held in perpetuity a cemetery for the burial of the faithful dead, the sacrament of baptizing children, and the other offices and sacraments pertaining to the faith of Christianity. We have decreed that the grant made to the said citizens by our said predecessor shall have the force of firm validity, saving the right of the diocesan of the place, for the time being, to choose and present a suitable person to them as parish priest. We also wish that the person who holds the dignity and benefice of the aforesaid church shall, as formerly at the feast of St Michael, be paid four pounds of Groningen money by the lawful priest of the aforesaid church, and that through this the aforesaid church be exempt from all right and power of that person; and that the aforesaid church be frequented by the citizens of Vtingaeluch and Westercluch as before. So that these things may remain valid and unshaken, we have confirmed them by the protection of our writing and the impression of our seal. If anyone presumes to attempt anything opposed to this our writing, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and our excommunication. Done at Groningen in the year of the Lord 1246, on the Wednesday after Palm Sunday. Witnesses: Brother, the provost of Tiel; Hermann and Gerhard, our scribes from Drijen; Albert and Swether of Worst; Hijsbert of Buchorst; Walter Radingus and Bartold Radingus, and many others.
